## 5. Pācittiya Kaṇḍa
## 1. Musāvāda Vagga
## 1. Musāvāda Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the first training rule of the Musāvāda Vagga, regarding the word "khuddakānaṃ," it is said that the word "khuddaka" is a synonym for the word "bahu" (many). "Tattha" means either in those vaggas or in those many training rules. When others argue that the reason (hetu) "jānitabbato" (because it is to be known) is inconclusive (anekantika) because it also applies to Nibbāna, which is the opposite, the speaker says, "I did not state this reason," and to conceal that reason, he says again, "I only said jātidhammato," and so forth. Since the term is indicated by eliding the nasal (niggahīta) where "sampajānaṃ" should be said, it was stated as "jānanto" (knowing).

"Sampajāna-musāvāde" (in deliberate lying) involves telling a lie while knowing the falsity of the matter to be spoken beforehand and also knowing it at the moment of speaking. Therefore, it was stated as "knowing," etc. The word "musāvāde" is in the locative case (sattamī vibhatti) in the sense of cause (nimitta). Therefore, the meaning should be understood in this training rule, as well as in other subsequent training rules of this nature, that a Pācittiya offense is incurred because of the cause of telling a lie.
2: It is called 'vācā' (speech) because it is spoken by this means; thus it is said as 'micchā' etc. Just as in expressions like 'shot with a bow,' it is said as 'oḷārikena' (by gross means) because it is intended in the sense of being evident, as in 'seen with the eye.' In the phrase 'he will have gone,' a lie occurs because it is spoken with certainty. 'Āpatti' refers to a Pācittiya offense, not a Dubbhāsita. This Pācittiya occurs for a monk who speaks mockingly to another using the ten grounds of insults (akkosavatthu) such as birth, etc. 'Cāresuṃ' means they carried or brought. In this Musāvāda, there are three factors: falsity of the matter (vatthuviparītatā), the intention to deceive (visāmbādanapurekkhāratā), and the effort to make that person understand the intended meaning. If there is no falsity of the matter but one makes another understand with an intent to deceive, it is not Musāvāda but merely a Dukkaṭa. Therefore, that falsity of the matter should also be taken as a factor. For one who tells a lie to make known a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), it is a Pārājika; if spoken by circumlocution (pariyāyena), it is a Thullaccaya; if spoken to accuse someone of a Pārājika without grounds, it is a Saṅghādisesa; in cases of accusing of a Saṅghādisesa or insulting speech, it is a Pācittiya; if insulting unordained persons or novices, it is a Dukkaṭa; if insulting mockingly regarding high or low birth, it is a Dubbhāsita; and if telling a mere lie, it is stated as a Pācittiya according to this training rule. ## The Commentary on the Musāvāda Training Rule is finished. ## 2. Omasavāda Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā In the second training rule, 'when reaching again the place where it stood before' means that the part of the wheel rim that first stood on the ground turns and then stands on the ground again. 'Pubbe' refers to the occasion of origin (aṭṭhuppatti). Those called 'pupphachaḍḍaka' are those who discard impurities such as birth-waste. 'Tacchakakamma' refers to the craft of a carpenter, such as stone-carving. 'Hatthamuddā-gaṇanā' is counting by bending the fingers. 'Acchiddaka-gaṇanā' means counting in sequence by placing wooden sticks in places of ones, tens, etc. By the word 'ādi,' one should include collective counting (piṇḍagaṇanā) performed by means of addition, multiplication, subtraction, division, etc. One who is proficient in that art of counting, upon merely seeing a tree, knows, 'In this tree, there are this many leaves in this place...'
3:
"...there are this many leaves." Because of the phrase 'yabha-methune,' it is stated as 'the syllable ya, the syllable bha,' and so forth.

'Not by the previous training rule' means not by the Musāvāda training rule. A monk who speaks with insults intensified by prefixes (upasagga), etc., should be dealt with only by a Pācittiya offense, according to the words 'that monk also by an offense.'

Since 'Dubbhāsita' is stated in a general sense, teachers say that insults not directly mentioned in the Pali or spoken behind one's back are also only a Dubbhāsita offense. This is because there is no offense lower than Dubbhāsita, and it is inappropriate to say there is no offense in this case. In the term 'sabbasattā' (all beings), those who know the meaning of the words also include animals and others.

For those who speak with the intent to instruct (anusāsanī) or out of a desire to blame evil, there is no offense even if anger arises intermittently, because the mind has a nature of changing rapidly. Since insulting (omasana) can occur even by a mere bodily gesture, it is stated as 'having three origins, a bodily action.' However, in the Parivāra, it is stated, 'By the fourth origin of offense... would one incur a Dubbhāsita? It should be said no,' etc. By rejecting other origins and stating only the fifth, it is said, 'In this case, the Dubbhāsita offense arises from speech and mind.' In truth, for one who insults with body, speech, and mind out of a desire to mock, only speech and mind are the factors of the offense; the body, though present, is not considered a factor by mere bodily gesture alone, similar to the offense regarding Dhamma teaching. However, for a monk who insults mockingly, although a Dubbhāsita offense is not incurred here, it should be understood that only a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred according to the training rule prohibiting bodily play (kāyakīḷā). There are three factors here: direct insult to an ordained person regarding birth, etc.; knowing that it is an insult; and the absence of intent for welfare or instruction.

## The Commentary on the Omasavāda Training Rule is finished.

## 3. Pesuñña Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the third training rule, they are called 'bhaṇḍanajāta' because a quarrel has arisen among those monks. It is called 'pisuṇā' (slanderous speech) because it grinds or crushes; it means speech that causes those who are united to divide. One who possesses such speech is called 'pisuṇa' (a slanderer), and his act is called 'pesuñña' (slander); thus the meaning should be understood here.
4:
In this Pesunña Sikkhāpada as well, a Pācittiya offence is incurred only by a monk who conveys malicious speech (slander) by means of the ten grounds such as birth (jāti), etc. For a monk who conveys it by means of other grounds for abuse (akkosa-vatthu), there is an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). It is said that for a monk who conveys it by means of words that are not grounds for abuse, there is also only an offence of wrong-doing. There are three factors here: (1) conveying malicious speech to another monk after hearing it from a monk who is abusing someone without specifying them by birth, etc.; (2) having one of two intentions—either the desire to be loved or the desire to cause division; and (3) the understanding of that [other] monk.

## The Commentary on the Pesunña Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Padasodhamma Sikkhāpada

In the fourth training rule, "similar to the preceding syllable" means the word 'anicca' in the phrase "vedanā aniccā" which is similar to the word 'anicca' in the phrase "rūpaṃ aniccaṃ". A collection of letters (syllables) without a case-ending is called 'akkharasamūha'. A word with a case-ending is called 'pada'.

"Ekaṃ padaṃ" refers only to a single line (pāda) of a verse (gāthā). "Padagaṇanāya" means by the count of the lines of the verse. "Apāpuṇitvā" means without reciting together. By this, it is shown that if a novice (sāmaṇera) recites the first line, etc., while [the monk] is reciting the last line of the verse, an offence is indeed incurred; the other person should recite only when that novice has become silent.

"Aṭṭhakathānissita" refers to the ancient commentaries (porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā) established in the three councils. Even now, there are commentary words such as "Just as a leopard, having hidden itself, catches its prey," and so on. It is said that the words spoken by teachers such as the Venerable Buddhaghosa according to the method of the ancient commentaries should also be included here. "Pāḷinissita" refers to texts such as the Udānavagga-saṅgaha, etc. "Vivaṭṭူpanissita" refers to the Dhamma based on Nibbāna. "Therassa" refers to the treatises of the Elder Nāgasena, such as the Maggakathā, etc.

Although in the Pāḷi text, words like "akkharāya" are spoken with a gender-reversal, the meaning should be taken as "akkharena", etc.

"Excluding the precinct (upacāra)" means excluding the precinct within twelve cubits of the assembly, and without preaching to the laypeople or novices who are standing or sitting together, but intending for others...
5: There is no offense for a monk who recites while targeting other monks (outside the twelve-cubit range of the audience). However, if he recites targeting a novice (sāmaṇera) who is sitting far away, there is indeed an offense. 'Opāteti' means reciting together. The three factors here are: being unordained (anupasampanna), teaching the Dhamma of the stated characteristics word by word (padaso), and reciting together. ## The Commentary on the Padaso-dhamma Training Rule is finished. ## 5. The Commentary on the Sahaseyya Training Rule 50-51. In the fifth training rule, regarding the phrase 'tatridaṃ nidassanaṃ', the remaining words should be supplied. This is an example for the case where the Venerable Rāhula desired the training. In the term 'dirattatirattaṃ', the inclusion of the word 'diratta' (two nights) is for the purpose of ornamenting the word 'tiratta' (three nights). It should be understood that it also has the purpose of showing that an offense is incurred only by a monk who sleeps for four days or more after staying for three consecutive nights without interruption, and not by a monk who sleeps on alternate nights and so forth. Indeed, when 'tiratta' is specified by 'diratta', it indicates three consecutive nights. 'With five types of roofing' means roofing with bricks, stones, plaster, grass, or leaves. 'By way of oral recitation' means by way of mastery. The height of one and a half cubits should be measured by a carpenter's cubit. A monastery that one enters by a single path and can walk everywhere without going out into the open is called 'ekūpacāra' (a single enclosure). Such a monastery is a single enclosure even if it has many doors. However, if it is partitioned by walls and the like and a separate door is installed, it becomes 'nānūpacāra' (different enclosures). If it is merely partitioned but no separate door is installed, it should be understood that 'this monastery is also a single enclosure, like a room whose door is closed with clay and the like.' Otherwise, there would be no offense even for one who, to be free from the offense of sleeping together with unordained persons lying in the front of the room after entering the inner chamber, has the chamber door closed with clay and the like and has it opened only at dawn. In the sentence 'For every effort of theirs, there is an offense for the monk,' some teachers say, 'It is called an offense originating from non-action (akiriya-samuṭṭhāna) due to not getting up, because at that moment of sleeping, there is no action. In fact, this training rule sometimes originates from action (kiriya) and sometimes from non-action. Its nature of originating from action is stated by way of the frequency of such actions.' They also say that, like this sleeping together, sleeping during the day also originates from non-action due to not getting up and not guarding the doors. This statement seems appropriate and should be accepted after investigation.

“For a mansion with walls not connected to the upper floor”—this statement is made to show that there is no need to mention a mansion with connected walls. Because there is no cause for doubt for a monk sleeping on the upper floor, the words “in the lower mansion” and so forth are stated. *Nānūpacāre* refers to a level that must be ascended by an external ladder.

*Sabhāsaṅkhepena* means in the manner of an assembly hall. By the word “*aḍḍhakuṭṭake*,” the shape is shown. In a dwelling where walls are constructed on three or two sides, but do not reach the roof, having only half-walls, such a dwelling is called *aḍḍhakuṭṭaka*. A *vāḷasaṅghāṭa* is a joint (beam) made with figures of beasts above the pillars and such within the enclosure. In the phrase “*parikkhepassa bahigate*” (gone outside the enclosure), if there is no enclosure on a particular side and the ground-base is higher than the natural ground, there is no offense even within the drip-ledge on the two sides below that high ground-base; this is because there is no designation of it being a “dwelling” (*senāsana*) below that base. Otherwise, if the ground-base is low and level with the natural ground and stays below the dwelling, then in that unenclosed area, an offense is committed in all places within the drip-ledge because there is no boundary; it should be understood that there is no offense only outside the enclosure. The words beginning with “*parimaṇḍalaṃ*” are spoken with reference to a dwelling that has an open courtyard in the middle for rainwater to fall. In that context, *aparicchinnagabbhūpacāre* means rooms where the passage in front of each room is not partitioned, and walls not less than one and a half cubits in height are built with an entrance from the open courtyard; it refers to rooms not made in such a manner. The term *gabbhaparikkhepa* is spoken with reference to the walls of rooms situated all around in square mansions and the like.

*Pāṭekkhasannivesā* means separate constructions, either because there are rows of rooms in one direction and no rows of rooms in other directions, or even if they exist, they are not connected to each other by walls and roofs. In the phrase “*taṃ... pe... sandhāya vuttaṃ*,” it means there is no offense of *pācittiya*; it does not mean there is no offense of *dukkaṭa*. For the porch of such a row of rooms, if there are no walls on three sides and it is fully roofed only by the room wall on one side, it is called “slightly enclosed” (*cūḷaparicchanna*). Therefore, it is only an offense of *dukkaṭa*. However, if a wall is made on one or all of the other sides of that porch, then because it becomes fully roofed and half-enclosed and so on, it should be understood that it is indeed a *pācittiya* offense. In the phrase “*bhūmiyaṃ vinā jagatiyā pamukhaṃ sandhāya*,” this is stated to mean there is no *pācittiya* offense for an unenclosed porch of a house built on the ground without making a high ground-base.
7:
If the porch has a high ground-base, it means that the porch is counted as enclosed by that base. “*Tattha*” refers to the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*. In stating the measurement of the ground-base, it means the height of the ground-base is such that a person lying on the natural ground cannot see a person lying on top of the ground-base.

A mansion built long and straight in one direction is an *ekasālasannivesa* (single-hall construction). Mansions built in two, three, or four directions in the shape of a crossroad and so forth should be known as *dvisāla* constructions and so on. The difference here from what was said before is merely the illustration of the different types of halls. The phrase “*parikkhepo viddhasto*” is spoken with reference to the enclosure of the porch.

Since it is shown in the Pali that an offense of *dukkaṭa* is committed in a dwelling that is half-roofed and half-enclosed, other cases such as a dwelling that is fully roofed and half-enclosed, though not directly mentioned in the Pali, are shown only as a basis for a *pācittiya* offense. This is because it is a prescribed fault (*paṇṇattivajja*) of the training rule and because one should stand by the graver penalty. The phrase “seven *pācittiyas*” is spoken by taking the two *pācittiyas* mentioned in the Pali together as one general category.

In the Pali, the statement “leaving before dawn on the third night and staying again” is spoken by way of the maximum limit (*ukkaṭṭha*). Even if a monk does not go outside before dawn, but gets up and sits under the roof, there is no offense for sleeping together on the next day. “It is like the *Senambamaṇḍapa*” refers to an assembly hall of that name in Sri Lanka which has a high ground-base and is fully roofed but not fully enclosed.

In this context, one-fourth (enclosure) is called *cūḷaka* (slight). Two parts are called *upaḍḍha* (half). Two parts out of three are called *yebhuyya* (majority). In this way, slight roofing, slight enclosure, and so forth should be understood. The three factors here are: being a dwelling that is a basis for a *pācittiya* offense, sleeping together with an unordained person in that dwelling, and the setting of the sun on the fourth day.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Sleeping Together is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Sleeping Together

In the sixth training rule, for a monk who sleeps with a woman on the fourth day, only one offense is committed by this training rule. Although some teachers say there are two offenses because an offense is also committed by the previous training rule, that statement is not appropriate because the word “with an unordained person” (*anupasampannena*) is spoken in a non-feminine gender. For a monk who sleeps on the fourth day, it is appropriate to state a *pācittiya* along with a *dukkaṭa*. In this training rule, although the Pali mentions *dukkaṭa* only by way of a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch), because of similarity with that *paṇḍaka*, a *dukkaṭa* is committed by this second *sahaseyya* rule for a monk who sleeps with a male hermaphrodite (*purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka*). By the previous first *sahaseyya* rule, a *pācittiya* along with a *dukkaṭa* is committed on the fourth day. A female hermaphrodite (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*) is just like a woman. This is our preferred decision. They say there is no offense in the case of a dead woman. The three factors here are: being a dwelling that is a basis for a *pācittiya* offense, sleeping together with a woman in that dwelling, and the setting of the sun.

## The Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Sleeping Together is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Teaching Dhamma

In the seventh training rule, the words “not with a *yakkha*” and so forth are connected with the words “except with a wise man.” The commentator means the meaning should be taken as: teaching Dhamma to a woman who is there, excluding a wise man but not excluding a *yakkha* and so forth.
8: It is proper to say that a monk who sleeps with a eunuch (napuṃsaka) on the fourth day incurs a pācittiya offense along with a dukkaṭa. Although in the Pāḷi of this training rule, only the dukkaṭa offense is taught by way of a paṇḍaka, because of the similarity to that paṇḍaka, a monk who sleeps with a male hermaphrodite (purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka) incurs a dukkaṭa by this second Sahaseyya training rule, and a pācittiya along with a dukkaṭa on the fourth day by the previous first Sahaseyya training rule. Our preference is that a female hermaphrodite (itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka) is of the same status as a woman. Some say there is no offense in the case of a dead woman. The three factors here are: a lodging that is a basis for a pācittiya, lying down together with a woman in that lodging, and sunset. ## The Commentary on the Second Sahaseyya Training Rule is finished. ## 7. The Commentary on the Dhamma-desanā Training Rule In the seventh training rule, the words 'na yakkhena' and so forth are connected with 'aññatra viññunā'. The intention of the commentator should be understood as: 'Except for a wise male human, if one teaches Dhamma to a woman who is with a yakkha or the like, there is an offense.' Indeed, it is not proper to teach a woman who is standing with such a yakkha or the like. It is certainly proper to teach the meaning in various local languages as one pleases. Non-action (akiriya) here refers to not changing one's posture and not calling a man within the twelve-cubit range. The five factors here are: teaching more than six words of the Dhamma of the stated characteristics, the woman being of the stated characteristics, the absence of changing posture, the absence of a wise man, and not being the answering of a question. ## The Commentary on the Dhamma-desanā Training Rule is finished. ## 8. The Commentary on the Bhūtārocana Training Rule In the eighth training rule, 'antarā' also refers to the time before the Parinibbāna. 'Atikaḍḍhiyamānena' means being urged or pressed by questions such as, 'Venerable sir, what have you attained?' If there is such a reason, it should certainly be told. In the phrase 'suta-pariyatti-sīla-guṇa', it should be understood that mastery of the meaning is the 'suta' quality, and mastery of the Pāḷi text is the 'pariyatti' quality. By the phrase 'cittakkhepassa vā abhāvā', it shows that Noble Ones (ariyas) do not have mental derangement or the state of being overwhelmed by pain.
9:
"Pubbe avuttehi" refers to the origins (samuṭṭhāna) not mentioned in the fourth Pārājika. This training rule is strictly an origin without intention (acittaka-samuṭṭhāna) due to ignorance of the regulation. This is because Noble Ones (Ariyas) do not transgress a regulation. For those who have attained Jhanas, telling the truth about their superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) is impossible if they have a mind of resentment to transgress the Teacher's command, as they would lose their Jhanas. There are four factors in this training rule: (1) the superhuman state is true, (2) telling it to an unordained person, (3) immediate understanding [by the listener], and (4) not referring to another person.

## The Explanation of the Bhūtārocana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 9. Duṭṭhullārocana Sikkhāpada

In the ninth training rule, "tattha bhaveyya" means "someone might have this view regarding that matter." To firmly establish the words of the Commentary through logical reasoning, the words beginning with "imināpi cetaṃ" were spoken.

"Ādito pañca sikkhāpadါနိ" refers to the first five training rules, such as Pāṇātipāta. "Sesāni" refers to the remaining training rules, such as Vikālabhojana. Acts like "sukka-vissaṭṭhi" are indeed transgressions (ajjhācāra). There are three factors: (1) the occurrence of a Saṅghādisesa offense with its basis for a monk who has not committed a Pārājika offense, (2) telling it to an unordained person, and (3) the absence of authorization (sammuti) from the monks.

## The Explanation of the Duṭṭhullārocana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 10. Pathavီခဏန Sikkhāpada

In the tenth training rule, since earth with little dust or clay is stated as a basis for no offense, it should be understood that earth with about half dust or clay also results in a Pācittiya offense. This is because such earth with half dust or clay cannot be called a basis for a Dukkaṭa offense. The reason is that there is no third type of earth distinct from natural earth (jāta-pathavī) and non-natural earth (ajāta-pathavī).

"Vaṭṭati" means it is permissible to say "Dig a pond in this place" because the specific spot is not designated. In saying "Dig this creeper," an offense is incurred under this Pathavī-khaṇana training rule because it refers to digging the earth; it is not an offense under the Bhūtagāma training rule.
10:
If one intends both digging the earth and cutting a vine, two Pācittiya offenses are incurred. Udakapappaṭaka refers to when water enters the ground, covering the upper part, and thin dust or fine clay forms a layer and remains floating (or falling). Even when that water dries up, that layer of earth remains shaking when the wind blows; it is called udakapappaṭaka.

The word akatapabbhāre is said to indicate a place that should not be used. This is because anthills usually occur in such places. Mūsikukkara refers to the heap of dust dug out and pushed outside by mice. Because words like acchadana (covering) are mentioned, it should be understood that only earth moistened by rainwater falling directly from the sky is jātapathavī (natural earth). Earth moistened by water that falls on a roof etc. and flows down from there is not jātapathavī. Maṇḍapatthambha refers to a pillar of a pavilion roofed with branches. Uccāletvā means lifting or raising. Tato means from the old monastery.

Mahāmattika refers to a lump of fine clay used for plastering walls. Being natural earth (jātapathavī), perceiving it as natural earth, and digging it oneself or causing another to dig—these three are the factors of this training rule.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Digging the Earth is finished.

## The First Chapter on Lying is finished.

## 2. Bhūtagāma Vagga

## 1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Vegetation

In the first training rule of the second chapter, "niggahétuṃ asakkonto" means that when a celestial mansion situated on a branch is about to be destroyed because the branch is being cut, even if the deity places their child on that tree to prevent the cutting, the monk is unable to stop the momentum of the falling axe. Rukkhadhamma refers to the nature of a tree. Just as trees do not get angry even when they are cut, the deity not getting angry is called rukkhadhamma.

Uppatitaṃ means 'arisen'; bhantaṃ means 'running' (chariot); vāraye means 'should restrain (or suppress)'. Itaro means that one who cannot suppress the arisen anger is not a 'noble charioteer', like a person who merely holds the reins of a king or sub-king. Visaṭaṃ sappavisaṃ is like black snake venom that has spread through the body from the fang marks. Jahāti orapāraṃ means abandoning the five lower fetters (saṃyojana) through the third path (the Path of Non-returning). Orapāraṃ means 'this shore' (or the lower fetters which are like this shore). Alternatively, that person is a monk who stays after removing anger through the third path, and through the Path of Arahantship, abandons 'this shore' and 'the further shore', namely one's own self-identity and the self-identity of others.
11:
Alternatively, it means that the monk, having removed anger through the third path (Path of Non-returning), abandons 'this shore' and 'the further shore' through the Path of Arahantship. In that context, 'this shore' (ora) refers to one's own self-identity (sakat-tabhāva) or the internal sense bases (ajjhattikāyatana). 'The further shore' (pāra) refers to the self-identity of others or the external sense bases (bāhirāyatana). One who abandons desire and lust (chandarāga) for both is said to 'abandon this shore and the further shore'.

"Bhavanti" means they increase (grow). "Ahuvunti" means they have become. Therefore, it was said 'arisen and grown'. Bhūtagāma is a collection of great elements (mahābhūta) united in the form of green grass and so on. To show that there is no other group separate from that collection, it is said 'the elements themselves are the group (gāma)'. In the word pātabya, referring to the meaning of the root pā as 'consuming', it is called 'the state of being consumable'. Since that state of being consumable occurs only through cutting etc., it was said 'arisen for that bhūtagāma due to the cause of cutting etc.'.

Here, the word jāta is synonymous with vijāta. Since it expresses 'giving birth' (arising) as in the words 'a woman gives birth to a son', it is said 'born' (pasūtāni), meaning leaves and roots have emerged.

Wishing to show those seeds, since the cause (seed) is taken by showing the effect (plant), it is said 'the seed is shown by the plant arisen from the seed'.

The expression "bhūtagāma arisen from a seed is called a seed" shows that this is a usage where the latter word is dropped (uttarapada-lopa), like calling a flower arisen from a lotus bush a 'lotus'. The seed called bhūtagāma refers to a seed from which leaves and roots have emerged. Yathārutaṃ means as it is in the Pali text.

"Sañcicca" (intentionally) is said; therefore, rising up even while knowing that earth is sticking to the body is allowable, because there is no perception of 'I will remove that earth'. By the mention of anantaka, moss about the size of a mustard seed is taken; this is the name of that species of moss. Because roots and leaves are not complete, it is called 'incomplete bhūtagāma'. It is included within bījagāma (community of seeds). Although it does not grow, because it is based on bhūtagāma, it is said to be 'included in rootless bhūtagāma'. Regarding the coconut tree, it is spoken of specifically (āveṇika).
12:
Seleya is a type of perfume originating from stone. 'Pupphitakālato paṭṭhāya' means starting from the time of blooming. 'Chattakaṃ gaṇhanto' means taking a mushroom that has bloomed. It is not allowable to take a mushroom bud even without damaging the bark of the tree, but it is allowable to take a bloomed one. 'Hatthakukkuccena' means by fidgeting of the hands (restlessness of the hands).

'Drinking water should not be scented (with flowers)'—this statement refers to scenting water intended for one's own drinking with flowers dedicated to oneself. For others (laypeople, novices), it is allowable because it is not prohibited. Therefore, it was said, 'one who wishes to eat it oneself.' For trees whose branches grow even without roots descending, just by the emergence of leaves, it is allowable to destroy cut coconut palms, bamboo poles, etc., without making them kappiya.

Because it is said, 'I will show the place for walking,' there is no fault for one who treads with the intention of walking in the cloister or with the intention of traveling on a path, nor for one who sits with the intention of sitting on grass.

'Samaṇakappehi' means by the allowable terms of ascetics. Fruits without seeds and fruits from which seeds must be removed are called 'samaṇakappa' because they are allowable. Seedless fruits (abīja) include young mangoes and the like. Fruits from which seeds must be removed (nibbaṭṭabīja) include jackfruit and the like. In the phrase 'only by saying kappiyaṃ,' although it is stated as a preceding action, at the very moment of speaking, a wound (mark) must be made on the bījagāma with fire, a knife, or similar tools. It is not allowable to do so before speaking. In making it kappiya, one should only show cutting or splitting without severing it into two parts. The monk performing it must only do so when told 'Kappiyaṃ karohi' (Make it allowable) in any language. This is because the instruction to make it kappiya again to free it from being bījagāma was already established from the beginning. Since it is said, 'it can also be done in a bowl,' it is certainly allowable to pierce the pulp or seed taken out of the shell anywhere. In this training rule, there are three factors: (1) being vegetation (bhūtagāma), (2) perception of it as vegetation, and (3) destroying or causing to destroy.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Vegetation (Bhūtagāma Sikkhāpada) is finished.

## 2. Aññavādaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the second training rule, 'aññaṃ vacanaṃ' (another word) refers to covering up a statement made by others to reveal a fault by speaking another statement that is inconsistent with it.
13:
A statement that occurs by way of covering with another word, which sets aside the meaning of what was asked and speaks or shows something else, is called 'aññavādaka' (prevarication). Therefore, it was said, 'this is the name for covering with another word.' 'Tuṇhībhūtassa etaṃ nāmaṃ' means this is the name for being silent, or this is the reading itself. 'Aññavādakaṃ āropetuṃ' means to charge with prevarication. 'Vihesakaṃ' means the state of harassing.

In the Pali, 'na ugghāṭetukāmo' means having the desire to conceal.

The dukkaṭa offense mentioned in the Pali as 'when prevarication is not yet charged' is appropriate through the power of covering with another word. According to the method in the Commentary, for a monk who covers up with a lie, there is a dukkaṭa along with a pācittiya. Once charged with prevarication, there is only a pācittiya by this training rule. Some teachers say, 'two pācittiyas along with the musāvāda pācittiya'; this should be investigated. For the ādikammika (the first doer), it should be understood that there is no offense by this rule even in lying. The three factors here are: being charged by a formal act (dhammakamma), being questioned about an offense or a matter, and prevaricating with another word or remaining silent with the desire to conceal.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Prevarication (Aññavādaka Sikkhāpada) is finished.

## 3. Ujjhāpanaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the third training rule, the root 'jhe' in the sense of thinking has many meanings; since the sense of looking is possible, it is said 'olokāpenti' (making them look). The word 'chandāya' is a gender shift, meaning 'chandena' (by desire).

Speaking disparagingly (avaṇṇa) of a monk to others to make them think poorly of him is called 'ujjhāpana' (complaining). Revealing a monk's fault by talking among themselves without telling others is called 'khiyyana' (grumbling). This is the difference between them.

'Aññaṃ anupasampannaṃ ujjhāpeti' means making another unordained person (layperson or novice) disparage. 'Tassa vā taṃ santike' means disparaging that monk (ordained) who is authorized by the Saṅgha in the presence of that unordained person. In this training rule too, since disparaging by lying etc. can occur, the instances of dukkaṭa and the non-offense of the ādikammika are [determined] by this very rule...
14:
It should be understood that in all cases, because one does not escape the pācittiya offense of lying (musāvāda), the offense is incurred by this training rule alone. In this regard, there are these six factors: (1) being authorized by a formal act (dhammakamma), (2) being ordained (upasampanna), (3) the absence of following a wrong course (agati), (4) the desire for that monk's harm, (5) the person in whose presence one speaks being ordained, and (6) complaining (ujjhāpana) or disparaging (khiyana).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Complaining is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the First Training Rule on Lodgings

In the fourth training rule, "apannāte" means at a time when it is not known as rain (when it is not raining). Taking this specific meaning of placing [bedding] in pavilions and so forth for eight months, the Blessed Buddha laid down this training rule from the beginning. Having manifested this meaning through words similar to a supplementary regulation such as "Monks, I allow [it] for eight months," a separate supplementary regulation was not spoken. However, in the Parivāra, because this word of allowance stands in the place of a supplementary regulation, it is called "one supplementary regulation."

"Navavāyimo" refers to a bed that is currently wrapped with newly woven thread. "Onaddho" refers to a bed covered with allowable leather. These beds do not perish quickly due to rain. The phrase "ukkaṭṭha-abbhokāsika" (a strict open-air dweller) is merely to show that monk's comfortable practice; even for one who undertakes the highest open-air practice, a robe-hut (cīvarakuṭi—a small hut made of robes) is indeed allowable. By the word "kāyānugatikatā," it shows the monk's state of staying only in that robe-hut; by that same word, it shows that an offense is incurred for a monk who goes elsewhere by himself out of fear of rain. Even if a bed is given by donors with the intention of it getting wet for those practicing the open-air dhutaṅga, it must be protected just as one protects oneself.

By the words "reflecting that clouds have not arisen," it shows that even in the summer, if clouds arise, it is not allowable to leave [the bed, etc.] in the open. "Tatra tatra" refers to those various open spaces such as the courtyard of a cetiya where [the bed, etc.] is specifically placed. The phrase "from the center towards the place of the footprints" refers to a place where, by sweeping from all around and always gathering rubbish in the middle of the courtyard, sand has accumulated in the center. This is said to show the procedure to be performed in such a place. Sand should be spread towards the base of a high ground or towards the base of a wall. Alternatively, some teachers say the meaning is that if sand is piled in the corners, it should be spread from that sand-pile towards other directions. Some teachers, however...
15:
...say that in order to avoid spoiling the swept area with footprints, one should stand on the unswept area and spread the sand towards one's own footprints. In the view of those teachers, the purpose of the words "starting from the center" is not seen.

A crab-footed (kuḷīrapadaka) bed is distinct from other beds merely by having curved legs, not by a special way of inserting the legs into the frame; to show this, the words "whoever..." and so forth were spoken. "Tassa" (his) refers only to an ordained monk (upasampanna).

In the sentence "Having sat... etc... there is a pācittiya offense," for a monk who goes away with the thought, "I will come back and remove it later," knowing that no clouds have arisen, there is no offense. That monk must indeed return later. "Having obtained permission" (kappam labhitvā) means having received the words spoken as "Go, do not stay here."

"The burden (responsibility) lies only with the resident monks" means that even if visiting monks (āgantuka) leave after sitting without saying anything, thinking "The resident monks (āvāsika) will surely remove it," the responsibility lies only with the resident monks. However, in the Mahāpaccari commentary, the meaning is that the responsibility lies only with the visiting monks who sat there, even if they did not say "This place belongs to us." Because it is said "having spread or having caused to be spread," the reason for the dukkaṭa offense is stated even for spreading without giving an order. "Ussāraka" refers to a monk who recites with a pleasant voice (sarabhāṇaka). He is called an ussāraka because he causes the Pali text to be recited or proceed higher and higher.

"Made for the sake of protecting the color" means it is made by sewing with pieces of cloth and so forth. "Should be spread on the ground" means if there is a coarse cloth mat (cimmilikā), it should be spread on top of that; if not, it should be spread on the bare ground. By the statement "The prohibition is only in the carrying of lion skins and so forth," it shows that only carrying for one's own sake—such as spreading them on beds and stools and then folding them back to keep—is not allowable. However, use by way of spreading on the ground and so forth is not considered "carrying for oneself." For in the Cammakkhandhaka, regarding the matter of carrying by spreading on beds and so forth for one's own sake, thus: "Monks, large skins—lion skin, tiger skin, leopard skin—are not to be carried. For the monk who carries them, there is a dukkaṭa offense" (Mahāvagga, 255)—thus it was prohibited.
16:
The rejection has been made. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood only by the method already stated. *Dārumayapīṭha* refers to a bench made of planks. *Pādakathalika* refers to wooden planks and such, where one rubs and washes unwashed feet.

113. Because of going with the intention, "I will put it away after returning," there is no offense for a monk who, though not drying it in the sun, has spread it for another reason and has the expectation of returning. For that very reason, in the Mātikā Commentary, six factors are stated along with the lack of disregard: "the bed etc. being *saṅghika*, spreading or causing to be spread in a place with the stated characteristics, the absence of obstruction by anyone, the absence of danger, the lack of disregard, and exceeding the distance of a stone's throw."

## The Explanation of the First Lodging Training Rule is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Second Lodging Training Rule

116. In the fifth training rule, *pāvāra* and *kojava* are special types of long-haired rugs kept only for the purpose of spreading. "Only this much is stated" is said in the commentaries. *Senāsanato* means from the very last lodging.

In order to specifically show the meaning stated in the Kurundī Commentary, the passage beginning with "*kiñcāpi vutto*" is undertaken. Because the foot of a tree is well-known, it is said "there is nothing to be said." *Palujjati* means it perishes.

117. That with which they weave or cover a bed or a bench with leather etc. is called *mañcapīṭhakavāna*. *Siluccayaleṇa* means a mountain cave. By this statement, "Asking permission is a duty," it shows that there is no offense. There are seven factors here: being a spread with the stated characteristics, that spread being *saṅghika*, spreading or causing to be spread in a monastery with the stated characteristics, the absence of anyone to forbid it, the absence of danger, departing for another direction without disregard, and exceeding the precinct boundary.

## The Explanation of the Second Lodging Training Rule is finished.
17:
## 6. Explanation of the Encroaching Training Rule

In the sixth training rule, "*anupavisitvā*" means having entered near. "*Upacāraṃ ṭhapetvā*" means leaving aside the precinct which is one and a half cubits (1.5 cubits) in distance. The factors of this training rule are: (1) it being a *saṅghika* monastery, (2) knowing the state of one who should not be made to get up, (3) having the desire to crowd [him], (4) sitting or lying down within the precinct. These four are the factors of this training rule.

## The Explanation of the Encroaching Training Rule is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Expelling Training Rule

In the seventh training rule, "*koṭṭhakāni*" means gatehouses. This statement, "It is not proper to expel from the entire monastery grounds," is said because it is inappropriate. The reason is that for a monk who causes another to be expelled with a mind that is not angry because he blames evil, there is no offense by this training rule because it is preached as "being angry and displeased." No offense is seen regarding other considerations. In the Pali, in words such as "expels a shameless (*alajjī*) monk," even if anger arises occasionally due to the nature of the mind changing quickly, there is no offense because the undertaking of expelling is only due to the reason of being shameless etc. The factors of this training rule are: (1) it being a *saṅghika* monastery, (2) the monk being free from being a maker of quarrels etc., (3) expelling or causing to be expelled by oneself out of anger. These three are the factors of this training rule.

## The Explanation of the Expelling Training Rule is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Upper-room Hut Training Rule

The eighth training rule is very clear in meaning. The factors of this training rule are: (1) it being a *saṅghika* monastery, (2) it being a hut with an open space high enough not to hit the head, (3) using the lower floor, (4) sitting or lying down on a bed with removable legs (*āhaccapādaka*) fitted into the sockets without closing the door. These four are the factors of this training rule.

## The Explanation of the Upper-room Hut Training Rule is finished.
18:
## 9. Mahallakavihāra Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth training rule, because it is stated as "a large dwelling with an owner," it is said that there is no offense for a hut built for one's own use (saññācikakuṭī). "Yassa" means of the dwelling. "That dwelling may also be incomplete in its surroundings (upacāra)" means that the opened door leaf strikes a wall, and that wall is approximately the width of the door leaf and lacks surroundings. The door leaf is called "ālokasandhī" because it connects or fits the light-opening (window). For a monk who repeatedly applies plastering and so forth in places other than the surroundings of the main door and the window, a Pācittiya offense is incurred according to the number of lumps of clay.

Some teachers, however, say: "Since the Pācittiya offense is not mentioned in the Pali text, it is only a Dukkaṭa offense." "Adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ" means it should be managed or arranged. He manages it while standing in a field containing green beans or green branches. "Dukkaṭa offense" means that a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred by a monk who stands in a field containing green beans or green branches and covers [the roof]. Some teachers say: "A Dukkaṭa offense is incurred by a monk who builds a dwelling in such a field," but this statement does not agree with the Pali text.

"Straight covering only" means covering straight with bricks and so forth from the edge of the roofing up to the ridge-pole, the peaked roof, the roof-finial, and so forth. In this way, if the entire dwelling is covered once, that covering is taken as "one course" (ekamagga), and in the Pali text, it is stated as "two courses" (dve magge) and so forth. They say that covering in succession (pariyāya) should also be applied in this same way; this statement agrees with the Pali text "he caused it to be covered repeatedly" and the Commentary statement "all this covering should be understood as being above the [previous] covering."

In the Pali text, the words "for one covering by course, for one covering in succession" are spoken to show the distinction in the manner of covering with bricks and so forth, and with grass and leaves. Some teachers say: "Taking one straight covering upwards from the edge of the roofing above a roof already covered in a row as one course, it is stated as 'two courses' and so forth, but it does not refer to covering the entire dwelling. This same method applies to covering in succession." This statement does not agree with the Pali and Commentaries.

In the phrase "tatiyāya maggaṃ," the word "tatiyāya" is a dative case ending used in the sense of the accusative; it means "the third course." Alternatively, "tatiyaṃ maggaṃ" itself is the original reading. The phrase "obtained by grass and leaves" is spoken referring to covering with grass and leaves and then applying plastering inside and out on top.
19: It is stated that there is no offense only in the case of a grass hut. "Tiṇṇam maggānam" refers to the three layers of roofing covered in succession. In the phrase "tiṇṇam pariyāyānam" as well, it should be understood in this same way. These three—being a large dwelling, being one's own residence, and constructing more than two or three layers—are the factors of this training rule. ## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Large Dwellings is finished. ## 10. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Water Containing Living Beings. In the matrix (mātikā) of the tenth training rule, it means if one pours or discards water containing living beings with grass or with clay. Or, the meaning should be understood by supplying the words: taking water and pouring it outside, and then bringing grass or clay and putting it into that water. Therefore, it is said: "Even if it is as much as a cartload," etc. "Idam" refers to the procedure of putting in grass and clay. "Vuttam" means what is stated in the matrix as "with grass or with clay," or what is stated in the commentaries. This training rule is also spoken regarding external use based on the object, because internal use will be discussed separately. Since it is prescribed for pouring water while considering it "containing living beings" but without the intention to kill, it is called "paṇṇattivajja" (a fault by prescription). However, it should be understood that if there is an intention to kill, the Pācittiya offense is incurred under a different training rule, not this one. These four—the water containing living beings, knowing that "beings will die by pouring," and pouring such water on grass etc. for some purpose without the intention to kill—are the factors of this training rule. ## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Water Containing Living Beings is finished. ## The Second Chapter on Lodgings (Senāsana-vagga) is finished. ## "Bhūtagāma-vagga" is also a name for this chapter.
