## 3. Ovāda Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Ovāda Training Rule
In the first training rule of the third chapter, 'tiracchānabhūta' means contrary or external. 'Samiddha' means complete. 'Sahitattha' means endowed with benefit. It is called 'gambhīra' (profound) because of the depth of its meaning and so forth.

145-147. 'Parato' means beyond. 'Karontovā' means doing so with the intent to exclude. 'Vibhaṅge' refers to the Jhāna-vibhaṅga. 'Caraṇa' is the Dhamma that is like feet for going to Nibbāna.

'Yadassa' should be resolved as 'yaṃ assa'. 'Dhāreti' means to preserve without loss. 'Parikathanattha' is for the purpose of preaching the Dhamma defined by way of miscellaneous discourses (pakiṇṇakakathā). The three types of Anumodanā (rejoicing) are: the Anumodanā related to the benefits of giving in Saṅgha meals and so forth, such as the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta; the Anumodanā in auspicious ceremonies like housewarmings, such as the Maṅgala Sutta; and the Anumodanā in inauspicious events like funeral meals, such as the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta. 'Kammākammaviniccaya' is the decision stated in the Kamma-vagga at the end of the Parivāra. 'Samādhivasena' means by way of having tranquility (samatha) as a precursor. 'Vipassanāvasena' means by way of dry-insight (sukkhavipassanā) such as the purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi). He is called 'cātuddisa' (one of the four directions) because he is worthy of going to any of the four directions he desires without depending on others to guard his virtue, or because he is good in the four directions.

'Abhivinaye' refers to the discipline of restraint (saṃvaravinaya) known as the Pātimokkha-saṃvara, or the Vinaya Piṭaka that explains it. 'Vinetuṃ' means to teach or explain. 'Paguṇa vācuggata' means mastered by way of both text and meaning, and committed to memory. In these two Vibhaṅgas, the connection is also made by way of the meaning. 'Abhidhamme' refers to the phenomena of mind and matter (nāmarūpa-dhamma) defined by way of characteristics (lakkhaṇa), functions (rasa), and so forth. It is said that in ancient times, the Great Elders, in order to prevent the disappearance of the Pariyatti, handed over specific portions of the Dhamma, such as the Dīgha Nikāya, to each group, saying, 'You must maintain this portion by way of both text and commentary; if you are able, learn even more than this.' Thus, they handed over the entire Dhamma according to the texts. At that time, those monks were called Dīghabhāṇaka or Majjhimabhāṇaka according to the name of the text. Those monks, having given up the portion that was their responsibility...
21:
...did not get the opportunity to learn other texts. With reference to that, it was said, 'If he is a Majjhimabhāṇaka,' and so forth.

In that sentence starting with 'Sace,' the 'lower three vaggas' are these three: the Sagāthaka-vagga, Nidāna-vagga, and Khandha-vagga, which are below the Mahā-vagga. The phrase 'below the Tika-nipāta' refers to the Ekaka-nipāta and Duka-nipāta. The Dhammapada, along with its stories (vatthu), should be learned by a Jātaka-reciter (Jātakabhāṇaka) together with his own Jātakas. The opinion of the Mahāpaccarī is that it is improper to learn less than that. 'From here and there' means that learning by selecting from the Dīgha Nikāya and so forth is rejected as 'improper' because it does not lead to the stability of the True Dhamma, nor to the monk's skill in the sequence of preceding and following contexts (anusaṃdhi). Regarding the statement 'Nothing is mentioned about learning in the Abhidhamma,' it should be understood that because the divisions like the Kusala-triads (kusala-tika) in the Vinaya, and the path of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā-magga) in the Suttas, cannot be understood without the Abhidhamma text—it would be like entering into darkness—therefore, by the acquisition of the Sutta and Vinaya, the acquisition of the Abhidhamma is already stated; thus it is not mentioned separately. Just as when it is said 'food should be eaten,' even if it is not said 'curry should be consumed,' it is already stated because they are inseparable; this should be seen as a complete example.

'Parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā' refers to speech in which the syllables (byañjana) such as soft (sithila) and hard (dhanita) are complete within the words. It is called 'porī' because it is speech originating in the city (pura), meaning the speech of city-dwellers. In the word 'anelagaḷā,' 'elā' means saliva; it refers to speech free from the dripping of that saliva. In the word 'kalyāṇavākkaraṇa,' the speech itself is the 'vākkaraṇa,' the sound of utterance. He is called 'kalyāṇavākkaraṇa' because he has noble and sweet utterance of speech. A monk becomes incapable (abhabba) of monkhood only through sexual intercourse with a nun (bhikkhunī), not with a sikkhamānā or a sāmaṇerī. Therefore, it was said, 'Or physical contact with a bhikkhunī,' and so forth.

'Garukehi' means with heavy articles (garukabhaṇḍa). The term 'ekatoupasampannāya' uses the locative case in the sense of the accusative. A nun ordained in the presence of monks refers to nuns who have changed their sex or the five hundred Sakyan princesses. For one who exhorts such 'one-sidedly ordained' (ekatoupasampanna) nuns, only a Pācittiya offense is incurred.

149. 'Not wishing to go after being invited' means they have no desire to return after the meal is finished, but wish to stay right there. 'Yato' means from the nunnery. 'Yācitvā' means requesting, 'We will live only by the exhortation you have brought.' 'Tattha' means in that nunnery. A Pācittiya offense is incurred by a nun who spends the Rains-retreat in a monastery where there are no monks; a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred by a nun who leaves. To answer the question 'Which of these two offenses should be avoided?' it was said, 'That offense should be guarded.' The offense arising on account of the Rains-retreat should be guarded. In other Pācittiya rules, there are grounds for non-offense. Therefore, it was said, 'Except in times of danger,' and so forth. 'Ovādatthāya' means for the purpose of requesting exhortation. 'Dve tisso' means by two or three. In fact, this term uses the nominative case in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa). 'Pāsādikena' means by way of inspiring physical conduct and so forth.
22:
"They wish to stay" means (having been invited and eaten, they do not wish to leave but) they wish to stay in that very place. *Yato* means from the bhikkhunīs' quarters. *Yācitvā* means having requested, saying, "We too shall stay only with the instruction brought by you." *Tattha* means in that bhikkhunīs' quarters. A bhikkhunī who spends the rains-retreat in a residence where there are no monks commits a Pācittiya offense; if she leaves, she commits a Dukkaṭa offense.

Answering the objection as to which of these two offenses should be avoided, he said, "That [offense] should be guarded against." This means the offense rooted in the commencement of the rains-retreat should be guarded against; the meaning is that there is a reason for non-offense in the other Pācittiya. Therefore, he said the words beginning with "*Āpadāsu hi*."

*Ovādatthāya* means for the purpose of requesting instruction. *Dve tisso* means by two or three [monks]; this word uses the nominative case in the sense of the instrumental. *Pāsādikena* means by way of physical actions, etc., that inspire faith. *Sampādetu* means to fulfill the threefold training. The three factors here are: not being authorized, the bhikkhunī being fully ordained, and giving the eight *garudhammas* by way of instruction.

## The Commentary on the Ovāda Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Atthaṅgata Sikkhāpada

In the second training rule, *kokanada* is a special kind of *paduma* lotus; that lotus is said to have many layers and is endowed with beauty. The meaning here is: just as one looks at the *paduma* lotus called *kokanada*, so too, look at the Blessed One, called Aṅgīrasa, who has a lotus-like face with unfading fragrance, who shines with his own power like the sun in the stainless sky, who is magnificent for that very reason, and who has radiance emanating from his limbs. *Rajoharaṇa* is the name of a foot-wiping cloth because it wipes the dust from the body. A verse spoken after emitting rays of light is called an *obhāsagāthā*. In the *Visuddhimagga* and other texts, the verse beginning with "*Rāgo rajo na ca pana reṇu vuccati*" is called an *obhāsagāthā*, but this verse "*Adhicetaso*" is not. This verse is not in the *Udāna Pāli* as the *udāna* verse of Elder Cūḷapanthaka; it is stated in that *Udāna Pāli* that this is the *udāna* verse of Elder Ekudāniya. However, since it is stated in the Pāli text here, it should be taken as the *udāna* verse of the Elder [Cūḷapanthaka] as well. Here, even with the *garudhamma*...
23:
...for a monk who instructs, it is only a Pācittiya. The three factors here are: the sun having set, being fully ordained, and instructing.

## The Commentary on the Atthaṅgata Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Bhikkhunūpassaya Sikkhāpada

The third training rule is quite clear in meaning. The four factors here are: going to the bhikkhunīs' quarters, being fully ordained, it being the wrong time, and instructing with the *garudhammas*.

## The Commentary on the Bhikkhunūpassaya Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Āmisa Sikkhāpada

In the fourth training rule, even if one instructs without regard for material gain (*āmisa*), if a monk speaks with the perception that he is instructing for the sake of material gain, there is no offense because this training rule is *sacittaka* (dependent on intention). The remaining points here are quite clear. The four factors here are: being ordained, having obtained authorization according to the Dhamma, having no mind regarding material gain, and speaking thus with the desire for disparagement.

## The Commentary on the Āmisa Sikkhāpada is finished.

The fifth, the Cīvaradāna Sikkhāpada, is quite clear in meaning.

## 6. Commentary on the Cīvarasibbana Sikkhāpada

In the sixth training rule, *kathinavatta* is said with reference to going to help fellow practitioners who are making robes during the Kathina month. *Vañcetvā* (having deceived) means not saying "the robe of your relative bhikkhunī" but saying only "the robe of a bhikkhunī," so that when those monks hear "the robe of a bhikkhunī," they have the perception that she is a non-relative. Therefore, it is said, "because of urging in an improper matter." The three factors here are: it being the property of a non-relative bhikkhunī, it being a garment for wearing or covering, and sewing it or having it sewn in the manner described.

## The Commentary on the Cīvarasibbana Sikkhāpada is finished.
24:
## 7. Saṃvidhāna-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the seventh training rule: regarding the phrases in the Pali text, "Sister, let us go" and "Venerable sir, let us go," the former is an arrangement initiated by a monk, and the latter is an arrangement initiated by a bhikkhunī. "Ekaddhānamagga" refers to a journey on a single path. "Hiyyo" (yesterday) here means tomorrow (suve). "Pare" refers to the third day.

"Dvidhā vuttappakāro" (stated in two ways) refers to the two modes: traveling on foot and traveling by flight (with wings). "Upacāro na labbhati" (the vicinity is not obtained) means that the usual vicinity, such as a stone's throw in an enclosed village, is not applicable in this training rule because the villages are too close to each other. By this statement, it should be understood that in this training rule, "village" refers only to the inhabited area (antaraghara) and not the entire village field (gāmakhetta). Within that inhabited area, it is shown that an offense occurs only upon entering the vicinity where such vicinity is applicable. Therefore, the phrase beginning with "ratanamattantaro" (an interval of a cubit) is stated. Here, "entering the vicinity" (upacārokkamana) means actually entering within the vicinity. Even if one does not enter the vicinity, a monk traveling on a path within half a league (addhayojana) of the village vicinity is still said to be passing through all the village vicinities located within half a league on both the left and right sides of the path. If one travels on a path beyond half a league, the decision is not based on the number of village vicinities but only on the distance of half a league. In this way, the validity of incurring an offense based on the number of village vicinities for a monk traveling by boat along a village bank in the next training rule is established. This is because it is impossible to enter the village vicinity by boat. A junction of three roads is called "siṅghāṭaka." The phrase "etthantare saṃvidahite" means that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred not only for making an arrangement on the aforementioned main roads but also for making an arrangement between paths.

"Addhayojanaṃ atikkamantassa" refers to a monk who crosses half a league in a place where there is no village. Even in a forest that is part of a village field, if there is no village within half a league, it is intended in this training rule as a "forest without a village," not referring to great forests like the Viñjhā forest.

"Raṭṭhabhede" refers to the ruin of the country. "Cakkasamāruḷhā" means mounting the "cycle" of postures or mounting a cart wheel. The five factors of this training rule are: (1) making an arrangement by both parties to travel, (2) not deviating from the appointment, (3) it not being the exempted time, (4) the absence of danger, and (5) entering another village or crossing half a league. For a monk who makes an arrangement and travels with a bhikkhunī ordained on one side (ekatoupasampannā), etc., he incurs an offense under the Mātugāma-sikkhāpada.

## The Commentary on the Saṃvidhāna Training Rule is finished.
25:
## 8. Nāvābhiruhana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the eighth training rule: "Ekaṃ tīraṃ... nirantaraṃ" refers to the continuity of villages situated within half a league of the river. The phrase "ekaṃ agāmakaṃ araññaṃ" is said because of the absence of such situated villages. The phrase beginning with "agāmaka-tīrapassena" is stated with reference to a river wider than half a league. In fact, even when traveling in the middle of a river narrower than half a league, since both banks are within half a league, the offenses must be determined by the number of villages reached and the number of half-leagues crossed. Therefore, it is said: "Yojana-vitthatā... addhayojana-gaṇanāya pācittiyāni" (a league wide... pācittiyas by the count of half-leagues). Indeed, for a river less than a league wide, the count of offenses is already stated by way of the banks situated within half a league.

Through the phrase beginning with "sabba-aṭṭhakathāsu," the aforementioned meaning is confirmed. In that context, although a pācittiya offense is not mentioned regarding oceans and large lakes, it should be understood that for a monk who boards for the purpose of play/pleasure in those oceans and lakes, it is only a dukkaṭa offense. It should be understood that the nature of this training rule as a 'prohibition by regulation' (paṇṇattivajja) and its 'three-minded' nature (ticittata) are stated because an offense can occur upon entering another village, etc., for a monk who initially boards for play but later falls asleep on the boat, or for one who is practicing wise reflection. The remaining text is easy to understand.

## The Commentary on the Nāvābhiruhana Training Rule is finished.

## 9. Paripācita-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the ninth training rule: the phrase in the Pali text, "Sikkhamānā... pañca bhojanāni thapetvā sabbattha anāpatti," is stated with reference to the absence of offense under this training rule. For a monk who consumes requisites arising from intimation (viññatti) or roundabout talk (parikathā) made by the five co-religionists, there is only a dukkaṭa offense. The five factors here are: (1) the state of being caused to be cooked by a bhikkhunī, (2) knowing that it was caused to be cooked by a bhikkhunī, (3) the absence of initiative by householders, (4) it being one of the five types of food, and (5) the swallowing of that food.

## The Commentary on the Paripācita Training Rule is finished.
26:
## 10. Commentary on the Rahonisajja Training Rule
In the commentary on the tenth training rule, the Rahonisajja-sikkhāpada, the phrase "Upanandassa catuttha-sikkhāpadena" (by the fourth training rule of Upananda) refers to the training rule prescribed regarding sitting in a private place with a woman. Although this training rule on sitting in a private place with a woman is the fifth in the Acelaka Vagga, it should be understood that it is called "Upananda's fourth training rule" because it is the fourth among the training rules laid down due to the Venerable Upananda.

## The Commentary on the Rahonisajja Training Rule is Finished.

## The Third Chapter, the Ovāda Vagga, is Finished.

## 4. Bhojana Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Āvasathapiṇḍa Training Rule
In the first training rule of the fourth chapter, "imesaṃyeva" means only for these types of sects (pāsaṇḍa). "Ettakānaṃ" means for this many persons in this sect.

Regarding the phrase "going or coming," this should be understood as traveling a distance of half a yojana. Almsfood intended for other sects, or almsfood offered generally by non-believers (titthiya) who have no faith in the monks, is also not allowable for monks. In this training rule, there are three factors: it being almsfood provided for guests (āvasathapiṇḍa), not being ill (agilāna), and eating after staying there.

## The Commentary on the Āvasathapiṇḍa Training Rule is Finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Gaṇabhojana Training Rule
In the second training rule, "abhimāre" refers to the archers who were dispatched to kill the Blessed One after being subdued. One might ask: Is it not established that this training rule was laid down during the time of King Ajātasattu, according to the statement "he also caused the King to be killed"? If that is so, does it not contradict the Pali which states, "At that time, the King of Magadha... (etc) ... a relative had gone forth among the Ājīvakas... (etc) ... he said this to King Bimbisāra"? It does not contradict. It is said that the Ājīvaka had been inviting the monks and giving offerings intermittently since the time of King Bimbisāra. Even after the training rule was laid down during the time of King Ajātasattu, he sent a messenger to the monks. The monks, being scrupulous, refused. Therefore, it should be understood that the story is presented from the very beginning.
27:
A kingdom that is different from one another is called 'virajja'; those who come from such a different kingdom are 'verajjaka'. Since they are diverse in terms of birth, clan, etc., the meaning is also 'nānāverajjaka' (those from various different kingdoms).

217-8. Although it is evident from the origin story of this training rule that it becomes a group meal (gaṇabhojana) due to requesting (viññatti), it should be understood that in the word-analysis (padabhājanī), it is shown as a group meal due to invitation (nimantana) which was not yet completed, without mentioning the requesting. Therefore, it is said, "dvīhākārehi" (in two ways), etc. Because it is said "by whatever synonym," it becomes a group meal even by a general name such as "take the food," etc. In the Pali, regarding the scruples arising over the statement "eat only here" in the stories of traveling, etc., it should be understood that this occurred only because the name of the food, such as 'rice' (odana), etc., was used. "Taking together" means standing together and taking without leaving the twelve-cubit space (hatthapāsa) of one another.

Because of the statement "give almsfood for all four of us," and because it is stated in the Pali (commentary) as "you give almsfood for one monk," etc., only food requested by the name of food becomes a group meal. It should be noted that even if that group meal is requested by another person, it applies to all monks who receive it together. However, for a monk who eats food requested and received individually, there is only an offense under the training rules such as the Paṇītabhojana-sikkhāpada.

'Āgantukapaṭṭa' refers to a robe made by adding a strip of cloth without cutting. "Ṭhapeti" means placing one end by way of fastening it to the robe. "Piccāgataṃ sibbati" means sewing the second end that is brought back by turning. "Āgantukapaṭṭaṃ bandhati" means repeatedly fastening with thread here and there while making it adhere to the robe. "Ghaṭṭeti" means taking it according to measurement and striking it with sticks, etc. "Suttaṃ karoti" means twisting it by way of making it into strands, etc. "Valeti" means twisting many strands of thread by hand or by a wheel-axle to make them one. "Parivattanaṃ karoti" means making a revolving spindle-machine; having inserted the ball of thread into that machine and placing it in bamboo tubes, etc., they make it revolve and pull from the end of the thread.

'Animantita-catuttha' refers to a group of four monks where the fourth monk is one who has not been invited. The same principle applies to the remaining groups of four. Therefore, it is said, "pañcannaṃ catukkānaṃ" (of the five groups of four). "Sampavesetvā" means having joined with those monks. "Gaṇo bhijjati" means the meaning is that it is no longer the invited Saṅgha.
28:
In the phrase "adhivāsetvā gatesu," at the moment of accepting an improper (akappiya) invitation, there is no dukkhaṭa offense in the preliminary effort (pubbapayoga). However, in the case of a group meal (gaṇabhojana) arising from a request (viññatti), it should be understood that at the moment of making the request, a dukkhaṭa offense is incurred according to other training rules such as the one regarding fine food (paṇītasūpodana). "Nimantanaṃ sādiyatha" means "Accept the meal invitation." "Tāni ca" refers to barley bread (kummāsa) and so on; because these were accepted later by another monk, they are not considered as being accepted together.

By the statement "bhattuddesakena paṇḍitena bhavitabbaṃ...pe... moce tabbā," it is shown that if the meal-allocator (bhattuddesaka) delights in an improper invitation, all the monks are considered to have delighted in it. It is also shown that for monks who accept together, an offense of group-dining (gaṇabhojanāpatti) occurs. "Gāmadvāre aṭṭhatvā" (without standing at the village gate) is said out of fear that the messenger might come to the door and say again, "Please accept the meal." The three factors here are: being a group meal (gaṇabhojanatā), the absence of a proper occasion (samayābhāva), and swallowing (ajjhoharaṇa).

## The Explanation of the Gaṇabhojana Training Rule is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Paramparabhojana Training Rule

In the commentary on the third training rule, "bhattapaṭipāṭi aṭṭhitā" means that the sequence of meals offered in succession by families continues without interruption or stopping. Gruel (yāgu) and so on, cooked with jujube fruits (badara), is called "badarasāḷava."

In the Pali text, "paramparabhojana" refers to eating the meal of another person before eating the meal of the person who first invited him (resulting in an offense). Although the performance of formal assignment (vikappanā) is not included in the Matika by way of supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) in this training rule, it is counted as one of the "four supplementary regulations" in the Parivāra. In that regard, although the Mahāpaccari commentary establishes the assignment in one's absence (parammukhā-vikappanā) by mentioning it later, the assignment in one's presence (sammukhā-vikappanā) should also be accepted. Therefore, in the Matika commentary, it is said: "Whichever monk, to one of the five classes of fellow-practitioners (sahadhammika), says in their presence: 'I give my expectation of a meal to you' or 'I make an assignment'..." and so on.

"Milk or broth" (khīraṃ vā rasaṃ vā) refers to what is placed on top of the meal along with the five kinds of staple food. Since milk and so on are not considered staple food (abhojana), there is no offense even if one drinks them out of sequence. Therefore, it is said: "To the monk who is eating..." and so on.
29:
Because of not performing the formal assignment (vikappanā), this training rule also arises through speech by way of non-action (akiriya); thus it is called "verbal action" (vacīkamma). In this training rule, there are these three factors: (1) being a meal out of sequence (paramparabhojanatā), (2) the absence of a proper occasion (samayābhāva), and (3) swallowing (ajjhoharaṇa).

## The Explanation of the Paramparabhojana Training Rule is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Kāṇamātā Training Rule

In the Pali of the fourth training rule, "paṭiyālokaṃ" means the western direction or the back direction. Since this training rule is independent of intention (acittaka), an offense is incurred even for a monk who accepts with the perception that it was prepared for the sake of provisions for a journey and so on. Because an offense can be incurred even by saying "Give it into the hand of this person" for one's own sake, it is called "verbal action" (vacīkamma). In this training rule, there are these five factors: (1) being the described flat cakes or round cakes, (2) having no remainder, (3) the journey not yet being cancelled, (4) being a non-relative, and (5) accepting more than two or three bowlfuls.

## The Explanation of the Kāṇamātā Training Rule is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the First Pavāraṇā Training Rule

In the fifth training rule, by the Pali "ti-kāraṃ avatvā," it is shown that the word "iti" obtained by the power of the word to be performed should not be said after the Vinaya act is completed. However, in this training rule, it should be understood that even if monks who do not know use the word "iti," the act of making an extra allowance (atireka) is indeed accomplished.

238-9. "Pavārito": To show that this word is formed in the agent sense (kattu-attha), "katapavāraṇo" and so on is said. To establish that the word "bhuttāvī" (having eaten) has no special significance, "vuttampi cetaṃ" and so on is said. "Tāhi" means with parched rice (puthuka). "Sattumodaka" is an uncooked cake made by moistening flour. Specifically, if one grinds flour, moistens it, makes a cake, and fries it, that cake does not cause one to be "pavārita" (one who has refused further food). Since it is said, "One is said to refuse only when one refuses what is present in a place where it should be refused," it should be understood that for a monk who refuses the property of a shameless person (alajjī) or communal property (saṅghika) that has not yet reached him, he does not become "pavārita."

"The nearest limb" (āsannataraṃ aṅgaṃ) means that when someone stands outside the reach of a forearm (hatthapāsa) and leans over to give, the head is the nearest part; it should be delimited by the near edge of that head.
30:
"Apanāmetvā" means bringing forward. In saying "Please take this almsfood," it is said without even a slight inclination. Since mere verbal offering is not intended, if one makes an effort to take it with a ladle, even if the ladle is not lifted, it is said "it is indeed brought forward" with the intention that Pavāraṇā occurs because it was previously brought forward in this way. "Uddhaṭamatte" means just at the moment of being separated from the vessel. "Dvinnam samabhārepi" means even if both the server and another person carry the same load of the alms-basket.

In saying "Take the broth," because it is spoken by the name of mere meat broth which does not cause Pavāraṇā, Pavāraṇā does not occur for the monk who refuses. In words such as "fish broth," because both the fish and the broth are possible meanings, and because the substance of fish curry is of such nature, Pavāraṇā occurs. Even for a monk who refuses what is brought forward while remaining silent without saying "Take this," Pavāraṇā indeed occurs. "Karambaka" is a designation for something mixed. That which is made by mixing many things is called "karambaka."

In the thought "It is made specifically for me," because the object is allowable, it is said "he is indeed one who has refused (pavārito)." If that thing is indeed made specifically [for him], there is no refusal (Pavāraṇā). "Ayameṭṭha adhippāyo" refers to the meaning stated as "without asking," etc. Here, the reason is difficult to see. Because the almsfood is abundant, the reason for the possibility of Pavāraṇā is difficult to see. Otherwise, in karambaka (mixed food) also, if fish etc. are abundant, Pavāraṇā would occur. Just as the reason is difficult to see here, it should be understood that the reason is also difficult to see in the subsequent passage "Take the mixed thing." Although the reason is stated as "This thing is indeed mixed with almsfood," etc., that statement does not agree with the saying "A very small amount does not cause Pavāraṇā." "Giving by separating" should be understood as giving by separating verbally, such as "Take the broth," etc. It does not mean separating the broth etc. with the body. Even if not so separated, because Pavāraṇā cannot occur for the one who refuses, and because it is spoken by the name of something that does not constitute Pavāraṇā, it is like the instances where one brings gruel mixed with almsfood and says "Take the gruel." Otherwise, the meaning should be taken here in a way that does not contradict the preceding and following [statements].

In words such as "a boat or a bridge," even if one stands for a moment at the time of boarding the boat etc., because boarding must be done, it is not called "standing" as the focus is on traveling. However, one should not [stand] in cases where there is no space due to a crowd of people. "Without moving" means...
31:
Without moving from the stated place to another seat or upwards, one is allowed to turn around in that very place. Therefore, He said the words "By whichever side," etc.

"Unallowable food" refers to food arisen through "corrupting families" (kuladūsana), etc. By this word "unallowable," it is shown that rice etc. mixed with those unoffered fruits etc. are indeed atiritta (leftover). Therefore, if there are unoffered roots, fruits, etc. in that bowl, one should remove them and eat the remaining almsfood.

"That person cannot do it again" means if it is done in that very vessel, because it becomes done together with what was done first, that first monk himself does not get the chance to do it again, but another monk does. For, because it was done by another, another gets the chance to do it again. In another vessel, however, it is allowable for that monk or another to do it. Therefore, He said, "He who has not done it, he should do it; that which has not been done, that should be done." "Thus done" refers to almsfood done in another vessel. If, in this phrase "a place mixed with food (āmisa)," even the food sticking to the mouth etc. must be cleaned before eating the almsfood made leftover (atiritta).

It should be understood as having non-action as its origin (akiriya-samuṭṭhāna) because of not having the leftover made by verbal command. The three factors here are: the state of being one who has refused (pavārita), the food not being made leftover (anati-rittatā), and swallowing during the [allowable] time.

## The Explanation of the First Pavāraṇā Sikkhāpada is Finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Second Pavāraṇā Sikkhāpada

In the sixth training rule, because it is stated in the matrix (mātikā) as "having eaten," a Pācittiya offense is incurred at the conclusion of the meal. The five factors here are: the state of being one who has refused (pavārita), the perception of being such, the expectation of enjoyment (tasting), the invitation/offering with food not made leftover, and the conclusion of the meal.

## The Explanation of the Second Pavāraṇā Sikkhāpada is Finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Vikālabhojana Sikkhāpada

In the seventh training rule, the dancing activities of actors are called "naṭanāṭaka." Dramatic stories such as the abduction of Queen Sītā are included.

248-249. "The purpose of nutriment in nutriment" means neither the function of nutriment existing in snacks such as cakes, nor the purpose or benefit called the removal of hunger performed by snacks...
32:
(They) do not complete the function of nutriment (in snacks etc., nor the benefit of removing hunger). In some regions, it might fulfill the function of nutriment, but in other regions, due to the nature of the soil etc., it might not fulfill the function of nutriment. Therefore, it is said, "in various regions," and so forth. Some teachers, however, say that this statement is made to show that "if it fulfills the function of nutriment in one region, it is certainly not allowable in other regions at the wrong time either." "Pakati-āhāravasena" means fulfilling the function of nutriment by its own nature alone, without being mixed with other yāvakālika substances. "Confusion would only arise" means that because there are names with many meanings and obscure names, confusion would indeed arise. For this reason, in this context, we shall also refrain from showing the various synonyms of mūlaka (radish) and so forth, as they should be understood only through instruction.

"Yaṃ" refers to a round tuber (vaṭṭakanda). "Muḷāla" refers only to a large tender root. The phrase "the tips of trees and creepers" is a summary of the meaning already stated below. To show that the unripe fruits of acchivāda and so forth are yāvajīvika, it is said, "unripe fruits." Regarding the phrase "the seeds of harītakī (myrobalan) and so forth," some say that the kernel (or flesh) inside the seed is yāvakālika, but this is improper because it is not mentioned in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).

The resin that drips from the hiṅgu tree is called hiṅgu (asafoetida). Hiṅgujatu and so forth are also varieties of hiṅgu. Among those varieties, hiṅgujatu refers to the resin made by boiling the stems and leaves of the hiṅgu tree. Hiṅgusipāṭikā refers to the resin made by boiling the hiṅgu leaves. Some also say it is made by mixing with other leaves. "Taka" is the resin that comes out from the very tip. "Takapatti" is the resin that comes out from the leaf. "Takapaṇṇi" is the resin made by roasting the leaves. Some also say it is the resin that comes out from the stem. Being at the wrong time, being yāvakālika, and swallowing—these three are the factors of this training rule.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Eating at the Wrong Time is Finished.

## 8. Sannidhikārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

252-3. In the eighth training rule, "of such nature" refers to alms-food without curry. Although in the Pāḷi text, only yāvakālika is included by the words khādanīya (consumables) and bhojanīya (nutritives), and yāmakālika is not included, nevertheless, "if one stores yāmakālika within the watch and eats it, there is no offence" is stated in this training rule and—
33:
"Bhikkhus, if sattāhakālika... yāvajīvika are accepted on the same day with yāmakālika, it is allowable within the watch; if the watch has passed, it is not allowable" (Mahāvagga, 305)—this has been taught.

Because it is taught elsewhere (in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka) and due to the power of the word "yāmakālika," the teachers of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), who know the intention of the Blessed One, state that yāmakālika that has been stored up (sannidhikāraka) is indeed a basis for a pācittiya offence. "Yaṃ" refers to the bowl. This word "yaṃ" is in the accusative case (upayogavacana) in relation to the action of scraping (ghaṃsana). "Fingerprints are visible" means that even in the absence of grease, they are visible because of the excellent luster of the bowl. "Yaṃ" refers to yāvakālika and yāmakālika. "Only that which is not relinquished" refers only to substances such as yāvakālika that have not been given to an unordained person or abandoned without attachment; it does not refer to the acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa) of that substance. It is not possible to relinquish the acceptance of a substance without relinquishing the substance itself, nor is there any such statement. If there were, it would contradict the statement: "If the bowl is difficult to wash... there is a pācittiya for one who eats." This is because one who is striving to remove food particles (āmisa) by washing cannot have attachment to the acceptance. The attachment that exists toward the bowl also exists toward the food particles within that bowl; therefore, non-attachment to food particles cannot be found here. Thus, it is said that not relinquishing the acceptance of food particles causes a pācittiya on the next day.

If it is argued that "just as non-attachment to food particles cannot be found here, non-attachment to the acceptance also cannot be found," then it would follow that wherever there is attachment to food particles, attachment to the acceptance also does not disappear. If this were the case, there would be no need to separately mention the relinquishing of acceptance without attachment. In the Commentary, if this is intended as the cause for relinquishing the acceptance, it should be stated separately and more clearly, similar to how the relinquishing of the determination (adhiṭṭhāna) of a robe is done by paccuddhāra even while attachment to the robe remains. If this method exists, the meaning already stated—that there would be no such thing as proper rotation in bowls with knots or bumps—is valid. Therefore, the statement in the Sāratthadīpanī, "Even if a substance is not yet given to another, if the acceptance is relinquished by non-attached abandonment, it is allowable on the second day," and so forth, should not be accepted as the essence.

"Pakati-āmisa" refers to allowable yāvakālika substances such as rice. "Two" refers to: one offence due to the factor of storing (sannidhi) for a monk who eats yāmakālika accepted in the morning with a mouth containing food particles, and because it takes on the nature of yāvakālika by being mixed with yāmakālika...
34:
Two Pācittiya offenses are certainly incurred due to the reason of not making [food] leftover (anatiritta). 'Vikappadvaye' refers to both the side with flesh (sāmisa) and the side without flesh (nirāmisa). 'Thullaccaya and Dukkaṭa' means: if one eats human flesh, it is a Thullaccaya offense; if one eats the remaining types of flesh, it is a Dukkaṭa offense. Being yāvakālika or yāmakālika, storing (sannidhi), and swallowing that which is stored—these three are the factors of this Sannidhikāraka Sikkhāpada.

## The Explanation of Sannidhikāraka Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 9. Explanation of Paṇītabhojana Sikkhāpada

In the ninth explanation, 'paṇītasamsaṭṭhāni bhojanāni' is a compound with the middle term omitted (majjhelopīsamāsa). In the Ṭīkā, since the foods were mentioned previously and are well-known, they are not shown again. Because those foods are mixed with such superior flavors, they are called superior foods (paṇītabhojana). To show the varieties of those superior flavors, the words beginning with 'seyyathidaṃ sappi navanītaṃ' (such as ghee, butter) are stated. In the term 'sappibhatta', although the meaning can be understood as rice mixed with ghee or as ghee and rice, since it is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) that 'there is no such thing as sappibhatta like sālibhatta (rice-meal)', no other meaning can be asserted. Only the teachers of the Commentaries are the authority in such matters.

'Mūla' refers to allowable items (kappiyabhaṇḍa). Therefore, in the phrase 'tasmā anāpatti', although there is no Pācittiya offense due to a misunderstanding, they say one is not exempt from the Dukkaṭa offense of [requesting] curry and rice (sūpodana). The phrase 'kappiyasappinā akappiyasappinā' is stated by way of animals with allowable flesh and animals with unallowable flesh.

The Mahānāma Sikkhāpada refers to the Cātumāsapaccaya-pavāraṇā Sikkhāpada which will come later. A monk who is not ill, even if he requests in a place where he is not invited, if he sets a limit on time or a limit on medicine, he is similar to a monk who requests beyond that limit from a place where he was invited by the Saṅgha, or a monk who requests medicine for an illness that does not require medical treatment even within the limit. Therefore, it is said, 'He should be dealt with according to the Mahānāma Sikkhāpada'. Being superior food, not being ill, obtaining by an unmade request (viññatti), and swallowing—these four are the factors in this training rule.

## The Explanation of Paṇītabhojana Sikkhāpada is finished.
35:
## 10. Explanation of Dantapona Sikkhāpada

In the tenth training rule, 'ghanabaddho' means having a body connected with solid flesh, composed of firm flesh.

'Mukhadvāra' (mouth-door) refers to the opening below the mouth, which is the gullet (galanāḷika). Because the mouth-door is interpreted as the gullet, even if [something] enters through the nose, it is considered as having entered the gullet; however, merely placing it in the mouth is not yet considered as having entered [the gullet]. 'Āhāra' (nutriment) refers to the four types of kālika (period-restricted items) to be swallowed; it does not include water. For although that water is included in medicine, it is only the kālika of the item that has been formally accepted; water itself is akālika (not time-restricted). Formal acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa) does not apply to water. For that reason, even if a monk eats food (āmisa) together with water that has been heated, water that was accepted a long time ago, or water kept in an unallowable hut (akappiyakuṭī), the faults such as 'cooking for oneself' (sāmapāka) do not occur. It will be stated later (in the Pācittiya Commentary): 'A monk heats water for the sake of gruel... it is allowable'. However, at that time, the monks did not yet know the meaning of this word 'āhāra'. Therefore, it is said: 'Without properly reflecting on the meaning', and so on.

'Rathareṇumpi' refers to dust similar to the dust that rises when a chariot travels. It shows that even the visible dust finer than that, which floats in the air, is negligible (abbhohārika). 'Akallako' means an ill monk (gilāna).

By the words 'to take... or by the near end of that person', it is shown that for a monk standing upright in the air and taking an object lifted up by another, the hatthapāsa (forearm's length) should be measured starting from the sole of the foot, which is the nearest limb, and not from the head. In that sentence, the word 'orimantena' should be understood as 'heṭṭhimantena' (by the lower end).

Regarding this formal acceptance, in the commentary on the Pavāraṇā Sikkhāpada, it is shown that 'if a monk is sitting, [the distance is measured] starting from the back end of the seat', etc., showing the measurement from the far end of the nearest limb of the recipients. Therefore, here too, for a recipient standing in the air, the hatthapāsa should be measured starting from the lower surface of the heel, which is the far end of the nearest limb (the toe); and for the giver, it should be measured starting from the lower surface of the toe, which is the near end. In this same way, for a monk lying on the ground and receiving from the hand of one sitting at the head of the bed, [it is measured] from the edge of the neck, which is the far end of the nearest limb, the head...
36:
The *hatthapāsa* (hand-reach distance) should be measured starting only from the outer edge of the toes; it should not be measured from the sole of the foot. When giving in this manner while lying down, it should be understood according to the circumstances. For it is said, "Whichever limb is nearest."

"*Paṭiggahaṇasaññāya*" means with the perception that has arisen, "I will receive it by means of a couch, etc." By this, it is shown that there is no need to say "I receive it" verbally. In some commentaries or in some regions (it is so). "*Asaṃhārime phalake*" refers to a wooden plank that cannot be moved by a man of average strength. "Having wiped and then receiving" is said with the intention of receiving if there is a doubt that dye powder might remain even after wiping; it is not so if there is no doubt. "*Taṃ pana*" refers to the almsfood taken from above without receiving the almsfood that has fallen. The statement that there is no offense is because there are no faults such as *durūpaciṇṇa* (improper conduct), etc. Saying "I will give it to a non-ordained person (unordained)," etc., is also said to avoid the *vinaya-dukkaṭa* offense. Even if one takes it without such a thought, there is no offense for the monk who receives and consumes it. The phrase "having given it to a non-ordained person" is also said to be consistent with the initial intention.

"*Carukena*" means with a small vessel. "*Abhihaṭattā*" is said with reference to the moment of giving. However, they say that when removing it after giving, if ashes or drops fall, it should be received again because the act of offering (*abhihāra*) has ceased. If one acts to remove them so they do not fall, it is appropriate. If one removes them in the normal way and the act of offering is not interrupted, it is considered already received. It is also allowable to stretch out the hand and touch the upper part of the rim of the pot.

"*Pādena pellitvā*" means treading with the perception "I will receive it with the foot." "*Keci*" refers to the teachers residing at Abhayagiri. "*Vacanamattameva*" means that the distinction is merely in the term *paṭibaddhappatibaddha* (connected to what is connected); in reality, it is only direct bodily connection (*kāyapāṭibaddha*). Therefore, the meaning is that the words of those teachers should not be accepted.

"*Tena āharāpetuṃ*" means if an object has reached a certain monk, it is allowable for another monk to have him bring it by commanding, "Bring it here." "*Na tato paraṃ*" is said with reference to an object that has not yet been personally received on that same day. However, they say that an object received on that same day may be consumed on subsequent days even without being received again.

"*Khiyyanti*" means they come to an end; the meaning is that because of those powders, *thullaccaya* offenses and offenses due to not receiving do not occur. By the words "*navasamuṭṭhitaṃ*" it should be understood that because it is newly attached to sugarcane, etc., it is not *abbohārika* (negligible). The phrase "*esa nayo*" is said with reference to the fault of *sannidhi* (hoarding), etc. Therefore, the words beginning with "*na hi*" are spoken. By those words, even if the five factors of receiving are complete, it is only called "received" if it is taken with the intention to swallow. This is because receiving is permitted only for food that is to be swallowed. Likewise, oil, etc., kept for external use...
37:
The meaning is that the words of those *Keci* teachers should not be accepted. "*Tena āharāpetuṃ*" means if an object rolls toward a certain monk, it is allowable for the monk who is to receive it to have it brought by commanding, "Bring it to this place." "*Na tato paraṃ*" is said with reference to an object that has not yet been personally received on that same day. However, they say that an object picked up on that same day may be consumed on subsequent days even without being received again. "*Khiyyanti*" means they come to an end. The meaning is that because of the existing powders, the *thullaccaya* offense and the *pācittiya* offense incurred by not receiving do not occur.

By the text "*navasamuṭṭhitaṃ*", it should be understood that because it is newly attached to sugarcane, etc., it is not *abbohārika* (negligible). The phrase "*esa nayo*" is said with reference to the fault of *sannidhi* (hoarding), etc. Therefore, He said "*na hi*", etc. By that text, even if the five factors of receiving are complete, it is only called "received" if it is taken with the intention to swallow. This is because receiving is permitted only for food that is to be swallowed. Likewise, oil, etc., kept for external use should be received and used only if there is an intention to swallow.

In the passages beginning with "*kesañci*", an object placed somewhere for the sake of laypeople or novices does not lose its status of being received just by being released from the hand; rather, it loses its status of being received only when it falls into a vessel. If a monk looks forward to that vessel for the next day, the food in that vessel might be thought not to lose its status of being received, like almsfood in an improperly washed bowl. Therefore, it should be understood that it was said, "It should be placed in the hand of the novice." In such matters, one should not seek logic but should practice according to what is stated in the commentary. By the Pali "*pattagatā*", it is shown that even if it touches the rim of the bowl, the gruel (*yāgu*) in the pot is neither received nor has its receiving lapsed because the monk touched it unintentionally. "*Āropeti*" means making the hand touch. A "load suitable for receiving" (*paṭiggahaṇūpagaṃ bhāraṃ*) is a weight that a man of average strength can lift. The phrase "*na pidahitabbaṃ*" is said with reference to what is released from the hand; there is no fault if one covers the pot in the hand with the other hand, or if one drops a lid from above without touching it even if it is released from the hand.

"*Paṭiggaṇhāti*" means that if a large branch held above for shade should break for some reason and the dust on that branch might fall into the mouth, one has it made allowable (*kappiya*) and then receives it. "*Kuṇḍake*" refers to a large pot. "*Tasmimpi*" refers to a large water jar. "*Gāhāpetvā*" means making one take the *kālika* (time-bound food/medicine) that has not yet been received.

"*Dutiyattherassa*" means giving to the second elder after having the senior elder relinquish it to oneself, saying, "Please give me the elder's bowl." "*Ettha pana*" refers to the exchange of bowls. Regarding the word "*kāraṇaṃ*", they give the reason that just as the thought "The novices are giving to us from here too" might arise, such a thought does not arise regarding this branch, etc.; that statement is appropriate. If a monk does not have such a thought, he may consume it even without exchanging. "*Niccāletuṃ*" means shaking to remove stones, gravel, etc.
38:
"Niccāletuṃ" means moving to remove stones, gravel, and so forth. The phrase "uddhanaṃ āropetabbaṃ" (should be placed on a stove) is said with reference to a stove without fire. When stirring rice cooking on a stove, the uncooked grains on top go down and get cooked; therefore, it is said, "It is indeed self-cooked" (sāmaṃpāka).

"Ādhārake patto ṭhapito" (the bowl placed on a support) refers to a bowl containing food that has not yet been formally offered, placed there for the purpose of being offered again. "Ekaggahaṇeneva" (by a single taking) refers to taking what was already taken by novices without it being given up. The statement "it is fit to be consumed" is said because the smoke-stick was formally offered on that very day. The passage beginning with "bhattuggāro" (belching of food) shows the decision regarding eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana) in connection with what is negligible (abbohārika). "Samuddodakena" (with ocean water) refers to unoffered water. "Himakarakā" (hailstones) are special forms of frozen water, like stone inscriptions, that sometimes fall with rain; there is no requirement for formal offering (paṭiggahena) for these hailstones. Therefore, it is said, "They are of the nature of water." By the phrase "it is fit only before noon," it is shown that while it may be negligible (abbohārika) regarding offenses of non-offering, it is significant (sabbohārika) regarding offenses of eating at the wrong time.

"Laggati" (it sticks) indicates the appearance of the color of fine clay on the mouth and hands. "Bahalaṃ" (thick) means it must be formally offered even if it does not stick to the hands and mouth. By the phrase "vāsamattaṃ" (merely a scent), the absence of pollen and nectar is shown. The phrase "that which is sprinkled must be formally offered" is said because the nectar is evident.

"In the great elements" (mahābhūtesu) refers to the elements such as earth residing in the bodies of living beings. "Everything is fit" (sabbaṃ vaṭṭati) means everything residing in one's own or others' bodies, such as tears and saliva, is fit. The meaning is that it does not produce offenses such as Thullaccaya because it is analogous to allowed meat. "Patati" (it falls) means it falls after being detached from one's own body. Because it is said "having cut from a tree," it should be understood that it is fit to consume even if not formally offered, such as digging the earth for fine clay, or cutting other medicinal roots and leaves for an antidote without making them into ash. The four factors here are: not being formally offered, not being permitted, the absence of being negligible like smoke, and swallowing.

## The Explanation of the Dantapona Sikkhāpada is finished.

## The Fourth Chapter, the Bhojana Vagga, is finished.

## 5. Acelaka Vagga
## 1. Explanation of the Acelaka Sikkhāpada
In the first training rule of the fifth chapter, the words "to me (give)" refer also to food and snacks given by a monk after placing them on the ground. The four factors here are: being an ascetic of another sect (titthiya), not being permitted, being swallowable, and giving into a vessel that has not been set down by one's own hand for the purpose of swallowing.
## The Explanation of the Acelaka Sikkhāpada is finished.
## 2. Explanation of the Uyyojana Sikkhāpada
In the second training rule, the three factors are: the desire to practice misconduct, the sending away of an ordained monk for that very purpose, and the crossing of the boundary (upacāra) by the monk who was sent away.
## The Explanation of the Uyyojana Sikkhāpada is finished.
## 3. Explanation of the Sabhojana Sikkhāpada
In the third training rule, regarding the term "in a small house" (khuddake ghare) in the Pali, a small house is intended to be one with a width of less than five cubits. In such a small house, even if one does not leave the reach of the hand (hatthapāsa) from the door-post, there is the crossing of the ridge-pole (piṭṭhivaṃsa); therefore, it is said, "having crossed the ridge-pole." "Of a house made in whatever way" means a house made whether the ridge-pole has been mounted or not.

In the Pali, "those free from lust" (vītarāgā) includes those whose lust is not aroused and Non-returners (Anāgāmīs). "With the mind" (sacittakaṃ) means sitting with the intention of entering and staying nearby. The four factors here are: the presence of a husband and wife whose lust is aroused, it being a bedroom, the absence of a second monk, and sitting by intruding/crowding.
## The Explanation of the Sabhojana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Cāritta Sikkhāpada
In the sixth training rule, because it is said, "There is no such thing as the task of searching and informing," if a monk who need not be searched for is seen in a place suitable for approaching, one should approach and ask him even if he is standing beyond the range of hearing ordinary speech. Therefore, it is said, "Moreover... whatever person he sees, he should ask him," and so forth.

In the section on non-offense (anāpatti), since only monasteries and so forth within the village are mentioned, an offense occurs even for a monk who crosses from the monastery to the village street without a permitted reason, and not only for one who crosses the boundary of a house.

In the Pali, the passage "for one entering the boundary of another's house... with the first step he crosses the threshold," and so forth, is said with reference to one who has entered a village. Even so, for a monk who does not enter another's house boundary but goes along the middle of the street, stands in front of the door of whatever house he desires, looks at people, and then goes on, there is only a Pācittiya offense. In that regard, some teachers say, "For a monk crossing in the street, offenses occur according to the number of house boundaries." Other teachers say, "According to the number of families for whose sake he went." The five factors here are: consenting to an invitation with any of the five kinds of food, not asking a present monk, approaching another house from the house where he was invited for a meal, not having passed noon, and the absence of times of danger.

## The Explanation of the Cāritta Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Mahānāma Sikkhāpada
In the seventh training rule, Mahānāma was the son of Sukkhodana, the elder brother of Elder Anuruddha and the Teacher (the Buddha). Elder Ānanda was the son of Amitodana, while Elder Nanda was the son of Suddhodana himself.

In the Pali, "I will bring in time" (kālaṃ āharissatha) means "let today's time pass," or "I will bring medicine tomorrow." In the third section, where it is said, "There are invitations limited by medicine and invitations limited by the night," the specified medicine must be taken only within the specified time, not beyond that.
41:
If taken in any other way than what has been stated, it should be understood that there is no distinct benefit. The factors of this training rule are: inviting a limited Saṅgha, requesting medicine beyond that limit, and not being ill.

## The Explanation of the Mahānāma Training Rule is finished.

## 8. Uyyuttasenā Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth training rule, the term 'ekamekaṃ' includes an army with two divisions or three divisions. The factors of this training rule are: going to see a fourfold army that has marched out of the city without a proper reason such as a specific cause, and seeing it in an unauthorized place.

## The Explanation of the Uyyuttasenā Training Rule is finished.

## 9. Senāvāsa Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth training rule, the factors are: the sunset of the fourth day while staying within the army, and not being ill.

## The Explanation of the Senāvāsa Training Rule is finished.

## 10. Uyyodhika Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth training rule, in the Pāḷi text, 'kati te lakkhāni laddhāni' means "How many strikes (blows) have you received?" The factors of this training rule are: going to see a battle etc. without a proper reason, and seeing it in an unauthorized place.

## The Explanation of the Uyyodhika Training Rule is finished.

## The Fifth Chapter, the Acelaka Vagga, is finished.

## 6. Surāpāna Vagga

## 1. Surāpāna Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the first training rule of the sixth chapter, in the Pāḷi text, 'kiṇṇapakkhittā' refers to liquor made by adding what is called yeast, such as grain seeds, without adding flour etc. 'Sambhārasamyuttā' refers to liquor mixed with many ingredients such as mustard.

Liquor made from the juice of flowers such as Madhuka, palm, or coconut, which has been fermented for a long time, is called 'pupphāsava'. Similarly, juice from fruits like jackfruit is called 'phalāsava'. Grape juice is called 'madhvāsava'. Sugarcane juice is called 'guḷāsava'. Liquor made from the juice of various ingredients such as triphala and trikaṭu, fermented for a long time, is called 'sambhārasamyutta'. 'Bīzato paṭṭhāya' means from the time the aforementioned flour etc. is put into a vessel for the purpose of becoming liquor.

Loṇasovīraka and Sutta medicines are special medicines prepared with many ingredients. Since the worldly fault (lokavajja) in the 'acittaka' (offenses regardless of intention) of the Uyyutta training rules has been explained previously, nothing is said there. In this Surāpāna training rule, because it is established by a specific object not shared with those rules, it should be understood that 'vatthuazānanatāya cettha' etc. is stated to show the distinction of being a worldly fault even in the aspect of lack of intention, due to the presence of unwholesome consciousness. Everything that should be said regarding this training rule has been explained in detail in the Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, the commentary on the first Pārājika, by way of clearing up contradictory points, and should be taken from there. The factors of this training rule are: the state of being liquor, and the drinking of that liquor.

## The Explanation of the Surāpāna Training Rule is finished.

## 2. Angulipatodaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the second training rule, the factors are: the intention to laugh/joke, and touching the body of a monk with one's own body.

## The Explanation of the Angulipatodaka Training Rule is finished.
43:
## 3. Hasadhamma Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the third training rule, in the Pāḷi text, in sentences such as 'hasadhamme hasadhammasaññī', the meaning should be understood as: considering mere diving and surfacing etc. as a 'sporting act' (hasadhamma), or considering diving and surfacing performed when there is a duty to be done as a 'sporting act'. 'Ussārento' means pushing a boat that is in the water onto the shore.

'Patanuppatanavāresu' is said in reference to a single potsherd thrown to move across the surface of the water by way of falling and rising like the movement of a frog. The factors are: the water exceeding the ankle, and playing with the desire to laugh/sport.

## The Explanation of the Hasadhamma Training Rule is finished.

## 4. Anādariya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth training rule, 'suttānuloma' refers to the four Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa). They are also called the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). The factors are: speaking to a monk regarding a rule, and acting with disrespect.

## The Explanation of the Anādariya Training Rule is finished.

## 5. Bhiṃsāpana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth training rule, the factors are: being a monk, and making an effort with the desire to frighten him within the range of sight or hearing.

## The Explanation of the Bhiṃsāpana Training Rule is finished.

## 6. Joti Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth training rule, 'alātaṃ patitaṃ' means a firebrand that has fallen out of the fire-pot. 'Vijjātaṃ' means a Pācittiya offense for a monk who puts an extinguished firebrand into a fire-pot where the flame has gone out and ignites it. Similarly, it applies to one who merely puts in fuel, or one who ignites an extinguished fire-pot with the breath of the mouth etc. The factors are: the absence of reasons such as illness, the desire to warm oneself or roast something, and lighting the fire (adding fire).

## The Explanation of the Joti Training Rule is finished.
44:
## 7. Nahāna-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh training rule, regarding the phrase "nagare thakite" in the Pāḷi, it should be understood that when a king, wishing to bathe for a long time, gave permission saying, "I will stay in the outer garden under protection; close the city and guard it," the people then closed the city. "Asambhinnena" means with unspoiled or undissolved soft perfume. The meaning is that on that day, one has just woken up without yet taking up any ornaments. In the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), bathing before the half-month has passed and the absence of the specified occasions are the two factors (aṅga).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Bathing is finished.

## 8. Dubbaṇṇakaraṇa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth training rule, regarding the phrase "paṭiladdhanavacīvarena," it is said that this also includes a robe obtained temporarily for the purpose of wearing for a few days, upon which the prescribed smudge-mark (kappabindu) has not yet been made.

Since it is stated generally as "navam nāma akatakanappaṃ" (new means that which has not been marked), it should be noted that if another monk has already made the smudge-mark and used the robe, whether that monk uses it himself or gives it to another after receiving it, it is considered already marked and cannot be called "new." Since it is said "for the purpose of wearing or dressing," it is also said that a smudge-mark must be made on the shoulder-cloth (aṃsabaddhaka) as well, because it is also worn. "Cammakāranīla" (cobbler's blue) refers to the blue color used when preparing leather to be blue. Some teachers say it is simply natural blue. The three factors are: the aforementioned robe not having a smudge-mark made, the robe not being lost, and the act of wearing or dressing.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Discoloring is finished.

## 9. Vikappana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth training rule, "yena" means with whom or in whose presence. The three factors are: not having revoked the assignment (paccuddharaṇa) of a robe that one personally assigned (vikappana), the robe being of a kind suitable for assignment, and using it without trust (vissāsa).

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Assignment is finished.
45:
## 10. Cīvara-apanidhāna-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth training rule, regarding the phrase "antamaso hasāpekkho pi" in the Pāḷi, the word "api" includes the intention to cause distress out of anger without the intent to steal, as well as the desire to disparage. For this reason, it is called "tivedanaṃ." The two factors are: hiding the bowl and other requisites of a monk, and the desire to cause annoyance.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Hiding Robes is finished.

## The Sixth Chapter, the Chapter on Drinking Fermented Liquor, is finished.

## 7. Sappāṇaka-vagga

## 1. Sañciccapāṇa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
In the first training rule of the seventh chapter, one who shoots arrows is called an "issāsa" (archer). The connection of the text is that in the cessation of this life-faculty (jīvitindriya), there is no such thing as a separate "soul" that exists. In this context, "pāṇa" refers to a living being. "The duty should be performed without negligence" means that duties such as sunning robes or sweeping should be performed after carefully observing so as not to cause harm even to tiny insects. The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Intentionally Killing Living Beings is finished.

## 2. Sappāṇaka-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
In the second training rule, "udakasaṇṭhānakappadese" refers to ground consisting of mud, stones, and so on. "Tattha" refers to the allowable water that has been poured. The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Water with Living Beings is finished.

## 3. Ukkoṭana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā
In the third training rule, because it is said "having gone to the presence of that monk," a Pācittiya offense is incurred by a monk who reopens (disturbs) a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) that has been settled by a formal act of the Saṅgha, only if he does so in the presence of the monk involved. If it is done behind his back, it is only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
46:
Since it is stated, "If one reopens a legal issue thinking it is an unrighteous act when it was actually a righteous act, there is no offense," reopening a case is not inherently unwholesome in itself, like disrespecting a person or the Dhamma. However, it becomes unwholesome only when one reopens it while perceiving it as a righteous act or while having doubt. The three factors are: the fact that the case was settled according to the Dhamma, the knowledge of that fact, and the act of reopening it.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Reopening a Legal Issue is finished.

## 4. Duṭṭhulla-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth training rule, the statement "he certainly incurs an offense" is said in the context of giving up the effort (to conceal). "Vatthupuggala" refers to the person who has committed the offense. Indeed, the mention of informing another is only when there is an intention to conceal. Since informing the person who committed the offense does not constitute concealment, the meaning is that it is only concealment (when informing others is avoided). "The end is cut off" means that even if there is a giving up of the effort (to conceal) with the thought "I will conceal it," if the information does not reach a succession of persons, the continuity of the offense is broken.

Regarding the statement, "Emission of semen and bodily contact for a layperson is called gross misconduct (duṭṭhulla-ajjhācāra)," this should be investigated as it contradicts the statement in the commentary on the Duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpada: "For a layperson... the first five training rules are called gross misconduct, the rest are not gross. Only emission of semen, bodily contact, and seeking sexual pleasure with coarse words are his misconduct." In this training rule, for a monk who conceals out of affection for a person, at the moment of concealing due to fear that "others will blame him," only resentment (paṭigha) arises. Therefore, it should be noted that it is called "painful feeling" (dukkha-vedanā). The two factors are: knowing a monk's grave offense (saṅghādisesa), and giving up the effort with the intention to conceal.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Concealing Grave Offenses is finished.

## 5. Ūnavīsativassa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth training rule, "rūpasippa" refers to the art of money-changing or goldsmithing. One is called "gabbhavīsa" (twenty years from the womb) because the twentieth year is completed including the time spent in the mother's womb.
47:
"Nikkhamanīyapunnāmāsī" refers to the full moon day of Sāvaṇa (Wagaung), which is the full moon immediately following the full moon of Āsāḷhī (Waso). "Pāṭipadadivase" occurs on the day of entering the later rainy season retreat. It means that higher ordination is conferred upon one who has stayed in the mother's womb for twelve months and is born on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā (the full moon of Thadingyut). Because it is said, "Thirty days and nights make a month, twelve months make a year," it is stated that "four months are deficient." "Pulling the rainy season upwards" means that the month of Waso is designated as an intercalary month (adhikamāsa), discarded, and then the retreat is entered. Therefore, once every three years, there is a year with thirteen months. "Taking those two months" means taking the two months obtained from the intercalary month for the two months that have not yet arrived from the full moon of Wagaung until the day of birth, which is the day of the Great Pavāraṇā. Hence the statement: "After performing the Pavāraṇā, he will be twenty years old," etc. "Being without doubt" refers to taking one intercalary month within eighteen years and, besides that, within twenty years, reducing four months for the cātuddasī (14th day) days, thus intending the state of being fully twenty years old at all times. "After performing the Pavāraṇā, he will be twenty years old" means that when the day of the Great Pavāraṇā has passed, he will be twenty years old including the period in the womb. "Therefore" means because the months in the womb are also included in the count. "Twenty-one years old" refers to one who is twenty years old after birth.

"Ordains another" means ordaining by being a preceptor (upajjhāya) or a teacher (ācariya). "He also" means that even though he ordains another, he himself does not become ordained. There are these two factors: the state of being under twenty years old, and ordaining as a preceptor while knowing that the person is under twenty years old.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Being Under Twenty Years Old is Finished.

In the sixth training rule, there are three factors: being a caravan of thieves, making an arrangement while knowing it, and traveling together according to the agreement.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on a Caravan of Thieves is Finished.
The seventh training rule is just as previously explained.

## 8. The Explanation of the Ariṭṭha Training Rule

In the eighth (Ariṭṭha training rule), "antarāya" is called an obstacle because it comes in between; it refers to present misfortune, etc. "Ānantariyadhamma" means the mental states such as volition (cetanā) that are fixed on producing results in the immediately following life. The phrase "na saggassa" (cannot reach heaven) is stated because the act of violating a nun is not an ānantariya kamma. However, for one who forcibly violates noble female disciples (ariyasāvikā) or a woman who is a virtuous worldling (kalyāṇaputhujjana), it is similar to an ānantariya kamma. "Being an obstacle to liberation" (mokkhantarāyikatā) is stated because for one who violates a nun who, though flighty, possesses natural virtue, the arising of the Path in that existence is impossible.

Only the ahetukadiṭṭhi, akiriyadiṭṭhi, and natthikadiṭṭhi, which do not turn back in that existence, are the fixed wrong views (niyatamicchādiṭṭhi). The inclusion of eunuchs (paṇḍaka), etc., is merely for the sake of illustration (nidassana). All two-rooted (duhetuka) and rootless (ahetuka) rebirths are obstacles to the result (vipākantarāya), because the Path cannot arise for two-rooted individuals either.

"Ayaṃ" refers to Ariṭṭha. "Rasena rasaṃ" means combining the taste of using the four blameless requisites with the taste of enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Upanento viya" means as if connecting; or it is just as the reading "so eva".

In the term "aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā", the bone itself is called "kaṅkala" because it is devoid of flesh. "Palibhañjanatṭhena" is because of the meaning of causing one to fall without fail. "Adhikuṭṭanatṭhena" is because of the meaning of being a place of excessive chopping. In the Pali, the words "I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One... is not able to cause an obstacle" are stated in accordance with the story of Ariṭṭha. Even otherwise, for a monk who takes any word spoken by the Blessed One wrongly and does not give it up even when forbidden by others, one may perform the formal act of admonishment (samanubhāsana) suitable for that monk according to the stated method to charge him with an offense, or perform the act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) by taking any of the three preferred reasons such as not seeing the offense, etc. Even without performing the formal admonishment, it should be understood that it is allowable to perform the act of suspension for the dukkaṭa offense caused by not giving up the view merely upon being told by monks, "Venerable, do not say so." The two factors are: the act being according to the Dhamma, and not giving up the view despite being admonished through the formal procedure.

## The Explanation of the Ariṭṭha Training Rule is Finished.

In the Pali, because it is stated generally as "under one roof," even if the physical boundaries (upacāra) are different, if they sleep under the same roof, a pācittiya offense occurs even for an Arahant who is unaware of the disciplinary rule, as well as for those monks who follow the views of the expelled monk. The two factors are: the state of not having been restored, and knowingly engaging in communion (sambhoga) and so forth.

## 8. Sahadhammika Vagga

## 1. Sahadhammika Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the first training rule of the eighth chapter, the two factors are: being spoken to by a monk regarding a training rule that has been laid down, and speaking in such a way as a pretext by a monk who does not wish to train.
