## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Mahākhandhaka
## Commentary on the Bodhikathā
In the Mahāvagga, the phrase "of the two Pātimokkhas" refers to the two texts: the Bhikkhuvibhanga and the Bhikkhunīvibhanga, which are the analysis of the Pātimokkha. "Which Khandhaka they chanted in rehearsal" is the grammatical connection. It is called "Khandhaka" because it is a collection of Vinaya rules, or because it explains the Vinaya rules. In this context, the word "Khandha" intends the collection of prescriptions of training rules regarding conduct (cāritta) and avoidance (vāritta), such as ordination (pabbajjā), etc. In the Padabhājanīya, the construction (yojanā) is: the meanings of which words are explained by which methods of the commentary. Or, it should be construed as: which meanings are explained. In this latter method, the word "hi" is to be understood as a mere filler (pādapūraṇa).

"Special reason" refers to a reason that prevents the use of the locative case, like the reason stated: "At that time, a reflection arose in the Venerable Sāriputta as a cause for requesting the prescription of training rules; at that time," etc. "Of this" means: what is the purpose in the Vinaya prescription for explaining the Teacher's conduct from the time of Supreme Enlightenment? It implies: if there is no special reason. The construction is: showing the origin (nidāna) is the purpose. Here, the word "nidāna" intends the cause such as the story (vatthu) and person (puggala) which are the reasons for prescribing the training rule, not just the place of prescription. Therefore, the text says "yā hī", etc.

In the word "Uruvelāyaṃ", the word "uru" means great. The word "velā" is a synonym for shore or bank. It is called "velā" because it is like a shore due to being high, etc. A great shore is Uruvelā; in that Uruvelā (He dwelt). Therefore, the text says "mahāvelāyaṃ", etc. "Mariyādā" refers to the boundary (sīmā) of virtues such as morality (sīla). "Pattapuṭena" means with a basket woven from leaves such as palm leaves.

The word "paṭhamābhisambuddho" is a designation (niddesa) made by dropping the nasal (niggahīta), so it is stated as "paṭhamaṃ abhisambuddho". "Paṭhamaṃ" is also a neuter designation showing an adverbial sense. Therefore...
84:
It should be understood that the construction (yojanā) is: 'Having fully realized [the Four Noble Truths], he first stayed at the foot of the Bodhi tree.'

In the Pali text, regarding the phrase 'Atha kho', the word 'atha' carries the meaning 'at that time' because particles have multiple meanings. The word 'sattāhaṃ' is a word in the accusative case used in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga). The term 'Atha kho' is a particle indicating a change in the subject matter. By this, it shows the transition to contemplating Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) after temporarily ceasing the experience of the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha). 'Paṭicca' means having approached and depending on one another. By this word 'paṭicca', the multiplicity of causes is shown, and by the word 'sahita', the multiplicity of effects is shown. 'Anulomaṃ' is a neuter grammatical designation indicating an adverb. 'Sveva' refers to that very Dependent Origination. Alternatively, 'stated according to the previous method' means the mode of conditions taught by the method starting with 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise' (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā). 'Pavattiyā' refers to the occurrence of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra).

In the Pali text, in the phrases such as 'avijjāpaccayā', ignorance (avijjā) is the lack of knowledge regarding the Truth of Suffering and so forth. Volitional formations (saṅkhārā) are mundane wholesome and unwholesome intentions (cetanā). Consciousness (viññāṇa) is only mundane resultant consciousness (vipāka). Name (nāma) is the collection of the three mental aggregates such as mundane feeling and so forth, while form (rūpa) is the materiality consisting of the great elements and derived matter. The six sense bases (saḷāyatana) are the six bases divided into sensitive matter (pasāda) and consciousness. Contact (phassa) is all resultant contact, and feeling (vedanā) is also all resultant feeling. Craving (taṇhā) is lust (rāga). Clinging (upādāna) is strong lust and the three types of wrong view (diṭṭhi). Existence (bhava) is twofold: kamma-existence (kamma-bhava) and rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava). Therein, kamma-existence is only the wholesome and unwholesome intentions that are objects of the taints (āsava), while rebirth-existence is the five aggregates that are objects of clinging. The arising of those aggregates is birth (jāti). Ripening is aging (jarā). Breaking up is death (maraṇa). Sorrow (soka) is grieving based on those very aggregates. Lamentation (parideva) is wailing. Suffering (dukkha) is bodily pain. Grief (domanassa) is mental pain. Despair (upāyāsa) is excessive sorrow.

The word 'sambhavati' (arises) should be understood as being connected to each individual term. Therefore, the phrase 'In this manner' (iminā nayena) and so forth is stated. By the term 'of the mass of suffering' (dukkharāsissa), it is shown that this is not the arising of a 'being' (satta), nor the arising of beauty (subha) or happiness (sukha).

'Have' is a particle used in the sense of 'evidently'. Regarding the statement 'The factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) are the means for the realization of Dependent Origination in forward order', although the reverse order (paṭiloma) of Dependent Origination appears in the first section with 'With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance' and so forth, it is stated thus because the realization of Dependent Origination in forward order (anuloma) is taught as the cause, as in 'When he understands the nature of things along with their causes' (yato pajānāti sahetudhammaṃ). Just as in this first watch, so too in the second watch, because it is stated in the verse 'When he understood the destruction of causes' (yato khayaṃ paccayānaṃ avedi), it should be understood that the phrase 'the destruction of causes' and so forth is stated.

The question 'Who touches?' (ko phusati) is improper and should not be answered. This is because it assumes a non-existent self (attā) to be real and asks about the actions of that self, similar to asking 'Which son of a barren woman touches?'. 'Sixteen doubts' (soḷasa kaṅkhā) refers to: 'Was I in the past? Was I not? What was I? In what way was I? Having been what, what did I become in the past?' and 'Shall I be in the future? Shall I not be? What shall I be? In what way...'
85:
It should be understood that the phrase 'called destruction' (khayasaṅkhāta) and so forth is stated. 'An improper question' (no kallo pañho) means a question that is not fit to be answered because it is logically unsound. The meaning is that it is like asking 'Which son of a barren woman touches?', because it asks about the action of a self (attā) by establishing a non-existent self as real.

'Sixteen doubts' (soḷasa kaṅkhā) are: 'Was I in the past? Was I not? What was I? How was I? Having been what, what did I become in the past?'—these are five regarding the past. 'Shall I be in the future? Shall I not be? What shall I be? How shall I be? Having been what, what shall I become in the future?'—these are five regarding the future. 'Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Where did this being come from? Where will it go?'—these are six regarding the present. Thus, there are sixteen kinds of doubts: five in the past, five in the future, and six in the present.

Among those doubts, 'What am I?' refers to doubting based on one of the categories such as human, deity, etc., or warrior (khattiya), etc. 'How am I?' refers to doubting based on shape, appearance, etc., or based on a cause such as a creator (Issara). 'Having been what, what did I become?' refers to doubting whether one was first one thing and then another among humans and so forth. 'Am I?' and so forth refers to doubting one's own current existence or non-existence, as well as one's nature and manner. 'Vapayanthi' means they disappear or vanish. Therefore, it is said, 'They disappear, they cease.'

'By that power' (tassa vasena) means by the power of knowing Dependent Origination and by the power of attaining the destruction of conditions (Nibbāna). 'Each individual group' (ekekameva koṭṭhāsaṃ) means each group according to the forward and reverse orders. 'Contemplated thus in the three watches of the night' means that in all three watches of the night, he contemplated only the forward and reverse orders in the manner found here in the Khandhaka Pali.

## Commentary on the Ajapāla Story
'At the end of those seven days' (tassa sattāhassa accayena) means after the seven days spent on the throne (pallanka) had passed. 'From that concentration' (tamhā samādhimhā) means from the concentration of the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala-samāpatti). For the contemplation of Dependent Origination occurred only at intervals; during all the remaining time, the Blessed One spent his time in the attainment of the fruit (phala-samāpatti). With reference to that attainment of the fruit, it is said 'from that concentration'.
86: Ratanacaṅkame refers to the jewel walkway created by the deities, having known the Blessed One's desire to walk after standing for a long time. Ratanagharaṃ refers to the house made of jewels created by the deities, having known the Blessed One's desire to sit. Tatrāpi means not only in the Ratanaghara; it means that even at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, while contemplating the Abhidhamma, he experienced the bliss of liberation (arahattaphala) from time to time. This is because, even at the foot of that Ajapāla banyan tree, the six-colored Buddha-rays, produced by the joy of the Fully Enlightened One as he investigated the Samantapaṭṭhāna of infinite methods, emerged just as they did in the Ratanaghara. One who makes the sound 'Huṃhuṃ' means making the sound 'Huṃhuṃ' with the intention of saying 'Begone!'—either out of pride, thinking 'Let no one of low birth approach me,' or out of anger towards those who have approached near. Brahmanyaṃ means the state of being a Brahmin. Antaṃ means Nibbāna, or the fruit of Arahantship which is the end of the deities or the end of the path-knowledges. ## Commentary on the Mucalinda Story. In this term mucalindamūle, 'Mucalinda' refers to the Nicula tree (Barringtonia acutangula). Uppannamegho refers to a great cloud that arose, filling the entire world-system. Vaddalikā is a name for rain itself in the feminine gender. Because that rain fell for seven days, it was said, 'There was continuous rain for seven days.' Because that day of drizzling rain was spoiled by the cold wind and mixed water drops, it was said, 'mixed with cold wind and water drops,' and so on. Ubbiddhatā means appearing distant, thus it was said, 'became distant with the disappearance of the clouds.' The sky is called Devo because it shines like an emerald (indanilā). Etamatthaṃ viditvā means having known the blissful nature of seclusion (viveka). Because the path-knowledges completely eradicate discontent, it is called 'contentment with the four path-knowledges.' Akuppanabhāvo means the nature of not being angry. ## Commentary on the Rājayatana Story. Paccagghe means brand new. Only this meaning is praised; the previous meaning is not praised. This is because Buddhas do not use very expensive bowls.
87:
## Brahmayācanakathāvaṇṇanā

The five cords of sensual pleasure are called *ālaya* because they are resorted to (clung to). Therefore, it is said, "Beings delight in *ālaya*." *Suṭṭhu muditā* means being exceedingly joyful. *Thānaṃ sandhāya* is said in reference to the word 'thāna'. *Imesaṃ* refers to the meaning of effects such as formations (saṅkhāra). In the Pāḷi, terms like *sabbasaṅkhārasamatha* are synonyms for Nibbāna. *Apissu* is a particle used in the sense of conjunction. It means not only did this thought occur, but these verses also became clear.

"I have attained it with difficulty" is said in reference to the fulfillment of the perfections (pāramī), not in reference to the difficult practice (dukkhapaṭipadā). This is because, for the Buddhas, the four paths are only pleasant practices (sukhapaṭipadā). The word *ha* is a particle used in two senses: clarity and certainty. It distinguishes 'alaṃ' (useless/enough) as being clear or certain. Alternatively, *halaṃ* can be a single particle.

In the Pāḷi, *sahampatissa* refers to a senior monk named Sahaka during the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha. Having attained the first jhāna, he was reborn as the chief of Brahmas in the first jhāna realm. Therefore, they knew that Brahma as 'Sahampati'. *Assavanatā* means because of not hearing. This is because hearing itself is called *savanatā*, similar to the word *devatā*.

*Dhammo asuddho* refers to the doctrine of wrong view. *Samalehi* refers to the six teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa. *Apāpura* means 'Open with the hand of teaching'. The word *dvāraṃ* is said in reference to the Noble Path.

*Sele* means on a mountain made of solid rock. In the word *tathūpamaṃ*, the word 'tathā' should be understood in the sense of 'taṃ'. Therefore, it means the Dhamma for which that rock mountain is a simile, or the Dhamma that has that rock mountain as its simile. Alternatively, it means the Dhamma that has a simile by way of that mountain, etc. *Dhammamayaṃ* means a palace made of supramundane Dhamma. *Uṭṭhāhi* means 'Arise from this seat with the body for the purpose of preaching Dhamma and wandering, or with the mind from the state of being unconcerned.' Alternatively, *uṭṭhehi* is the original reading. Therefore, he urged him in both physical and mental effort, saying, "Wander, preach." The four words starting with *vīra* are addresses by way of praise.

*Buddhacakkhu* refers to the knowledge of the degrees of faculties (indriyaparopariyattañāṇa) and the knowledge of dispositions and tendencies (āsayānusayañāṇa). This is because these two knowledges are named 'Buddha-eye'. *Svākārā* refers to those who have good qualities such as the faculty of faith (saddhā).
88:
It should be understood that those whose qualities such as faith are good are called 'svākārā' (those of good disposition). They are easy to instruct and are accustomed to seeing the faults in the next world as a danger.

In this context, there are lotuses; therefore, both a thicket and a pond are called 'uppalinī'. Here, however, 'uppalinī' refers to a pond. The same applies to other terms like 'paduminī'. Those that have not yet emerged from the water are called 'udakānuggatāni'. They grow and thrive while remaining submerged; these are called 'antonimuggaposīni'. 'Accuggammā' means rising by way of surpassing the water.

'Apārutā' means opened. 'Tesaṃ' means for those beings who possess the supporting conditions. 'Dvārā' means the doors of the Noble Path. This statement, 'The doors are opened for them,' was spoken by the Buddha with reference to his seeing, through his self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhūñāṇa), the arising of the Path for those beings who have the supporting conditions. In the passages beginning with 'vihiṃsasaññī', the meaning should be understood as follows: 'If I teach this profound Dhamma, which I have well-mastered, to people who cannot understand it, it will result in weariness of body and speech.' Thus, with the perception of weariness, he did not speak and did not wish to speak. But now, let those who are endowed with the cause open their vessels of faith; I shall fulfill their aspirations.

## Pañcavaggiyakathāvaṇṇanā

Āḷāra is the name. Kālāma is the clan. Regarding the statement, 'Knowledge also arose in the Blessed One,' one might ask: 'Did knowledge only arise now? Did he not see all things of the three periods and those beyond time in every aspect at the foot of the Bodhi tree?' It is true that he saw them. However, because omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) occurs in a single thought-moment, it was not yet differentiated by way of name and so forth.

Indeed, because conflicting differentiations cannot occur simultaneously, it is not possible to differentiate the individual and infinite divisions of all things, such as name and birth, with a single thought. With this omniscience, it is only possible to see all things as they are, free from differentiation. The way differentiation arises by taking as an object a desired aspect of the things seen is like the differentiation that arises regarding a variegated cloth seen with eye-consciousness. Here too, immediately after reflecting on Āḷāra, the knowledge of all aspects arose. Not only that, but knowledge also arose concerning everything, such as: 'The Group of Five (Pañcavaggiya) will be the first to understand the Dhamma; with them as the leaders, the deities will also understand; Āḷāra has passed away and is reborn in the Sphere of Nothingness (Ākiñcaññāyatana); and Uddaka is reborn in the Sphere of Neither-perception-nor-non-perception (Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana).' To show the rarity of being endowed with the moment of a Buddha's appearance, he looked in sequence, and it is as if he knew only when the deity informed him...
89:
Because it is bound to the course of sound, even though it is known by a single knowledge, when spoken, it appears as if known sequentially. The deity also reported the very meaning that the Blessed One already knew. Therefore, it should be understood why it was said, 'Knowledge also arose in the Blessed One.' The same applies in other places where the Teacher's seeking of welfare is shown, such as: 'While surveying the world, he saw such a person; if I go there, what will happen?' and so forth. Although it appears to occur sequentially according to the course of words in all instances, it should be understood that the complete realization occurs through a single knowledge. The statement, 'The Group of Five are very helpful to me,' was said with reference to the existence of their past service. It was not said because they were the cause of the Dhamma teaching, for he teaches even those who have not been helpful.

'Between Gayā and the Bodhi tree' means in a place three gāvutas between Gayā and the Bodhi tree.

'Sabbābhibhū' means standing having conquered all things of the three realms. 'Anūpalitta' means unstained by the smear of defilements. For that very reason, he is the 'renouncer of all' (sabbañjaho). 'Released in the destruction of craving' means released by way of making Nibbāna, the destruction of craving, the object. Thus, having known all things by himself, he meant, 'Whom should I point to as my teacher?'

'The city of Kāsī' refers to the city of Vārāṇasī. 'I shall beat' means I shall strike. The Teacher's Dhamma teaching is called the 'Drum of the Deathless' (amatadundubhi) because it proclaims the attainment of the Deathless Nibbāna. 'I go to beat the Drum of the Deathless' is the meaning.

'Worthy of being called Anantajina' means it is appropriate for him to have the name Anantajina. He is 'Anantajina' because he has infinite knowledge, because he has conquered with infinite knowledge, or because he has conquered infinite faults. Alternatively, he is 'Anantajina' because he has conquered and taken hold of the infinite Nibbāna, which is free from the interval of arising and passing away, having crushed the enemies that are defilements.

'It may be so' means that such knowledge should exist in such a jewel-like physical body. This proclamation of his name became a supporting condition (upanissaya) for Upaka, who was endowed with such potential, to approach the Blessed One, ordain, and realize the Path and Fruit when he encountered suffering in the future. That is why the Blessed One traveled the path on foot to meet with Upaka.
90:
"Bāhulliko" refers to one who is greedy for the four requisites. "Padhānavibbhanto" refers to one who has fallen away from the practice of austerities (dukkara-cariyā), which is the means to abandon defilements. In this state of a monk, there are no household duties such as plowing or cattle-rearing, which are for the benefit of a householder; therefore, it is called "anagāriyā" (homelessness). They enter into that state of a monk. "Tadanuttaraṃ" refers to that unsurpassed (Fruit of Arahantship). "Brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ" is the Fruit of Arahantship, which is the culmination of the noble practice of the Path. For the sake of that Fruit of Arahantship, sons of good family go forth into homelessness. "Diṭṭheva dhamme" means in this very life. "Sayaṃ" means by oneself, without relying on others. "Abhiññā sacchikatvā" means having realized for oneself through one's own knowledge. "Upasampajja" means having attained.

"Iriyāya" means by means of a posture that is difficult to practice. In "uttari-manussadhamma" etc., it is called "alamariya" because it is capable of producing the noble state (ariya) that is higher than mundane human knowledge. "Ñāṇadassanaviseso" refers to the distinction in knowledge and vision (Path Knowledge) which precedes Omniscience. The word "no" has the same meaning as the word "nu". "Bhāsitametaṃ" refers to this kind of speech. Those five monks also remembered with a single word, thinking, "If this Great Monk had said 'I am an Arahant' during the time of practicing austerities, we would have believed him, but he did not say so then. Now, however, he speaks only of a quality that truly exists." Thus, reverence arose in them, thinking, "The Buddha is born," and they abandoned the address "Friend (āvuso)" and addressed him, "Venerable Sir (bhante), it is not so." "Aññā cittaṃ" is the mind of attaining the Fruit of Arahantship.

"Antā" refers to the two portions or parts. "Kāmesu kāmasukhallikānuyogo" is the enjoyment of sensual pleasure in the objects of sense. Alternatively, it should be noted that it is called "kāmasukhallika" because it clings to defilements themselves through the pleasure of material things. "Gammo" means the property of those living in a village. "Attakilamathānuyogo" is the repeated devotion to the suffering of self-mortification, such as sleeping on thorns. "Ubho ante" means that the aforementioned greed or eternalism is one extreme, and hatred or annihilationism is the other extreme.

In "cakkhukaraṇī" etc., it is called "cakkhukaraṇī" because it produces the eye of knowledge associated with oneself. The second term (ñāṇakaraṇī) is a synonym for that very "cakkhukaraṇī". "Upasamo" is the stilling of defilements. "Abhiññā" and "sambodho" are the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. "Nibbānaṃ" is the unconditioned element (asaṅkhatadhātu). He praises the practice, saying it leads to the benefit of this stilling of defilements, etc. "Sammādiṭṭhi" is knowledge. "Sammāsaṅkappo" is thought. The remaining factors of the Path are easily understood by their own nature.
91: Having thus shown the four Paths together, he now spoke the words beginning with "Idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave" to show the Four Noble Truths that are to be penetrated by those Paths. In the words "jātipi dukkhā" etc., the very first arising of the phenomena of mind and matter (rūpārūpadhamma) of beings being born in various existences is called "jāti" (birth) here. That birth is "dukkha" (suffering) because it is the basis for the suffering, etc., found in those various existences. In the same way, in old age (jarā) etc., the state of being suffering should be understood because they are the basis of suffering. The five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā) are indeed suffering by way of the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkha), the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkha), and the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha). "Ponobbhavikā" means that which produces renewed existence (punabbhavakaraṇa); it is called "punabbhava" by dropping the latter word; because it has the nature of producing renewed existence, it is called "ponobbhavikā". In the term "nandirāgasahagatā", it is called "nandī" because it delights in and cherishes forms, etc. That very delight is lust (rāga), so it is called "nandirāga". This is an exposition emphasizing the state of being, meaning "the state of delight and lust". Because it is accompanied by that delight and lust, it is called "nandirāgasahagatā". "Tatra tatra" means in various existences. The craving that proceeds by way of enjoying sensual pleasure in the six objects such as forms is called "kāmatanhā". The craving that proceeds together with the eternalist view is "bhavatanhā". The craving that proceeds together with the annihilationist view is "vibhavatanhā". By the words "asesavirāganirodho" etc., only Nibbāna is spoken of. Therein, "virāga" means fading away or departure. "Nirodha" means cessation. By both terms, only the complete departure is intended. That by which the fading away and cessation of craving without remainder occurs is "asesavirāganirodho", which is Nibbāna itself. And because, having reached that Nibbāna, they give up, relinquish, are liberated from, and do not cling to craving and the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), it is called "cāga" (giving up), "paṭinissagga" (relinquishment), "mutti" (liberation), and "anālaya" (detachment). The terms "cakkhu" etc. are merely synonyms for knowledge. "Yāvakīvañca" means for as long a time. "Tiparivaṭṭaṃ" is the knowledge and vision having three rounds by way of the three rounds known as the knowledge of the truth (sacca-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the function (kicca-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of accomplishment (kata-ñāṇa). Herein, the knowledge that knows the Four Noble Truths as they really are, such as "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering, this is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering," is called "sacca-ñāṇa". The knowledge that knows the task to be done regarding those very truths, such as "It should be fully understood, it should be abandoned, it should be realized, it should be developed," is called "kicca-ñāṇa". The knowledge that knows the state of that task having been completed, such as "It has been fully understood, it has been abandoned, it has been realized, it has been developed," is called "katā-ñāṇa". "Dvādasākāraṃ" means having twelve aspects by way of the three aspects in each of those four truths. "Abhisambuddho ti paccaññāsiṃ" means "I did not claim that I have known the Four Noble Truths and reached the Fruit of Arahantship." "Yato ca kho" means from the time he was sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
92:
Starting from the time [he] stayed at the foot of the Bodhi tree, it means 'thereafter I'. The statement 'Knowledge arose in me' is said with reference to reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). The words beginning with 'My liberation is unshakeable' show the manner in which that reviewing knowledge occurs. In that context, 'My liberation is unshakeable' refers to the fruition of Arahatship (arahatta-phala). Its unshakeable nature should be understood both by way of its cause, known as the Path, and by way of its object.

'In this exposition (veyyākaraṇa)' means in this discourse which is without verses. 'When it was being spoken' means while it was being preached. 'Dhamma-eye (dhamma-cakkhu)' here refers to the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) because it performs the function of an eye regarding the truths of the Four Noble Truths. The words beginning with 'Whatever [is of the nature to arise]' were spoken to show the occurrence of non-delusion by way of its function, even though Nibbāna is the object.

'Dhamma-cakka' is called the 'Dhamma-wheel' because both the Dhamma of penetrative knowledge (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and the Dhamma of teaching knowledge (desanā-ñāṇa) are like a wheel in the sense of turning. 'Radiance (obhāsa)' is the radiance that arose through the power of the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), produced by the weather (utu) which has the mind as its cause, and which remained pervading the ten-thousand world systems.

This person has seen the Dhamma of the Noble Truths, therefore he is called 'one who has seen the Dhamma (diṭṭhadhamma)'. This same method applies to the remaining terms. Because it is attained by one's own direct realization, one does not depend on another; because it does not occur in this Dhamma through the faith of another, it is called 'independent of others (aparappaccaya)'. Some say that by merely saying 'Come, monk (ehi bhikkhu)', the state of a novice and the state of a monk (upasampadā) are accomplished; therefore, the limitation is shown in that phrase by the word 'iti'. However, other teachers say that the higher ordination is accomplished only at the conclusion of the words 'for the making an end of suffering'. The statement in the Commentary, 'by the words of the Blessed One, "Come, monk"', is said by way of the initial phrase, referring to the speech characterized by the words 'ehi bhikkhu', just as in the case of the 'Musāvāda-vagga' and so on. That statement agrees with the words in the Commentary on the First Pārājika: 'The Blessed One said... "Come, monk, lead the holy life for the making an end of suffering."' Whatever the Blessed One says as a rule, all of that is indeed a factor [of the ordination]. For trainees (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana), this speech is said in full; but for those beyond training (asekha), it should be understood that he says the speech ending with 'lead the holy life', because they have already perfected the three trainings. Because it is a fulfillment (sampadā) that is superior to and higher than mundane fulfillments, it is called 'Upasampadā'.

## 19-21.
'Nīhāra-bhatta' refers to food that monks have brought out from a village and offered. 'Is it proper?' means 'Is it suitable?'. The words beginning with 'This is mine' show the grasping through craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and views (diṭṭhi) respectively.
93:
22-23. In the phrase 'tasmā tiha', 'tiha' is merely a particle; the meaning is 'tasmā' (therefore). 'Nibbindati' means he becomes disenchanted by way of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā). 'Virajjati' means he does not lust by way of the four Paths. 'Vimuccati' means he is liberated by way of Fruition. The words beginning with 'When liberated' show the realization through reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). 'Brahmacariya' refers to the holy life of the Path (magga-brahmacariya). 'Karaṇīyaṃ' (what is to be done) refers to the sixteen-fold task, such as full understanding (pariññā) and so on, to be performed individually regarding the Four Truths by the four Paths. 'Nāparaṃ itthattāya' means he knows, 'There is no further task of developing the Path for me, either for the sake of these sixteen tasks or for the sake of the destruction of defilements.' Alternatively, 'itthattāya' means 'there will be no further continuity of the aggregates for me other than this present continuity of the aggregates'.

## Pabbajjākathā-vaṇṇanā
'Āḷambara' refers to a drum (paṇava). 'Vikesika' refers to one with disheveled hair. 'Vikkheḷika' refers to one with saliva trickling out. 'Thinking it to be like a cemetery' should be connected as: he saw his own attendants as if they were in a cemetery. 'He uttered an inspired utterance' means he let out words that occurred by the power of spiritual urgency (saṃvega). 'Upassattha' means the assembly of beings that is mixed with suffering, or overwhelmed by suffering.

'This, Yasa...'—the Blessed One said this with reference to Nibbāna. 'Anupubbiṃ kathaṃ' refers to a gradual talk (anupubbī-kathā). 'Ādīnava' means fault. 'Okāra' means the state of being low because of being resorted to by low people. 'Saṃkilesa' means the defilement of beings by those [defilements], or it means the object of defilement. 'Kallacitta' means having a healthy (ready) mind. The teaching of the Truths is called 'Sāmukkaṃsikā' because it is an exaltation or a lifting up [of the teaching] by [the Buddha] himself. The specific form of that teaching is shown by the words 'Dukkha' and so on.

'Assadūte' refers to messengers on horseback. 'Iddhābhisaṅkhāra' means a feat of psychic power. 'Abhisaṅkharesi' means he performed.

'As it was seen (yathādiṭṭhaṃ)' means for one who reviews or sees with the remaining three Paths the plane of the Four Truths seen by the first Path (sotāpatti-magga). In the phrase 'mātu no jīvitaṃ', 'no' is merely a particle; the meaning is 'the life of the mother'. Because Yasa was one whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava), the Blessed One gave him the higher ordination (upasampadā) with only these words: 'Come, monk, the Dhamma is well-expounded; lead the holy life.' For those whose taints are destroyed, the higher ordination is authorized with only this much, because suffering has already been completely destroyed even before being called 'ehi bhikkhu'. The words 'lead the holy life' are spoken with reference to the fulfillment of the training rules known as the holy life of the Dispensation (sāsana-brahmacariya), not the holy life of the Path (magga-brahmacariya).
94:
"Seṭṭhānu-seṭṭhīnaṃ" refers to those families who have had great merchants and subordinate merchants in succession. "Orako" means an inferior person.

32-33. "Mā ekena dve" means that two monks should not go together on a single journey. He is called "Māra" because he kills pure beings or virtues. He is called "Pāpimā" (the Evil One) because he is associated with evil.

"Sabbapāsehi" means by all the snares of defilements. "Ye dibbā ye ca mānusā" means there are snares of defilements based on celestial sensual pleasures and snares of defilements based on human sensual pleasures; it means by all those snares. The words "You are the Buddha" were spoken by Māra with reference to the acceptance of the offerings and honors made by devas and humans.

The snare of lust is called "antalikkhacara" (wandering in the sky) because it binds even those possessing the five higher powers (abhiññā) who wander in the sky. Māra, however, thinks that the snare itself wanders in the sky. "Mānaso" refers to that which is associated with the mind.

"Jānāti maṃ" means that after Māra spoke, thinking, "Will the ascetic Gotama turn back out of fear, thinking that another powerful deity is forbidding him?", and when the Buddha said, "Evil One, I have defeated you," Māra fled dejectedly, thinking, "He has recognized me."

"Parivitakko udapādi" means that since the desire to ordain would arise even in those lacking the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the "Ehi Bhikkhu" ordination, and the Buddhas do not ordain them in that way, it should be understood that He reflected thus to show the procedure for their ordination as well. Those endowed with the supporting conditions approach the Blessed One and ordain only through the "Ehi Bhikkhu" method. "Ye paṭikkhittapuggalā" is a syntactical connection. In the phrase "sayaṃ pabbājetabbo," according to the teaching beginning with "having the hair and beard shaved," the acts of cutting the hair, wearing the saffron robes, and giving the refuges are called "pabbajjā" (going forth). Among these three, the last two—wearing the robes and giving the refuges—must be performed or caused to be performed by the monks themselves. The word "pabbājehi" is spoken with reference to all three types. The phrase "khaṇḍasīmaṃ" is said to avoid neglecting the announcement of the head-shaving. It is not proper to command another to "cut this person's hair" within the same boundary (sīmā) without informing the monks. "Pabbājetvā" is spoken with reference only to the cutting of the hair, because "having caused them to wear the saffron robes" is mentioned separately. "Pabbājetuṃ na labhati" is spoken with reference to the giving of the refuges; a refuge given by one who is not fully ordained (a layperson or a novice), even by the command of a monk, is not valid.

"Yasassī" means being endowed with a retinue. By the Pali term "nijjiivanissattabhāvaṃ," one should understand the method: "Hair is a separate part of this body, without consciousness, indeterminate (avyākata), void, not a being, and merely the earth element," and so forth.
95:
It includes the method beginning with "void, not a being, the harsh earth element." Everything should be understood according to the method found in the Visuddhimagga. "Pubbe" refers to the times when previous Buddhas appeared. "Madditasaṅkhāro" is spoken by way of insight (vipassanā). "Bhāvitabhāvano" is also spoken by way of tranquility (samatha).

In the passage "kāsāyāni tikkhattuṃ vā ...pe... paṭiggāhāpetabbo," one should first make the request, "Venerable Sir, please grant me the going forth out of compassion, taking these saffron robes for the sake of liberation from all suffering," or "having given those saffron robes," and then cause the robes to be accepted. "Athāpi" etc. shows the procedure to be performed after causing the robes to be accepted three times. "Athāpi" means "and after that." Some teachers, however, say that "athāpi" is said to show a different variety of going forth without causing the robes to be accepted; "athāpi" means "or else." By the words "that which is not given is not proper," it shows that the going forth does not take effect.

"Pāde vandāpetvā" means causing one to bow down towards the feet. Even paying homage from afar is called "paying homage to the feet." In the phrase "upajjhāyena vā," the one from whom one takes the preceptor is the preceptor (upajjhāya). The teacher to whom one is entrusted for training in the duties of conduct (ābhisamācārika) is the teacher (ācariya). If the preceptor himself teaches everything and does not entrust the student to another, the preceptor is also his teacher. For example, at the time of higher ordination (upasampadā), the preceptor who himself recites the formal act (kammavācā) is also the kammavācā-teacher.

Because there should be no interruption in the middle when giving the refuges ending with the nasal sound (niggahīta), He said "continuously (ekasambandhāni)."

## "He should be trained in the duties of conduct (ābhisamācārika)" shows that novices (sāmaṇeras) must practice the Sekhiya rules, the Khandhaka duties, and other training rules concerning worldly reproach (lokavajja) such as the emission of semen (sukkavissaṭṭhi), etc. A novice who does not practice these duties is shameless (alajjī) and deserves punishment (daṇḍakamma).

## The explanation of the talk on going forth (Pabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā) is finished.

## Commentary on the Second Story of Māra
In the Pali text, regarding the words "Anuttaraṃ vimuttiṃ anupāpuṇātha" (Attain the unsurpassed liberation), it should be understood that the Buddha gave this advice so that the monks would not stop their efforts due to the force of habitual tendencies, thinking, "We have become Arahants; what benefit is there for us in practicing meditation?" Instead, they should spend their time in fruition attainment (phala-samāpatti) in secluded dwellings, and by seeing them living in such fruition attainment, others might follow their example.

## The Commentary on the Second Story of Māra is finished.

## Commentary on the Story of the Bhaddavaggiya
"Idaṃ nesaṃ pubbakammaṃ" (This was their former deed) refers to the past meritorious deeds of the thirty princes that led to their collective realization of the Truth. It should be understood that these princes possessed much wholesome merit as a support for Nibbāna (the end of the cycle of rebirth), acquired through hearing the Dhamma, taking refuge, giving, observing virtue, and practicing concentration and insight during the times of previous Buddhas. Otherwise, the realization of the Truth on that very day and the attainment of the distinction of "Ehi Bhikkhu" (Come, Monk) ordination would not have been possible.

## The Commentary on the Story of the Bhaddavaggiya is finished.

97:

"Paṃsukūlaṃ uppannaṃ hoti" (A rag-robe was obtained) means it was obtained by searching for the rag-robe made of hemp, infested with worms, which had been discarded after being wrapped around the corpse of a slave girl named Puṇṇā. It is said that the Blessed One, while causing the earth to shake, wore that robe and later gave it to the Elder Mahākassapa; this was said in reference to that robe. The reflection beginning with "Kattha nu kho" (Where indeed...) was made to show various miracles to the ascetics. "Phāliyantu, Kassapa, kaṭṭhāni" (Let the wood be split, Kassapa) should be understood as what the Buddha said when requested by Uruvela Kassapa. The same method applies to the remaining words.

In the phrase "antaraṭṭhakāsu himapātasamaye," the eight nights between the last four days of the month of Māgha and the first four days of the month of Phagguṇa are called "antaraṭṭhakā." "Udakavāhako" means a flood or current of water. "Reṇuhatāyā" means covered with dust, meaning not wet by rain. "Nāvāyā" means by means of a raft. "Idaṃ nu tvaṃ mahāsamaṇā" means "Are you here, Great Ascetic?" The letter 'dha' was changed to 'da' and the anusvāra was added to say "idaṃ nu," similar to the usage in "ekamidāhaṃ" and other passages. He asked, "Are you indeed standing in this place?" "Ayammahamasmi" means "Here I am, I am standing here."
98:

Aggihuttamiissaṃ means together with the equipment for fire-offering.

52-53. Upasaggo means misfortune or danger. The phrase "three thousand five hundred miracles" (aḍḍhuḍḍhāni pāṭihāriyasahassāni) is said excluding the fifteen miracles such as the taming of the Naga; it should be understood that a small additional amount does not count towards the [round] number.

Gayāyaṃ means in the village called Gaya, so named because it is situated not far from the river named Gaya, using the feminine gender. Gayasīse means on the stone slab of that name.

[pe]... or pleasure," [the Buddha] shows the burning nature of the remaining mental aggregates by way of the feelings of joy, grief, and equanimity in the eye-consciousness cognitive processes. ## The Explanation of the Story of the Meeting with Bimbisāra

Yaññā abhivadanti means they say they prosper because of sacrifice. In this context, upadhīsu refers to the four types of upadhi (substrates of rebirth) in the sense of being the basis for suffering, pleasure, etc.: kāmūpadhi, khandhūpadhi, kilesūpadhi, and abhisaṅkhārūpadhi. Among these four, because the khandhūpadhi (substrate of aggregates) is intended here, it is said: "Knowing them as a stain among the substrates of aggregates" (khandhūpadhīsu malanti ñatvā). Yaññā means because of the cause of sacrifice. Yiṭṭhe means in the performance of a great sacrifice (mahāyāga). Hute means in the daily fire-offering. Kiṃ vakkhāmi means "What shall I say?"

57-58. Āsīsanā means the heart's desire (manoratha). Siṅgīsuvaṇṇanikkhena means by a mass of Singī gold. Among types of gold, yuttikata gold is inferior. Rasaviddha gold is more excellent than that. Ākaruppanna gold is more excellent than that. Any kind of dibba-suvaṇṇa (divine gold) is more excellent than that.
99:
...is more excellent than that; among those divine golds, cāmīkara gold is more excellent; then sātakumbha gold; then jambunada gold; and siṅgī gold is more excellent even than jambunada gold. A nikkha of that Singī gold has the weight of five suvaṇṇas. They also mention various other divisions such as eight suvaṇṇas. Regarding "in the ten abodes of the noble ones" (dasasu ariyavāsesu):

"Here, monks, a monk has abandoned five factors, is endowed with six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has dispelled individual truths, has well relinquished searches, has unclouded thoughts, has tranquillized bodily formations, has a well-liberated mind, and has well-liberated wisdom."

(This refers to) the ten abodes of the noble ones as mentioned thus.

In that text, "abandoned five factors" refers to being free from the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). "Endowed with six factors" refers to the six-fold equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā), which is the opposite of joy, etc., regarding the six objects such as the desirable. "A single guard" means having established mindfulness. That monk has four supports (apassena), namely: reflecting on use, enduring, avoiding, and dispelling; therefore, it is said "has four supports," and by this phrase, those supports are shown. One who has dispelled the truths of views individually held by those with wrong views is called "one who has dispelled individual truths"; by this, the abandoning of views through mundane knowledge is meant. Because he has well relinquished the searches known as the search for sensual pleasure (kāmesanā), the search for existence (bhavesanā), and the search for the holy life (brahmacariyavesanā) without deficiency, he is called "one who has well relinquished searches." By this, the absence of the three searches is meant. By the phrase "unclouded thoughts," the state of having a mind unclouded by sensual thoughts, etc., is meant. By the phrase "tranquillized bodily formations," the state of being free from distress through the attainment of the fourth jhāna is meant. By the phrase "well-liberated mind," the Path (magga) is meant. By the phrase "well-liberated wisdom," the Fruition knowledge (phala-ñāṇa) is meant, by way of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa). Noble ones dwell in these ten states; therefore, they are called "abodes of the noble ones" (ariyavāsa).

Because he has dwelt in, used, and accomplished those abodes of the noble ones, the Blessed One is called "one who has dwelt in the abodes" (vutthavāsa). Dasabala means being endowed with the ten physical strengths and the ten knowledge strengths. There are these ten types of elephants:

"The Kāḷāvaka elephant, the Gaṅgeyya elephant, the Paṇḍara elephant, the Tamba elephant and the Piṅgala elephant;

The Gandha elephant, the Maṅgala elephant and the Hema elephant; the Uposatha elephant and the Chaddanta elephant."
100: These ten classes of elephants mentioned are endowed with strength ten times greater than each preceding class. Among them, the strength of ten Chaddanta elephants, the greatest of all, is known as the ten [physical] strengths of the Blessed One's body. That strength is equal to the strength of a thousand crores of ordinary elephants called Kāḷāvaka, and the strength of ten thousand crores of average men. That strength is also called 'Nārāyaṇasaṅghātabala'. In the Pali, the ten powers of knowledge (dasabala-ñāṇa) are: the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the results of kamma (kammavipāka-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the way leading to all destinations (sabbatthagāminīpaṭipadā-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the world with its many and various elements (anekadhātunānādhātuloka-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the various dispositions of beings (sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikatā-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the maturity of the faculties (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments (jhāna-vimokkha-samādhi-samāpattīnaṃ saṃkilesa-vodāna-vuṭṭhāna-ñāṇa), the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa). These are called the Blessed One's ten powers. 'With the ten factors of one beyond training (asekha)' means being endowed with the ten asekha qualities associated with the fruit of Arahantship, as stated in the Pali: 'Asekha Right View... Asekha Right Concentration, Asekha Right Knowledge, Asekha Right Liberation.' Here, Right View, mentioned in the sense of seeing, is also called Right Knowledge in the sense of knowing. All other factors such as contact (phassa) associated with the fruit-consciousness are to be understood as Right Liberation. ## The Commentary on the Meeting with Bimbisāra is finished. ## Commentary on the Going Forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna. He is called Sāriputta because he is the son of the Brahmin woman Sārī. He is called Moggallāna because he is the son of the Brahmin woman Moggallī. 'Channaparibbājakassa' refers to a wanderer (paribbājaka) who wanders covering his private parts with a white cloth. By this word, it is shown that he is not a naked wanderer. The term 'upaññātaṃ' is explained as 'having been known,' and the term 'maggaṃ' is explained as 'the path that has been approached.' Therefore, in the term 'upaññātaṃ', the word 'ñāta' is a synonym for knowledge (ñāṇa). In the term 'maggaṃ', it refers to the path itself through a change of gender. It is shown that the prefix 'upa' has the meaning of approaching and should also be connected with the word 'magga'. This is the intended meaning:
101: Because what is called 'following' is the knowledge attained by those who desire it, and it is also the path reached by them; therefore, (he thinks), 'It would be good if I were to follow.' 'Upanyātaṃ nibbānaṃ' means Nibbāna known through inference (anumāna). The explanation of the word 'maggaṃ' is 'magganto,' meaning searching for Nibbāna known through inference in order to see it through direct perception. To show that the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca) and the truth of the path (magga-sacca), which is the cause of cessation, are called 'nirodha' by the method of ellipsis (ekasesa), he said 'atha vā,' etc. 'Paṭipādento' means concluding. 'Ito uttari' means even if the other three paths beyond this path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) that I have attained do not yet exist, this very Dhamma is the Nibbāna that I have sought. 62-3. 'Tadārammaṇāya' means by the liberation of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala-vimutti) which has Nibbāna as its object. 'Tesaṃ āyasmantānaṃ' means the retinues of those two venerable ones reached the fruit of arahantship (arahatta-phala) at that very moment upon hearing the Dhamma of the Blessed One. As for the two chief disciples (aggasāvaka), because the task of their knowledge was great, they reached the fruit of arahantship only after a few days. Therefore, he said 'evaṃ,' etc. Intending the state of being the object of the action of attending, it is said 'upayogatthevā.' ## The Explanation of the Story of the Ordination of Sāriputta and Moggallāna is finished. ## Explanation of the Duties towards Preceptors. 'Vajjāvajjā' means minor and major faults. In the word 'uttiṭṭhapattaṃ,' 'uttiṭṭha' means wandering for alms, as in the Pali passages such as 'Uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyya' (Dhp. 168). A bowl taken for the purpose of wandering for alms is called 'uttiṭṭhapattaṃ'; therefore, he said 'a bowl for wandering for alms.' Because one might ask what fault there is in tilting that bowl, he said 'tasmiṃ hi,' etc. 'Tasmā' means because people have the perception of impurity (ucchiṭṭha) in the alms-bowl (uttiṭṭhapatta), thinking 'these monks eat in this very vessel.' Therefore, it is called 'uttiṭṭhapattaṃ'; by the word 'uttiṭṭha' itself, the state of being impure in the perception of people is understood. Some teachers, however, say, 'The word uttiṭṭha has the same meaning as the word ucchiṭṭha.' Because 'uttiṭṭhā' is also a word ending in the suffix 'tvā,' he said 'having risen.' 'Upajjhāyaṃ gahetuṃ' means to take the state of a preceptor in mind, or to take the consent of that preceptor through words of request.
102:
"Upajjhāyattaṃ" means taking the state of a preceptor into mind, or taking the consent of that preceptor through words of request.

"Patissayana" is "patisso" (dependence). It means the state of practicing in dependence on a teacher, or any form of respect. Being with respect is called "sappatisso." It means practicing under the instruction of another, having made them the leader. Therefore, it is said, "having established the state of being a leader." "Sāhu" means good or excellent. "Lahu" means not heavy, the state of being easy to support. "Opāyika" means connected with a means; it means such practice is a means for liberation from Saṃsāra. "Patirūpa" means this action is a respectful deed. "Pāsādikena" means to fulfill it with bodily and verbal actions that inspire faith. "Kāyena" means making it known through the body, showing hand gestures and so on that convey that meaning. "Sādhu" refers to acceptance. When the preceptor says "Sāhu" and so on, it means the co-resident's word of acceptance "Sādhu," and thus it is said "he makes it known by the body," etc. "Āyācanadānamattena" means merely by the co-resident's initial request, and then merely by the preceptor's words such as "Sāhu."

"Assa" means belonging to the co-resident (saddhivihārika). The phrase "two robes" refers to the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and the double-layered outer robe (saṅghāṭi). "Ito paṭṭhāya" (starting from here) begins from the letter "na" (not) in the phrase "na upajjhāyassa bhaṇamānassa" (not while the preceptor is speaking). By this, it shows there is no offense in the duties prohibited by the letter "na," such as "nātidūre" (not too far), etc. "Sabbattha dukkaṭāpatti" (an offense of wrong-doing in all cases) means that except for cases of danger, madness, mental distraction, or being oppressed by pain, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) occurs even for a monk who speaks without knowing the Vinaya regulation, or even for a sick monk. Indeed, in times of danger, it is allowable to speak intermittently. The same applies to other duties prohibited by the letter "na" of this nature. However, in other duties not prohibited by the letter "na," even a sick monk is not exempt from the offense. In the Pali, the phrase "having touched even under the couch" is said to avoid clashing with alms-bowls and so on placed there previously. It is certainly allowable to place the bowl after looking with the eyes or knowing that there are no other items. "Āpattiyā āsanna" means the very act of committing an offense.

"Gāme" means in such a place as a pavilion within a village. "Antaraghare" means inside a house. "Paṭikkamane" means in a rest house. "Dhotavālikāya" means in clean sand, free from dust, in a place where water has flowed. "Niddhūme" means in a place free from the smoke of a burning fire in a sauna (jantāghara). Indeed, a sauna is a place for making the body sweat to prevent oppression by diseases and so on caused by snow in regions where snowfall is heavy. Because it is covered in darkness in that sauna, many...
103:
A sauna (sweat house) is a place for making the body sweat to prevent illnesses and so on that can occur due to snowfall. Because it is dark in that sauna, many monks also enter together, put down their robes, smear their faces with fine clay to protect against the heat of the fire, sweat their bodies as much as desired, rub themselves with powder and so on, and then bathe. Therefore, it is said in the Pali, "the powder should be kneaded" (cuṇṇam sannetabbaṃ) and so on. "Ullokaṃ" means the place for looking upwards (the upper part).

"Aññattha netabbo" means if dissatisfaction with the Dispensation (Sāsana) arises in the co-resident while living in his monastery, he should be taken from there to another place endowed with good friends (kalyāṇamitta) and so on. The phrase "visabhāgapuggalānaṃ" (dissimilar persons) refers to monks, whether conscientious (lajjī) or shameless (alajjī), who do not desire the progress of the preceptor. If a shameless preceptor does not even take advice, and conscientious monks are incompatible (visabhāga) with that preceptor, then one should leave that preceptor and enjoy material requisites and so on only with the conscientious monks. In this case, the status of being a preceptor and so on should not be considered the standard. "Pariveṇaṃ gantvā" means going to the preceptor's enclosure. The phrase "na susānaṃ" (not to the cemetery) is merely an illustration (upalakkhaṇa); a co-resident who wishes to go outside the precinct (upacārasīmā) must not go without asking permission.

## The Explanation of the Duties toward the Preceptor (Upajjhāyavatta-kathā-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## The Explanation of the Duties toward the Co-resident (Saddhivihārikavatta-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

In the explanation of the duties toward the co-resident, regarding the words "saṅgahetabbo anuggahetabbo" (should be supported, should be assisted) and so on, preceptors and teachers who do not support their co-residents with Dhamma or material things due to disrespect commit an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) because of the breach of duty. Therefore, it is also said in the Parivāra, "If he does not give, he incurs an offense." The remaining words are easy to understand.

## The Explanation of the Duties toward the Co-resident (Saddhivihārikavatta-kathā-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## The Explanation of Not Practicing Properly (Nasammāvattanādikathā-vaṇṇanā)

In the explanation of not practicing properly, "not fulfilling the duty" (vattaṃ na pūreyya) means, despite knowing that it is the time for performing the duty, he does not fulfill it due to pride, laziness, and so on...
104:
If one fails to perform [the duties] towards the preceptor (upajjhāya) and others, either out of disrespect or out of ignorance, thinking 'It is not improper to not do it,' it is merely an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa). However, for one who does not perform them unintentionally or through lack of mindfulness, etc., there is no offense. In truth, since all duties (vatta) are indeed sekhiya duties, all decisions here should be understood according to the method stated in the Sekhiya rules. Gehassitapema means affection based on loving-kindness (metta-pema).

Not knowing whether one is pleased or not pleased means: 'If I am pleased, those who do not perform the duties commit an offense; if I reject it and am not pleased, there is no offense'—thus one does not know. According to the statement, 'Among them, one monk who is accomplished in the duties... there is no offense for them,' if someone says, 'I will attend to your sick (gilāna) saddhivihārika or antevāsika, and I will perform all necessary tasks such as giving advice and instruction,' or if those saddhivihārikas and others say, 'Please remain unconcerned,' or if they are not pleased with the duty, there is no offense for the teachers and preceptors either.

## The explanation of the section beginning with 'Not behaving properly' (nasammāvattanādi) is finished.

In the story of Radha the Brahmin in the Pali, uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāta means a pale yellowish color has appeared over the whole body. The repetition (vicchā) is made to show that the pale color has spread throughout the entire body. Adhikāra means a favor (service). Katavedino are those who make known the favor done to them by others through a reciprocal action. The words to be spoken in the ordination ceremony (upasampadā-kammavācā) will be mentioned at the end. Parimaṇḍalehi means 'completely' or 'perfectly'.

71-73. Paṇṇattivītikamma means the transgression of a training rule (sikkhāpada). In the Pali, piṇḍiyālopa-bhojana means food sought by the strength of the calves of the legs, wandering and collecting morsel by morsel. Atirekalābha means gains in excess of the alms-food. The distribution of Saṅgha-meals and so on will become clear in the Senāsanakkhandhaka. Vihāra means the entire monastery (saṅghārāma) enclosed by a wall, including grass-roofed huts and so on. Aḍḍhayoga means a long mansion with a single hall. Some say it is a long mansion shaped like the back of an elephant or like a garuḍa bird. Pāsāda means a square...
105:
...high mansion, which is a mansion with many stories. Hammiya is a mansion with a flat roof, provided with a moon-deck (balcony), and not very high. Guhā means a mountain cave. Pūtimutta means the urine of cattle.

## Explanation of the Duties towards a Teacher (Ācariyavatta)

'Sahadhammikaṃ vuccamāno' means being exhorted by a training rule such as 'It should be worn in this way.' 'Vādaṃ āropetvā' means by way of refuting (reproaching), such as 'What fault is there in wearing [the robe] hanging down? If there were a fault, there would also be a fault in wearing it all around evenly,' and so on. 'Taṃyeva titthāyatanaṃ' means the view (diṭṭhi) itself is called titthāyatana because it is the cause (āyatana) for the arising of suffering. 'Āyasmato nissāya vacchāmi' means 'I will live depending on the venerable one'.

## The explanation of the Duties towards a Teacher is finished.

## Explanation of the Section on Dismissal and Forgiveness

The connection (sambandhayojanā) should be understood thus: by the same characteristic that was stated previously, an offense should not be known (there is no offense) for a pupil living in dependence (nissayantevāsika). However, in the manuscripts, in the phrase 'na teneva lakkhaṇena', they omit the word 'na' and write 'by that same characteristic, an offense should be known for the nissayantevāsika'; that writing is a mistake made through negligence. The reason is that if one takes it as an offense by that same characteristic, then whether one is released from dependence or not, it would be an offense, and thus one would fall into an offense by the characteristic stated in the duties of a saddhivihārika. If that were so, it would contradict the subsequent statement: 'As long as a nissayantevāsika lives depending on a teacher, for that long he must perform all the duties towards the teacher.' Also in the Visuddhimagga:

'For the nissayācariya, uddesācariya, nissayantevāsika, uddesantevāsika, and samānācariyaka, as long as the dependence (nissaya) and the instruction (uddesa) are not interrupted, for that long they should be looked after and attended to.'
106:
It has been stated thus. Therefore, by the method already mentioned, bringing in the letter 'na' (negation) that was omitted here, the meaning should be taken as follows: by the same characteristic mentioned for that saddhivihārika, an offense is not to be known (i.e., no offense is incurred) for the nissayantevāsika (a pupil living in dependence).

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Salutation and Asking for Forgiveness is finished.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Cessation of Dependence (Nissaya-paṭippassaddhi)

In the discussion on the cessation of dependence, by the passage "Dependence should be taken in the presence of one with whom there is common use and common communion," the taking of dependence is directed only towards conscientious (lajjī) persons. This is because it is prohibited with regard to the shameless (alajjī).

In this context, since the use of the four requisites is already included by the word 'sambhoga', the word 'paribhoga' is used to include communion (saṃvāsa) such as performing legal acts together (ekakamma) and so on. By this (the term ekasambhoga-paribhoga), it is shown that one should not engage in common use and communion with the shameless. The phrase "parihāro natthi" means there is no protection from an offense (i.e., an offense is incurred). "Tādiso" refers to such a person in whose presence dependence was previously taken and with whom there is common use and communion. "Tathā vuttaṃ" means when it has been instructed, "I will return quickly." The phrase "four or five days" is merely an illustration (upalakkhaṇa). If compatibility (sabhāgatā) is evident within one or two days, dependence should indeed be taken on the day it is known. However, if it is not evident even after four or five days, one should wait for as many days as it takes for it to become evident. One should not, however, make an excuse (deception) saying, "I will wait to see the compatibility."

In the phrase "dahara suṇanti," even if one does not hear (the teacher's words), if there is the perception that "he will come, he is delayed by some obstacle," protection (no offense) is indeed obtained. Therefore, it is said, "If he sends word saying, 'I will stay right here,' there is no protection (an offense is incurred)."

The statement "there is no protection even for a single day" is said with reference to a lack of effort in going. For a pupil who makes an effort, however, there is no fault even if a few days pass due to tasks such as tidying up the lodgings and so on.

"Should stay right there" means one should stay and take dependence only in that place of compatibility. By the passage "In that very monastery... it is proper to stay," it is stated that the cessation of dependence occurs through meeting the preceptor (upajjhāya) only as long as that preceptor is supporting/favoring the pupil. In that case, if...
107:
...if the preceptor does not support the pupil, either due to anger or due to indifference toward the group, it is shown that the dependence taken from other teachers does not cease.

The method mentioned in the cessation of teacher-dependence (ācariya-nissaya), such as "koci ācariyo" and so on, should be applied to the departure of the preceptor (upajjhāya-pakkamana) etc., and the method mentioned in those cases of preceptor-departure etc., should also be applied here to the cessation of teacher-dependence, and should be conjoined as appropriate.

"Staying in another monastery beyond two clod-throws (leḍḍupāta)" means staying in another monastery outside the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā) beyond two clod-throws from the dwelling place of the resident pupils (antevāsikas). By saying this, it is shown that even if it is outside the precinct, if one stays in a nearby place within two clod-throws from the dwelling place of the resident pupils etc., the dependence does not cease. Within the precinct boundary, however, for a monk staying even beyond two clod-throws, the dependence certainly does not cease.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Cessation of Dependence is finished.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Five Factors for Ordination

In the discussion on the characteristics of preceptors and teachers, "a novice should not be made to attend" means one should not ordain a novice by acting as the preceptor. Because it is the property of an adept (asekkha), it is called 'asekkha'; it refers to the group of virtue (sīlakkhandha), both mundane and supramundane.

'Antaggāhikāya' refers to the wrong view that grasps the portions of eternalism (sassata) and annihilationism (uccheda). "The last two" refers to these two factors: being one of little learning and being one of little wisdom. "The last three" refers to these three: being unable to dispel arisen remorse (kukkucca) according to the Dhamma, not knowing offenses, and not knowing the emergence from offenses. Indeed, the inability to dispel remorse according to the Dhamma, which is defined by the method of the Pali and Commentaries, is simply being unskilled (avyatta); therefore, that inability is also stated as a factor regarding offenses.

Conduct that is exceedingly distinguished and noble is called 'ābhisamācāra'; it is the virtue (sīla) concerning major and minor duties. The training (sikkhā) defined as the Khandhaka training rules, which are laid down with reference to that ābhisamācāra, is called 'ābhisamācārikā sikkhā'. Indeed, even that training rule is called 'sikkhā' because it must be trained in by those desiring fulfillment through methods such as learning and so on. The training that is the beginning and the cause of the holy life of the Path is called 'ādibrahmacariyaka sikkhā'; it refers to the training rules included in the Ubhatovibhaṅga.
108:
Therefore, in the Visuddhimagga also, it was said: "The training rule included in the Ubhatovibhaṅga is called ādibrahmacariyaka (fundamental to the holy life); the training rule included in the Khandhakavatta is called ābhisamācārika (pertaining to good conduct)." Therefore, in the term "Sekkhapaṇṇatti", it is called "sekkha" because it is to be practiced, and "paṇṇatti" because it is prescribed by the Blessed One. All prescriptions of training rules included in the Ubhatovibhaṅga should be understood as "Sekkhapaṇṇatti".

In the term "Nāmarūpapariccheda", it refers to the wisdom that knows by distinguishing mind (nāma)—which consists of the four groups such as the feeling aggregate (vedanākkhandha) along with Nibbāna, as taught through the Kusala Triads etc., by way of distinctions such as birth (jāti), plane (bhūmi), person (puggala), association (sampayoga), base (vatthu), object (ārammaṇa), kamma, door (dvāra), characteristic (lakkhaṇa), and function (rasa)—and matter (rūpa), which consists of the great elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādārūpa). It also refers to the treatise that explains this wisdom. By this, it is shown that one must be proficient in the meaning of Abhidhamma. "Sikkhāpetum" means to cause to learn (to cause to study).

## The Explanation of the Five Factors for Ordination is finished.

## Explanation of the Story of Former Members of Other Sects

In the discussion of the probation for members of other sects (titthiyaparivāsa), among the words such as "ājīvakassa vā", an akiriyavādī (proponent of the non-action doctrine) is called an Ājīvaka. However, the Nigaṇṭhas, who are kiriyavādī (proponents of the action doctrine), and other naked ascetics are included under the term "acelaka". In every respect, the probation for members of other sects is prescribed only for a naked ascetic. To show that this probation is prescribed for one who comes to the presence of the monks in that naked form, and not for one who comes covered, the words "sace sopi" etc. were said. There, "sopi" refers to the Ājīvaka.

"Āmisakiñcikkhasampadāna" means the repeated giving of a small gift. "Rūpūpajīvikā" refers to women who live by depending solely on their physical beauty. A prostitute's house is called "vesiyāgocara" because it is the place where she frequently resorts. This method is the same in all cases. "Yobbannātītā" refers to an elderly maiden (thullakumārī) who has reached old age without having had relations with a man. "Ādāya" means taking (gahana).

## The Explanation of the Story of Former Members of Other Sects is finished.
109:
## Explanation of the Story of the Five Diseases

88-9. In the stories of the five diseases etc., the words in the Pāḷi "somhi arogo vibbhamissāmi" mean "I am free from disease, I will return to the lay life." "Nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇa" refers to the size of the nail of the little finger. Since it is stated, "If it is the size of a fingernail in a hidden place and is in a state of not increasing, it is allowable," it is automatically understood that such a disease is not allowable in an unhidden (exposed) place, and even in a hidden place, a disease that is in a state of increasing is not allowable. To refute the view of those teachers who might hold that even in a prominent (exposed) place, leprosy that is smaller than the size of the little finger's nail and not increasing is allowable, the words "mukhe pana" etc. were said.

"Kolaṭṭhimattakopi" means even if it is the size of a jujube seed. In the phrase "even if it is in a state of not increasing, it is not allowable," the word "pi" indicates that a boil (gaṇḍa) is not allowable even if it is smaller than the size of a jujube seed. Therefore, it was said "sacchaviṃ kāretvā", which means making it have skin. Or there is a variant reading "sañchaviṃ", which means making it have well-formed skin. Even when boils etc. have healed, a discolored scar may occur in that place; that is allowable.

"Padumapuṇḍarīkapattavaṇṇa" means having a color like the petals of the red lotus (paduma) and the white lotus (puṇḍarīka). By the phrase "kuṭṭhe vuttanayeneva" (in the same manner as stated for leprosy), it shows the method already mentioned: that a non-increasing disease in a hidden place is allowable, but in other places, not even the slightest disease is allowable. "Sosabyādhi" is the disease of consumption (tuberculosis). "Yakkhummāra" is a disease like being possessed by a demon (yakkha), which occurs occasionally, causing one to fall to the ground and rub limbs such as hands and face on the ground.

## The Explanation of the Story of the Five Diseases is finished.

## Explanation of the Story of the Royal Servants

The request for permission, "O King, I am no longer a servant of the King," is said with reference to the rank or position granted by the King himself. If a person is appointed by royal officials such as ministers, or is a servant of the ministers themselves, it is proper for that person to ask permission from those respective ministers etc.

## The Explanation of the Story of the Royal Servants is finished.
110:
## Commentary on the Story of the Robber

Therefore, because the Blessed One is himself the Lord of the Dhamma (Dhammassāmī), he ordained Aṅgulimāla by the "Ehi Bhikkhu" formula. However, it should be understood that when he was prescribing the training rule (sikkhāpada) for the monks, he spoke in this way. "They know thus" means they know that he has become virtuous (sīlavā).

"They cease" means they abstain. "Having broken" means having broken the foot-shackles (andubandhana). "Having cut" means having cut the iron chains (saṅkhalika). "Having untied" means having untied the rope bonds (rajjubandhana). "Having opened" means having opened the village gates and so forth among the village bonds. "While they do not see" means in the absence of the guards who are stationed to protect the man.

"Just as in the previous method" means in the same manner as mentioned in the phrase "beaten with a whip, punished with a penalty" (kasāhato katadaṇḍakammo).

## The Commentary on the Story of the Robber is finished.

## Commentary on the Story of the Debtor

"Even if he flees" refers to one who flees out of fear upon knowing that the creditors (iṇasāmika) are coming. "He is liable" (gīvā hoti) means that while knowing he is in debt, he was admitted into the state of a monk, which is free from debt, through a lack of respect; therefore, he is liable. "A little, a little" refers to repaying bit by bit. By the words "it must indeed be given," it is shown that the debtor monk must make an effort to repay the wealth, whether the creditor accepts it or not. Other monks should also assist as companions, saying, "Do not lay down the burden (dhura)." Indeed, if he lays down the burden (by not paying), he should be dealt with according to the value of the goods (bhaṇḍaggha).

## The Commentary on the Story of the Debtor is finished.

## Commentary on the Story of the Slave

"Bought by imposing the conduct of a slave"—by this statement, buying for the purpose of liberation from slavery is prohibited. In truth, such a person bought with wealth is not a slave. "By the power of such and such conduct" means in those various districts (it follows the method of making one a non-slave, such as by burning the slave records).
111:
By such methods of making one a non-slave as burning the slave records, and with reference to the release of all bonds during coronation ceremonies (abhiseka) and the like, it is said "in a way common to all."

Regarding self-enrollment as slaves: it is not proper to do so. Those free women, thinking "Let us also become royal slave-women," have their own names written in the kings' slave records for the sake of their own protection. Their children also become royal slaves. Therefore, it is not proper to ordain them. They should not be ordained without the permission of their owners; if there are many owners, they should not be ordained even if only one of them does not give permission.

Regarding the propriety of ordaining after making them free: if those temple attendants (ārāmika) have been given to a certain monastery, it is proper to ordain them after informing the Saṅgha of that monastery and making them free by paying compensation (phātikamma). In some districts, when making someone a non-slave, they pour buttermilk (takka) on the head; it is said that by this act, they become non-slaves. The giving of an ārāmika is also to be understood in this same way. Even if given in such a manner, because he is still a temple slave of the Saṅgha, it is said "he should not be ordained." Since it is said "temporarily" (tāvakālika), everything given for a fixed period or with the desire to take it back later must be regarded as temporary. An "ownerless slave" (nissāmikadāsa) refers to a slave whose owner's family has perished through death without any relatives, leaving no heir. Such a slave should be ordained only after being made free by those of the same class, by the inhabitants of his village, or by the authorities. Deva-slaves (devadāsa) are also slaves. In some places, they are royal slaves, and in some places, they are monastery slaves; therefore, it is not proper to ordain them. If a monk, after ordaining a slave, removes him to hide him upon seeing the owners, he should be dealt with by an offense of taking what is not given (adinnādāna) for every footstep. However, there is no offense for a slave who runs away on his own.

## The Commentary on the Story of the Slave is finished.

## Commentary on the Story of the Goldsmith's Son and Others

In the discussion concerning the request for the shaving (bhaṇḍukamma) and so forth, "Kammārabhaṇḍu" refers only to a goldsmith's boy who, because of his youth, has a shaven head without a topknot. In the term "Tulādhāramuṇḍaka," "Tulādhāra" refers to one who [holds] the scales for copper, gold, and so forth with the hand...
112:
Smiths are called "Tulādhāra" because they hold scales with their hands. Among them, it refers to a young boy with a shaven head. Therefore, he is called "a young boy with five topknots" (Pañcasikha Taruṇadāraka). Tying a single topknot into five coils is called "Pañcasikhā," and one who has such topknots is called "Pañcasikha." They ordained that boy by cutting his topknots without informing any [other] monks. For that reason, the Buddha allowed the practice of asking permission from the Saṅgha for the bhaṇḍukamma (shaving the head). "Sīmāpariyāpanna" means within the baddha-sīmā (fixed boundary) if one exists, or within the upacāra-sīmā (vicinity boundary) if not.

Although it is only stated here, "Monks, I allow you to ask the Saṅgha for bhaṇḍukamma," and no offense is mentioned for not asking, the Commentary states: "Thinking that all have been asked... there is no offense for the one who ordains [the person]." Therefore, it should be understood that a monk who intentionally shaves someone's hair without asking permission commits a dukkaṭa offense. Since shaving hair also falls under the terminology of making someone a samaṇa or pabbajjā, He said, "making this person a samaṇa," etc. In the context of "Ekasikhā-mattadhara," some say "Ekasikhā" means a topknot made of a single hair, but it should be understood as a topknot with a small amount of hair. Cutting even a single hair without asking permission is indeed improper.

"Vāmahatthena" (with the left hand) is said because one eats with the right hand (thus holding with the left).

103-4. Regarding the groups of five and six in the duties of one released from dependence (nissaya-muccanaka), all these details in "ubhāyani kho panassa pātimokkhāni... anubyañjanaso" can be known if the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā is known. The phrase "āpattiṃ jānāti, anāpattiṃ jānāti" should be understood as referring to offenses, etc., in the places known to oneself.

## The explanation of the story of the smith's shaven-headed boy (Kammāra-bhaṇḍu-vatthu), etc., is finished.

## Explanation of the story of Rāhula (Rāhula-vatthu)

"Pokkharavassa" (lotus-leaf rain) is rain that rolls off the bodies of those who do not wish to be wet, like water on a lotus leaf. It is said that when it rains, only those who wish to be wet get wet, not others. Thinking, "There is no one who goes saying 'Accept almsfood,'" and that he himself would enjoy all the kingship and wealth he possessed (King Suddhodana thought so). Out of respect, King Suddhodana also did not invite [the Buddha].
