However, he went to the palace and spent the whole night preparing a great offering and arranging and decorating the seating for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.

"No one... took the bowl" means they did not take it, thinking that the Blessed One would only go to his father's palace. "Kulanagare" means in the city of relatives. "Piṇḍacāriya-vatta" means the duty of wandering for alms from house to house even in the villages of one's relatives. Because he wanders for the sake of alms, he is called "Bhikkhācāra"; by this term, the Khattiya king is meant.

"Uttiṭṭhe" means the almsfood to be received by standing and intending at the doors of others' houses; "nappamajjeyya" (should not be negligent) means one should not be negligent in that alms-round, rejecting the excellent food received through invitations, etc. "Dhammaṃ" means one should practice that practice of alms-gathering (bhikkhācariya-dhamma) well, wandering from house to house and abandoning improper search (anesana). "Sukhaṃ seti" means living happily in the four postures.
113:
King Suddhodana also did not invite the Blessed One out of respect. However, he went to the palace and spent the night preparing a great offering and arranging the seating and decorating the area for the Saṅgha headed by the Blessed One.

With the perception that "The Blessed One will only go to His father's palace," no one took the bowl. "Kulanagare" means in the city of relatives. "Piṇḍacāriya-vattaṃ" means the duty of wandering for alms from house to house even in the villages of one's relatives. Because there is wandering for the sake of begging, it is called "Bhikkhācāro"; by this word, the king (Khattiya) is referred to.

"Uttiṭṭhe" refers to the almsfood to be received by standing and intending at the doors of others' houses. "Nappamajjeyya" means one should not be negligent in wandering for alms, rejecting the excellent food obtained through invitations and so forth. "Dhammaṃ" means one should practice that virtue of alms-gathering, wandering from house to house and abandoning improper search (anesana). "Sukhaṃ seti" means living happily in all four postures.

In the second verse, "na naṃ duccaritaṃ" means one should not practice the aforementioned Dhamma as misconduct by wandering in improper places (agocara) such as the houses of courtesans. The rest is as previously stated. It means after hearing this second verse spoken by the Blessed One, who was seated in the palace, concerning His alms-round in the assembly of relatives...

In the words "Dhammapāla Jātaka" etc., it is stated to show the events of King Suddhodana's life in later times, up to his Parinibbāna, as appropriate. Therefore, it was said, "having realized the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala)," etc. In the phrase "Sirigabbhaṃ gantvā," it should be understood that the Blessed One went because He knew that if He did not go and see her on that very day, Queen Yasodharā would die of a broken heart.

"Taṃ divasameva" means on that very day He saw the mother of Rāhula. In the Dhammapada Commentary, however, it is said: "The Teacher went to Kapilavatthu and on the third day, He had Prince Nanda ordained." "Kesavissajjanaṃ" means the loosening of the topknot tied during childhood for the royal crown; they say that when doing so, they perform a ceremony. In the Sāratthadīpanī, however, it is said to be the shaving of hair according to family custom. "Paṭṭabandho" is the binding of a golden plate on the forehead, signifying "This person is the king." The ceremony of entering a new palace is called the house ceremony (Gharamaṅgala). The ceremony of raising the parasol is called the parasol ceremony (Chattamaṅgala).
114:
"Janapadakalyāṇī" refers to a woman who is beautiful in the district. She is so called because she is endowed with the five beauties—hair, flesh, bone, complexion, and age—which are not shared by others. "Tuvaṭaṃ" means quickly. "Anicchamānaṃ" means being mentally unwilling. Verbally, however, when the Blessed One said, "Nanda, you shall go forth," he did not dare to refuse out of respect and said, "Very well." The Blessed One gave him the going-forth on this pretext.

"Brahmariūpavaṇṇaṃ" means having an appearance similar to that of a Brahma. "Tyassa" means "te assa" (those pots of gold of yours). "Nivattetum na visahī" means he was unable to turn [Rāhula] back because the Blessed One had said, "Do not turn him back." The seven kinds of noble wealth are:

"The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of shame and fear of wrongdoing,
the wealth of learning, generosity, and wisdom is indeed the seventh wealth."

These are the seven kinds of noble wealth mentioned. "Adhimattaṃ Rāhule" means that when Rāhula went forth, the suffering was even greater than the suffering that arose when Prince Nanda went forth. "Ito pacchā" means that in the days following this occurrence of sorrow, Non-returners (Anāgāmīs) no longer experience thoughts of attachment or aversion toward relatives. In the Pali, the words beginning with "puttapemaṃ" were spoken by King Suddhodana to show the intensity of a father's love for his son. Love for a son is said to "pierce the skin... and remain touching the marrow," because the material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) arising from the force of joy (pīti) co-nascent with oneself shake the entire body. The phrase "attano piyatara" (dearer than oneself) refers to the Blessed One. The word "putte" refers to Rāhula. "Saddahantena" means believing his words without doubt. If there is doubt, an offense (āpatti) is indeed incurred.

## The Explanation of the Story of Rāhula is finished.

## The Explanation of the Story of the Training Rules and Punishment

In the training rules for novices and so forth, "sikkhāpadāni" in the Pali refers to the groups of training. Alternatively, they are the means for attaining the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā). "Pāṇa" (life) in the ultimate sense is the life faculty (jīvitindriya). The act of striking down and overcoming [that life faculty] with weapons and so forth, not allowing it to continue in its sequence, is called "pāṇātipāta." It means the killing of a living being.
115:
In terms of ultimate reality, that pāṇātipāta is the murderous volition (vadhaka-cetanā) that triggers the effort to cut off the life faculty of a living being, while perceiving that being as a living being. Therefore, because it is the cause of enmity, abstinence from killing is called "veramaṇī" because it removes (manati) the evil states (vera) such as killing. Alternatively, it is called "veramaṇī" because one abstains (viramati) by means of it; according to the method of linguistics (nirutti), the abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-virati) is called "veramaṇī." This method applies to the remaining terms such as adinnādāna as well.

Taking what is not given is called adinnādāna; it is simply the volition of theft. "Abrahmacariya" means non-noble conduct; it is the sexual volition (methuna-cetanā) that triggers the practice of the sexual path with a sexual organ. "Musā" means a false matter; the speaking of that false matter, the volition to communicate it as truth while knowing it to be false, is called "musāvāda." Liquor produced from flour, cakes, and so forth, and fermented spirits of various kinds such as those from flowers or fruits, are called "surāmeraya." That same substance is called "majja" (intoxicant) because of its intoxicating nature, and "pamādaṭṭhāna" (ground for heedlessness) because it is the cause of heedlessness. This term is a designation for the volition with which one drinks that intoxicant.

The period from dawn until noon is the time for the meal of the noble ones; any other time is called "vikāla" (the wrong time). In this context, the name "bhojana" (food) refers to all "yāvakālika" (temporary food) because of the sense of being edible. Here, "bhojana" is intended as the act of swallowing, using the method of dropping the subsequent word. Swallowing yāvakālika at the wrong time is called "vikālabhojana." Alternatively, the meaning should be taken as eating or swallowing yāvakālika at the wrong time. In terms of ultimate reality, it is simply the volition to swallow yāvakālika in the afternoon.

A sight that is like a thorn because it is inconsistent with the Dispensation is called "visūkadassana." It is a name for watching and listening to dancing, singing, etc., as well as all forms of games such as quail-fighting and gambling. Here, the word "dassana" (seeing) also includes "savana" (hearing), as it can be subsumed under the term "dassana" due to the nature of the five consciousnesses observing their respective objects. It should be understood that dancing and singing performed by oneself are also included by the words nacca, gīta, and vādita.

"Mālā" (garland) refers to anything worn for the purpose of adornment, whether tied or untied, even if made of thread and so forth. "Gandha" (fragrance) refers to any other kind of fragrance besides scented powders and ointments. "Vilepana" (ointment) refers to fragrances that are ground and used to color the skin. "Dhāraṇa" means wearing. "Maṇḍana" means filling in deficient places. Enjoying [these things] for the sake of fragrance or skin coloring is called "vibhūsana." In the case of garlands and so forth, wearing and so forth...
116:
In the words beginning with mālā (garlands), the terms such as dhāraṇa (wearing) should be applied in order. The primary cause for these acts of wearing, etc., is specifically the intention of transgression (vītikamma-cetanā).

The word uccā is an indeclinable (nipāta) synonymous with the word ucca. A seat or bed that exceeds the standard measurement, such as an āsandi (long chair), is called uccāsayana (high bed). A place spread with unallowable coverings or with a red canopy is called mahāsayana (large bed). Indeed, in these contexts, sitting and sleeping are included in the terms uccāsayana and mahāsayana by eliding the latter part of the compound (uttarapada-lopa). In the phrase jātarūpa-rajata-paṭiggahaṇa (accepting gold and silver), the word rajata (silver) includes all forms of currency (rūpiya) such as wooden tokens (dārumāsaka), etc. It should be understood that pearls, gems, etc., as well as grain, fields, and buildings, are also included here. By the word paṭiggahaṇa (accepting), personal acceptance, causing others to accept, and consenting [to the gift] are included. Nāsanavatthu (grounds for expulsion) refers to the cause for the destruction of the monk's status because it pertains to the level of a pārājika offense.

In the Pāḷi, 'sabbaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ āvaraṇaṃ karonti' means they prohibit entry into the entire monastery. 'Saṅghārāmo āvaraṇaṃ kātabbo' means the monastery should be barred, or a barring should be made in the monastery. For this reason, it is said 'tattha āvaraṇaṃ kātuṃ' using the locative case (bhumma). The same method applies to Pāḷi passages like 'āhāraṃ āvaraṇaṃ'. By the phrase 'yattha vā vasati', it refers to the permanent dwelling place or lodging obtained by a novice according to his seniority (vassagga) or his own property. By the phrase 'yattha vā paṭikkamati', it refers to the dwelling place of the teachers and preceptors (ācariya-upajjhāya). Therefore, it is said 'attano' (one's own), etc. 'Attano' means by oneself, or belonging to the teacher or preceptor. Because one is disciplined by this barring, etc., it is called daṇḍa (punishment). That punishment itself, being an action to be performed, is called daṇḍakamma (disciplinary act), which refers to barring, etc. 'Udakaṃ vā pavesetuṃ' means immersing in water such as a lotus pond.

## The Explanation of the Story of Disciplinary Acts regarding Precepts is finished.

## Explanation of the Story of Barring without Asking, etc.

The phrase 'saddhivihārika-antevāsikānampi' is said with reference to those who are ordained (upasampanna). Indeed, if those teachers and preceptors do not restrain their disciples in the manner they themselves refrain, then other monks must certainly perform the disciplinary act (niggahakamma) such as barring. 'Saṅgaṇhanti' (they win over) means they favor them with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu) such as giving, with the intention: 'I will take them after splitting them from another's group.'
117:
They win them over either through the four bases of sympathy such as giving, or by means of coaxing and enticement, with the intention of splitting and taking over another's group. Whether that other group is split or not, an offense is incurred for every effort (payoga) of the monk who so favors them. 'It is not proper to take by splitting' means both splitting is not proper and taking is not proper. However, it is proper to speak of faults out of respect for the Dispensation (sāsana) or out of compassion for others; it is not proper to speak with a desire for popularity among the group.

By the words 'the acceptance of lodging also ceases (paṭippassambhati)', the interruption of the rains-retreat (vassaccheda) is shown. Even for those ordained, because the novice status—including the taking of refuges—is destroyed due to the commission of a pārājika offense, the acceptance of lodging ceases; it should be understood that they also do not receive the Sangha's gains. By the words 'the refuges are taken again in the first rains (purimā vassa)', it shows the entry into the rains-retreat on that very day along with the taking of the refuges. The words 'the rains-residence gift in the later rains (pacchimā vassa)' merely show the taking of the rains-residence gain. Whether before or after that later rains, a novice who has entered the first rains and whose virtue is not impaired certainly receives the rains-residence robe and the season-robes (kālacīvara) that arise for the Sangha during the robe-months. If it is said 'they are taken in the later rains', it shows the entry into the later rains and the broken rains-retreat. This is because a novice who enters the later rains (or has a broken retreat) does not receive a share of the season-robes. Therefore, it is said 'the gain should be given after asking permission (apaloketvā)'. As for the rains-residence gain, if the donors who are the owners of the lodging say, 'The rains-residence gift should be given even to the novice who stays in our lodging, having entered the later rains and performed his duties for the sake of protecting the lodging,' then it may be given even without asking permission. In the Sāratthadīpanī, it is said: 'He will receive the rains-residence gift in the later rains because he has entered the rains again in the later rains.' If that statement is made based on this intention of the donors regarding the rains-residence robe, it is excellent. However, if it is said with reference to the communal season-robes, it should be understood as inappropriate.

'Without knowing' means that a novice who drinks thinking it is not 'liquor' does not fall into the destruction of all virtues such as abstaining from taking life, nor the destruction of the refuges. However, there is the occurrence of unwholesome states and the breach of the precept of abstaining from intoxicants, just as in the case of wearing garlands, etc. 'The remaining precepts' refers to abstaining from eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana), etc. For even those precepts such as abstaining from eating at the wrong time are broken for one who transgresses them intentionally. Because the precepts other than the one transgressed are not broken, the factors for expulsion (nāsananga) do not occur. For that very reason, the word 'broken' is used in the phrase 'when those [precepts] are broken'.
118:
"He should be made to confess his fault" means that after making him confess in the midst of the Saṅgha, saying, "Venerable sir, a fault has overcome me," and so forth, the refuges and the precepts should be given. This is said because those novices have committed a pārājika offense. Therefore, it is said, "He should be expelled by destroying his outward appearance (liṅga-nāsanā)." Here, only the destruction of the outward appearance (liṅga-nāsanā) is intended. This is stated because speaking dispraise of the Triple Gem and so forth occur together with the causes for the destruction of the outward appearance, such as taking life and so forth.

An objection may be raised: The novice Kaṇṭaka was also one who held wrong views, yet in his case, only expulsion by punishment (daṇḍakamma-nāsanā) was mentioned below. But here, for one with wrong views, expulsion by destroying the outward appearance is mentioned. What is the distinction between these two novices? Keeping this objection in mind, it is said, "one who holds either the eternalist view or the annihilationist view." The meaning here is: if someone firmly clings to and speaks of any eternalist or annihilationist view conceived by sectarians, such as "the self or the sovereign Brahmā is permanent and stable," or "the self will be annihilated and perish," that view of his becomes a ground for pārājika. Such a person should be expelled by destroying the outward appearance. However, if someone does not hold such a view but, being an adherent of the Dispensation, merely misunderstands the meaning of the Buddha's words and continues to speak so without relinquishing it even when exhorted by the monks, his view does not constitute a pārājika. He should be expelled only by the Kaṇṭaka-expulsion (kaṇṭaka-nāsanā).

## The explanation of the story beginning with the case of entering without asking is finished.

## Explanation of the Story of the Eunuch (Paṇḍaka)

In the story of the eunuch, these three—the āsitta-paṇḍaka, the usūya-paṇḍaka, and the pakkha-paṇḍaka—are also individuals with rootless rebirth (ahetuka-paṭisandhi) who possess the nature and physical characteristics of a man. Because of the strength of the eruption of their defilements, they are similar to the neuter eunuch (napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka) and are thus called "eunuchs" (paṇḍaka). Among them, the eruption of defilements in the āsitta-paṇḍaka and the usūya-paṇḍaka can still be prevented from transgression through wise attention and so forth; therefore, it is said that they may be ordained. For the pakkha-paṇḍaka, however, during the dark fortnight, the fever of defilements comes over him like madness, and it only subsides after reaching the point of transgression. Therefore, it is said that he should not be ordained during that fortnight. To show this distinction, the passage beginning with "To whom others..." is stated. In that text, "āsittassa" refers to one's own [semen] poured into the mouth...
119:
The fever is calmed by the emission of semen. "When envy arises" means that when the lustful desire to indulge arises through the power of envy, the fever is calmed by the emission of semen.

Because it is said, "the testicles are removed," if only the male organ is removed while the testicles remain, one does not become a eunuch (paṇḍaka). For a monk, if that organ is removed for a reason other than illness, there is only a grave offense (thullaccaya); he does not, however, become a eunuch. But if the testicles are removed, the male organ also becomes incapable of sexual intercourse through lust; the state of manhood disappears, and the male characteristics such as the beard, as well as the status of a monk, also disappear. The fever of defilements also leads to transgressions that are difficult to prevent, just as in the case of a neuter eunuch. Therefore, teachers say that such a person, even if already ordained, should be expelled (destroyed).

If that is so, why was a pārājika offense not prescribed for the removal of testicles? Regarding this objection, some teachers say, "This was already prescribed by the Blessed One because he said, 'Monks, a eunuch who is not ordained should not be ordained; if he has been ordained, he should be expelled.'" Other teachers, however, say, "Because one does not yet become a eunuch at the moment the testicles are being removed, a pārājika was not prescribed for that moment. That monk whose testicles have been removed later becomes a eunuch in the manner described; he becomes 'one without sexual nature' (abhāvaka), and is no longer a fit basis (vatthu) for monkhood; for that reason, his monkhood disappears. Therefore, from the time he becomes a eunuch, because he becomes similar by birth to a neuter eunuch, he is called 'unfit' (abhabba) in the sense that 'even if he has been ordained, he should be expelled,' but this does not refer to the time before that." They say that even if this person was one with roots (sahetuka), because of the destruction of his nature, he becomes like one without roots (ahetuka), and thus the Path cannot arise for him.

Still other teachers say, "The statement 'if he has been ordained, he should be expelled' refers to one who became a eunuch through effort before being ordained; but if he becomes a eunuch through effort after being ordained, his monkhood does not disappear." But that statement is not proper. For, if one becomes unfit (abhabba) through effort before being ordained, one must also be unfit if it happens afterwards; this should be accepted after careful consideration.

Because this person lacks the state of a woman and so forth, he is called "one without sexual nature" (abhāvaka). In the phrase "going forth is not prohibited," by the word "going forth" (pabbajjā), higher ordination (upasampadā) is also included. Therefore, he said, "In this Dispensation, for whomsoever going forth is prohibited," and so forth. In the phrase "only in that fortnight is his going forth prohibited," however, during the fortnight when he is not a eunuch, he can obtain only the status of a novice; higher ordination (upasampadā) is not allowable even then. It should be understood that when the fortnight in which he is a eunuch arrives, he should be expelled from the Dispensation by destroying his outward appearance.

## The explanation of the story of the eunuch is finished.
120:
## Commentary on the Story of the One Who Lives in Communion by Theft

In the story of the one who lives in communion by theft, 'Kolaññā' refers to those born in a clan, or those well-known and famous in that clan, or it is the name for relatives who know that clan. In this Dispensation, even the mere taking of the monk's appearance with the intent to steal is considered communion (saṃvāsa); therefore, it is said, "There are three types of those who live in communion by theft." 'Na yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vandanaṃ' means not consenting to the salutation of monks or novices. 'Yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vandanaṃ' means consenting to the salutation of monks according to the seniority of years shown by one's own false speech. However, if a junior novice consents to the salutation of senior novices, or a junior monk consents to the salutation of senior monks, he does not become one who lives in communion by theft. 'Imasmiṃ atthe' means in the sense of a thief of communion (saṃvāsa-tthenaka).

The phrase 'bhikkhu-vassāni' (monk years) is stated by the power of the text mentioned regarding the thief of communion; however, one who ordains himself and counts novice years is also a thief of both (ubhaya-tthenaka). Not only a man, but also a woman who conducts herself in this way among bhikkhunīs is a female who lives in communion by theft (theyya-saṃvāsikā). In this matter, even the first-doers (ādikammika) are not exempt. Since the first-doer is mentioned in relation to offenses (āpatti) prescribed only for monks, in this case of communion by theft, the first-doer is also not exempt. In the phrase 'rāja... pe... bhayena' (fear of kings, etc.), the word 'bhaya' (fear) should be understood as connected to each item. 'Yāva so suddhamānaso' means as long as he has a pure mind, without the impure thought, "I will deceive the monks with this appearance and live with them."

Indeed, if the appearance is taken with an impure mind, whether he later lives with the monks or not, he is a thief of the appearance (liṅga-tthenaka). Even if he lives with them later, he does so as one who is ineligible (abhabba) for the Dispensation. Therefore, it should be understood that a thief of both (ubhaya-tthenaka) is included within the thief of appearance (liṅga-tthenaka). If a person takes the appearance with a pure mind due to fear of kings, etc., and while wandering, later develops the impure thought, "I will live by counting monk years," he does not become one who lives in communion by theft by the mere arising of that thought, because the appearance was taken with a pure mind. However, if that person goes to the monks and performs actions such as counting novice years, then he should be regarded as a thief of communion (saṃvāsa-tthenaka) or a thief of both (ubhaya-tthenaka). The statement made later regarding the laying down of the burden (confession), "This person is also one who lives in communion by theft," refers to the laying down of the burden by way of consenting to communion by associating with monks. Therefore, it is said, "As long as he does not consent to communion." It should be understood that until then, he cannot be called one who lives in communion by theft. In this context also—
121:
Because he has a pure mind, if he takes the appearance with an impure mind, whether he later associates with monks or not, he is a thief of appearance (liṅga-tthenaka). Even if he associates later, he does so as one who is ineligible; thus, it should be understood that a thief of both (ubhaya-tthenaka) is included only within the thief of appearance (liṅga-tthenaka). If a person takes the appearance with a pure mind due to fear of kings, etc., and while wandering, later develops the impure intention, "I will live by counting monk years," he does not yet become one who lives in communion by theft by the mere intention. This is because he took the appearance with a pure mind. If that person goes to the monks and performs actions such as counting novice years, then he becomes a thief of communion (saṃvāsa-tthenaka) or a thief of both (ubhaya-tthenaka). The statement "With the laying down of the burden (confession), this person is also one who lives in communion by theft" is said with reference to the laying down of the burden by way of consenting to communion through associating with monks. Therefore, it should be understood in connection that as long as he does not consent to communion, he is not called one who lives in communion by theft.

In this teaching, even if one takes the appearance not because of fear of thieves, etc., but with the intention of playing, and while showing the guise of a monk in the presence of monks, he does not consent to salutation, etc., or if he takes it with a pure mind, thinking, "Does the monk's appearance look good on me?" etc., he should be noted as not being one who lives in communion by theft.

'Sabba-pāsaṇḍiya-bhattāni' refers to meals that are made common to all those of various beliefs. Since communion (saṃvāsa) could occur when taking meals intended only for monks, it is called a meal common to all. Even if one eats monastery meals in places where there are no monks, without consenting to communion, he does not become one who lives in communion by theft. 'Kammantānuṭṭhānena' means by performing work such as plowing. 'Patta-cīvaraṃ ādāya' means by carrying them on the body in the guise of a monk.

"One who wears [the robes] in this way is called one who lives in communion by theft" is merely an illustration. In fact, even if he does not know the name "one who lives in communion by theft," if he knows, "It is not proper to do this," or "By doing this, one does not become a true monk," or "If I tell them, they will discard me," or "By any means, ordination is not valid for me," then he is one who lives in communion by theft. If a person initially thinks, "I have taken the state of a monk," and merely does not speak because he is ashamed to show a defect such as wearing white clothes, he is not one who lives in communion by theft. In the phrase 'anupasampanna-kāleyeva' (only during the time of being unordained), by the word of emphasis (eva), it shows that if he knows the characteristics of one who lives in communion by theft at the time he is a bhikkhu and does not report it out of deception, he is still not one who lives in communion by theft. Because he took the appearance with a pure mind, he is not a thief of appearance (liṅga-tthenaka); and because he has attained full ordination and consents only to the communion that is appropriate for that ordination, he is not a thief of communion (saṃvāsa-tthenaka). A novice, however, is a thief of appearance because he has taken the appearance that is worthy of communion; and by the mere consenting to communion, he becomes a thief of communion.

'Saliṅge ṭhito' means staying in one's own appearance. "He is not one who lives in communion by theft" means he is not a thief of appearance because he has not abandoned the appearance given by the monks, and he is not a thief of communion because he has not abandoned the claim to be a monk. The reason stated in the Mātikā Commentary, "He is not a thief of communion because he consents to the communion that corresponds to his appearance," is also said with reference to this very reason.
122:
If it were not so, and if it were taken in a manner consistent with the appearance, then even for a novice (sāmaṇera), because he delights only in the communion (saṃvāsa) consistent with the appearance in matters such as the counting of the monk's years (seniority), he would not become a saṃvāsatthenaka (communion-thief). Why is that? Because the appearance given by the monks is common to both monks and novices. Just as a monk in this context does not become a saṃvāsatthenaka when he gives up the training, so too it should be understood that one who has committed a pārājika offense does not become a saṃvāsatthenaka because he has not abandoned his claim to be a novice. The phrase "accepting that it is beautiful" means laying down the burden of wearing the saffron robes and accepting the status of a layman.

The phrase "any person who ordains when old" is said with reference to a novice. "In the mahāpeḷā, etc." refers to specific types of alms-bowls or vessels placed at the doors of houses made of bamboo strips and so on. By this statement, it shows the non-performance of counting years (seniority) and so forth together with the monks in the monastery.

## The Explanation of the Story of the Communion-Thief is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Story of One Who Has Gone Over to a Sect

In the discussion of the titthiyapakkantaka and so forth, the phrase "merely taking their appearance" means merely wearing the appearance on the body with the decision "I will become a sect-member (titthiya)", without any intention such as testing or investigating. "By himself" means wearing garments made of kusa grass and so on by himself even within the monastery grounds, without going to the sect-members. "I will become an ājīvaka... he goes" means going to the ājīvakas with the intention "I will become an ājīvaka" according to their method of ordination. Although that monk has the decision to reach the status of a sect-member, because he thinks "I will go and become one", only an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is stated for every step. Although dukkaṭa is not explicitly mentioned in the Pāḷi text, it is stated because it is consistent with the dukkaṭa of preliminary effort (pubbappayoga) mentioned in cases such as sexual intercourse. By this, it should be understood that if one accepts the appearance by way of decision, it is a pārājika; in the effort prior to that acceptance, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is stated. A monk who turns back and regrets at the moment of the thullaccaya can be freed from the offense by confessing it. Just as in this case of titthiyapakkantaka, so too in the cases of causing a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda) and causing a Buddha to bleed (lohituppāda), the boundary of being freed from dukkaṭa, thullaccaya, and pārājika in the preliminary efforts of monks should be understood. Because it is contrary to the Dispensation (Sāsana), no "no-offense" (anāpatti) is stated even for the first-doers (ādikammika) in these cases of titthiyapakkantaka and so forth. However, to show the state of being ineligible for ordination, these cases of titthiyapakkantaka, saṅghabhedaka, and lohituppādaka, as well as others like mātughātaka (matricide), are stated here in the Abhabbakaṇḍa (Section on the Ineligible) without showing them as pārājika etc. by a separate training rule in the Pārājika chapter.
123:
The phrase "that view" is said with reference only to taking the state of the sect-member's appearance as being superior. Indeed, even if one holds the eternalist (sassata) view of those sect-members, if he does not accept the appearance (marks), he does not become a titthiyapakkantaka. Even without taking that view, if he accepts the appearance thinking "The practices and conduct of these people are good," he indeed becomes a titthiyapakkantaka. "Due to the absence of the view" means due to the absence of the view that leads to becoming a sect-member because of his attachment to the state of a monk. By this statement, it shows that for a monk who wears garments of kusa grass etc. during times of danger, there is no offense, just as for a naked monk.

"Stated by an ordained monk"—in this context, the saṅghabhedaka (schism-maker) is also stated only by an ordained monk; however, it should be noted that mātughātaka (matricide) and so forth are stated even by unordained persons (laypeople or novices).

## The Explanation of the Story of One Who Has Gone Over to a Sect is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Story of the Animal

The phrase "water-dwelling, frog-eating serpent body" should be connected. "Vissarabhayena" means due to the fear that the monk might cry out or scream upon seeing the serpent's body. A serpent's body does not appear during the "monkey-sleep" (kapimiddha) and so forth; wishing to show the limit of the appearance of that serpent body, he said "vissaṭṭho" (relaxed) and so on.

## The Explanation of the Story of the Animal is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Story of Matricide, etc.

Apavāhana means cleansing. Compared to non-human births such as animals, only in those of human birth are qualities like loving-kindness (mettā) towards children sharp and clear, like supramundane qualities (lokuttara-guṇa); therefore, he said "the mother who is a human female, the progenitor." Just as the occurrence of wholesome states (kusala) is sharp and clear only for humans, so too is the occurrence of unwholesome states (akusala); therefore, he said "even by himself, being of human birth" and so on. In the word "ānantariyena" (by immediate karma), the result of rebirth in hell immediately after death is called anantara; that which is joined with the state of being the progenitor in that immediate rebirth is called ānantariya. It occurs through that ānantariya karma. The phrase "son of a prostitute" is merely an illustration (upalakkhaṇa); even the son of a high-born woman who commits adultery, if he kills his father without knowing him, he is indeed a pitughātaka (patricide).
124:
"Avasesa" refers to those starting from the Non-returner (Anāgāmin). All that should be said regarding this killing of an Arahant (arahantaghātaka) has already been stated in the [commentary on] the Pārājika concerning human beings (Manussaviggaha Pārājika).

The phrase "This person is a schismatic" is said with reference to a monk of normal status (pakatatta). Even if one who has already incurred a Pārājika or whose ordination is invalid due to a defect in the object (vatthuvipatti) etc. splits the Saṅgha, he does not incur the heinous crime (anantariya-kamma). However, the Saṅgha is indeed split. It should be understood that his status as a novice is also not prohibited.

The meaning already stated as "with a corrupt mind" is clarified as "with the intent to kill." "Causes blood to flow" means that because the Tathāgata's body is of such a nature that it cannot be destroyed by enemies, no one can use force to cut the skin etc. and cause blood to flow externally. However, due to being struck by a weapon etc., the blood moves from its original place and, being disturbed, collects in one spot. By this much, the one who strikes, like Devadatta, is called a "shedder of blood" (lohituppādaka). For one who destroys a Cetiya, a Bodhi tree, or an image, although it is not an anantariya-kamma, it is a great fault similar to an anantariya-kamma. However, a dry branch that saps the vitality of the Bodhi tree, or a branch that is damaging a Cetiya containing relics, should be cut. In such cutting, only merit is produced.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Matricide etc. is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Case of a Hermaphrodite

"Female hermaphrodite" (itthī-ubhatobyañjanaka) means a hermaphrodite endowed with the female faculty (itthindriya). The other kind is endowed with the male faculty (purisindriya). Both faculties do not arise simultaneously in one person, as this is rejected in the Yamaka. The second sign (organ), however, arises without the faculty, due only to unwholesome consciousness accompanied by kamma. Even for normal women and men, kamma alone is the cause of the signs and gender characteristics. The faculty is not the cause, as the Paṭṭhāna does not state that faculty as a condition.

The commentaries state "depending on the female faculty, female signs etc. arise" only to show the occurrence of signs in those who possess the faculty. But here, it is meant that due to the power of unwholesome kamma, signs can arise even without the faculty. In both types of hermaphrodites, when lust for a woman arises, the male sign becomes manifest and the other (female) sign is hidden. When lust for a man arises, at that time...
125:
...the female sign becomes manifest and the other (male) sign is hidden. In that context, "vicāraṇakkamo" (the sequence of investigation) is the sequence of investigating the meaning in order to show the inappropriateness of the statement in the Kurundī which explains the manifestation of female and male signs at the very moment of rebirth. Indeed, in the Atthasālinī, it is stated: "Female signs etc. arise having proceeded depending on the female faculty." The connection is "He has no novicehood." If a monk ordains someone as a novice or a monk knowing them to be an ineligible person (abhabba) who is rejected, or an eligible person (bhabba) [who is restricted, such as one with severed hands], he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). It should be understood that for a monk who does not know, there is no offense regarding any of these persons.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Case of a Hermaphrodite is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Case of One Without a Preceptor etc.

In the cases of those without a preceptor etc., the phrase "the training rule was not yet laid down" is said with reference to the training rule that is about to be laid down in this very Pabbajjākkhandhaka: "Monks, one without a preceptor should not be ordained." The phrase "The act (kamma), however, is not invalid" is said because even if there is no preceptor, the preceptor is mentioned in all the Kammavācās by using the name of a deceased preceptor, or a former preceptor who has disrobed, or any other non-existent person, saying: "This person named so-and-so is a candidate for ordination from the Saṅgha, with the preceptor named so-and-so." If the preceptor were not mentioned, there would be a failure of the act (kammavipatti), which is described as "not referring to a person." Therefore, it is called "anupajjhāyaka" (without a preceptor) in the Pali. In its commentary as well, it is not said "without reciting the preceptor's name," but the meaning is given as "without having the candidate take a preceptor, being entirely devoid of a preceptor in every way." 

In the Pali, "with the Saṅgha as preceptor" means reciting the Saṅgha itself as the preceptor in the Kammavācā thus: "This person named so-and-so is a candidate for ordination from the Saṅgha; this person named so-and-so requests ordination from the Saṅgha, with the Saṅgha as preceptor." Similarly, in the phrase "with a group (gaṇa) as preceptor," the connection should be understood as: "This person named so-and-so is a candidate for ordination from the group," and so on. Even when said in this way, the act is not invalid, as only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated. Otherwise, it would say, "And that person is not ordained." Therefore, He said "saṅghena" etc. In that context, among the acts performed with preceptors such as eunuchs (paṇḍaka), if the quorum of a group of five etc. is completed excluding the eunuch etc., the act is not invalid; otherwise, it should be understood that it is invalid.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Case of One Without a Preceptor etc. is Finished.
126:
## Explanation of the Story of Those Without Alms-bowls, etc.

Regarding the cases of those without alms-bowls and robes, even if the bowl and robes are absent, because it is recited in the formal act (kammavācā) that "he is complete with bowl and robes," it is not stated as a failure of the formal act (kammakopa), but only a dukkaṭa offense is declared. Alternatively, because of the deficiency in the recitation of the kammavācā, it would indeed be a failure of the act.

Some teachers say: "Just like those ordained by the first authorized kammavācā, even now, if one is ordained by a kammavācā without saying 'he is complete with bowl and robes,' the ordination is still valid." This statement is not appropriate. Because from the time of authorization onwards, not using the prescribed words is indeed a failure due to deficiency in the recitation, just like the deficiency in the phrase "Such-and-such a person requests ordination from the Saṅgha."

That phrase "Such-and-such a person requests ordination from the Saṅgha" was also authorized later. If a monk ordains someone without the request "Venerable Sir, I request ordination from the Saṅgha," but says "This such-and-such a person requests ordination from the Saṅgha" when performing the kammavācā, the act is well-performed; if he performs it without saying so, it fails. At the very end, it is not proper to omit anything from the authorized kammavācā; it is simply a deficiency in the recitation. The connection is "Other monks also wish to give."

"Anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapāta" refers to alms-food from which the first portion has not yet been taken by monks. In the term "sāmaṇerabhāgasamako," although there is no separate "novice's portion" because novices are given an equal share of material gifts, this is said to show that these candidates (paṇḍupalāsa) are like novices because their going forth is connected only to the preparation of the bowl and robes. This portion is given only to one whose going forth is certain and imminent. Therefore, it is said "until the bowl is fired," etc.

"Āmisabhāga" refers to the Saṅgha-meal offered at the monastery and the material gifts arising there; it does not refer to gifts offered by donors at their homes. Therefore, ticket-food (salāka-bhatta), etc., is excluded, saying "donors might become remorseful." By the word "bhesajja" (medicine), etc., it shows that the fault of providing medical treatment to laypeople does not occur here.

## The Explanation of the Story of Those Without Alms-bowls, etc., is Finished.
127: ## Explanation of the Stories of Those with Severed Hands, etc. In the stories of those with severed hands, etc., the phrase 'at the base of the ear' (kaṇṇamūle) is said with reference to the severing of the entire ear. 'Of the ear-flap' (kaṇṇasakkhalikāya) means the edge of the ear. 'To whom the ear is pierced' (yassa kaṇṇāviddha) is said with reference to the hole for wearing earrings, etc., below. That hole is not suitable for joining. 'At the tip of the nasal bone like a goat's foot' (ajapadake) means at the tip of the nasal bone resembling a goat's foot. Above that tip of the nasal bone like a goat's foot, it does not sever. The phrase 'it is possible to join' is said with reference to joining without disfigurement; joining that results in disfigurement causes one to be a spoiler of the assembly. 'One with a crooked body' (khujjasarīro) means one with a bent body. The Blessed One, whose body is straight like that of a Brahmā, is called 'brahmujjugatta' (one with a body straight like Brahmā). 'Parivaṭuma' means one whose body is rounded all around; by this, he shows that such dwarfs are not suitable (for ordination). 'One with a head full of lumps of flesh' (kūṭakūṭasīso) is expressed with repetition (āmeḍita) to show the state of having lumps of flesh in many places. Therefore, he said 'with a head like a cluster of palm fruits'; a cluster of palm fruits is called 'piṇḍi.' 'With a head that is gradually tapering' (anupubbatanukena sīsena) means with a head that is gradually thin like the pinnacle of a pagoda. One endowed with a head that is uniformly thick and high from the beginning to the end like a thick bamboo node is called 'nāḷisīsa.' 'Kappasīsa' means one whose head is split into two like the frontal lobes of an elephant. The explanation of the phrase 'or hair like an earring' (kaṇṇikākeso vā) is 'by insects,' etc. Intending the growth of hair even on the forehead as on a monkey's forehead, he said 'with head-hairs,' etc. 'One with monkey-eyebrows' (makkaṭabhamuko) means one whose eyebrows cannot be distinguished from the forehead hairs. 'With eye-orbs' (akkhicakkalehi) means with the black circles of the eyes. 'Kekara' means one who looks askance. 'Water-star' (udakatārakā) means the reflection of those who look into the water; some teachers say 'water-bubble.' 'Eye-star' (akkhitārakā) means the shadow of those standing in front; they also call it 'eye-socket.' 'One with very pale eyes' (atipingalakkhi) means one with pale eyes like a cat's eyes. 'Madhupingala' means having a pale color like the color of honey. In the word 'one without eyelashes' (nipphakhumakkhi), the word 'pakhuma' is well-known for eyelashes; because of the absence of those eyelashes, one is called 'nipphakhumakkhi.' 'By eye-disease' (akkhipākena) means by a disease of the eyelid margins that leads to a state of putrefaction.
128:
Cipiṭanāsika means one with a flat (non-prominent) nose. Paṭaṅgamaṇḍūka refers to a large-mouthed frog. Bhinnamukha means one whose mouth is open at the end [of an action], or one whose mouth is always open. Vaṅkamukha means one whose lower jaw is shifted to one side. Oṭṭhacchinnaka means one who has had flesh removed from somewhere on both lips, either from birth or later by a knife or similar instrument. Eḷamuka means one whose mouth is constantly dribbling saliva.

Bhinnagala means one with a bent neck. Bhinna-ura means one with a very sunken middle of the chest. Bhinnapiṭṭhi (deformed back) is also the same. All this is said with reference to "Kacchugatta" (scabby-bodied) and so on. Since the decision here has already been stated regarding leprosy (kuṭṭha) and so on, it says "Viniccayo" (the decision) and so forth.

Vātaṇḍika means one who has a swollen scrotum due to the disease of orchitis; even if covered by the undergarment, the swelling is apparent, and such a person should not be ordained. Vikaṭa means one with splayed feet; when walking on a walkway, the knees go outwards. Paṇha means one with backward-turned feet; when walking on a walkway, the knees go inwards. Mahājaṅgha means one with large calves. Mahāpāda means one endowed with large soles of the feet. Pādavemajjhe means in the middle of the back of the foot; by this, it shows that the toes and the heel are similar.

"Majjhe saṅkuṭitapādatta" explains the reason for having bow-like feet. "Agge saṅkuṭitapādatta" explains the bird-like gait due to bow-like feet. "Piṭṭhipādaggena caṅkamanto" (walking on the upper part of the foot) refers to walking on both the outer and inner edges of the soles of the feet.

Mammana means one whose speech has improper syllables due to the lack of purity in the places and instruments of articulation. Because of the imitation of speech, he is called a stammerer (mammana). Even one who, though endowed with proper articulation, repeats a single syllable like the sound "hi" many times, is also included here. However, if a person can suppress the "hi" sound and speak smoothly without repeated syllables, he should be ordained.

"Āpattito na muccati" means only one who acts knowingly is not free from the offense. There is no offense for a monk who, against his will, gives physical consent due to dangers such as a threat to life. "Appatto osāraṇaṃ" means he is unfit for rehabilitation (osāraṇā).

## The explanation of the cases of severed hands and so on is finished.
129:
## Explanation of the Case of Dependence on a Shameless Monk

In the cases connected with dependence (nissaya), one who has a share of qualities such as views and virtue similar to the monks is called bhikkhusabhāga; the state of being one who has a share similar to those monks is called bhikkhusabhāgatā.

## The explanation of the case of dependence on a shameless monk is finished.

## Explanation of the Case of Dependence for Travelers and So On

In the term "Nissayakaraṇīya", taking dependence is called nissaya; it should be understood that the qualifier is placed at the end, meaning "one for whom that taking of dependence is a duty." In the phrase "Vivāsā vā... anāpatti", there is no offense because of the effort to travel; just as a monk traveling while a teacher is present commits no offense, so too it means there is no offense if there is no teacher in that place. By this, it shows that an offense is committed by a monk who stays depending on the sufficiency of lodgings and so on without any hardship. It is said that such an offense is committed daily due to the reason of not traveling. Even if sent by teachers for tasks such as dyeing robes, one should stay only until the task is completed, and not beyond that. It should be understood that teachers should send young monks who love virtue only for temporary tasks, not for permanent ones. Since it is said, "For one going by boat... there is no offense," it should be understood that except for such uncontrollable circumstances, it is not proper to enter the Vassa in a place where there is no teacher to give dependence.

"Tassa nissāya" means depending on that [teacher]. In the sentence "In the month of Āsāḷha... one should go to that place," if the day for entering the Vassa occurs while waiting, thinking "this named Elder will come here, will come here," then so be it; without entering the Vassa in the place where one is staying, one should go to a place where dependence can be obtained, even if it is far, and enter the later Vassa (pacchimikā vassa).

"Gottenapi" means also by the clan name, without mentioning the name, such as "the candidate for ordination of the Venerable Pippali." By this, the fact is clear that when asked "What is your preceptor's name?", the candidate should say "Venerable Kassapa" by the clan name. Therefore, whether it be some other well-known name or a name designated at that moment for ease of recognition, the formal act (kammavācā) should be recited using all those.
130: Just as the name of the preceptor is recited, so too should the name of the candidate for ordination be recited, whether by clan name (gotta) or by a name given at that moment, during the proclamation of the Kammavācā. At that moment, the monks who assign a name such as "This person is named Tissa" or "named Nāga" should do so before the appointment of the instructor (anusāsaka). Even if this is not done, at the time of instructing and questioning regarding the obstructive factors (antarāyika-dhamma), the monk who makes it known, saying, "What is your name? Sir, my name is Nāga. What is your preceptor's name? Sir, my preceptor's name is Tissa," etc., should ensure that the perception "This is my name" arises in the minds of both the candidate and the preceptor. If, however, one speaks with the original name (pakati-nāma) at that moment and later proclaims the Kammavācā with a new name like Tissa, it is not proper. In that proclamation, even if the preceptor's name is not specifically taken but the person is referred to as "Tissa's candidate for ordination," etc., the act is well-performed, just like the ordination act of those without a preceptor; for even if there is no preceptor or if the person is unsuitable (abhabba), the act is successful if the person is referred to by the Kammavācā. However, if the candidate's own name is omitted and the Kammavācā is proclaimed with another name, the act fails; that person remains unordained. This is because the person whose name was taken is not present there, and the name of this candidate was not spoken in the proclamation, making him like any other unordained person or novice present in the boundary. Therefore, a monk who wishes to change the candidate's original name and proclaim it sequentially as Nāga, etc., must first make it known, saying "You are named Nāga," etc. Then, at the moment of questioning regarding the instruction and obstructive factors, he should make it clear to both the candidate and the Saṅgha before proclaiming the name as Nāga, etc. If one person has many names, it is proper to take one of them. The name taken for the candidate and the preceptor in one place must be the same name used in the motion (ñatti) and in all the proclamations (anussāvana). For if a name other than the one taken is used, the phrasing (byañjana) is considered broken, and the act fails. Only the motion and proclamations that are not divergent in meaning and phrasing are proper. Regarding the preceptor's name, there is no fault whether the word "Āyasmanta" (Venerable) is added in all places before the name, such as "Āyasmato Tissassa," or if it is not added. Although in the Pali text, the word "Āyasmato" is placed after the name as "itthannāmassa āyasmato," [it continues...] "Āyasmā Sāriputto..."
131:
...since the usage of the word "Āyasmanta" before the name is seen in such phrases as "Āyasmā Sāriputto atthakusalo," its usage before the name is more appropriate. Even if that word "Āyasmanta" is used in one place and not in another, or used before the name in one place and after it in another, it does not constitute a deficiency in the proclamation because the name itself has not been omitted. For this very reason, it is said that in the Pali text, after using it in one place as "itthannāmassa āyasmato," it is not used in phrases such as "itthannāmena upajjhāyena." Despite such views, it should be understood that proclaiming the Kammavācā by either using it or not using it in a uniform manner in all places is more commendable.

## The explanation of the story regarding the requirements (nissaya) for travelers, etc., is finished.

## Explanation of the story regarding two candidates for ordination, etc.

"Ekānussāvana" (single proclamation) refers to those candidates for whom the Kammavācā is proclaimed at the same time, in a single moment. To perform the ordination for such candidates with a single proclamation. Therefore, it was said: "To perform with a single proclamation" (ekānussāvane kātuṃ). This term "ekānussāvane" should be understood as a single word without dropping the case ending. "Or by one" (ekena vါ) means that when proclaiming for two candidates at the same moment with a single Kammavācā, it is done by a single teacher. The method of a single teacher proclaiming for two candidates at the same moment should be understood in this way: "This Buddharakkhita and this Dhammarakkhita are the candidates for ordination of the Venerable Saṅgharakkhita," etc. In this same way, the proclamation by a single teacher for three candidates at the same moment should be understood.

To perform the proclamation together according to the previous method means that, as previously stated in the method "one for one, another for the other," etc., two candidates are ordained by two teachers, or three by three teachers, or a single teacher performs the proclamation for all three together. In doing so, however, there must be only one preceptor. The phrase "but not with different preceptors" (na tveva nānupajjhāyena) is a prohibitive statement meaning it is not proper for a single teacher to perform the ordination for two or three candidates of two or three different preceptors at the same moment with a single proclamation. It is not that it is improper to perform the ordination for three candidates with different teachers and different preceptors. Therefore, it was said: "If, however, there are different teachers and different preceptors... it is proper."
132:
In this context, the statement "Elder Tissa is the co-resident of Elder Sumana, Elder Sumana is the co-resident of Elder Tissa," referring to the preceptors making the announcement (anussāvana) for each other's co-residents, is merely an illustration (upalakkhaṇa). Therefore, if Elder Tissa announces for Elder Sumana's co-resident, and Elder Sumana announces for Elder Nanda's co-resident, and they each complete the quorum (gaṇapūraka), it is indeed permissible. However, if the preceptor himself announces for his own co-resident, there is no need for further discussion; the formal act is well-performed. If ordination (upasampadā) can occur for a candidate without a preceptor when announced by any monk, how much more so should it be understood when the preceptor himself announces for a candidate who has a preceptor? For this reason, to show the impermissible side, the phrase "Sace pana" (But if...) and so forth was stated.

## The explanation of the story beginning with two candidates for ordination is finished.

## Explanation of the Procedure for Ordination

The word "Upajjhā" is shown to be an "ā-ending" word with the same meaning as "Upajjhāya". Alternatively, it is said that in the word "Upajjhāya", the letter "ya" is dropped in the accusative and nominative cases to form "Upajjhā"; it should be noted that the word "Upajjhā" is not used in the instrumental case and so on. In the Pali, "one should designate oneself by oneself" means that oneself as the agent and instrument should perform the act of designation towards oneself as the object. Or, the word "attānaṃ" is an accusative used in the sense of the nominative, meaning "one should be designated by oneself". This is not only here; in other instances such as the thirteen designations (sammuti), etc., by this same principle, one should indeed be designated by oneself. However, because one is the object of the formal act, the group (gaṇa) such as the group of four (catuvagga), etc., excluding oneself, is required in all cases.

"Saccakāla" (time of truth) refers to the time when you should desire only the truth, abandoning the deception of "I will hide it". "Bhūtakāla" (time of reality) refers to the time when, even without deception, the truth of the matter such as being human must necessarily be desired; otherwise, there is the intention that obstacles such as the failure of the formal act (kammakopa) may occur. "Maṅku" means with a downcast face. "Uddharatu" means let him establish [the candidate] in the state of higher ordination from the state of not being ordained.

To ensure proficiency in the meaning of all formal ritual texts (kammavācā), the meaning of this higher ordination ritual text should be understood as follows: "Suṇātu" (let [the Saṅgha] listen) is the third person singular in the sense of an injunction to listen.
133:
The word "suṇātu" is the third person singular in the sense of an injunction to listen. By this word "suṇātu", the Saṅgha is urged toward the act of listening. Although it should be said as "suṇāhi" in the second person singular because the Saṅgha is present, the use of the third person when associated with the word "Saṅgha" is the practice of grammarians. For example, "May the Blessed One Gotama accept my meal" (Adhivāsetu me bhavaṃ Gotamo), "It is time, O Sugata, for the Blessed One to prescribe the training rules for the disciples" (Etassa sugata kālo, yaṃ Bhagavā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeyya), "May the venerable one proceed" (Pakkamatāyasmā), "May the venerable ones listen to me" (Suṇantu me āyasmanto), and so on. Therefore, the third person is used here. Alternatively, it is said thus out of respect. Indeed, towards those in positions of respect, even where the second person should arise, the third person is used out of respect, as in "May the Sugata teach the Dhamma" (Desetu sugato dhammaṃ) and so forth.

Some teachers say that the third person is used here in consideration of the words "Bhante" and "Āvuso", but that is not appropriate. This is because even when those words "Bhante" and "Āvuso" are present, the second person is seen to be used, as in "Venerable Sir, be my teacher" (Ācariyo me bhante hohi), "Come, friend Upāli, question this monk" (Inghāvuso Upāli, imaṃ pabbajitaṃ anuyuñjāhi), and so forth.

"Me" is the genitive case used by the one making the announcement to refer to himself. "Bhante" is a respectful address used for seniors. The word "Āvuso" is an address for juniors. Both of these are indeclinables (nipāta) because their form does not change even in the plural, as in "Tumhe bhante" and "Tumhe āvuso". "Saṅgho" generally refers to a collection of persons of natural status (pakatatta), such as a group of four (catuvagga) and so on. However, here, it should be taken as a Saṅgha starting from a group of five (pañcavagga) in border regions, and starting from a group of ten (dasavagga) in the middle regions. The summary of this sentence is: "Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to my words." This is the speech to be spoken by a junior. However, if the announcer (anussāvaka) is senior to all the monks, he should say, "Suṇātu me, āvuso, saṅgho" (Friends, let the Saṅgha listen to me). Even if that senior says "Bhante", or a junior says "Āvuso", there is no failure of the formal act (kammakopa). Some teachers say there is no fault even if one says "Āvuso" in one place and "Bhante" in another, because the sense of address is accomplished by both.

Now, to show what matter he wishes to make known by urging the Saṅgha to listen with "suṇātu", he said "Ayaṃ itthannāmo" (This person named so-and-so) and so forth. In that statement:
134:
The word "ayaṃ" (this) indicates the presence of the candidate for higher ordination within the hatthapāsa (forearm's length). Because of this word "ayaṃ," it is established that only a candidate standing within the hatthapāsa can attain the status of a monk. This is because one who stands outside the hatthapāsa cannot be referred to as "ayaṃ" (this person). For this reason, when appointing [a monk] to instruct the candidate, the word "ayaṃ" is not used because the candidate is then standing outside the hatthapāsa. Therefore, the novice who is the candidate for higher ordination must be placed within the hatthapāsa. In the phrase "ayaṃ itthannāmo" (this person named so-and-so), the word "ayaṃ" must certainly be used. It should be understood that this word "ayaṃ" is to be used only during this first mention of the name. The term "itthannāmo" is an indefinite way of indicating the candidate's name. By both [words], the name is shown, such as "ayaṃ Buddharakkhito" (this [person] Buddharakkhita). The word "upasampadāpekkho" is a bahubbīhi compound in the sense of bhinnādhikaraṇa. It means "one who desires higher ordination from the Saṅgha." To show the connection with the candidate's preceptor (upajjhāya), the phrase "itthannāmassa āyasmato" (of the venerable so-and-so) is spoken. By this, the meaning is shown along with the connection of the name in this manner: "This Buddharakkhita, who is the saddhivihārika of the Venerable Dhammarakkhita, desires higher ordination." In this sentence, it is also permissible to say "ayaṃ Buddharakkhito Dhammarakkhitassa upasampadāpekkho" without mentioning the word "āyasmato." For this reason, in the Pali text, the word "āyasmato" is not mentioned in the phrase "itthannāmena upajjhāyena." What needs to be said here has already been stated below.

In this case, should the preceptor not also be required to be within the hatthapāsa, just like the candidate? If so, why is the word "ima" (this) not used when referring to the preceptor, as in "ayaṃ itthannāmo imassa itthannāmassa upasampadāpekkho"? There is no contradiction here. This is because even if the preceptor is absent, the formal act (kamma) is not invalidated. Indeed, for the sake of completing the formal act, the name of an absent preceptor is recited by the power of the existing words, even in cases such as the ordination of a candidate who has no preceptor present. Therefore, since the formal act is accomplished merely by referring to the preceptor even if he is not nearby, it is not appropriate to refer to him as "imassa" (of this one).

"Parisuddho antarāyikehi dhammehi" (pure from obstructive qualities) means being free from obstructive conditions that make one an unsuitable subject (avatthu) for higher ordination, such as being an "unfit person" (abhabba-puggala), as well as from obstructive conditions that merely cause an offense, such as having the five diseases or being one whose hands are cut off. Only when stated in this way does the higher ordination take effect, even if one is not free from obstructions that merely cause an offense, such as the five diseases; otherwise, it does not. "Paripuṇṇassa pattacīvaraṃ" means that the bowl and robes are complete for this candidate. Only when stated in this way does the higher ordination take effect even for a candidate whose bowl and robes are not complete; otherwise, it does not. Upasampadaṃ...
135:
The phrase "upasampadaṃ yācati" (requests higher ordination) refers to the act of requesting, as in "Venerable Sir, I request higher ordination from the Saṅgha." Even if the person does not request it from the Saṅgha himself, the formal act is successful and not invalidated only if it is said, "Such-and-such a person requests higher ordination from the Saṅgha"; otherwise, it is not successful. "Upajjhāyena" means that with such-and-such a person as the preceptor (the instrument), he requests the Saṅgha (the agent) to complete the granting of higher ordination (the object). Since the root yāc (to request) is a bitransitive verb, two objects are mentioned: "saṅghaṃ" and "upasampadaṃ."

In the phrase "yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ," because there is a suitable time for this formal act, it is called "pattakāla" (the time has arrived). This refers to the four types of formal acts of the Saṅgha, such as apalokana (announcement). This same "pattakāla" is expressed as "pattakallaṃ" by adding the suffix -ya in its own meaning. Here, however, the ñatticatuttha (motion-and-three-proclamations) formal act for higher ordination is intended; it is the suitable time for the Saṅgha to perform that act. The word "yadi" (if) makes known the suitability of the time for the formal act by obtaining the consent of the Saṅgha. This is because if there is any monk who considers it unsuitable, he will speak up in objection. Intending this very meaning, it is stated in the proclamations (anussāvana) of the kammavācā: "To whichever venerable one it is pleasing... let that one speak." That pattakalla (suitability) is comprised of these five factors: vatthu-sampadā (completeness of the candidate), purity from obstructive qualities (antarāyika-dhamma), sīmā-sampadā (completeness of the boundary), parisa-sampadā (completeness of the assembly), and the completion of preliminary duties (pubbakicca).

Among these five factors, vatthu-sampadā refers to a male human being who is other than the eleven types of "unfit persons" (abhabba-puggala) already mentioned or those who have committed a pārājika offense, and who is a full twenty years of age, whether a layman or a novice. Only when such a person is present is this formal act of higher ordination by the Saṅgha called pattakalla; if such a person is not present, it is not. Even if performed, it is simply invalid.

Purity from obstructive qualities (antarāyika-dhamma) refers to the candidate for higher ordination being free from the faults prohibited by the Blessed One, starting from having the five diseases and ending with not having parental permission, as well as faults such as having hands cut off. These faults are called "obstructive" (antarāyika) because they cause obstructions such as offenses for the Saṅgha performing the formal act. Only when there is freedom from such obstructions is this formal act called pattakalla; otherwise, it is not. Except for the case of a person under twenty years of age, a formal act performed [in other cases of minor obstructions] is indeed well-performed.
136:
The perfection of the boundary (sīmāsampadā) should be understood by way of the two types of boundaries—the fixed boundary (baddha-sīmā) and the unfixed boundary (abaddha-sīmā)—which are free from all defects, as will be explained in the Uposathakkhandhaka. Only when such a boundary exists is this formal act (kamma) called 'pattakalla' (timely and proper); it is not so in the absence of a boundary. Furthermore, an act performed without it fails. 

The perfection of the assembly (parisasampadā) is comprised of these four factors: (1) the presence of monks within the same boundary without leaving the hatthapāsa (forearm's length), who are eligible to perform the act, numbering no less than ten (in the Middle Country) or five (in the border regions), who have not committed a pārājika offense, have not been suspended (ukkhitta), and are of common communion (samānasaṃvāsaka); (2) the bringing of the consent (chanda) of those monks who are entitled to give it; (3) the lack of protest from those present; and (4) the absence within the Sangha's hatthapāsa of prohibited persons, such as unordained persons (anupasampanna) like laypeople who are excluded in the Uposathakkhandhaka, those who have committed a pārājika, those who have been suspended, monks of a different communion, and bhikkhunīs, excluding the candidate for ordination. Only when such perfection of the assembly exists is this act called 'pattakalla'; it is not so in its absence. Among these four, if any of the first three factors are missing, the act performed fails, but it does not fail merely due to the absence of the last factor (the absence of prohibited persons).

The completion of preliminary duties (pubbakiccanitthāpana) refers to the proper execution of the eight preliminary duties mentioned in the Pāḷi, such as 'first, he should be made to take a preceptor,' namely: (1) making him take a preceptor (upajjhāya); (2) announcing the bowl and robes; (3) then placing him outside the hatthapāsa and performing the formal act of appointing an instructor (anusāsaka); (4) the instruction by the appointed monk; (5) that monk returning first to inform the Sangha and calling the candidate into the hatthapāsa, saying 'Come'; (6) making him pay respects at the feet of the monks and request ordination; (7) then appointing an inquirer of the stumbling blocks (antarāyika-dhamma); and (8) the inquiry by the appointee. Only when these preliminary duties are completed is this formal act of ordination by the Sangha called 'pattakalla'; it is not so in their absence. However, even if these preliminary duties are not performed, if the aforementioned perfection of the object (vatthusampatti) and other perfections are present, the act performed is unshakeable (akuppa). Thus, it should be understood that 'pattakalla' in this context is comprised of these five factors. In this same manner, the state of being 'pattakalla' should be understood by applying it appropriately to all formal acts already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned.
137:
## Commentary on the Discussion of Ordination

'Itthannāmaṃ upasampādeyya' means that by bringing the state of ordination to completion, one should make that person endowed with ordination; this should be understood in the sense of a wish (patthanā) 'may he make,' or in the sense of a prescription (vidhi) 'let him make.' For example, when it is said, 'May he make Devadatta happy,' it means that by bringing happiness to completion, he should make Devadatta endowed with happiness; similarly here, by bringing his state of ordination to completion, he should make him endowed with ordination. This is the function of the causal agent (payojakabyāpāra). Just as a causal agent (hetukattā) is said to 'make happy' a simple agent (suddhakattā) by bringing about the cause of happiness, so too here, the Sangha, acting as the causal agent, is said to 'ordain' (upasampādeyya) the person who is the simple agent undergoing ordination, by bringing about the cause of ordination.

By this, it is established that there exists a conventional truth (sammutisacca) called 'ordination' (upasampadā) designated by the Noble Ones, based on the ultimate realities (paramatthadhamma) that arise in such a manner, just as happiness is given to a person by one who bestows happiness. In this formal proclamation (kammavācā) for ordination, because it is said, 'This person named so-and-so requests ordination from the Sangha,' and unlike in the case of probation (parivāsa) etc., it does not say 'should give ordination to so-and-so' in accordance with the request, but rather says 'should make so-and-so ordained' (upasampādeyya); therefore, it should be understood that this act of ordination is not included in the category of giving (dāna), but is included only in the category of the characteristics of a formal act (kammalakkhana). In this way, the meaning should also be understood in the phrases 'he ordains so-and-so' (upasampādeti) and 'he has been ordained by the Sangha' (upasampanno saṅghena). The only difference is that in those cases (upasampādeti, upasampanno), the distinction is by way of the present and past tense, whereas here (upasampādeyya), the distinction is by way of the untouched (future) time.

'Esā ñatti' (This is the motion) refers to the notification (ñāpanā) stated as 'the Sangha should be notified.' This statement is also made to indicate the existence of the proclamations (anussāvana). While this statement must certainly be made, it should not be said in a formal act consisting only of a motion (ñattikamma). In such a motion-only act, it should be understood that the act is completed just by uttering the syllable 'yya' (in ñāpeyya). 'Khamati' means it is pleasing or acceptable. The construction is: 'To whichever monk the ordination being given/completed by the Sangha is pleasing, he should be silent.' 'Tuṇhī' is an indeclinable (nipāta) in the sense of not speaking; the meaning is 'he should be one who does not speak.' It should be connected to the original text as: 'The Sangha approves of the ordination of the person named so-and-so.' The reason for the Sangha's approval is stated by the words 'tasmā tuṇhī' (therefore it is silent). There, the verb 'āsi' (was) is elided. Since the Sangha remained silent and noiseless even though it was said three times, 'He who does not approve should speak,' the meaning is that the Sangha approves. 'Evaṃ' means in this manner. The meaning is: 'By this very silence, I hold, know, and understand the Sangha's state of approval.' The word 'iti' is used in the sense of conclusion; it is not a factor (anga) of the kammavācā. Therefore, the reciter (anussāvaka) should conclude the recitation only at the end of the syllable 'mi' in 'dhārayāmi'; it should be understood that the word 'iti' must not be included. In this way, the meaning of all formal proclamations (kammavācā) should be understood.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Ordination Ends.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Four Supports etc.

The passage beginning with 'ekaporisā' (one man-length) shows the measurement of the extent of the shadow of living beings by measuring with feet. A shadow the length of six or seven feet is called a 'porisa' length. This measurement of the shadow and the announcement of the measure of the season are stated for the purpose of inquiring together with visiting monks to note the increase or decrease (of time) and to perform duties such as paying respects or receiving respects. It comes or it goes, therefore it is called 'utu' (season). Since the year (saṃvacchara) is compared and determined by that season, it is called a measure (pamāṇa). Therefore, it is said, 'The season itself is the measure of the season.' 'Aparipuṇṇā' (incomplete) refers to the incompleteness by way of the day of ordination. If one was ordained in the middle of a season, in that season...
138: It should be concluded by reciting only up to the syllable 'mi'; it should be understood that the word 'iti' should not be used. In this manner, the meaning of all kammavācās should be understood. ## The Explanation of the Procedure for Ordination is finished. ## The Explanation of the Four Requisites and So Forth. The phrase beginning with 'eka-porisā vā' (or one man's height) shows the method of knowing the shadow of a being's body by measuring it with feet. A shadow with a length of six or seven feet is called 'porisā'. This measuring of the shadow and the announcement of the measurement of the season, etc., were taught for the purpose of performing acts such as paying homage and receiving homage, after investigating together with visiting monks and knowing the state of the shadow's increase or decrease. It is called 'utu' (season) because it comes and goes. Because the year is compared and measured by that very season, it is called 'pamāṇa' (measure); therefore, it is said, 'The season itself is the measure of the season.' 'Aparippuṇṇā' (incomplete) refers to the incompleteness of the season by virtue of the day of ordination. If one was ordained in the middle of a season, the announcement of the remaining days in that season is shown as 'divasabhāgācikkhana' (announcing the portion of the day). Therefore, it is said, 'By however many days a certain person's certain season is incomplete, those days should be announced.' In that statement, the construction of the meaning is: 'By however many days the season pertaining to the person who has attained the status of a bhikkhu at that moment is incomplete, those days should be announced.' Because everything such as the shadow is combined and recited or spoken, it is called 'saṅgīti' (recital). Therefore, the phrase beginning with 'idameva' is said. Therein, the facts should be announced together. 'Tvaṃ kiṃ labhasīti' means: 'What year and what season do you get at the time of your ordination? At what time did you obtain the status of a bhikkhu?' 'Vassaṃ' refers to the rainy season (vassāna-utu). This announcement of the measure of the season cannot be known if spoken without the announcement of the year (saṃvacchara); therefore, it should be understood that by this very announcement of the season, it amounts to showing 'I obtain such a season' whether in the years of the Sāsana, or in the years of the Kaliyuga era, or in the thousands or hundreds. This word 'chāyā' (shadow) is said with reference to the sequence appearing in the Pāḷi text.
