However, according to the proper order of speaking, in the years of the Kaliyuga era, etc., which are well-known in all regions, it should be said: 'In such a year, in such a season, in such a month, in such a fortnight (waxing or waning), under such a constellation (nakkhatta) associated with a specific day and time, in such a portion of the day like the morning, at such a measurement of shadow or such a measurement of hours (nāḍikā), I obtained the status of a bhikkhu.' Thus it should be announced. 'Having well learned this sequence of words...'
139:
Visiting monks should be told to practice by knowing the order of seniority. In the Pali, 'Kissa tvaṃ' means 'Why did you do this for so long?' 'Upasampadaṃ yāci' means he asks for both novice ordination and higher ordination. In the word 'Passissāmi', the remaining word 'vadati' (he says) is implied; the same applies further on. By the word 'Osāretabbo', the previous state of being an expelled monk (ukkittaka) is not escaped even if one disrobes and obtains higher ordination again. Therefore, it shows that for monks, in matters of communion (sambhoga) etc., it is only a Pācittiya offense. In the phrase 'Anāpatti sambhoge saṃvāse', it should be understood that sleeping together (sahaseyya) is also included.

The intention here is: because this monk has been rehabilitated into the Saṅgha, he is a monk of normal status (pakatatta). Therefore, it should be understood that there is no Pācittiya offense here due to communion with an expelled monk. A monk who does not see an offense where there is one, due to the view that it is not an offense, and thus does not perform the remedy, is not called 'shameless' (alajjī) by that much alone. Only a monk who commits a transgression while knowing the regulation is called 'shameless'. It is said: 'He knowingly falls into an offense,' etc. Therefore, there is no fixed rule of a Dukkaṭa offense here due to communion with a shameless monk. Thus, it should be understood that even that Dukkaṭa offense is not mentioned here. Some teachers, not noticing this intention, say that by this Pācittiya rule 'Anāpatti sambhoge saṃvāse', it is stated as no offense, but one still falls into a Dukkaṭa offense due to communion with a shameless monk; such a fixed rule of offense should be understood as stated only when there is shamelessness, not when it is absent.

In the verses beginning with 'Vinayamhi', 'niggahānaṃ' means in the acts of rebuking. 'Pāpicche' means in rebuking evil persons and in praising the shameful (lajjī) ones; a monk who acts according to the meaning in the noble Vinaya, which brings happiness to those who love virtue, is said to practice properly. Therefore, the connection (yojanā) should be understood as 'I shall speak the summary (uddāna)'. The rest is easy to understand everywhere.

## the method of explaining the Mahākhandhaka is finished.
140: ## 2. Uposathakkhandhaka ## Explanation of the Authorization of the Assembly, etc. I shall further explain the Uposathakkhandhaka. They enter (otarantī) into this; therefore, it is called 'tittha' (a ford), meaning a view (laddhi). 'Ito' means from the view of the Dispensation (Sāsana). In the phrase 'āpajjitvā vā vuṭṭhito', the confession of an offense (desanā) is also included. Therefore, in the Mātikā Commentary, it is said: 'An offense that has been emerged from, or confessed, or made known... is said to be non-existent.' 'Manujena' means together with a human who is nearby. 'Pare' refers to other persons who are far away; the connection is that one should not speak to them. Because it is said, 'When it is made clear, there is comfort for him,' some teachers say that even a heavy offense (garukāpatti) is cleared just by making it clear (confessing). That is merely their opinion, as it contradicts the texts (suttas) prescribing probation (parivāsa) and so on. The intention here is: when a monk makes himself known as he truly is, virtuous monks, relying on the words 'he should be made to live on probation even if unwilling,' will use a means to give him probation and so on, and will certainly establish him in the state of purity. Then, through the absence of remorse and so on, there is comfort for him. 'Pathamaṃ pātimokkhooddesaṃ' refers to the Nidānauddesa. He prescribed the Nidānauddesa which did not exist before. It is not that He prescribed only this Nidānauddesa; rather, the Blessed One took all the training rules such as the Pārājikas that were prescribed before, made them into the Vinaya Mātikā by way of the Pārājika recitation (Pārājika-uddesa), etc., and having personally summarized them together with the Nidānauddesa, He prescribed them as the 'Pātimokkha'. Referring to that entire Pātimokkha, it is said: 'Monks, I allow you to recite the Pātimokkha.' 'Etaṃ veditabbaṃ' refers to the collection of meanings such as 'on whichever fourteenth or fifteenth day.' ## The explanation of the Authorization of the Assembly, etc., is finished.
141:
## Explanation of the Talk on the Authorization of the Boundary

"In the eastern direction" is merely an example. In fact, if there is no mark (*nimitta*) in that direction, one should start from where there is a mark, first reciting "in the south-east, in the south," and so on, and having proclaimed the marks in the surrounding places, one should again proclaim the first proclaimed mark, "in the south-east." This is because even a boundary (*sīmā*) shaped like a triangle can be authorized with three marks.

"One who connects the boundary circle three times" means that a Vinaya expert (*vinayadhara*), staying in one place himself, connects mark to mark around the boundary circle solely by the words of proclaiming the marks. Indeed, it is proper to proclaim them even without going to those respective locations of the marks. Since it is difficult to walk around a boundary of three *yojanas* three times in a single day, it is also proper for a Vinaya expert to proclaim, "This stone is a mark," etc., by noting the report of someone who says, "Venerable sir, it is a stone," according to what was previously determined by monks, even if he has not seen it himself.

"A mountain consisting only of earth" refers to one that is not man-made but is natural. The others are the same. "The other mountain" refers to mountains such as those consisting only of earth. "From the size of an elephant"—here, the part rising from the ground should be taken as the size of an elephant.

"With four or three" means with marks situated in four or three directions of the boundary land. It is not proper to authorize with many marks situated in only one direction. Nor is it proper with two marks situated in two directions. Therefore (because it is not proper with only one mark), in saying "placing that mark outside," it means that since the proclaimed mark is not the boundary, it is improper to include it within the boundary. Therefore, he said, "If," and so on.

The size of a lump of molasses (*palaguḷapiṇḍa*) of thirty-two *palas* should be taken by its shape, not by weight. The *pala* measurement by weight should be taken by the Magadhan weight. They say that the Magadhan weight is double the worldly weight. "Even if very large" means even if it does not rise to the size of an elephant from the ground but is many *yojanas* in thickness submerged in the ground below. If a peak the size of an elephant rises from it, it is classified as a mountain.

"Of trees with heartwood inside"—this is said with reference to trees that will have heartwood upon maturing, even if heartwood is not present at that moment due to their being young. A grove of four or five such trees with a girth of a stylus-shaft (or arrow-shaft) is also acceptable. By the phrase "mixed with trees having heartwood inside," he shows that a palm grove or coconut grove mixed with heartwood trees is also acceptable. The words "about four or five trees" refer to the heartwood trees.

"They make a forest monastery" means that in the midst of a thicket, without cutting the trees, they mark the boundary of the monastery with fences and so forth, and by making the precincts and leaf-roofed dwellings only among the trees within that forest, the interior of the monastery remains just like a forest. This is the meaning of making a monastery in such a manner. If all trees are cut down to make a monastery, it is no longer a forest; therefore, the forest surrounding that monastery should be proclaimed in only one place. But here, since the interior of the monastery is a forest, it is said, "the forest should be proclaimed." If that forest were proclaimed [otherwise], it would lead to the fault to be mentioned later, such as "the monastery is above the mark." "A portion" refers to a part of the forest situated on one side of a monastery built in a place devoid of trees. "The size of a stylus-shaft" means having the size of an arrow-shaft or a stylus-shaft.
142:
## 
It refers to a forest mixed with trees that have heartwood inside. By this term 'antosāramissakānaṃ', it is shown that a forest mixed with palmyra and coconut trees is also suitable as a boundary sign (nimitta). The phrase 'about four or five trees' is said with reference to heartwood trees. 'They build a monastery in the middle of the forest' means that without cutting down the trees within the forest thicket, they define the monastery's limits with fences and the like, and construct the surrounding area (pariveṇa) and leaf-huts (paṇṇasālā) only in the spaces between the trees, so that even inside the monastery, it remains like a forest. If they were to build the monastery by cutting down all the trees, the monastery would no longer be a forest; therefore, the forest surrounding it should be proclaimed as a sign in only one place. However, here, since it remains a forest even inside the monastery, it is said, 'one should proclaim the forest.' If one proclaims that forest as a sign, it leads to the fault mentioned immediately after, such as 'the monastery is located above the sign.' 'Ekadesa' (a portion) means a part of the forest; it refers to a part of the forest situated on one side of a monastery built in a place devoid of trees.

'The measure of a sūcidaṇḍaka' means having the length of an arrow shaft. Some say it is the length of a stylus (lekhani). However, in the Mātikā Commentary, in the decision on non-apportionable items (avebhaṅgiya), it is stated: 'Any bamboo even the size of an eight-inch sūcidaṇḍaka... is a heavy object (garubhaṇḍa).' Therefore, it should be understood as a very thin bamboo rod or a needle-stick. [This refers to trees] planted in bamboo joints, reed joints, or earthen vessels such as spittoons. The word 'taṅkhaṇampi' (even instantly) is said with reference to young saplings that have the nature of growing without wilting. As for mature trees which, even if uprooted and planted with their roots, wilt like a cut branch and only survive after a long time when new roots and shoots appear, or even die, it is not suitable to proclaim such as a sign. 'Etaṃ' (this) refers to the emergence of new roots and branches.

'In the middle' means the interior of the major directions of the boundary (sīmā). 'Corner' refers to the meeting point of two roads at each of the four corners of the boundary. The intention is that one may proclaim all four roads in the four directions as signs, with one road in one direction and another road in another direction among the roads that extend outside those four corners. How is it known that the state of being connected is removed merely by proclaiming in this way? Are these not the same four roads when going to another place? Indeed, it has been said, 'they go in four directions.' Therefore, the underlying reason should be investigated in this matter.

'To a bhikkhunī crossing a river'—this phrase is mentioned in the Pāḷi text in the training rule for bhikkhunīs on crossing a river (nadīpāragamana) to show the characteristics of a river. For monks, even a river that is just deep enough to wet the inner robe (antaravāsaka) is suitable as a sign. By the passage 'in the same way for a group of four rivers,' it is shown that it is not suitable to proclaim again when going to another place after proclaiming in one place. For this reason, the word 'unmixed' (asammissa) is used, as in 'one should also proclaim four unmixed rivers.' 'Mūla' (root/original) means at the beginning. 'Having destroyed' means that farmers who do not want the water, being unable to stop the great flow of water, destroy the riverbank (meaning diverting the water).

'Ukkhepima' refers to a well from which water is drawn by a pot or bucket attached to a long rope. 'With unmixed stones' means [proclaiming signs] using only mountains in all directions, or using stones that have no other signs mixed with them.
143:
Thus, by the statement "In the case of the four rivers, the same method applies," it is shown that after proclaiming a marker in one place, it is not proper to proclaim it again in another place where it has reached. For this very reason, the word asammissa (unmixed) is used in the phrase "It is proper to proclaim even the four unmixed rivers." Mūle means at the beginning. Nadiṃ bhinditvā means just as farmers who do not want water are unable to stop a great flood, likewise, by breaking the river bank.

Ukkhepima refers to water that is drawn up and poured using a pot attached to a long rope.

Asammissehi means only by mountains located in all directions, or by any one of the markers such as stones that are not mixed with other markers. Sammissehi means by eight markers situated such as a mountain in one place and a stone in another. By the phrase "even by hundreds of markers," it is shown that it is proper to proclaim many markers even in a single direction, such as: "What is the marker in the eastern direction? Venerable Sir, it is a mountain. Again, what is the marker in the eastern direction? Venerable Sir, it is a stone," and so on. Siṅghāṭakasaṇṭhāna refers to a boundary that is triangular in shape. Caturassa means perfectly square, while mudiṅgasaṇṭhāna (drum-shaped) is oblong. It may be contracted at one end and wide at the other. Sīmāya upacāraṃ ṭhapetvā means setting aside a precinct sufficient for a sīmantarika (inter-boundary space) outside the limits of those monasteries for the boundary to be bound in the future. Those monasteries where a boundary is bound are called baddhasīmā. Pāṭekkaṃ means individually. Baddhasīmāsadisāni shows that just as monks staying within bound boundaries are allowed to perform legal acts individually without depending on the consent (chanda) of others, so too are monks staying within village boundaries (gāmasīmā). Āgantabbaṃ is said in the sense of mere respect. Therefore, it is said, "the coming also," and so forth.

In the phrase pabbajjūpasampadādīnaṃ, the word pabbajjā is taken with reference to the request for the bhaṇḍukamma (shaving of the head). "Twenty-one monks" is said with reference to those sitting. This is also said for the purpose of having enough monks for the abbhāna rite along with the monk who is the subject of the act. The statement "stones reaching the markers should be placed" is said because tree-markers and the like are difficult to find in the desired place, and because trees grow and cause the mixing of two bound boundaries, whereas stone markers do not grow, and because it is easy to bring and place them from any place. Likewise, the same applies to the statement "stones for the sīmantarika should be placed." "Even the measure of four finger-breadths" means that just as a space of four finger-breadths of the marker-stones extends all around outside the limit of the khaṇḍasīmā, and the remaining part is within the khaṇḍasīmā, so too, when those stones are placed, it should be understood that there is a sīmantarika of four finger-breadths.
144:
Sīmantarikapāsāṇā refers to the marker-stones of the Great Boundary (mahāsīmā) placed in the sīmantarika (inter-boundary space) of a khaṇḍasīmā. When proclaiming those stones, they should be proclaimed only while circumambulating to the right. How should they be proclaimed? To explain in detail: standing at the west of the khaṇḍasīmā facing east, one should proclaim all the markers in that direction in order, saying, "What is the marker in the eastern direction?" Likewise, standing at the north facing south, one should proclaim in order, "What is the marker in the southern direction?" Likewise, standing at the east facing west, one should proclaim in order, "What is the marker in the western direction?" Likewise, standing at the south facing north, one should proclaim all the markers in that direction in order, "What is the marker in the northern direction?" Once again, standing at the west facing east, one should proclaim again as previously proclaimed. In this way, the sīmantarika stones of many khaṇḍasīmās should be proclaimed individually.

"Tato" means after proclaiming the sīmantarika. "Avasesanimittāni" refers to the remaining markers on the outside and inside of the Great Boundary. "Ubhinnampi na kopenti" means they do not invalidate the legal acts of both.

"Kuṭigehe" refers to a grass-roofed hut built on the ground. "Udukkhalaṃ" refers to a small pit similar to a mortar-hole. "Nimittaṃ na kātabbaṃ" means that neither that line nor the small pit should be made a marker. Although it is clear that these are not suitable because they are not included among the eight kinds of markers mentioned, this is said to prevent failure (vipatti) from afar, fearing that some ignorant person might out of delusion make them a marker, thinking them to be an indelible sign. In the statements above such as "without proclaiming the wall," the reason for repeatedly stating what is already clear should be understood. Because a failure of the boundary (sīmā-vipatti) is the root of the failure of all legal acts such as ordination (upasampadā), everything that should be said has been said by the teachers to close every door to failure in every way, and thus they have established the decision in this matter.

"Bhittiṃ" refers to a wall made of bricks, wood, or clay. In the case of a wall made of stone, however, it is proper to proclaim a single stone sufficient to be a marker in each respective direction. It is not proper to proclaim an entire wall built of many stones, because it must be said in the singular: "This stone is the marker." In the phrase "antokuṭṭameva," it should be understood that even within the wall, the boundary is only the area inside from where the markers are situated. "Pamukhe nimittapāsāṇe ṭhapetvā" means that stones should be placed and the boundary consecrated in the front porch area outside, facing the room, in a space the size of the room's width. Only by consecrating in this way, including the wall between the front of the rooms, will the boundary be square in shape both inside and outside. "Bahi" means outside all around the entire hut-dwelling.
145:
"It is a boundary both inside and outside" means it is a square-shaped boundary (sīmā) including the wall situated in the middle.

By the statement "It occurs only in the upper palace (pāsāda)," it is shown that because the wall situated between the inner chamber and the front room is a single unit, and because there is no space for twenty-one bhikkhus at that wall, the boundary does not descend below; rather, only the upper wall stands as the boundary. "A wall on the lower floor" refers to the walls situated in the four directions of the lower floor. Indeed, if walls exist in only two or three directions, it does not descend below. The statement "It also descends below" is said because twenty-one bhikkhus can be accommodated within the four walls, including the walls themselves. When it descends, it descends according to the dimensions of the upper boundary. However, on the lower ground level defined by the exterior and interior of the four walls, it descends as far as the water level. It does not descend even a hair's breadth outside the walls. "From the palace wall" means from the wall on the upper floor. Whether it descends or not should be understood in the same manner as previously stated; this is said in reference to the walls in the four directions of the lower floor, which are included within the dimensions of the upper boundary, being connected with the crossbeams, and the smallest boundary dimensions being within those walls, and so on.

In this boundary, although projections (niyyūhaka) and such do not become the boundary at the moment of binding because they are the locations where the signs (nimitta) are placed, they should be regarded as being situated within the boundary once the boundary is bound. The phrase "of the outermost pillars" refers to the stone pillars placed as signs. The statement "It is connected with the upper floor" is said because there are no pillars situated within the boundary between the walls. If there were pillars situated within the boundary, even if the wall were not connected to the upper floor, the palace situated above the pillars within the boundary would still be within the boundary.

If a boundary is bound by placing sign-stones within the outermost row of pillars on the ground below a palace built upon many rows of pillars, what happens in that case? Here, it should be understood that the upper floor above the beams supported only by the pillars within the boundary is entirely within the boundary; there is no dispute on this point. However, regarding the upper floor above the beams supported equally by a row of pillars within the boundary and a row of pillars outside the boundary, some teachers say that half is the boundary. Others say the entire floor is only a village boundary (gāma-sīmā). Others say it is indeed a bound boundary (baddha-sīmā). Therefore, when bhikkhus perform a formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma), they should stand in a respected place free from doubt, and perform the act only after clearing all such doubtful areas. Alternatively, they should investigate the reasons for a firm conclusion and act in accordance with those reasons.
146:
"Tālamūlaka mountain" refers to a mountain resembling the root of a palm tree. A mountain that is thick at the base and gradually becomes slender as it rises is said to be like a palm root. "Vitāna-shape" means having the shape of a mushroom (ahicchattaka). "Paṇava-shape" means having a shape that is slender in the middle and wide at the base and the top. "In the lower part or in the middle" refers to the lower part of a mountain shaped like a mudiṅga drum or the middle part of a mountain shaped like a paṇava drum (meaning the boundary dimensions are not met there).

"A mountain like a snake's hood" means a mountain that is hunched like a snake's hood, with its peak leaning towards a place other than its base. "Ākāsapabbhāra" refers to a mountain cleft (overhang) not enclosed by walls (an open cleft). "Boundary dimension" refers to a stone that has the minimum boundary dimensions along with the internal space. By the statement "That stone also stands within the boundary," it is shown that a boundary is established only in a ground area defined by such hollow stones, caves, walls, and so on, and not in an undefined area. It shows that those stones and such are called "boundary" only because they stand within the boundary, and they are not boundaries by their own nature, like a couch (mañca) and such situated within a boundary. If that hollow stone hangs in the air without touching the ground, the boundary does not descend. Hollow stones themselves become the boundary because they are connected to the boundary. How is this statement—that the boundary does not descend through these hollow stones and such which lack the minimum dimensions—to be believed? It should be believed on the authority of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā).

Furthermore, in such a descent, there is no process of descending to the lower surface of the boundary by following the hollow stone wall, as mice and such might do. However, if the space below, which has the minimum boundary dimensions, is enclosed—either entirely or for the most part—by stone walls and such about two finger-breadths thick that touch the upper surface, then the boundary bound above also stands simultaneously on the lower ground separated by those stone walls, along with the upper surface. This is like a nadīpāra-sīmā (boundary across a river) standing on both banks separated by the river. Even if the caves and such are removed, the boundary that has descended below does not disappear until the disappearance of the Dispensation (Sāsana). Specifically, even if the boundary is first bound above and the caves and such are made later, the boundary certainly descends to the ground below. Some teachers do not accept this. Although it stands in two places, above and below, that boundary is one and the same. It should be understood as one, like a lineage (gotta) or birth (jāti) existing in different individuals. This is because all bound boundaries (baddha-sīmā) and unbound boundaries (abaddha-sīmā) pervade their respective natural bases—such as villages, forests, rivers, etc.—entirely and simultaneously at one moment according to their definition. Although they do not exist in the ultimate sense (paramattha), based on those respective ultimate realities that serve as bases, or based on specific actions, worldly people...
147:
The monks included in the Sasana also have a single nature in terms of support (nissaya), because they are designated as one in a fitting and certain manner. This is true; in the world, [terms like] 'a village', 'a forest', 'a river', 'a lake', 'an ocean' [are used]. In the Sasana, it is seen that a single designation is used, such as: 'That sīmā is authorized by the Saṅgha.' (Mahāvagga 143). 'Monks, in a forest without a village, the area within seven abbhantaras is a single communion (samānasaṃvāsa) and a single Uposatha (ekūposatha). The area within a splash of water (udakukkhepa) is a single communion and a single Uposatha.' (Mahāvagga 147). In the ultimate sense, however, a single nature does not pervade many phenomena. Because it is not like the specific conceptualization of a portion of a kasiṇa and so on, it falls away from being a single entity; this is our opinion.

'Below it' (assa heṭṭhā) means in the open mountain valley below the Sappaphaṇa Mountain. 'Of the cave' (leṇassa) means if a cave is made, it refers to that cave. To show the decision on whether the boundary descends or does not descend by distinguishing that same cave in five ways, he said: 'But if below...' (sace pana heṭṭhā) and so on. There, the word 'below' (heṭṭhā) is connected with the phrase 'it is a cave' (leṇaṃ hoti). 'Inside' (anto) is said with the meaning that the cave below is in the same place; it means inside the mountain, at the foot of the mountain. To distinguish that same word 'inside' (anto) by the boundary limit, it is said: 'beyond the upper boundary limit.' Although one should say 'on this side' (orato) with respect to the foot of the mountain, it should be understood that it is said 'on that side' (pārato) referring to the mountain peak which is the support of the sīmā. For that very reason, wishing to specify the word 'outside' (bahi) in the term 'outside cave' (bahileṇaṃ), he said: 'on this side of the upper boundary limit.' In the phrase 'the sīmā does not descend outside,' 'outside' (bahi) is said referring to the cave at the foot of the mountain; it means the sīmā does not descend to the lower part of the upper boundary limit which is outside the cave. 'Inside sīmā' (anto sīmā) means it does not descend into its own proper place of descent within the cave and the foot of the mountain. In these words, 'the sīmā does not descend outside, the sīmā does not descend inside,' it should be understood that it shows the sīmā does not descend in any way because there is no cave in its own proper place of descent. Even if it does not descend, it remains only above. By the words 'that which falls outside is not a sīmā' (bahi patitaṃ asīmā) and so on, it should be understood that it shows that a sīmā situated on unstable supports such as palaces (pāsāda) also perishes with the destruction of those palaces.
148:
'They dig a pond; it is just the sīmā.' In this phrase, if an underground river (umanganadī) already exists below, not less than the size of a sīmā, and the sīmā is bound later and exists only above the river, it should be known that when the pond is dug touching that river, the sīmā perishes. 'Below the surface of the earth' (heṭṭhāpathavitale) means in the open space of the ground in between. 'In the sīmā-terrace' (sīmāmāḷake) means in the courtyard of the khaṇḍasīmā. The term 'Banyan tree' (vaṭarukkha) is mentioned because it is endowed with branches capable of reaching very far with the support of aerial roots (pāroha). The connection of all trees, creepers, etc., with one another is also certainly not allowable. For that very reason, connection by means of boats, ropes, or bridges is also rejected. 'From that' (tato) means from the branch. In the phrase 'the surface of the earth of the great sīmā' (mahāsīmāya pathavitalaṃ), because the bound boundary (baddhasīmā) is taken without taking the very close village boundary (gāmasīmā), there is no fault of overlapping boundaries (sambhēda-dosa) even when the village boundary and the bound boundary are connected by trees and so on. This should be understood because they exist in the state of support and supported by one another. If there were a fault of connection even in those [cases], how could a bound boundary be authorized within a village boundary? If there is a fault in connecting with a certain sīmā, it is not allowable to bind [a sīmā] there. It is like not being allowable to bind a baddhasīmā within [another] baddhasīmā or an udakukkhepasīmā, and like an udakukkhepasīmā [not being allowable] within its own support, the gāmasīmā. For that very reason, by saying 'If a branch of a tree or an aerial root coming from it is situated in a monastery sīmā or a village sīmā outside the river bank' (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 147) and so on, he showed the fault of connection of the udakukkhepasīmā only with the gāmasīmā, etc., which are not its support; he did not show the fault of connection with the river sīmā (nadīsīmā) which is its support. In the same way, it should be understood here regarding this gāmasīmā and baddhasīmā. This meaning will become clear above. 'Touching' (āhacca) means having contacted.

'Or having cleared the great sīmā' (mahāsīmāṃ vā sodhetvā) means having cleared the entire great sīmā by bringing all the monks within the great sīmā into the hatthapāsa (forearm's length) or by removing them [from the area], etc. By this statement, he shows that even if [boundaries] were well-bound previously, having been freed from all failures (vipatti), there is such a fault of overlapping (sambhēda-dosa) not directly mentioned in the Pāḷi text, which arises later due to connection by trees and so on. And that sambhēda-dosa is shown by the teachers of the Council (Saṅgītikāras) who knew the intention [of the Buddha]. Since the overlapping and encroaching of bound boundaries upon one another is rejected by the words 'Monks, a sīmā should not be overlapped by another sīmā' and so on, and since it is established that binding them while touching one another is not allowable—just as overlapping is not allowable—by the Buddha's allowance to bind a sīmā only after leaving an inter-boundary space (sīmantarika) between two bound boundaries, saying 'Monks, I allow one authorizing a sīmā to authorize it after leaving an inter-boundary space' (Mahāvagga 148), therefore, even for those already bound, it is not allowable for them to later stand touching each other through a single tree. This is because it is a non-action conformity (akiriya-anuloma) with the fault of connection rejected at the time of binding the sīmā.
149:
## 
It was determined by the compilers of the Council (Saṅgītikārakas), who understood the intention of the Blessed One, that it is also not allowable to stand while touching [the boundary] with a single tree or such. This is because it follows what is unallowable (akappiyānuloma), in accordance with the fault of connection (sambandhadosa) that is rejected at the time of consecrating a boundary.

This fault of connection, however, because it arises later in boundaries that were previously well-consecrated, is not capable of making them a non-boundary, unlike at the moment of consecration. Therefore, as soon as the connection with the tree etc. is removed, those boundaries return to their normal state. Just as this connection with a tree etc. is not allowable later, it should be understood that if such a connection exists at the moment of consecration, it is not allowable to consecrate those boundaries.

Some teachers say regarding the phrase "having cleared the Mahāsīmā" that it only means monks within the Mahāsīmā should be cleared so that they do not touch those branches or roots with objects connected to their bodies; it does not mean clearing the entire boundary. This statement is inappropriate because it contradicts the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). For the Commentary states: "It stands touching the ground of the Mahāsīmā or the trees etc. grown there," thus citing only the branches and roots touching the Mahāsīmā as the cause of the fault of connection. It does not mention the monks standing there touching the branches etc.

If the monks touching the branches etc. were the only cause, then it should have been stated that a monk touching a branch or a root protruding from it that has entered the Mahāsīmā is the cause. This is because whatever is the cause for clearing the Mahāsīmā should be primarily shown in that sentence. It is not only the monk touching the branch etc. that stands touching the boundary who must be cleared; even a monk touching a branch etc. that is in the air must be cleared. Therefore, the phrase "standing while touching [the boundary]" would be useless. Regarding branches in the air, only the monk's touching is stated as the cause, and the clearing is stated as clearing that monk by bringing him into the hatthapāsa etc. But here, the clearing is stated with a general term for the entire boundary: "having cleared the Mahāsīmā."

Furthermore, if only the clearing of a monk touching a branch etc. were intended, the specific mention of "the ground of the Mahāsīmā" would be useless, because a monk touching a branch etc. must be cleared regardless of where he is, even if he is in the air.
150:
## 
Because of the statement "having cut them, they should be made to be outside," which refers to separating them from the state of being established in that Mahāsīmā, and because the touching of dissimilar boundaries (visabhāgasīmā) is the cause for clearing the entire boundary, it must be accepted that this single fault of connection (sambandhadosa), as established in the Commentary, indeed exists. For that very reason, in the discussion of the water-boundary (udakukkhepasīmā) as well, it is stated: "standing in a monastery boundary (vihārasīmā) or a village boundary (gāmasīmā)," and "it is not allowable [to perform a legal act] in a boat tied to a post driven into the riverbank," and "if a bridge or the pillars of a bridge stand on the outer bank, it is not allowable to perform the act." Thus, only the touching of branches etc. in dissimilar village boundaries is stated as the cause of the fault of overlap (saṅkaradosa), not the monk's touching.

This is true: tying a boat to a tree growing within the river and performing the act is allowed because it is similar (sabhāga) to the river boundary as a support for the water-boundary. If the fault of connection were stated for all places based only on the monks' touching, then tying in the river would also have to be forbidden. For in that river as well, the monk's touching would be a cause for the failure of the act. Therefore, in similar boundaries (sabhāgasīmā), when one has entered and stands on a branch etc. (whether touching the ground or not), only the monk touching that branch etc. must be cleared. In dissimilar boundaries (visabhāgasīmā), however, when a branch etc. stands touching [the boundary], all monks must be cleared even if they do not touch that branch etc. But if the branch etc. stands without touching, only the monk touching that branch etc. must be cleared. This is the conclusion that should be reached here.

Regarding this matter, some teachers say: "Just as between two bound boundaries (baddhasīmā), so also between a bound boundary and a village boundary, and all other boundaries of the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka); if there is a connection by trees etc. between them, both should be cleared as if they were a single boundary and the act performed in only one place. An act performed in the other place fails. There is no distinction of similar (sabhāga) and dissimilar (visabhāga) in this matter." That is merely their opinion. This is because the absence of the fault of overlap between similar boundaries and the presence of that fault only in dissimilar boundaries is established by the methods of the Vinaya, such as the Sutta and Suttānuloma.

This is true: with the words "I allow you, monks, to agree upon a boundary," the consecration of a bound boundary is allowed only within a village boundary. Their similarity (sabhāgatā) through the relationship of support and being supported, and the absence of faults such as overlap (sambheda) and overspreading (ajjhottharaṇa), is established by the Sutta itself. By the conformity (anuloma) of the connection allowed at the time of consecration, a connection by trees etc. that grow later is also allowable for those boundaries. For it is stated: "Whatever, monks... conforms to what is allowable and inhibits what is unallowable, that is allowable for you." Thus, first, the similarity between a bound boundary and a village boundary and the absence of faults such as overlap...
151:
This [compatibility] is established through the Sutta and the method in accordance with the Sutta (Suttānuloma) found in the Vinaya. For this reason, the consecration of a baddha-sīmā (bound boundary) is permitted only within a gāma-sīmā (village boundary). The compatibility of these two, based on their relationship as support and supported, and the absence of defects such as overlapping or encroachment, is established by the Sutta. Regarding how it is established by the method in accordance with the Sutta: since it is consistent with the permitted connections at the time of consecration, any connection with trees etc. that grow later between the gāma-sīmā and baddha-sīmā is also allowable. Why? Because it is said: "Monks, whatever object... is in accordance with what is allowable and prohibits what is not allowable, that object is allowable for you." Thus, the mutual compatibility and absence of overlapping defects between a baddha-sīmā and a gāma-sīmā are established by the Sutta and the method in accordance with the Sutta. In the same way, the mutual compatibility and absence of overlapping defects between an arañña-sīmā (forest boundary) and a sattabbhantara-sīmā, and between a nadī-sīmā (river boundary) and an udakukkhepa-sīmā (water-splash boundary), should be understood as established.

Because the consecration of one baddha-sīmā within another baddha-sīmā or within boundaries like a river is prohibited, and because the consecration of a baddha-sīmā within a gāma-sīmā is prohibited by the power of the Sutta which specifies that udakukkhepa-sīmā and sattabbhantara-sīmā are to be made only in rivers etc., the mutual incompatibility (visabhāga) of these boundaries is established. Furthermore, the possibility of defects such as overlapping through trees etc., either at the moment of consecration or later, is clearly established by the Sutta and the method in accordance with the Sutta as previously mentioned. Therefore, in the Commentary, the defect of connection is shown only for incompatible (visabhāga) boundaries using examples like the banyan tree, while the defect of connection for compatible boundaries like baddha-sīmā and gāma-sīmā is not mentioned. Not only is it not mentioned, but it is also made known in the Pāḷi and Commentaries that there is no defect even if these compatible (sabhāga) boundaries are connected by trees etc. This is true because in the Pāḷi, growing markers such as "mountain-marker, stone-marker, forest-marker, tree-marker" are permitted. By permitting these, it is made known that there is no defect of overlapping between a baddha-sīmā and a gāma-sīmā even when these tree-markers grow. However, such a connection between two baddha-sīmā is not allowable. Indeed, it is said: "Even a single tree can be a marker for two boundaries; however, when that tree grows, it causes an overlapping of boundaries (sīmā-saṅkara); therefore, it should not be done." This meaning is also made known by the words: "Monks, I allow the consecration of a boundary up to three yojanas in extent." Since a baddha-sīmā and a gāma-sīmā will inevitably be connected by trees, creepers, bushes, etc., at the edges around a boundary of three yojanas, the Commentary does not say, "A boundary should be consecrated only after destroying such connections."

If the failure of a legal act (kamma-vipatti) were to occur here due to the connection of trees etc., it would certainly have been mentioned. In fact, to avoid failure, the Teachers repeatedly stated even in places where there is no doubt, such as "without mentioning the wall," etc. But here, they spoke of the consecration of a boundary even in the middle of a dense forest where trees and creepers are continuous, saying "they build a monastery in the middle of a forest; the forest should not be mentioned," etc. Similarly, regarding mansions etc. built on top of pillars, the consecration of a boundary on the upper floors is mentioned in various ways even though they are connected to the pillars below. Therefore, the connection of trees etc. between a baddha-sīmā and a gāma-sīmā was directly permitted and prescribed by those Teachers. Alternatively, since gāma-sīmā are individually similar to baddha-sīmā, monks performing a legal act in one gāma-sīmā would have to clear other connected villages, forests, rivers, and oceans, even if connected only by wood or grass. If this were the case, a legal act could only be performed after clearing the entire island of Jambudīpa. If they were not cleared, and if the legal acts such as ordination and boundary consecrations performed since the time of the First Council were to fail, the doubt as to whether all monks are truly monks would be difficult to prevent. Such a doubt is inappropriate. Therefore, by the method already mentioned, there is a defect only when incompatible (visabhāga) boundaries are connected by trees etc.; it should be understood that there is no defect in compatible (sabhāga) boundaries such as baddha-sīmā and gāma-sīmā. Because it is difficult to clear a mahā-sīmā (great boundary), Saṅgha acts are mostly performed in a khaṇḍa-sīmā (small boundary); hence the phrase "in the sīmā-māḷaka" etc. is used. When a khaṇḍa-sīmā is insufficient for a large assembly of monks, this same method should be applied when performing a legal act in a mahā-sīmā. By the text "having caused to move," a monk who touches the boundary with an object connected to his body...
152:
Monks performing a formal act (kamma) in a certain village boundary (gāmasīmā) should clear connections even as small as wood or grass to successive other villages, as well as forests, rivers, and oceans. If it were so, the act should only be performed after clearing the entire island of Jambudīpa. If it were not cleared in this way, and if the higher ordinations (upasampadā) and boundary consecrations (sīmāsammuti) performed since the time of the First Council were to fail, then the doubt as to whether all monks are truly ordained would be difficult to prevent. This is not appropriate. Therefore, according to the method mentioned, the fault of connection with trees and so forth exists only in dissimilar boundaries (visabhāgasīmā); however, it should be understood that there is no fault in similar boundaries (sabhāgasīmā) such as a formal boundary (baddhasīmā) and a village boundary (gāmasīmā).

Because it is difficult to clear a great boundary (mahāsīmā), formal acts of the Saṅgha are mostly performed in a small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā); with this intention, it was said, "In the boundary terrace (sīmāmaḷake)," and so forth. However, when a large assembly of monks gathers and the khaṇḍasīmā is insufficient, if the act must be performed in the mahāsīmā, this same method should be adopted.

By the word "ukkhipāpetvā" (having caused to be lifted), it is shown that a monk who touches the boundary even with an object connected to his body is considered as one standing within the boundary (sīmaṭṭha). The phrase "purimanayepi" (also in the previous method) means that even in the case where a tree branch from a mahāsīmā enters a khaṇḍasīmā, a monk sitting on that branch is considered as one standing within the boundary; therefore, it was said, "he should be brought into the hatthapāsa (forearm's length)." In this matter, regarding a khaṇḍasīmā and a mahāsīmā connected to each other by tree branches and so forth, some teachers say that it is suitable to perform acts such as higher ordination with five monks who are positioned such that three monks are in the khaṇḍasīmā and two monks are in the mahāsīmā, without touching the inter-boundary space (sīmantarika) and without leaving the hatthapāsa. This statement is not appropriate. This is because of the word: "If a fourth monk standing in a different boundary should perform the act, it is not a valid act, and it should not be performed" (Mahāvagga 389), and so forth. For this very reason, in this case as well, it is prescribed to perform the act only in the maḷakasīmā after clearing the mahāsīmā. In another way, because of standing in different boundaries, the monk standing in that mahāsīmā cannot be a quorum-completer (gaṇapūraka), and thus it should be known that the act merely fails.

If this is so, how can the mahāsīmā be cleared by means of bringing consent (chanda) and purity (pārisuddhi)? The Vinaya experts do not desire such clearing by bringing chanda and pārisuddhi. In this case of connected boundaries, they only desire clearing by means of bringing the monks into the hatthapāsa or by making them go outside the boundary. It should be understood that even if chanda is given, if the monk does not come personally, the monk standing in the mahāsīmā causes the act to fail. If it is asked why he causes the act to fail if his chanda and so forth do not arrive, it is because of the fault of the connection between two dissimilar boundaries (visabhāgasīmā). This fault of connection should be believed based on the authority of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). Indeed, it should be known that logic (yutti) cannot be known in all matters of the Vinaya, because the Vinaya is the domain of the Buddha (buddhagocara). Some teachers, however, say: "If monks standing continuously without interruption across both boundaries perform the act, and if the entire group of monks completing the quorum, the candidate, and the chanter of the kammavācā are all present together in only one boundary, then that act is well-performed. If either the candidate for the act or the chanter of the kammavācā is standing in the other boundary, the act fails." This statement is also appropriate only in the case of similar boundaries (sabhāgasīmā) such as baddhasīmā and gāmasīmā. For example...
153:
When monks perform a Sangha act (saṅghakamma) while standing without an interval, if the group of monks, the candidate for ordination (upasampadāpekkha), and the chanter (anussāvaka) are all present together within a single boundary (sīmā), that Sangha act is indeed well-performed. However, if a monk eligible for the act or the chanter is standing in another boundary, they say the Sangha act is invalidated. This statement is appropriate only for compatible boundaries (sabhāga-sīmā) such as the Baddha Sīmā and Gāma Sīmā. In those boundaries, even if they are connected to each other by trees etc., there is no fault. But in incompatible boundaries (visabhāga-sīmā) where there is a fault, if there is a connection by trees etc., one standing on one side can indeed invalidate the Sangha act on the other side. Since the purification (sodhana) is generally mentioned in the Commentary, this is our view (khanti). It should be accepted after careful consideration.

'Does not descend' (na otarati) means that in drum-shaped mountains and the like, it does not descend to the bottomless part. In this context, although it does not ascend to the top of the mountain etc., which is beyond measure at the moment of binding the boundary, it becomes a boundary later because of its status of being established in the boundary. The drum-shaped area below, however, does not attain the name of a boundary even if the boundary is bound above. It is with reference to this non-descent to the bottom that it is said 'does not descend'; otherwise, it should have been said in connection with both ascending and descending. 'Whatever' (yaṃ kiñci) refers to everything sentient or insentient that exists above the established boundary, whether it existed before, arose later, or entered later. Indeed, a monk who is riding on a sentient being such as the back of an elephant within the boundary is also considered to be standing within the boundary. The phrase 'in the Baddha Sīmā' is also said by way of illustration (upalakkhaṇa) according to the context. Everything standing in all Abaddha Sīmās is also to be regarded as a boundary.

'Going by a single connection' is said with reference to trees, vines, etc., that grow there. Such a thing deserves to be called 'gone from here.' If there are ropes, sticks, etc., lying across both a Baddha Sīmā and a Gāma Sīmā, or an Udakukkhepa Sīmā and a River Sīmā, where it is impossible to say 'gone from here' or 'come from there,' what should be done? Here, the part established on the Baddha Sīmā side is Baddha Sīmā, and the part established on the Gāma Sīmā side is Gāma Sīmā, just like a mountain etc. established in both boundaries. The same principle applies if an aerial root of a banyan tree growing from a Baddha Sīmā is established in a Gāma Sīmā, or if an aerial root of a banyan tree growing from a Gāma Sīmā is established in a Baddha Sīmā. Since it is impossible to say 'gone from here' or 'come from there' from the time it takes root, that part becomes part of the boundary it has entered. Some say that the branch in the air between those aerial roots belongs to both boundaries according to the extent of the boundary limits. Our preference, however, is that although the aerial root coming from the branch of that banyan tree is rooted in another boundary, as long as it cannot stand without that branch, it does not yet abandon its status of the original boundary. Only when it can stand independently without the branch does that aerial root alone attain the status of the boundary it has entered. Therefore, the part of the branch in the air also does not abandon its status of the original boundary. Why? Because it does not abandon its status of having come from the original boundary. The same principle applies to Udakukkhepa Sīmā, River Sīmā, etc. In those boundaries, in an incompatible boundary...
154:
Some teachers say that by the measure of the boundary limits, it belongs to both boundaries. In our own view (sakavāda), however, although the aerial root (pāroha) coming from the branch of that banyan tree is established by roots in the entered boundary, as long as it cannot stand without the branch, it does not abandon its status of being in the original boundary. When it can stand independently of the branch, then only the aerial root attains the status of being in the entered boundary. Therefore, the entire part of the branch in the air does not abandon its status of being in the former boundary. Why? Because the part that has come from that former boundary has not been abandoned. This is our preference (khanti). The same principle applies to Udakukkhepa Sīmā, River Sīmā, etc. In those Udakukkhepa Sīmās and River Sīmās, if one enters an incompatible boundary (visabhāga-sīmā) in this way, the purification of the entire boundary, and if one enters a compatible boundary (sabhāga-sīmā), the purification of only the monk who is standing in contact, all follow the method previously mentioned.

'Pārayati' means it overspreads (ajjhottharati). A boundary established on both banks of a river is said to overspread the river. Therefore, it is said, 'overspreading the river' (nadiṃ ajjhottharantaṃ). Indeed, the boundary does not descend into the river. However, if the characteristics of a river are absent, it does descend. In that case, that boundary is not a 'boundary across the river' (nadīpāra-sīmā). Therefore, it is said, 'The characteristics of a river are as previously mentioned in the signs of a river.' 'Assa' means 'it should be.' The connection is that it must be a permanent boat (dhuvanāvā) that is definitely obtainable. By the phrase 'not by a boat' (na nāvāya), it is shown that even without a boat, the binding of a boundary is well-bound. The boat serves the purpose of avoiding offenses.

'Rukkhasaṅghāṭamayo' refers to a bridge made by joining many trees together. There is a remaining text: 'made by cutting a tree.' The phrase 'having made the monks standing within all the signs within arm's reach (hatthapāsa)' is said with reference to the two banks being a single village field (gāmakhetta). The phrase 'mountain-shaped' (pabbatasaṇṭhānā) is said because of the island peaks rising from one side.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Granting of Boundaries is finished.

## The Explanation of the Uposatha Hall etc.

'Samūhanitvā' means having destroyed or having removed. This is also said for the purpose of avoiding offenses.

'Yāni kānici' is said because the signs of the boundary for this Uposatha hall are not explicitly mentioned in the Pali text.

## The Explanation of the Uposatha Hall etc. is finished.
155:
## Explanation of the Talk on Allowing the Non-separation Boundary

The phrase "eighteen monasteries" is said with reference to the Andhakavinda monastery as well. "The boundary of those monasteries" refers to the boundary existing in those great monasteries (mahāvihāra). The opening for the word "mana" is "īsaka," which means drifting slightly. To show this very meaning, it is said, "the state of not reaching the point of drifting away occurred." By the words "one who does not attend to it," the reason for not exceeding by psychic power is stated.

"That person" refers to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. "Both kinds also" refers to the two types: the boundary of common communion (samānasaṃvāsa-sīmā) and the boundary of non-separation (avippavāsa-sīmā). The term "boundary of non-separation" is said with reference to the great boundary (mahāsīmā). This is because, for the most part, the designation of non-separation exists in that great boundary.

"Even though they do not know the boundary of non-separation"—this is said regarding monks who do not know the existence or non-existence of the great boundary, nor its external limits. Intending that even such monks who do not know, if they stand within the boundary and perform the act with the kammavācā, that boundary is indeed abolished, it is said, "they will be able to abolish and to establish." "In a place free from doubt" means in a place free from a fragmentary boundary (khaṇḍasīmā). This is also said because, even if a great boundary exists, a fragmentary boundary is desired for the ease of performing monastic acts; therefore, that fragmentary boundary should not be established in places where many people gather, such as the courtyard of a cetiya. Even in such a gathering place, if that fragmentary boundary is established, it is well-established just like a great boundary. The phrase "but they will certainly not be able to re-establish" is said with reference to establishing a great boundary, because the fragmentary boundary has not been abolished and because they do not know its non-existence. However, they are certainly able to establish a fragmentary boundary in a place free from doubt.

"Having caused an overlapping of boundaries" means, when a fragmentary boundary exists, causing an overlap by covering the fragmentary boundary with a great boundary; and even when a fragmentary boundary does not exist, causing a doubt of overlap by not ceasing to wonder if it might overlap. "They would make it not a monastery" means making it unsuitable for Saṅgha acts. The meaning is that, although in the past acts could be performed in places free from doubt such as the courtyard of a cetiya, now even that ability to perform acts has been destroyed. "Should not be abolished" means it should not be abolished by those who do not know the fragmentary boundary. "They do not know both" means they do not know the determination of the regions of both boundaries, or they do not know the existence or non-existence of either of those two boundaries; there is only doubt in every place. "They will be able neither to abolish nor to establish"—this is said with reference to the meaning that although they are able to abolish while standing in a place free from doubt, they are unable to re-establish the great boundary. "Nor can they perform the kammavācā"—this is said with reference to the kammavācā for establishing a boundary. "Therefore" means because they are unable to establish, therefore it should not be abolished.
156:
Some teachers say: In such monasteries (where it is unknown whether a fragmentary or great boundary exists), having taken about five or six monks, starting from the edge of the monastery, standing continuously at every space the size of a couch within the monastery enclosure and in the surrounding area about a stone's throw away, if the abolition of the boundary is performed first by way of abolishing the boundary of non-separation and then the boundary of common communion, then if a fragmentary boundary or a great boundary exists in that monastery, those monks who have reached the middle of those boundaries at some couch-position will surely abolish them. Because of that abolition, only the village boundary (gāmasīmā) will remain. In this abolition of the boundary, knowing the boundary or its limits is not a factor. Standing within the boundary and the performance of the kammavācā with the thought "we shall abolish" are the only factors here. This is because it is stated in the Commentary that "even if they know the fragmentary boundary but do not know the boundary of non-separation, they will be able to abolish and to establish," thus stating the abolition even when the limits of the great boundary are unknown. They say that when only the village boundary remains, it is proper to establish both types of boundaries as desired and to perform acts such as ordination (upasampadā). That statement seems appropriate. It should be accepted after investigation.

## The Explanation of the Talk on Allowing the Non-separation Boundary is Finished.

## Explanation of the Talk on Village Boundaries and So Forth

In the Pali, by the words "monks, in a boundary that is not designated," etc., the village boundary (gāmasīmā) is the field (territory) of the established boundary (baddhasīmā). This is just as the forest, river, etc., are the fields for the boundary of seven abbhantaras, the water-splash boundary (udakukkhepa), and so on. It is shown that the village boundary itself becomes a boundary of common communion in a place devoid of an established boundary. In the phrase "whatever village boundary of that village," the word "of the village" is said with reference to the entire village territory (gāmakhetta), including fields, forests, mountains, etc., both inside and outside the limits of the village boundary. It does not refer only to the houses within the village. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: there is a village boundary connected to that entire village territory. The intention is that the conventional term "village" (gāma), designated by the people of the world as a single entity for many portions of land such as the inner village and fields, is also called "village boundary" (gāmasīmā) here. Indeed, the village itself is the village boundary. By this same method, the nature of forest boundaries (araññasīmā), etc., should be understood for those areas of land such as the forest, river, ocean, and natural lake mentioned above, which are designated as single entities by the people of the world. In the world, however, the conventional term "village boundary," etc., occurs only for the limits of the village and so on. It does not occur in all places such as the village territory. In the Dispensation (sāsana), however, because of the sense of excluding those villages from other villages, they themselves are their own limits. Therefore, it should be understood that they are called by the name of boundary as "the village itself is the village boundary, the forest itself is the forest boundary, the ocean itself is the ocean boundary." The phrase "or of a market town" is said as an illustration (upalakkhaṇa) to include various types of village boundaries. Therefore, it is said, "a city is also certainly included." Although the phrase "they receive tax" is said in general, in reality, in the land limits presented on the king's gold plates as "this village has this much land limit," even if tax is not taken in certain places such as lakes, canals, cemeteries, and mountains, those places are also indeed the village boundary. Excluding rivers, streams, and lakes, the entire land limit defined by the king and others should be known as the village boundary. Therefore, it is said, "the king defines and gives to someone." In that village, the king...
157:
In the world, the term 'village boundary' (gāmasīmā) and similar designations apply only to the limits of a village and the like. They do not apply to all places such as village fields. In the Sasana, however, because these villages are excluded from other villages, they themselves constitute their own boundaries. Therefore, it should be understood that they are referred to by the term 'boundary' (sīmā), as in 'the village itself is the village boundary, the forest itself is the forest boundary... the ocean itself is the ocean boundary.'

The phrase 'or of a town' (nigamassa vā) is stated to show all varieties of village boundaries by way of illustration (upalakkhaṇa). Therefore, it is said, 'a city (nagara) is also included.' The phrase 'they receive tribute' (baliṃ labhanti) is stated as a general rule. In fact, regarding the portions of land recorded in royal plates or documents (rājapaṇṇesu) as 'this village is this much of a portion of land,' even if tribute is not collected in certain places like tanks, canals, cemeteries, or mountains, those places are still part of the village boundary. All portions of land demarcated by kings and others, except for rivers, estuaries, and natural lakes, should be known as village boundaries. Thus it is said, 'the king demarcates and gives to someone.' If the king joins a certain area with another village, that area then belongs to the boundary of the village it was joined to. The same principle applies if natural lakes in a river are destroyed and turned into reservoirs or filled and turned into fields.

Villages abandoned by people due to dangers from kings or thieves, which remain uninhabited for a long time, are still individual village boundaries if there are other villages surrounding them. This is because kings may collect tribute from those abandoned villages by having residents of surrounding villages cultivate them, or by marking the cultivated areas of whoever works there. Alternatively, they may merge them with another village. However, if villages are abandoned even by kings, have no adjacent village fields, and have merged with the great forest, they become forest boundaries (agāmakaraññasīmā) that are not associated with a village; the former village boundary is destroyed. Kings may establish a large village in a place like a forest, settling thousands of families there, and demarcate surrounding existing villages as 'fief-villages' (bhogagāma) for the residents of that new village. In such cases, if the old names and boundaries are not destroyed, those old villages remain individual village boundaries. Merely giving them in this way does not mean the former village boundary status is relinquished. The phrase 'that and the other' (sā ca itarā ca) is an explanation of the meaning of the Pali term 'of common communion and a single Uposatha' (samānasamvāsā ekūposathā). In that explanation, 'that' (sā ca) refers to the new visuṃgāma boundary created by the king's will. 'The other' (itarā ca) refers to the original natural village boundary (pakatigāma) that remains unchanged. Just as it is proper to perform all Sangha acts in a bound boundary (baddhasīmā), these visuṃgāma and natural village boundaries are similar to a baddhasīmā in their suitability for all acts. That boundary is of common communion...
158:
'Having a single Uposatha' (ekūposatha) means, in essence, being of common communion (samānasamvāsā). Generally, when it is said 'similar to a bound boundary' (baddhasīmā), people tend to think only of the boundary for not being parted from the three robes (ticīvarāvippavāsa-sīmā) as a baddhasīmā. Therefore, to dispel such a misconception and to show that the similarity to a baddhasīmā also exists in the seven-abbhantara boundary (sattabbhantara-sīmā) to be mentioned later, the word 'only' (kevala) and so forth are stated.

'In a forest like the Vindhya forest' refers to a place where there is no village designation such as 'this is the field of such-and-such a village,' and where there is no plowing or sowing. Small islands in the middle of the ocean, where fishermen do not go and which are not inhabited by people, are also included in this category of 'forest' (arañña). Every place that is not village land and is devoid of rivers, oceans, or natural lakes should be known as a forest boundary (araññasīmā). This forest boundary, without depending on a seven-abbhantara boundary, is naturally of common communion and similar to a baddhasīmā. Just as in boundaries like rivers, it is proper to perform all Sangha acts in this forest boundary.

The status of rivers, oceans, and natural lakes as boundaries is already established because the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) states, 'by their own nature, they are similar to a baddhasīmā.' But how is the status of the forest as a boundary established? It is established by the power of the Suttas and other texts that allow the seven-abbhantara boundary. Just as many baddhasīmās are allowed in a village boundary to prevent schismatic acts (vaggakamma), and just as an inter-boundary space (sīmantarikā) is allowed between two baddhasīmās to prevent them from overlapping, so too is the seven-abbhantara boundary allowed in this forest. Since the existence of an inter-boundary space between two such seven-abbhantara boundaries is prescribed in the Pali and Commentaries, it should be understood that the forest also naturally possesses the status of a boundary, like rivers. The seven-abbhantara boundary is allowed only to prevent schismatic acts. Only those standing within that boundary can perform a schismatic act within a boundary; it is not like those standing in the sky, which is not a boundary, who cannot perform an act of those standing in the sky. Taking this principle, it should be understood that the Commentary states that rivers, oceans, and natural lakes—even though they are rejected as baddhasīmās by the statement 'Monks, all rivers are not bound boundaries'—possess the status of a boundary by their own nature.

'From the place where that monk is standing' means starting from the position of that monk. Even if there are a thousand monks, when a boundary is considered starting from the outer limit of that standing place to prevent schismatic acts among the monks, the seven-abbhantara boundary that arises spontaneously along with that consideration is of common communion (samānasamvāsā). However, in a small forest where there is no concern about schismatic acts because it is filled with many monks, if there is no need to consider a seven-abbhantara boundary, then a seven-abbhantara boundary does not arise; the Sangha should perform the act in the forest boundary itself. The same principle applies to rivers and so forth. For it will be said later: 'If a river is not very long...'
159:
“If the Saṅgha sits in all places from the source of the river to its mouth, there is no act of water-throw boundary (udakukkhepasīmā-kamma),” and so forth, as will be stated (in the Mahāvagga Commentary, 147). By this statement itself, it should be understood that for the purpose of preventing a fragmented act (vaggakamma), the water-throw boundary (udakukkhepasīmā) and the seven-abbhantara boundary (sattabbhantara-sīmā) arise only when there is regard for the boundary (sīmāpekkha); they do not arise when there is no such regard.

Some teachers, however, say: “A boundary is created only by measuring seven abbhantaras all around and making a delimitation; it does not arise spontaneously.” That view should not be accepted. For if a boundary were to arise only by making an abbhantara delimitation, then an unfixed boundary (abaddhasīmā), which is accomplished through the specific actions of the monks, would not be possible. Furthermore, because there are many types of cubits in the world, such as the carpenter’s cubit and the natural cubit, and because the Vinaya does not specify a particular cubit measurement, when measuring with an indefinite cubit, there would be doubt (saṅkā) regarding the failure (vipatti) of the boundary, such as: “Was it measured with the cubit allowed by the Blessed One, or was it not?” Also, since those measuring would be unable to measure without even a slight deficiency or excess, there would only be failure. If this boundary were to increase by the power of the assembly (parisa), it would either increase or decrease according to the measurement of those monks. When the Saṅgha has performed the act and departed, would this boundary, which arose through the effort (payoga) of the monks, disappear by their effort or not? If it does not disappear, why would it not remain until the disappearance of the Dispensation (sāsanantaradhāna), like a fixed boundary (baddhasīmā)? And if it remains, why would there not be doubt about the overlapping of boundaries (sīmāsambheda) in the entire forest, as in old monasteries? Therefore, it should be understood that the boundary arises only through regard for the boundary (sīmāpekkha) and disappears with the disappearance of that regard. Just as in this seven-abbhantara boundary, the same applies to the water-throw boundary (udakukkhepasīmā) in rivers and so forth.

Indeed, in that water-throw boundary as well, a medium-sized man cannot be precisely identified. Likewise, throwing with full strength cannot be precisely known. In both the seven-abbhantara and the water-throw, if there is insufficient space for seven abbhantaras or for a water-throw in a certain direction, how could measuring or throwing take place there? If it were said that the boundary enters a place that is not its own territory because it has entered the village territory (gāmakhetta) and so forth, the boundary would be invalidated. However, when a boundary arises through regard for the boundary, in places where there is sufficient space, the seven-abbhantara and water-throw boundaries arise fully and spontaneously. But in places where there is insufficient space, they arise only within the extent of one's own territory and do not go outside. As for the mention of measuring the abbhantara and the act of throwing sand and so forth in this context, it is done to define the location of the boundaries that have already arisen, just like the description of the procedure for throwing clods of earth to know the village precinct (gāmūpacāra) and the house precinct (gharūpacāra). For this very reason, it was said in the Mātikā Commentary: “One either consecrates a boundary or defines a water-throw.” Even when this is done, because that delimitation cannot be known exactly as it truly is...
160:
Because that delimitation cannot be known exactly as it truly is, the monks staying inside should, after knowing it by comparative measurement, stay in a place free from doubt. Those monks who wish to exclude another monk should send him to a place far away that is free from doubt.

Other teachers, however, say: "Regard for the boundary (sīmāpekkha) is not necessary. When even a single monk enters a forest or a river for purposes such as traveling or bathing, a boundary of seven abbhantaras or a water-throw boundary arises spontaneously around that monk, like the light of a lamp. As soon as that monk reaches a village territory and so forth, that boundary disappears. For this very reason, in this context, it was allowed to maintain another seven abbhantaras or a water-throw as an inter-boundary space (sīmantarikā) between the two boundaries of two groups of Saṅgha performing separate acts. This is to prevent the boundary that arises around a monk sent for some business to the edge of a boundary from touching the boundary of others and causing an overlap of boundaries (sīmāsambheda). Otherwise, an inter-boundary space of only a cubit and four finger-breadths should have been allowed here. Alternatively, this point is also clear from the statement that an act is invalidated for a monk standing in the inter-boundary space in both boundaries. This is because the boundary that arises spontaneously around the monk standing in that inter-boundary space overlaps with both boundaries or with one of them. Otherwise, it would not be appropriate to say that the act is invalidated because of the monk standing in that inter-boundary space. It is also stated in the Mātikā Commentary: 'Whether one stands having abandoned the hand-reach (hatthapāsa) within the delimitation, or stands outside the delimitation without exceeding that same amount of delimitation, one invalidates the act (kammaṃ kopeti).' Furthermore, for a monk standing in a forest that is not a village, even if he has no desire to perform a communal act, the Blessed One allowed the being apart from the robes (cīvaravippavāsa) in an open space defined by seven abbhantaras. And that delimitation is indeed a boundary. Thus, the boundary arises without regard (apekkha). For this very reason, it is stated here: 'This boundary also obtains the exemption from being apart from the three robes (ticīvaravippavāsa-parihāra).' Therefore, it should be accepted that the boundary arises in the manner stated even without the desire to perform a communal act." That view is not appropriate. If a boundary could arise for every individual monk like the light of a lamp, then when the Saṅgha or a group (gaṇa) performs an act, the many boundaries arising individually around the monks standing there would lead to the fault of mutual overlapping (sankara). Also, the increase or decrease of that boundary would occur according to the strength of the assembly. New boundaries would arise for monks who arrive later, and the boundaries existing around the monks who depart would be destroyed.

In the Pali, however, it is stated: "Seven abbhantaras all around; this is the common communion (samanasaṃvāsa) there," and so forth, allowing only a single seven-abbhantara and water-throw. This boundary does not arise spontaneously by nature or by the power of a cause, like the light of a lamp.
161:
In truth, these boundaries arise only by the permission of the Blessed One. When the Blessed One allowed these boundaries, he did so only for the purpose of avoiding a group act (vaggakamma) and for the ease of performing legal acts for the monks. If that is so, how could the arising of those boundaries around monks who have entered for purposes such as bathing be without benefit? Even if there is a benefit, how could many boundaries arise according to the number of individual monks, when only a single beneficial boundary should exist? It is stated (in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā): "They stand within a single boundary without leaving the hand-reach (hatthapāsa)." There is also the mention of establishing an inter-boundary space (sīmantarika) between two boundaries with a measurement equal to those boundaries, and the mention of the invalidation of the legal act for monks standing in that inter-boundary space. That statement was made to avoid from afar the suspicion of overlapping boundaries and the suspicion of the invalidation of the legal act, because the limits of these boundaries are difficult to discern.

The seven-abbhantara limit shown by the Blessed One in the open for the sake of not being separated from one's robes (cīvarāvippavāsa) is not a sattabbhantara-sīmā. Like the limits of a field or a pond, it is merely a limit in this context. In that case of cīvarāvippavāsa, even if many monks are standing together, they must keep their robes within a seven-abbhantara limit around them, starting from their own respective standing positions. It should not be taken starting from the edge of the assembly. For if it were taken from the edge of the assembly towards the inside, a robe placed at the end of the abbhantara would be outside the abbhantara of a monk standing in the middle; thus, that robe could become a nissaggiya offense at dawn. A boundary (sīmā), however, must be taken only from the edge of the assembly. Here, the protection against separation from robes is mentioned only because there is a limit in the open. It is not mentioned because a boundary limit is obtainable, as in the case of the term 'boundary of non-separation' (avippavāsa-sīmā) in a great boundary (mahāsīmā). For even in a mahāsīmā, a robe becomes nissaggiya in a village or its precinct. Here too, a robe placed at the edge of the boundary of a monk standing in the middle becomes nissaggiya. Therefore, it is our preference that the arising of these sattabbhantara and udakukkhepa boundaries, and their disappearance without that regard for the boundary, should be understood only by the power of the aforementioned regard for the boundary (sīmāpekkha). This should be accepted after careful investigation. Otherwise, another method more suitable than this should be sought.

Regarding this sattabbhantara-sīmā, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Seven abbhantaras all around in the forest," and in the Commentary: "Seven abbhantaras all around in a forest like the Vindhya forest." Since the sattabbhantara-sīmā is prescribed even in a forest dense with trees and the like, there is no fault in the connection of this boundary with trees and the like, along with the forest boundary (arañña-sīmā) which is its own support. It should be understood that in a place supported by trees where there is no village, it is unnecessary to say that the protection of the open space is permitted for the sake of not being separated from robes (cīvarāvippavāsa), excluding the protection of the trees.
162:
"For the sake of the precinct" (upacāratthāya) means that for the sake of the inter-boundary space, more than seven abbhantaras is permissible.
