However, less than that is not permissible because the seven-abbhantara limit is difficult to discern. Therefore, even a single monk standing outside, apart from the Saṅgha, should cross another seven-abbhantara distance and stand very far away. Otherwise (if he does not cross the seven abbhantaras), there may be suspicion of the invalidation of the legal act. This same method applies to the water-splash boundary (udakukkhepa) as well. For this reason, it will be stated (in the Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā): "But less is not permissible." It should be understood that the prescription of the inter-boundary space in this sattabbhantara-sīmā is established in accordance with the Pāḷi that allows the inter-boundary space for two bound boundaries (baddha-sīmā).

In fact, although the Blessed One, by the power of the origin, allowed the inter-boundary space for two bound boundaries of the same category that depend on a single village boundary, in order to avoid the fault of mutual overlapping or encroachment; nevertheless, the teachers of the Commentaries, knowing that the Blessed One did not desire the mutual overlapping or encroachment of two sattabbhantara-sīmās or two udakukkhepa-sīmās of the same category that depend on a single forest boundary or a river boundary etc., nor their standing without an interval or inter-boundary space, established the prescription of the inter-boundary space here as well. It should be understood that even in the case of boundaries of different categories (visabhāga-sīmā), standing without an inter-boundary space results in overlapping only when the two factors are present: depending on a single boundary and being of the same category; if these are not present, it does not occur. By the very power of prescribing the inter-boundary space, it should be accepted that the mutual connection of trees and the like for these sattabbhantara and udakukkhepa boundaries is also not permissible, just as in the case of bound boundaries; this method is also thus demonstrated.

By the words "by nature itself" (sabhāveneva), it is shown that these are unbound boundaries (abaddha-sīmā) like a village boundary. By the words "it is permissible to perform all Saṅgha acts here," it is shown that they share the same communion (samānasaṃvāsa) and the same Uposatha. "By whatever [creature]" (yene keneaci) refers to a type of pond dug even by animals such as pigs. A large current of water falling from a high place to a low place, whether the hole it dug or eroded is small or large, if it possesses the required characteristics, it is a natural lake (jātassara) only. Here too, in a small pond, there is no need for the water-splash (udakukkhepa) procedure. In the ocean, however, because it is difficult to clear, the legal act must be performed entirely by means of the water-splash boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā) only.

"Again there" (puna tattha) means that in these three types of unbound boundaries such as rivers which are established by worldly convention, he intends to show the limit of the unbound boundary established by Sasana convention for the purpose of avoiding a group act. In the Pāḷi, in the phrases such as "that which a medium-sized man," it is called udakukkhepa because water is lifted and thrown there; it is called udakukkhepa because it is the place where the water falls. The meaning here, by the power of word-connection, is: starting from the edge of the assembly, all around, as far as a medium-sized man...
163:
The distance a man throws water and where it falls is the defined area; this area in rivers and such is another communal *udakukkhepa-sīmā* (water-throw boundary).

"Within that" (*tassa anto*) means within the area defined by that water-throw. A monk standing not only within that water-throw but also outside it [within a certain range] invalidates the legal act (*kamma*). The statement "it is not proper to stand within a single water-throw" is said because the extent of a water-throw is difficult to discern, leading to doubt about the invalidation of the legal act. Therefore, in the *Mātikāṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "A monk who stands within the defined area having abandoned the *hatthapāsa* (forearm's length), or a monk who stands outside the defined area without exceeding that same extent, invalidates the legal act; this is the conclusion in all Commentaries." Regarding this, the statement in the *Sāratthadīpanī* which says, "By the words 'a monk standing within that water-throw having abandoned the *hatthapāsa* invalidates the legal act,' a monk standing anywhere outside the defined area does not invalidate the legal act," and rejects the words of the *Mātikāṭṭhakathā*, saying "it is found neither in the Pāḷi nor in the Commentaries," etc., is not good. This is because here, the words of the Commentary and the *Mātikāṭṭhakathā* are consistent and connected in method.

The connection is as follows: without leaving a *sīmantarika* (inter-boundary space) of about a span and four finger-breadths between two water-throw boundaries, it is stated right here in the Commentary: "Another water-throw should be placed in the *sīmantarika*; more than that is certainly proper, but less is not proper." By this statement mentioning the *sīmantarika*, if it is placed less than a water-throw's distance, the invalidation of the legal act due to the overlapping of boundaries (*sīmasambheda*) is already stated. To whatever extent this is stated, to that extent, even if a single monk enters that *sīmantarika*, since he is standing within a boundary, the invalidation of the legal act is indeed stated. The statement in the Commentary "less is not proper" is also said to remove doubt about the overlapping of boundaries, even for one who finds the extent of a water-throw difficult to discern. Since it is stated that the *sīmantarika* should be arranged with that same extent between *sattabbhantara* boundaries, these also have extents that are difficult to discern, and the doubt about the invalidation of the legal act for those standing there is evident. It should be understood that the teachers designated even a place where there is doubt about invalidating the legal act as a "place of invalidation" in order to avoid it from a distance.

"That" (*taṃ*) refers to the boundary. By the words "it passes over very quickly," it shows that it is proper to perform the legal act in a boat that does not pass beyond that water-throw boundary but circulates only within it. Indeed, it is for the purpose of avoiding such doubt that the boundary is demarcated with sand and so on. Otherwise, doubt might arise as to whether the legal act is invalidated, wondering whether the boat has gone outside or not. "Of another proclamation" (*aññissā anussāvanā*) means in a river boundary alone...
164:
The proclamation (*anussāvanā*) occurs only in the river boundary (not mixed with the *udakukkhepa*). "Or on a tree grown within the river" means it can also occur on a tree standing outside the extent of the *udakukkhepa*. This is because the outer bank of the river is a *visabhāga-sīmā* (dissimilar boundary) and thus a place where a boundary should not be established, but the inner part of the river is not a place where a boundary should not be established, as it is similar in nature as a support. Therefore, by the words "on the outer bank of the river or in a monastery boundary," etc., only the bank is shown as a place where a boundary should not be established, but not the river. The words "even by those standing on a tree" are said with reference to a tree standing within the *udakukkhepa*. For it is not proper for monks to stand outside the *udakukkhepa*.

"Of the tree" means only of that tree standing within the *udakukkhepa*. "Having cleared the boundary" means clearing the aforementioned *vihāra-baddha-sīmā* (fixed monastery boundary) and *gāma-sīmā* (village boundary) by bringing the monks standing there into the *hatthapāsa* (forearm's length) or by making them go outside the boundary. Just as monks performing a legal act in a water-throw boundary must do so after clearing (other boundaries), so too monks performing a legal act in a fixed boundary or a village boundary must do so only after clearing the monks present in the water-throw boundary. By these words "having cleared the boundary," the fault of connection through trees and so on between the *sattabbhantara* forest boundaries and the water-throw boundary is also shown by way of method. In this same way, the fault of connection between the *sattabbhantara* boundary and the fixed boundary or village boundary, and between these and the *sattabbhantara* boundary, should be understood. In the Commentary, however, all this can be known by the method already stated, so only the arrangement between boundaries that are close to each other is shown.

Here, the way of taking the method in accordance with the *Suttas* is: just as a boundary consecrated in a fixed boundary becomes a *vipatti-sīmā* (defective boundary), and thus their mutual connection through trees and so on is not proper, so too a fixed boundary consecrated in rivers and such becomes a *vipatti-sīmā*, and thus its connection with those river boundaries through trees and so on is clearly not proper. By this method, it should be understood that the connection through trees and so on of the *sattabbhantara* boundary with village and river boundaries, and of the water-throw boundary with forest boundaries and such, is not proper. Thus, it should be understood as the method in accordance with the *Suttas* that if the fixed boundary, *sattabbhantara* boundary, and water-throw boundary allowed by the Blessed One are connected through trees and so on, whether with each other or with other boundaries that are not their own support, they fall into the fault of overlapping boundaries (*sambheda-dosa*).

However, with their own supporting village boundaries and so on, when the three types of boundaries such as the fixed boundary arise, it should be regarded that connection through trees and so on is also allowed, in accordance with the *sambhedajjhottharaṇa* (overlapping and covering) allowed by the Blessed One. If this is so, why is a *sīmantarika* (inter-boundary space) not arranged between the water-throw boundary, fixed boundary, and so on?
165:
Because of the difference in support and the difference in nature, they are naturally distinct (therefore, an inter-boundary space need not be established). This means that overlap occurs only in boundaries that have the same support and the same nature, when they are without an inter-boundary space (sīmantarikā). Because of this stated meaning, while the Saṅgha is performing a legal act (kamma) in a boundary established with a river as a mark, it is permissible for other monks to perform a legal act in a water-boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā) that is established within the river and touches the village territory.

The five types of boundaries established by worldly convention—village boundary (gāma-sīmā), forest boundary (arañña-sīmā), river boundary (nadī-sīmā), ocean boundary (samudda-sīmā), and natural lake boundary (jātassara-sīmā)—do not incur the fault of overlapping (sambhēda-dosa) even if they are connected to each other by trees and so on. This is because there is no worldly convention that they overlap. In the world, people do not say that villages and so on are overlapped with other villages or rivers merely because they are connected by trees and so on. The overlap or non-overlap of boundaries established by worldly convention must be understood only through worldly convention, and not otherwise. Therefore, in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), the method of overlap among these boundaries is not shown anywhere; only the boundary established by the convention of the Dispensation (Sāsana) is shown.

Among these boundaries, regarding the established boundary (baddha-sīmā), the lower limit is fully shown in the Commentaries with such statements as 'the boundary extends downwards to the water that supports the earth' (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 138). However, the lower limit of village boundaries and so on is not shown. How should this be known? Some teachers say, 'Village boundaries and so on also extend downwards, touching the water that supports the earth, just like the established boundary (baddha-sīmā).'

Other teachers, however, reject that statement and say, 'First, the river, ocean, and natural lake boundaries, as well as the water-boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā) depending on them, exist only on the upper surface of the earth and in places submerged by water; they do not exist below that because there is no water covering below. If, however, there is a place about a league (yojana) deep due to whirlpools and so on, those are indeed river boundaries and so on, but they do not exist below that depth. Therefore, a monk who has entered through a tunnel with its opening outside the bank below the river, or who has entered by psychic power, does not invalidate the legal act of the monks staying in the river. That monk, however, does invalidate the legal act of the monks in the nearby village. If that monk is sitting between two villages on both banks, he invalidates the legal act of the monks in both village areas. If the bank is not village territory but is merely a forest without a village, he invalidates the legal act of the monks performing a legal act in a small forest boundary (arañña-sīmā) alone, excluding the sattabbhantara boundary on both banks. If they perform the legal act in a sattabbhantara boundary, then if the limit of their sattabbhantara boundary extends beyond one sattabbhantara from the place where this monk is sitting inside the tunnel, the legal act is not invalidated; if it does not extend beyond, it is invalidated.

In a village boundary (gāma-sīmā), the area below where tunnels or pits can be dug, or where it is said that gold, gems, etc., can be excavated, is also considered the village boundary. A monk staying inside such a place by psychic power also invalidates the legal act. In a place where there is no even a notion that ordinary people can enter...'
166:
the legal act is invalidated. If it does not (extend beyond), the legal act is invalidated. In a village boundary (gāma-sīmā), however, in tunnels or pits where it is possible to enter, or where gold, gems, etc., are excavated and taken, or where there is a possibility that they can be taken, the area below to that extent is also the village boundary. A monk sitting inside there by psychic power also invalidates the legal act. In a place where there is no even a notion that ordinary people can enter, that entire area down to the water supporting the earth is only a forest boundary (arañña-sīmā), not a village boundary.

The same principle applies to the forest boundary (arañña-sīmā). In that forest boundary, as far as there is a possibility of entry, only that much of the upper surface is the forest boundary. Below that, it is not the forest boundary because it is not conventionally called 'the same forest' along with the upper surface. This is because people do not say that one who has entered under the ground has 'entered the forest.' Therefore, a monk staying under the ground does not invalidate the legal act of the monks in the forest area above, just as a monk staying in a tunnel-river does not invalidate the legal act of those in the river above. In a single world-system (cakkavāḷa), excluding the villages, rivers, oceans, and natural lakes, all the remaining uninhabited places, including the deva and brahma realms, are simply 'forest' (arañña). Because it is said, 'from a village or from a forest,' rivers, oceans, natural lakes, etc., are also technically forest. However, in this context of boundaries, since rivers and so on are taken as separate boundaries, only the remainder should be taken as forest. Among those forests, whatever area is conventionally called 'one forest' is one forest boundary (arañña-sīmā). For instance, the entire city of Indra (Indapura) is one forest boundary. Similarly, the cities of Asuras, Yakkhas, and so on. The celestial mansions of devas and brahmas in the sky, being delimited by the sky all around, are each individual forest boundaries, like mountain islands in the middle of the ocean. In all such places, the legal act should be performed either in a sattabbhantara boundary or in the forest boundary itself. Therefore, here too, because the earth below is not conventionally called 'forest' along with the forest surface above, it should be taken as a separate forest boundary. That is why, in the discussion of village and river boundaries in the Commentaries, the method shown for the established boundary (baddha-sīmā)—that 'a monk with psychic power staying below the ground invalidates the legal act' (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 138)—is not shown here.

This explanation of the lower limit of village boundaries and so on seems appropriate as it does not contradict the Suttas and other texts. It should be accepted after careful investigation. If accepted in this way, the established boundary (baddha-sīmā) designated within a village boundary covers the village boundary above and the forest boundary below that extends to the water. Thus, it is established that that forest boundary is also the territory (khetta) of that established boundary. The Blessed One stated that rivers, oceans, and natural lakes are 'without boundary' (asīmā) (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 147), meaning they are not the territory of an established boundary (baddha-sīmā), but He did not say so regarding the forest. Therefore,
167:
The forest boundary (arañña-sīmā) should also be understood as the territory (khetta) of the bound boundary (baddha-sīmā). If that is so, why is a boundary not bound in that forest? It is because there is no purpose, and because the seven-inter-fathom boundary (sattabbhantara-sīmā) arises immediately when a boundary is desired. Indeed, a bound boundary established over that seven-inter-fathom boundary would only become an invalid boundary (vipatti-sīmā) because it would conform to overlapping (sambheda) and submerging (ajjhottharaṇa) the existing boundary.

A boundary established by standing in a village territory and including a part of the forest that is not village territory, even if well-established, is valid because it does not mix with the seven-inter-fathom boundary ordained by the Blessed One in the non-village forest. Between the monks who enter within that bound boundary to perform a formal act and the monks who perform a formal act in the pure forest outside that bound boundary, three seven-inter-fathoms (sattabbhantaras) must be maintained. Otherwise, it would only be an invalidity (vipatti). Therefore, it should be understood that establishing a bound boundary in a non-village forest is entirely useless.

'A branch entering the river' refers to a branch that stands touching the ground of the river, and even more so to one that stands without touching it. The same principle applies to aerial roots (pāroha). By this passage, it is shown that it is not allowable to connect with a water-splash boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā) via branches and such that are connected to a different type of boundary (visabhāga-sīmā) which stands touching a similar river boundary. By this same passage, it should be understood that it is not allowable to connect with a small boundary (māḷaka-sīmā) via branches and such that stand touching a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) or a village boundary (gāma-sīmā).

By the words 'only within the river', the standing of bridge supports on the bank is excluded. By that passage, it is shown that there is no overlapping (sambheda) even if they stand within the river outside the limit of the water-splash boundary. Therefore, he said, 'those standing on the outer bank,' and so on. For if there were overlapping in the case of standing within the river outside the water-splash limit, then the bridge standing in the river should also be rejected because the invalidity of the act (kammakopa) would be the same; however, it is not rejected. Therefore, it should be understood that in all boundaries, there is no fault of overlapping (sambheda-dosa) with one's own supporting boundary.

'By an obstruction (āvaraṇa)' means by obstructing the water by driving in wooden stakes and such. 'By the construction of an embankment (koṭṭakabandhana)' means by an embankment made by filling with clay and such. By both terms, only obstruction is shown. The meaning already stated as 'having destroyed the river' is clarified by the passage 'an embankment is bound below'; the meaning is that the river is obstructed below and an embankment is bound. 'Saḍḍhitamodaka' means overflowing water. By the passage 'from the place where it flows submerging the river', it is shown that it is not allowable to establish a boundary in the place where water flows between a lake and a river. 'Uppatitvā' means becoming wide by way of breaking the banks and such. 'Vihāra-sīmā' refers to the bound boundary (baddha-sīmā).
168:
'Agamanapatha' refers to a journey where one cannot go and return on the same day. The statement 'it only reaches the count of a forest boundary' is said with reference to a forest boundary without a village, established by worldly usage. 'In that place' refers to small islands and such which are the paths of fishermen in the natural course.

'That place' refers only to the place where pits and such are made, not to where they are not made. 'Lōṇī' refers to a river (or channel) that flows in the form of a canal, being low due to the force of the rising sea tide.

'Sambhindanti' (they overlap) means that if one includes within one's own boundary even a hair's breadth of an area, starting from a place where four monks cannot sit, it is called overlapping the boundaries. It should be understood that if one includes the entire area, starting from a place sufficient for four monks to sit, it is called 'submerging' (ajjhottharanti). 'Saṃsaṭṭhaviṭapā' refers to trees whose branches and roots stand intertwined with each other; by this, the extreme proximity to each other is shown. For trees standing far apart may also have their branches touching; since that alone would not certainly constitute the characteristic of overlapping, the word 'viṭapa' (branch/root) is used to show that characteristic of overlapping. By doing this, if one includes an area insufficient for monks to sit within one's own boundary and builds an old monastery, it is called overlapping a boundary with another boundary; it is shown that it does not mean anything beyond that.

'Baddha hoti' (it is bound) is said with reference to the boundary of an old monastery. 'Amba' (mango tree) refers to the mango tree which serves as a marker (nimitta) of that old boundary for those who do not know because the enclosures and such of the old monastery have been destroyed in later times. The meaning is that they bind the boundary by including the area between the mango tree and the rose-apple tree (jambu) within their own boundary, having designated the rose-apple tree which stands in the old monastery boundary as a marker. Here too, it should be understood that it is stated by way of introduction that even if the mango tree, which is a marker of the old boundary and stands on village land, has its branches and leaves intertwined with the rose-apple tree within that old boundary, there is no invalidity at the time of binding the boundary, nor is there overlapping with the village boundary or invalidity of the act later on.

'Padesa' refers to a region sufficient for the Saṅgha to sit. By the words 'having left an inter-boundary space (sīmantarika)', etc., it is shown that even if boundaries are bound without an interval, touching each other without overlapping (sambheda) or submerging (ajjhottharaṇa), such a boundary is not a valid boundary. Therefore, an inter-boundary space of even one or two finger-breadths is allowable. However, because such a small space is difficult to discern, it is stated in the commentaries as four finger-breadths and so on. 'Dvinnaṃ sīmānaṃ' means it is the marker of two bound boundaries. The intention is that since the marker is outside the boundary, there is no fault of overlapping at the time of binding. It is not only because it is a marker that it causes commingling...
169:
...performs [so]. Furthermore, another tree standing in the sīmantarikā (boundary interval) also performs in the same way. Therefore, trees and such growing in even a small sīmantarikā are certainly not allowable. Here, since the fault of overlapping (saṅkara-dosa) is shown everywhere only regarding the entry of visible trunks, branches, etc., above [the ground], it is established that there is no fault in the entry of invisible roots, as they are considered the same as the ground. However, if roots also enter while being visible, it is indeed an overlap (saṅkara). Mountains and rocks, even if visible, are considered the same as the ground. If, at the very time of binding the boundary, a large tree stands touching both boundaries, it should be understood that the boundary bound later does not become a [valid] boundary.

Sīmā-saṅkara means the overlapping of boundaries (sambheda). The statement in the Sāratthadīpanī—"Performing sīmā-saṅkara is said because when a tree grows and enters the boundary area, the extent of the two boundaries is difficult to know"—is not appropriate. This is because it should also be said in the case of overlapping with a village boundary (gāmasīmā). For in that village boundary as well, when the marks (nimitta) grow, the extent of the village boundary and the bound boundary (baddhasīmā) is indeed difficult to know. However, since it is not mentioned regarding that village boundary but only regarding the overlap of two bound boundaries, it should be understood that only the aforementioned fault of connection (sambandha-dosa) is referred to by the word saṅkara. In the Pali text, although the invalidity of a boundary bound later is taught by way of the introduction (nidāna) as: "Monks, for those whose boundary is bound later, that act of theirs is unlawful (adhammika)," etc., it should be understood that the invalidity of both boundaries is shown when two groups of monks standing in two village boundaries make a connection or an encroachment between the boundaries, without leaving a sīmantarikā, or without separating the connection of tree roots, etc., and complete the kammavācā at the same moment, thereby consecrating them together.

## The Explanation on Village Boundaries, etc., is Finished.

## Explanation on the Divisions of Uposatha, etc.

In the phrase "adhammena vaggaṃ" (unlawfully and by a faction), if there are four monks within a single boundary, only the recitation of the Pātimokkha is permitted; if there are three or two, only the pārisuddhi-uposatha is permitted. Here, because it is not done in that way, it is called "adhammena" (unlawfully). Since the consent and purity (chanda-pārisuddhi) reach only the Saṅgha, and not a group (gaṇa) or an individual, it is called "vaggaṃ" (by a faction).

If two groups of monks, having brought each other's consent within a single boundary, perform separate Saṅgha acts (saṅghakamma) at the same moment, what happens in this case? Some teachers say that this act is allowable. That statement should not be accepted because it is an act by a faction (vaggakamma). In truth, the consent and purity of the monks performing the act do not reach the other Saṅgha. This should be understood because there is no such statement that the consent and purity reach [them], and because the boundary is permitted only for the purpose of performing acts separately. If, while the Saṅgha is present in a monastery boundary (vihārasīmā), three or two monks perform the pārisuddhi-uposatha in a khandhasīmā (temporary boundary) for some reason, it should be understood that since they are standing in a different boundary, that act is a lawful act (dhammakamma) and an act by a unified group (samaggakamma).

## The Explanation on the Divisions of Uposatha, etc., is Finished.

## Explanation on the Recitation of the Pātimokkha

In the phrase "Evametaṃ dhārayāmi, sutā kho panāyasmantehi," after saying "Thus I remember this,"...
170:
If two groups of monks, having brought each other's consent within a single boundary, perform separate Saṅgha acts (saṅghakamma) at the same moment, what happens in this case? Some teachers say that this practice is allowable; that statement should not be accepted because it is an act by a faction (vaggakamma). In truth, the consent and purity of the monks performing the act cannot reach the other Saṅgha. This should be understood because there is no such statement that it reaches [them], and because the boundary is permitted only for the purpose of performing acts separately. If, while the Saṅgha is present in a monastery boundary (vihārasīmā), three or two monks perform the pārisuddhi-uposatha in a khandhasīmā (temporary boundary) for some reason, it should be understood that since they are standing in a different boundary, that act is a lawful act (dhammakamma) and an act by a unified group (samaggakamma).

## The Explanation on the Divisions of Uposatha, etc., is Finished.

## Explanation on the Recitation of the Pātimokkha

In the phrase "Evametaṃ dhārayāmi" (Thus I remember this) and "Sutā kho panāyasmantehi" (It has been heard by the venerable ones), after saying "Thus I remember this," one should say: "Venerable ones, the introduction (nidāna) has been recited; the four pārājika rules have been heard by the venerable ones," and so on. In the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-aṭṭhakathā, Nidāna-vaṇṇanā), it is said in this very way. "Sutena" means by the word "suta."

"Savarabhaya" means danger from thieves wandering in the forest. Therefore, it is called "aṭavimanussabhaya" (danger from forest-dwelling savages). Before the recitation of the introduction is finished, it is not considered that the Pātimokkha has been recited; therefore, it is said: "in the second and subsequent recitations (uddesa)," and so on. "By three methods as well" means by way of osāraṇa (summarizing), kathana (expounding), and sarabhañña (intoning). Among these methods, summarizing the sutta because of wanting to speak the meaning oneself or wanting another to speak it is called "osāraṇa." Showing the meaning of that sutta is called "kathana." Chanting only the text with a melody is called "sarabhañña." "Having resolved upon recitation (sajjhāya)" means having produced the thought, "I will perform the recitation." "One who speaks by summarizing" means speaking by reciting the text oneself first and then explaining the meaning later.

## The Explanation on the Recitation of the Pātimokkha is Finished.

## Explanation on the Rejection of Unlawful Acts, etc.

"Of nine kinds" means: three kinds regarding the Saṅgha, the group (gaṇa), and the individual; three kinds by way of the recitation of the sutta, purity (pārisuddhi), and resolution (adhiṭṭhāna); and three kinds by way of the fourteenth day, the fifteenth day, and the day of unity (sāmaggi). Thus, it refers to the Uposatha of nine kinds.
171:
"Fourfold" refers to the four types of Uposatha acts performed illegally, such as the dissentient Uposatha (vagguposatha). "Twofold" refers to the two types of Pātimokkha, namely the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha and the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha. "Ninefold" refers to the nine types of Pātimokkha recitation (pātimokkhuddesa), consisting of five for monks and four for nuns.

## The explanation of the discussion on protesting illegal acts, etc., is finished.

## The explanation of the discussion on learning the counting of fortnights, etc.

The word "Kati" should be understood as feminine, in reference to the word "tithi" (lunar day).

"Utuvassa" occurs only in the winter and summer seasons.

In the word "Viññāpeti," "Viññāpana" (making known) should be understood as performing a bodily gesture after mental planning. In the Pali, "pārisuddhi given to another" means the monk who gives the purity gives it again in the presence of another monk. Since it is stated, "He reports only the true status of being a novice," for one who was ordained before reaching twenty years of age, one who has committed a Pārājika, or one who has renounced the training, etc., as long as their claim to be a monk (bhikkhu-paṭiññā) remains, the chanda-pārisuddhi (consent and purity) brought by them is valid. It should be understood that it is shown that only from the moment they admit their status as a novice, etc., does it no longer count. Indeed, in the Pali, it is said: "When one has given purity and reached the Saṅgha, if he disrobes... if he admits to being a paṇḍaka, if he admits to being an animal, if he admits to being a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka), the purity brought is valid." Therefore, it is established that for paṇḍakas and others as well, the chanda-pārisuddhi is valid during the time they claim to be monks. Thus, it is said: "This method is the same in all cases." For those who are normally insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by pain, even if they admit to being insane, etc., on the way, it should be understood that the chanda, etc., is valid just by their reaching the Saṅgha.

By the phrase "within the arm's length (hatthapāsa) of the monks," it shows that chanda-pārisuddhi does not reach groups or individuals. This is because it is stated in the Pali, "reached the Saṅgha." "Biḷālasaṅkhalika-pārisuddhi" refers to purity that is like a chain tied to a cat's neck. Just as the chain follows only when the cat comes and does not follow when the cat does not come because it is attached to that cat, this is the meaning of this purity (it arrives only when the monk who brings it arrives). Or, in another way, just as the first link of a chain...
172:
...reaches only the second link and not the third link, this purity is likewise. In this context, the mention of the cat should be understood as merely an illustrative example.

## The explanation of the discussion on the authorization to learn the counting of fortnights, etc., is finished.

## The explanation of the discussion on giving consent (chanda)

In the Pali, in the phrase "There are duties to be done for the Saṅgha," the word "duty" (karaṇīya) is used in the singular due to a grammatical shift (vacanavipallāsa).

The phrase "There is no duty of giving authorization (sammuti) to that monk" means that since the Pali mentions giving authorization only to a monk who occasionally remembers, even if there is no authorization for a monk who occasionally does not remember, his absence does not cause the act to be dissentient (vagga). However, some teachers say, "He too should be brought within the arm's length (hatthapāsa)," but that view should not be accepted.

The task to be performed before the assembly of the Saṅgha is known as pubbakaraṇa (preliminary duties), and the task to be performed after the assembly of the Saṅgha is known as pubbakiccam (preliminary acts). In the Pali, regarding "If he does not determine (adhiṭṭhaheyya), there is a dukkaṭa offense," there is no offense if it happens without intention or through forgetfulness. As in this case, it is the same in subsequent cases. Where there is an unintentional offense (acittakāpatti), we shall discuss it later.

"It is prescribed" shows that although there is no separate prohibition stating "Uposatha should not be performed by one with an offense," it is indeed prescribed by the power of the aforementioned Sutta. In this same way—according to the Sutta method beginning with "Monks, it is impossible and out of the question that the Tathāgata would perform Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha in an impure assembly"—it should be understood that performing Uposatha together with shameless monks (alajjī) is also prohibited, as all training rules are for the purpose of suppressing the shameless. By the phrase "by the prescription of giving purity (pārisuddhi)," it is indicated that a monk with an offense should not give purity either. In the phrase "Both incur a dukkaṭa offense," for one who confesses and one who accepts the confession merely by the name of the offense without knowing it is a common offense (sabhāgāpatti), it is (according to some teachers) only an unintentional (acittaka) dukkaṭa offense.
173:
It is said that just as the Saṅgha, when fallen into a shared offense (sabhāgāpatti), is allowed to perform the Uposatha after setting aside the motion (ñatti), so too, three monks are allowed to perform the Uposatha after setting aside the group motion (gaṇañatti) in the manner already stated, such as 'Listen to me, venerable ones, these monks have fallen into a shared offense,' and having informed each other between the two monks. However, a single monk with an offense must go even a long distance to remedy that offense. If he is a monk who cannot reach [another monk], he should perform the Uposatha with the intention, 'I will remedy it when I find a monk.' After remedying it, he must perform the Uposatha again.

## The Explanation on the Giving of Consent (Chanda-dāna-kathā), etc., is finished.

## Explanation of the Fifteen Cases of No Offense (Anāpatti-pannarasaka), etc.

'Having gone for some business' (kenaci karaṇīyena gantvā) means having gone to a village or a forest that is outside the limits of the boundary (sīmā). By this statement, it is established that at the time of setting the Uposatha motion, those monks set the motion only in concord. Therefore, in the Pāli, it is said in all the fifteen cases (pannarasaka), 'It has been recited, it has been well recited.' As for the words 'being divided but perceiving themselves as united' (vaggā samaggasaññino), etc., it means that at the moment of saying 'What is the preliminary duty of the Saṅgha?' etc., after the motion is finished, the monks who come from outside enter the boundary, and thus at that moment, the monks are divided. Therefore, it is said, 'Because they have entered the boundary, they are divided,' etc. By this, it is shown that even at the moment of reciting the Pārājika section, etc., for the monks who recite while perceiving [the group] as divided, there is only an offense; however, because the motion was finished beforehand, there is no failure of the formal act (kammakopa). In this same way, the meaning should be understood in all subsequent sections (vāra).

In this matter of Uposatha, it is also said in the Pāli, 'When the whole assembly has risen... purity (pārisuddhi) should be informed in their presence.' Therefore, it is said that for monks who have not yet performed the determined Uposatha (adhiṭṭhita-uposatha), it is allowable to inform their purity in the presence of any monk who has reached the outside of the boundary.

## The Explanation of the Fifteen Cases of No Offense, etc., is finished.
174:
## Explanation of the Showing of Marks (Liṅgādi-dassana-kathā), etc.

'Aññātakaṃ' refers to someone not seen before, as expressed by 'the property of others.' 'Of others' means the property of those whom one has not seen before. 'Nānāsaṃvāsakabhāvaṃ' means the state of being of separate communion by way of view (laddhi).

In the Pāli, 'abhivitaranti' means they decide that [the others] are not of the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka).

'Uposathakārakā' means those who perform the Saṅgha-uposatha. Therefore, it is said, 'except by the Saṅgha.' Indeed, one who goes from a place where the Saṅgha-uposatha is performed should go only as the fourth [with three others]. However, one who goes from a place where three monks are staying is allowed to go even with one [other] monk. In the Pāli, the phrase 'a residence without monks' (abhikkhuko āvāso) is merely an illustration. It is said that because it is stated 'except by the Saṅgha,' members of a group (gaṇa-puggala) should not go even to a residence with monks from a place where the Saṅgha-uposatha is performed. 'Uposathaṃ karonti' means they perform either the Saṅgha-uposatha or the Gaṇa-uposatha. The phrase 'to his presence' (tassa santikaṃ) is said with reference to one who goes from a place where the Gaṇa-uposatha is performed. Otherwise, it would contradict the statement 'at the minimum limit, as the fourth [with three others].' 'Āraññakena' refers to a monk who wanders alone. 'Uposathantarāyo' means an obstacle to one's own Uposatha.

In the Pāli, in such phrases as 'bhikkhuniyā nisinnaparisāyā' (the assembly where a nun is sitting), the word 'bhikkhuniyā' etc., is in the genitive case (chaṭṭhī) used in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa).

## The Explanation of the Showing of Marks, etc., is finished.

## The Method of the Explanation of the Uposathakkhandhaka is finished.
175:
## 3. Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka

## Explanation of the Allowance for Entering the Rains (Vassūpanāyika-anujānana-kathā), etc.

In the Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka, 'aparasmī divase' refers to the second day, which is the first day of the waning moon.

'Aññattha aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpanena vā' means a monk who has expectations [of returning] goes without any necessary business and lets the dawn rise in another place. 'Parihāni' means the loss of qualities (guṇa).

In the Pāli, 'sattāhaṃ sannivatto kātabbo' means that instead of spending the entire seven days outside, one should make a return to the monastery within the seven days by way of connecting back to the monastery at the time of dawn-rise, which marks the end of the seven-day period. Here, the word 'sattāha' (seven days) refers to the end of the seven-day period. Because of the expectation of that time, it is expressed in the masculine gender as 'sannivatto.' 'Tīṇi parihīnāni' means they are diminished because [facilities] such as toilets (vacca-kuṭi) for nuns are prohibited.

'Na palujjati' means it does not perish because of the lack of proficiency of others or because of my own death.

## The Explanation of the Allowance for Entering the Rains, etc., is finished.

## Explanation of the Allowance [to go] when Sent (Pahiteyeva-anujānana-kathā)

By the phrase 'a man living with the monks,' it is shown that he is a person with no other refuge (ananyagatika). 'Gantabbaṃ' means one should go even if not sent for the Saṅgha's business. In this matter, it should be understood that it is allowable to go on a seven-day business (sattāha-karaṇīya) even if sent by lay followers who wish to know the nature of the Dispensation (Sāsana), or by those who see the increase of their faith.

'Ratticchedavinicchayo' is the decision regarding the 'break of the night,' which is defined as letting the dawn rise outside while having gone on a seven-day business. 'Gantūṃ vaṭṭati' means that while staying within the precincts (upacāra-sīmā), one should note the reason for the seven-day business and go with the mental resolution, 'I will return within seven days.' Even if one goes having made the resolution at the first moment but forgetting it at the moment of departure...
176:
There is no fault because it is stated (in the Mahāvagga Pāḷi) that "one who has business to attend to may depart." However, it is said that for a monk who goes without making any mental attention (ābhoga) in every respect, the Rains-residence is broken. If a monk, even in the absence of a reason for a seven-day business (sattāha-karaṇīya), goes with the intention "I will return within seven days" and does return within seven days, it is said that he only incurs an offense, but the Rains-residence is not broken because he returned by the dawn of the seventh day. This point should be accepted after careful investigation. "Bhaṇḍaka" refers to robe-material. "It is allowable if he cannot deliver it" means that because there is an effort to return on that very day, there is no breaking of the Rains-residence or an offense. "Ācariya" refers to the dependence-teacher (nissaya-ācariya) and the Dhamma-teacher (dhamma-ācariya) even if they are not ill; this is even more so in the case of the ordination-teacher (upasampadā-ācariya) and the preceptor (upajjhāya). Saying "it is allowable" is meant to indicate that there is no offense even if seven days are exceeded; however, the Rains-residence is indeed broken.

## The Explanation of the Allowance for One Who is Sent for is Finished.

## The Explanation of Non-offense and the Breaking of the Rains-residence in Case of Danger

In the Pāḷi, "gaṇhiṃsu" means they caught and ate. "Paripātiṃsu" means they made them flee, or they pursued them.

In the phrase "sattāhavārena aruṇo uṭṭhāpetabbo" (dawn should be made to rise within the seven-day turn), it means that after spending six days outside, one should enter within the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā) before dawn on the seventh day, let the dawn rise there, and then depart the next day after undertaking the seven-day period again. Some teachers say, "It is allowable to come on the seventh day and depart during that same day without letting the dawn rise," but this statement should not be accepted because it is stated that "dawn should be made to rise." It is with the intention of making the dawn rise at that monastery on the seventh day that it is also stated in the Pāḷi, "a seven-day return should be made." A monk who goes without letting the dawn rise, if he spends the seven days outside without entering the monastery, his Rains-residence will be broken because the dawn was made to rise only outside. Otherwise, the phrase "dawn should be made to rise" would be meaningless, as it is said that "one should enter the monastery within the seven-day turn and depart only after making the dawn rise." In other places as well, only the making of the dawn rise is mentioned. In the Cīvarakkhandhaka, it will be said: "A monk living in one monastery makes the dawn rise in another monastery within the seven-day turn."
177:
Furthermore, if those teachers should say, "The statement in the Commentary 'dawn should be made to rise' is meant in the sense that a monk who enters at any time on the seventh day is said to have made the past dawn associated with that day rise," that statement does not agree with the linguistic usage (saddagati). For one who enters after the dawn has already risen cannot be the causal agent (payojaka-kattar) who makes that dawn rise. If that were possible, then in the phrase "also for one who, after entering the Rains, departs on that very day for a seven-day business without making the dawn rise," the words "without making the dawn rise" would be contradictory, because that monk would also have made the dawn associated with that day rise.

Also, for a forest-dwelling monk who goes to a forest area endowed with the proper factors in the evening and returns at that very moment, the dawn would have been made to rise and the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) would be purified; but this is not appropriate, because it is said that the dawn is made to rise only at the time of dawn-rise. Indeed, it is stated in the Visuddhimagga: "One should set out early and make the dawn rise in a place endowed with the proper factors. If, at the time of dawn-rise, their illness increases, one should only attend to their needs; one should not be a purifier of the ascetic practice." Similarly, for those undergoing probation (parivāsa) and so on, who lay down their duties without making the dawn rise, a break in the nights is stated. For it is said in the Cūḷavagga: "The duties should be laid down only after the dawn has risen." Also, in the Sahaseyya training rule, it is said "having departed before dawn," etc., in order to be freed from the state of sleeping together with one who is not fully ordained. Thus, in all matters such as being separated from the robes (cīvara-vippavāsa), etc., the making of the dawn rise is shown only by means of the upcoming dawn at the end of the night, not by means of the past dawn. Therefore, the making of the dawn rise in this context should be understood only in the manner stated; otherwise, it would result in the breaking of the Rains-residence.

The statement regarding the departure of a monk with a seven-day business on the very day he entered the Rains without making the dawn rise is appropriate because departure is allowed whenever there is a reason from the time of entering the Rains. However, for a monk who has returned after a seven-day turn, departing again on that very day without making the dawn rise is not appropriate, simply because it is stated that "dawn should be made to rise." Alternatively, just as it is not allowable to not return during other seven-day periods, even though not returning during the final seven-day period is allowed by the words, "Bhikkhus, he departs on a seven-day business seven days before the Pavāraṇā; that bhikkhu may either return to that residence or not return," etc. Similarly, although departure without making the dawn rise is allowed in the first seven-day period, for a monk who returns in the seven-day periods following that first one, the dawn...
178: It should be decided here that going without letting the dawn rise is not proper. 'Brought here' means brought to the place of arrival outside the monastery. ## The explanation of the absence of offense in case of obstacles to the Rains-residence is finished. ## Explanation of Entering the Rains-residence in Cattle-pens, etc. Because of the absence of huts and so on, it is not proper to enter the Rains-residence by making a verbal statement like 'I enter the Rains-residence here.' In the Pali, 'pīsācillikā' means young spirits (pīsāca-dārakā). 'Joining the doorway' means making a door with door-leaves. 'Cutting a tree' means cutting the upper part of a hollow place. 'On the top of a stump' means on the top of a hollow stump. A 'ṭaṅkitamañca' is a couch made by piercing long legs and inserting the frame-ends (aṭani); even if it is spread upside down, it remains as before; they usually place it in cemeteries or shrines. A house made by spreading a stone slab over four stones is also called a 'ṭaṅkitamañca'. ## The explanation of entering the Rains-residence in cattle-pens, etc., is finished. ## Explanation of Unrighteous Agreements, etc. 'Mahāvibhaṅga' refers to the commentary on the fourth Pārājika. Later, in the Senāsanakkhandhaka, unrighteous agreements (adhammika-katikā) will also become clear. Because for a monk entering the Rains-residence in two monasteries with different boundaries, the first taking of residence (senāsana-ggāha) is cancelled as soon as he leaves the precinct (upacāra) with the thought 'I will stay in the second.' Therefore, in the Pali, it is said: 'Monks, for that monk, the first rains (purimikā) is not known,' referring to the first taking of residence. In the second taking of residence, however, the first rains is indeed known. If he stays in that second monastery for the three months...
179: ...is called the first rains (purima-vassa). Otherwise, if one passes the boundary (upacāra) from that second monastery on the second day etc., thinking 'I will stay in the first monastery,' it should be understood that the first rains is not evident. In the Pali, because it is said 'That monk departs on a seven-day business (sattāha-karaṇīya) seven days before the Pavāraṇā,' it should be understood that even on the Pavāraṇā day, it is not proper to go without a seven-day business. 'Komudiyā cātumāsiniyā' refers to the full moon day of Kattika. It is called 'Komudī' because water-lilies (kumuda) exist at that time. It is also called 'Cātumāsinī' because it is the end of the four months of the rainy season. ## The explanation of the unrighteous agreement (adhammika-katikā) etc. is finished. ## The method of explaining the Vassūpanāyika Khandhaka is finished.
180:
## 4. Pavāraṇākkhandhaka

## Explanation on uncomfortable living, etc.

In the Pavāraṇākkhandhaka Pali, "he should return for alms" (piṇḍāya paṭikkameyya) means he should depart after wandering for alms. "Avakkārapāti" is a vessel for placing leftover almsfood. "Avisayha" means something that cannot be lifted. "Vilaṅghana" is the same as "vilaṅgha," which means lifting; that vilaṅgha itself is called "vilaṅghaka." Since it means lifting with the hands (hatthavilaṅghaka), it is stated as "by lifting with the hands." Alternatively, it means with hands that cause lifting, meaning with hands clasped together.

"If, however, he is more senior" (sace pana vuḍḍhataro hoti) means if the monk who gives the Pavāraṇā is more senior. In the phrase "Thus, for him, the Pavāraṇā is performed for that purpose," it should be understood that when Pavāraṇā is performed in this way, even if that monk does not perform Pavāraṇā himself, the Saṅgha-pavāraṇā act is a harmonious act (samagga-kamma) merely by his arrival at the Saṅgha. "And by that monk" (tena ca bhikkhunā) refers to the monk who gives the Pavāraṇā.

"Even many of equal years are allowed to perform Pavāraṇā together" means that all monks who have attained ordination in the same year and thus have equal years of seniority are allowed to perform Pavāraṇā together.

In the Pali, "wrong view" (micchādiṭṭhi) refers to the wrong view that arises in the manner of "there is no result of giving," and so forth. "Antaggāhikā" refers to the view that takes an extreme, known as eternalism or annihilationism. In the passages beginning with "That which you" (yaṃ kho tvaṃ), it should be read by inserting the word "that" (taṃ) as "Whatever Pavāraṇā you set aside, you set aside that Pavāraṇā by sight."

"Revealing the object" (vatthuṃ pakāsento) is said with reference only to the object which is the cause for the arising of suspicion regarding a person. When it is said, "Only the person is known, not the object," the object intended there is not meant here. If, however, one sees the catching of fish from a pond in the place where that monk resides, then it should be said, "Both the object and the person are known." Therefore, it is stated, "As in the previous method, by thieves," and so forth. It should be understood that because of seeing the scent of flowers and the scent of ariṭṭha medicine on the monk's body, it is said, "Both the object and the person are known."

## The explanation on uncomfortable living, etc. is finished.
181:
## Explanation on the story of the quarrelsome monks

"There are two fourteenth-day observances" (dve cātuddasikā honti) means that in the third fortnight, there are two fourteenth-day Uposatha days along with the fourteenth day. By the statement, "For the quarrelsome monks, on the thirteenth or fourteenth day, these [monks] will perform the fifteenth-day Pavāraṇā," it is shown that the designation of the fourteenth or fifteenth day for monks starts from their own Uposatha day, and not by the power of the lunar day (tithi) established by the lunar movement.

Indeed, according to the words, "Monks, I allow you to follow the kings," although one follows the lunar day of the worldly experts in this matter, one should follow it only by making the fourteenth day as the fifteenth, or the fifteenth day as the fourteenth, according to one's own Uposatha sequence; but one should not follow it by making the sixteenth day or the thirteenth day an Uposatha day. For that very reason, it is said in the Pali, "The fourteenth-day Uposatha should be performed two or three times." Otherwise, it would have to be said that the Uposatha should be performed on the twelfth or thirteenth day. The statement "Once on the fourteenth or fifteenth of the fortnight" and so forth should also be taken as being said according to the sequence of the Uposatha observance, and not according to the sequence of the lunar day (tithi).

## The explanation on the story of the quarrelsome monks is finished.

## Explanation on the collection of Pavāraṇā

By the statement, "Having performed Pavāraṇā, they are allowed to depart on a journey even in the interval," it is shown that when the Pavāraṇā-saṅgaha (collection of Pavāraṇā) is performed, monks who wish to depart in the interval are allowed to perform Pavāraṇā by convening the Saṅgha.

## The explanation on the collection of Pavāraṇā is finished.

## The explanation on the Pavāraṇākkhandhaka is finished.
182:
## 5. Cammakkhandhaka
## Commentary on the Story of Soṇa Koḷivisa and Others
In the Cammakkhandhaka, the term "uṇṇapāvāraṇa" refers to a woolen cloak or upper garment made by raising the fibers on both sides. There is also a cloak woven by raising cotton fibers on both sides; the term "uṇṇapāvāraṇa" is used specifically to exclude that (cotton) cloak (and refer only to the woolen one).

"Aḍḍhacandapāsāṇe" refers to a half-moon-shaped stone slab placed at the base of a staircase, with half of it set into the structure. In the Pāḷi, "vihārapacchāyāyaṃ" means in the shadow at the edge of the monastery; some also say it refers to the lengthening shadow cast by the monastery.

The word "bhogā" is a nominative case used in the sense of the accusative (the object). "Accāyatā" refers to an overly taut and harsh tuning (of the lute strings). "Saravatī" means having a pleasant or sweet sound. "Atisithilā" refers to an overly slack and soft tuning. "Vīriyasamathaṃ" refers to concentration (samādhi) associated with energy (vīriya). When established in that serenity, just as a reflection of a face appears in a mirror, a certain sign (nimitta) arises; the meaning is: "Take up (bring about) that sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta), the sign of insight (vipassanā-nimitta), the sign of the path (magga-nimitta), and the sign of the fruit (phala-nimitta)." In this way, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) ending in the fruit of Arahatship was taught to the Elder Soṇa.

"Chaṭṭhānāni" refers to the six causes or grounds. "Adhimutto" means being firmly established through penetration. All the terms such as "nekkhamma-adhimutto" are spoken in terms of the fruit of Arahatship. Indeed, Arahatship is called "nekkhamma" (renunciation) because it is a departure from all defilements; it is called "paviveka" (seclusion) because it is secluded from those same defilements; it is called "abyāpajja" (non-ill-will) because of the absence of trouble; it is called "upādānakkhaya" (destruction of clinging) because it arises at the end of clinging; it is called "taṇhakkhaya" (destruction of craving) because it arises at the end of craving; and it is called "asammoha" (non-delusion) because of the absence of delusion.

"Kevalaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ" refers to mere faith that is not mixed with penetrative wisdom. "Paṭicayaṃ" means increase through repeated practice. "Vītarāgattā" means that because lust (rāga) has been removed through penetration by the Path, one remains having penetrated and realized the fruit of Arahatship, which is called renunciation (nekkhamma). In the remaining terms, the method should be understood in the same way. "Pavivekādhimutto" means declaring Arahatship by saying, "I am inclined toward the fruit of Arahatship, which is secluded from defilements."

"Sīlabbataparāmāsaṃ" refers to a mere attachment to views by misinterpreting rules and rituals. "Sārato paccāgacchanto" means knowing it as the essence (the noble). "Abyāpajjādhimutto" means declaring the fruit of Arahatship, which is free from trouble.
183:
"Amissīkata" means made unmixed. Defilements cause the mind to be mixed with sense objects; because of the absence of those defilements, it is called "amissīkata" (unmixed). "Bhusā vātavuṭṭhī" refers to a powerful mass of wind.

In the phrase "upādānakkhayassa ca," the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative (the object). "Disvā āyatanuppādaṃ" means having seen the arising and passing away of the sense bases (āyatana) such as the eye. "Cittaṃ vimuccati" means the mind is liberated through the power of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) by means of this practice of insight (vipassanā).

## The Commentary on the Story of Soṇa Koḷivisa and Others is finished.

## Commentary on the Rejection of Double-layered Sandals and Others

"Sakaṭavāha" refers to cartloads measured by two carts. Although the plural term "vāhe" is an adjective for "hirañña" (gold/money), the singular "hirañña" is used in a general sense.

"Addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā" means having a color like a wet soap-nut; some also say it is like the color of a wet crow's wing. The word "rajana" (dye/color) is spoken with reference to applied colors such as blue/black. Therefore, it is said, "wiping with a piece of cloth." That applied surface color disappears when wiped in such a manner. However, the color that arises from being dyed with black or red dyes to remove the bad smell of the leather cannot be removed by a cloth, etc., as it is integral to the leather. Therefore, sandals with such color should be regarded as permissible.

"Khallaka" refers to leather that covers the entire heel. It is permissible to merely place a covering over the upper part of the heel and bind it to prevent the sandal from slipping off. "Vicitrā" refers to cloth that is ornate in its shape or form; it does not mean ornate in color. This is because being ornate in color is included among the things to be entirely rejected, such as the khallaka. Because they have faces similar to cats, large owls (or bats) are called "pakkhibiḷālā" (bird-cats); the "skin" of these creatures refers only to their feathers or fur.

## The Commentary on the Rejection of Double-layered Sandals and Others is finished.
184:
## Commentary on the Prohibition of Sandals in the Monastery, etc.

In the phrase 'uṇṇāhi katapādukā', sandals made from woolen blankets are included.

'Gaṅgāmahakīဠikāya' means playing at the Ganges festival. At that Ganges festival, men and women go by vehicles to play in the water. 'Pīṭhakasivikaṃ' is a litter-vehicle made of planks and so on. 'Paṭapotalikaṃ' is a palanquin. Every kind of vehicle is permitted for a sick monk who is unable to travel even when wearing sandals.

'Vāḷarūpāni' are figures of wild beasts that are depicted. The phrase 'caturangulādhikāni' shows the distinction from uddhalomī and ekantalomī rugs. Rugs with hair less than four finger-breadths are included among uddhalomī and so on. 'Vānacitro uṇṇāmayattharaṇo' is a variegated rug woven with woolen threads of various colors in patterns such as wall-openings. 'Ghanapupphako' is a rug decorated with many colors. 'Pakatitūlikā' is a mattress stuffed with cotton. 'Vikatikā' refers only to rugs variegated with figures of wild beasts such as lions. 'Uddhalomī' is described in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary as 'a woolen rug with fringe on both sides'. 'Koseyyakaṭṭissamayaṃ' is a rug woven by inserting gold threads between silk threads. Gold thread is called 'kaṭṭissa' and also 'kasaṭa'. For this reason, they say that the Elder Dhammapāla called it 'koseyya-kasaṭamaya'. 'Ratanaparisibbitaṃ' is a rug smeared with liquid gold. 'Suddhakoseyyaṃ' is a silk rug without gem-stitching.

Because black antelope skins are very delicate, they are sewn in double or triple layers; therefore, they are called 'ajinappaveṇī'. 'Rattavitānena' means with a completely red canopy. A canopy that is variegated in color, whether woven or painted, is allowable. The same rule applies to red pillows placed at both ends. The phrase 'citraṃ ဝါ' (or variegated) is said because it is allowable in every way, not because pillows at both ends are unallowable. The word lohitaka (red) does not mean variegated, and because it is appropriate to include variegated rugs under the term paṭali. Robes, however, do not come under the designation of 'red' (lohitaka). Therefore, it is allowable for both the canopy and the pillows at both ends. The phrase 'sace pamāṇayuttaṃ' and so on is said to show the prohibition of pillows that exceed the standard size, not to show the nature of high and large beds, as it is not stated so. That pillow...
185: (That pillow) is allowable for laypeople observing the Uposatha. This is because at that time, only high and large beds and seats are not allowable for them. Although in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary etc. it is said, 'Except for mattresses stuffed with wool, all rugs such as gonaka embroidered with jewels are allowable,' the Vinaya Commentary alone should be taken as the authority in determining what is allowable (kappiya) and unallowable (akappiya). ## The explanation of the prohibition of wearing sandals within the monastery (ārāma) is finished. ## Explanation of the allowance of things prepared by laypeople etc.: 'Abhinissāya' means depending on. 'Visūkāyika-vipphanditānaṃ' means the agitation of views and the agitation of the mind which are antagonistic. 'Yatindriya' means having restrained faculties by way of the mind faculty. In the Pali, 'Aṭṭhakavaggikāni' refers to the sixteen suttas included in the Aṭṭhakavagga of the Sutta Nipāta. 'Evaṃ ciraṃ akāsi' means 'For what reason did you live among householders for such a long time without entering the monkhood?' It is said that he ordained in middle age; therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus. 'Etam-atthaṃ viditvā' means knowing this matter in every aspect: that having seen the danger in sense pleasures, they do not rush into the household life even after a long time. 'Ādīnavaṃ loke' means seeing the danger such as impermanence in the world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka). 'Nirupadhi' refers to Nibbāna. By the words 'The pure person does not delight in evil,' the reason for the words 'The Noble One (ariya) does not delight in evil' is stated. In that context, 'suci' (pure) refers to a purified person. 'Kāḷasīha' refers to a species of black-faced monkey. 'Cammaṃ na vaṭṭati' means it is not allowable to make a sitting rug (nisīdana), but it is allowable to use it as a monastery requisite by way of a floor covering etc. ## The explanation of the allowance of things prepared by laypeople etc. is finished. ## The method of explaining the Cammakhandhaka is finished.
186:
## 6. Bhesajjakkhandhaka

## Commentary on the Five Medicines, etc.

In the Bhesajjakkhandhaka, "pittaṃ koṭṭhabbantaragataṃ hoti" means that the unattached bile that pervades the body enters the intestines. This means the bile is disturbed.

261-2. In the text, "nacchādenti" means they do not produce delight. "Susukā" is a species of fish in the ocean; they also call it a crocodile. "Saṃsaṭṭhaṃ" means that which is strained.

"Piṭṭhehi" means with ground powders. "Kasāvehi" means with decoctions obtained by boiling bark and so on in water. "Ubbhidaṃ" means that which is made of alkaline soil. "Loṇavilaṃ" is a specific kind of salt.

264-5. "Chakaṇaṃ" is cow dung. "Pākatikacuṇṇံ" is unboiled bark powder. Scented powder, however, is not allowable. In the text, "cuṇṇacāliniṃ" is a sieve for straining medicinal powder pounded in a mortar. "Suvaṇṇageruko" refers to gold-colored orpiment and so on. In the text, "añjanūpapisanaṃ" is medicine to be ground for application as eye-ointment.

267-9. "Kabaḷikā" is a medicinal compress. "Gharadinnakābādha" is an illness arising from a medicine given by a housewife for the purpose of subjugation. "Tāya chārikāya paggharitaṃ khārodakaṃ" is alkaline water trickling down from the ashes when water is poured over them after placing the ashes in a filter. In the text, "akaṭayū Sena" means with unprepared mung bean soup. "Kaṭākaṭena" means with mung bean soup obtained by boiling mung beans and straining them without stirring.

## The Commentary on the Five Medicines, etc., is finished.
187:
## Commentary on the Allowance of Molasses, etc.
272-4. "Guḷakaraṇaṃ" means a sugar-cane shed. "Avissatthā" means they are suspicious or doubtful.

"Appamattakepi vārenti" means they refuse even a small donation, considering that it might cause hardship to the donors. "Paṭisaṅkhāpi" means they refuse after reflecting, "This much is enough for sustenance; let the rest be for other monks."

"Vatthipīḷanaṃ" means pressing the compress with the hand so that the oil, etc., in the compress enters the body. Since only surgery and douching (vatthikamma) in sensitive (narrow) areas are forbidden, cauterization (dahanakamma) is indeed allowable.

## The Commentary on the Allowance of Molasses, etc. is finished.

## Commentary on Rice Gruel, Honey-balls, etc.
282-3. In the Pali, "dasaṭṭhānāni" means giving ten benefits or reasons to the recipient. "Anuppaveccheti" means gives. "Vātañca byapaneti" should be connected as "removes wind," meaning it makes the wind favorable (eases flatulence). "Saggā te āraddhā" means "Heaven has been attained by you."

## The Commentary on Rice Gruel, Honey-balls, etc. is finished.

## Commentary on the Pāṭaligāma Story
"Pāṭaligāme nagaraṃ māpenti" means they are building a city named Pāṭaliputta in a vast forest area near Pāṭaligāma, which is the land of that village. "Yāvatā ariyam āyatanaṃ" means as far as there is a city that is a gathering place of noble people. "Yāvatā vaṇippatho" means as far as there is a city that is a place for merchants to sell goods or to reside. This Pāṭaliputta will be the chief city among all those cities. "Puṭabhedanaṃ" means a place for opening (unpacking) bundles of goods brought from various places by carts, etc., for sale. The word "saraṃ" is also used for lakes, etc.
188:
To prevent that misunderstanding, it is said, "In this context, 'sara' means a river." It is called 'sara' because it flows (sarati). "They crossed without a raft" means they reached the other shore without even touching this small amount of water and without a raft.

## The Commentary on the Pāṭaligāma Story is finished.

## Commentary on the Truths at Koṭigāma

In the Pali, "sandhāvitaṃ" means having run from one birth to another by way of taking rebirth. "Saṃsaritaṃ" is a synonym for that term. "Of mine and yours" means the running [through Saṃsāra] of mine and yours (or, by way of the Lord, of mine and yours) has occurred. "Saṃsaritaṃ" means wandering. Craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) is called "bhavanetti" because it leads from one birth to another.

To clarify the meaning of "they are blue," it is said "they are blue-colored," etc. "Blue-colored" means smeared with blue unguent. This method applies to all terms. "Paṭivaṭṭesi" means struck. "Ambakāya" means mother. This is a figurative expression (upacāra) meaning a woman. "Reflect" means "The Tāvatiṃsa gods are of such a nature; consider this." This was said to inspire a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in the monks, not for the sake of taking a beautiful sign (subhanimitta). This is because all the Licchavī princes will soon meet with destruction because of King Ajātasattu.

## The Commentary on the Truths at Koṭigāma is finished.

## Commentary on the Story of General Sīha, etc.

"In the assembly hall" refers to the great assembly made for conducting royal affairs and for investigating without bias. "Preparation for going" means making an effort to go. "Dhamma in accordance with Dhamma" means a reason consistent with the reason you stated, a meaning suitable to the meaning you stated. "Legitimate follow-up of the argument" means your view, being well-reasoned due to the reason stated by others...
189:
...or the follow-up of that view hereafter. To say "one does not reach even a slight blameworthy point" means "there is no blameworthy reason in your view."

"Anuviccākāra" means acting after knowing (investigating). One performs acts such as going for refuge to the Triple Gem. It means "Do not act hastily and then be regretful later." "Patākaṃ parihareyyuṃ" means they wander about the city proclaiming, "Such a person has become a disciple who has gone to our refuge," while raising flags and banners.

"Nimittakammassa" refers to the act of killing (pāṇātipāta) that arises because of (the cause of) eating meat.

## The Commentary on the Story of General Sīha, etc. is finished.

## Commentary on the Allowance of Allowable Ground

"Anuppage eva" means very early. "Oravasaddaṃ" means a loud noise. Even if that word is not spoken, the word "pi" allows for saying it (as a kappiyakuṭi). "In the Commentaries" means in the other Commentaries excluding the Andhaka Commentary. "Common characteristic" means a statement common to all Commentaries including the Andhaka Commentary.

"Cayaṃ" means a high foundation which is a base. "Starting from where" means starting from which brick, etc.; it means starting from which [point] they wish to raise the wall. "But the pillars go upwards, therefore they are allowable"—by this, it is established that even if bricks and stones are placed below, if they stand raised even a finger's breadth from the masonry or from the ground, they are allowable.

"Ārāma" means the entire monastery precinct delimited by the surrounding boundary (upacārasīmā). "Senāsana" means the dwellings of the Saṅgha, such as grass huts, etc., inside the monastery precinct. "Vihāragonisādikā" is the same as "senāsanagonisādikā." Even if the dwellings themselves are enclosed, they are called "gonisādikā" because the monastery precinct (ārāma) is not enclosed. By the phrase "even if half-enclosed," it is shown that a dwelling with less than half an enclosure is mostly considered unenclosed; therefore, it falls into the category of being unenclosed. "In this context" refers to a dwelling that is half-enclosed, etc. "It is allowable to obtain a kappiyakuṭi" means...
190:
Due to the absence of a gonisādikā, it means that any one of the three remaining types of kappiya-kuṭi (allowable storehouses) should be constructed.

In the phrase "the houses of those lay devotees," it should be understood that even if a house is built for the residence of monks, as long as it has not yet been offered, it remains the property of those lay devotees. "Vihāraṃ ṭhapetvā" means excluding the monastery built for the residence of those who are ordained (upasampanna). "Gehaṃ" refers to a residential dwelling. Any other building, such as an uposatha hall, which is not a residential dwelling, is the fifth type of kappiya ground, distinct from the four types of kappiya-kuṭi. Even if it is the property of the Saṅgha, in such a building, even if there is a well-enclosed precinct, there is no fault such as antovuttha (storing food indoors) and so on, just as in the open air. The fault of antovuttha and so on occurs only in a residential dwelling of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha that is roofed and enclosed by whatever means and is sufficient for sleeping together; it does not occur elsewhere. Therefore, he said "Yaṃ pana," etc. In that context, although the phrase "saṅghikaṃ vā puggalikaṃ vā" is generally stated for bhikkhunīs, it should be understood that the saṅghika and puggalika property of monks, as well as the saṅghika and puggalika property of bhikkhunīs, stands in a place like the property of laypeople for the monks.

Mukhasannidhi means that the fault of antosannihita (storing within) causes an offense due to the reason of entering the mouth; not otherwise. Therefore, it is called "mukhasannidhi."

"They are broken in various places" means they are broken more than halfway. "When the entire roof is destroyed" refers to when the roof made of grass, leaves, etc., which protects against rain, is destroyed. Even if the rods tied with creepers remain above the rafters, they are still considered abandoned materials. "Pakkhapāsakamaṇḍala" refers to the roof made of grass, leaves, etc., situated above three rafters on one side.

By saying "it should be given to an unordained person (anupasampanna)," etc., it shows that even if one stays in an unallowable storehouse (akappiya-kuṭi), it becomes allowable if given to an unordained person. In this matter, giving with expectation is allowable; it is shown that it is not like receiving (paṭiggahena).

In the Pali, "kantāre sambhāvesi" means he arrived at a difficult journey where food is scarce.

## The explanation of the allowance of the kappiya ground is finished.
191: ## Explanation of the Story of Keṇiya the Matted-hair Ascetic. Jaṭila refers to a Brahmin who bears matted hair that can be moved, assumes the appearance of an ascetic, is engaged in sacrifices, and is honored by the world. Pavattāro refers to those who speak by the power of the prescribed word. It means that this collection of Vedic texts belongs to those teachers, or that those teachers composed these Vedas. The three terms gītaṃ, pavuttaṃ, and samihitaṃ are synonyms for one another. Tadanugāyantīti means they sing in imitation of those Vedas previously composed by those great teachers. The same applies to the remaining terms. The phrase yāvakālikapakkānanti is said with reference to ripe fruits. Although not explicitly stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, a drink given after being crushed in cold water and strained by laypeople or novices is indeed allowable even in the afternoon. Because this meaning is not explicitly stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is said starting with "Kurundiyaṃ panā". Although the phrase "ucchuraso nikasaṭo" is mentioned in the explanation of yāmakālika because it is similar in being a drink, that sugarcane juice should be understood as being only sattāhakālika. These four juices are fruit juice, leaf juice, flower juice, and sugarcane juice. In the Pali, aggihuttamukhā refers to those for whom fire-sacrifice is foremost. Chandaso means of the Vedas (prosody). The meaning is that the Sāvittī text should be recited first. Tapatam means of those who have a bright and shining radiance. ## End of the Explanation of the Story of Keṇiya the Matted-hair Ascetic. ## Explanation of the Story of Roja the Mallian, etc. Bahukato buddhe vā means one who has great reverence for the Buddha. "Venerable Ānanda, I was terrified of the punishment of my kinsmen" is the remainder of the sentence. Only when this remainder is included is the use of "Evaṃ ahaṃ" (So I...) appropriate. Vivari means opened just by thinking "Let it open," not by getting up and using hands. Aññataro refers to the elder monk named Subhadda. Dve dārakā refers to two sons who were in the stage of novices. Nāḷiyāvāpakenāti means storing with a tube and a bag. The meaning is "Collect rice and so on with these vessels." Bhusāgāre refers to a house made of straw. It means in that straw-house made by pulling straw from the inside of a straw pile and making it like a house. ## End of the Explanation of the Story of Roja the Mallian, etc.
192:
## Explanation of the Four Great Authorities
Parimaddantā means reflecting and investigating. The phrase "two garments are mentioned only by the name of the region" is a term showing the identity of the pattuṇṇa garment called by that regional name. It is not a term excluding other things. This is because the pattuṇṇa garment is also called by the name of the region.

Tumba refers to vessels (or pots). Phalatumba is a pot made from gourds and so on. Udakatumba is a water pot. Kilañjacchatta is an umbrella woven from bamboo strips. Sambhipparasa means having a mixed taste.

## The explanation of the Four Great Authorities is finished.
## The method of explanation for the Chapter on Medicines is finished.
193:
## 7. Kathinakkhandhaka
## Explanation of the Talk on the Allowance of Kathina
In the Kathinakkhandhaka, 'sīsavaseana' means primarily or by way of the chief. 'Kathina' means firm because it is capable of establishing the five advantages (ānisamsa) within itself. In the sentence 'that [advantage] will be to them,' using 'to them' (nesaṃ) instead of 'to you' is appropriate. 'Those who have spread the Kathina' means it will occur not only for you but for others who have spread the Kathina as well. Alternatively, 'vo' (you) is used to collectively refer to the monks present at that time along with future monks who are not yet present; thus it means 'to you.' Here, 'so nesaṃ' should be understood as 'so tesaṃ.' Therefore, He said: 'Monks, these five [advantages] will be allowable for you who have spread the Kathina.' 'Matakacīvara' is the robe of a deceased monk.
