The phrase 'by way of spending the Vassa' also applies to those who spent the later Vassa; thus it is said: 'Those who, having entered the earlier Vassa, are invited at the first Pavāraṇā, receive [it].' The phrase 'even if they enter, they do not receive' is said with reference to monks who have completed the later Vassa.

'Khalimakkhitasaṭaka' refers to new, unwashed cloth. By the phrase 'should not remain without doing,' it is shown that if one remains [without doing so] out of disrespect, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa) is committed.

'Having asked permission' (apaloketvā) refers to the procedure to be followed when one wishes to give [the robe] only to the one who will spread the Kathina without giving it to other monks who have completed the Vassa. If that is the case, why is giving by a formal act (kammavācā) not mentioned? It is because, unlike the Kathina robe, it is not suitable to give by a formal act; thus it means it should be given only after asking permission.

'Mahābhūmika' means having a wide scope, and it is said to be very extensive because it possesses twenty-four modes. 'Pañcaka' refers to a five-fold robe (with five segments), and this method applies to the remaining terms as well. 'Paṭhamacimilikā' is one's own natural cloth layer other than the Kathina cloth. 'Sewing with an inner lining' is said to be the name for sewing strong old layers together. It is also said that the statements in the Mahāpaccari and Kurundī commentaries are made to show that the difference is only in phrasing, not in meaning. 'Piṭṭhi-anuvātāropanamattena' means merely by attaching the border along the length. 'Kucchi-anuvātāropanamattena' means merely by attaching the border along the width. 'Rattinissaggiya' occurs by the passing of the night.
194:
'Hatavatthakasaṭakena' means very worn-out cloth. In the passage beginning with 'na hi tena,' even if the text from the Parivāra is not brought and mentioned here, nothing is lacking in what should be known by the monk spreading the Kathina, because all of that has been stated right here in this Khandhaka.

It is called 'mātikā' (matrix) because it is like a mother (mātā); here, the suffix '-ka' should be understood in the sense of 'like' (iva). To show the meaning accomplished by that suffix '-ka,' it is said 'mātikāti mātaro,' etc. 'Assa' means to that matrix. The removal of the Kathina ending in departure (pakkamanantika-ubbhāra) itself arises as its own matrix; thus it is called 'mātikā' by way of metaphorical identification (abhedūpacāra). This is because it arises only at the end of departure which is the cause for removal, and because there is no matrix apart from that removal. In this context, the Pali text that explains that removal is also appropriately called 'mātikā.' That [Pali] is called 'pakkamanantikā' because it explains the removal ending in departure. This same method applies to the remaining removals. Here, by the word 'pakkamananti,' the crossing of the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā) should be understood.

## End of the Explanation of the Talk on the Allowance of Kathina.

## Explanation of the Seven Cases of Taking [the Robe] Away

'I will not return again'—this phrase shows the cause for the cutting off of the residence-impediment (āvāsapalibodha). During the five robe-months, at any time one crosses the precinct boundary with the thought 'I will not return,' the residence-impediment is cut. For one who has already gone outside the precinct, it is cut the moment the thought 'I will not return' arises anywhere. The statement 'first, the robe-impediment (cīvarapalibodha) is cut' is said because the robe-work is finished even before departing. This is because it is said, 'taking the finished robe.' For a monk who has spread the Kathina, as long as there is expectation of a robe (cīvarāsā), thinking 'I will receive a robe from the Sangha or from donor families, etc.,' or as long as there is the desire to make it (karani-icchā), thinking 'I will cut and make the double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi), etc.,' after obtaining the cloth and the necessary assistance of companions, etc., the robe-impediment remains uncut. However, when the expectation of a robe ceases because robes are not obtained at all from the desired place, or when the desire to make it disappears because the obtained robes are finished, or because they are lost or destroyed, or because of indifference toward the robe, then the robe-impediment is cut.
195:
The cutting off of this robe-impediment (cīvara-palibodha) is also shown here by the words "taking the finished robe." Similarly, in all the subsequent headings (mātikā), it should be understood that the prior or posterior cutting off of these two impediments is stated based on the sequence of the Pali text. In every way, the removal of the Kaṭhina (kathiṇubbhāra) occurs only through the cutting off of both these impediments, not just one. It should be understood that these eight headings are established to show the cutting off of those impediments either sequentially or simultaneously. The words "within the boundary" (antosīmāyaṃ) are spoken because the impediment is cut off at the very moment the robe is finished. By the words "they will not have this robe made," it shows the cutting off of the impediment of making (karaṇa-palibodha) because the concern for the robe has ceased. If a certain monk, either due to fewness of wishes or lack of need, does not accept the robe at all and goes outside the boundary, since he has no robe-impediment in any way, it should be understood as the removal of the Kaṭhina ending with a decision (sanniṭṭhānantikā) merely by the decision "I will not return." "So pana" refers to the cutting off of the impediment. "Ayaṃ pana" refers to the removal of the Kaṭhina by the cutting off of expectation (āsāvacchedika), which is explained separately in detail and is not mentioned here; this is how it should be connected.

"Obtaining without expectation" means obtaining from any place where the expectation (āsā) "we shall obtain a robe from this family" has never arisen before. "Not obtaining despite expectation" means not obtaining in the place that was desired. "Not mentioned here" means not mentioned immediately after this "ending with hearing" (savanantikā). "Therein" means in that "ending with the crossing of the boundary" (sīmātikkantikā). What is called "ending with the crossing of the boundary" arises from crossing the limit (sīmā) known as the final day of the robe-season. Some teachers consider that "crossing the time outside the boundary is sīmātikkama"; according to their view, even if the robe-time expires within the precinct (upacāra), the removal of the Kaṭhina would not be established, which is not appropriate. Therefore, the expiration of time in any place should be understood as sīmātikkama. Here, in the Pali regarding this sīmātikkantikā, the words "one who has a finished robe" are merely an indication; for a monk whose robe is not yet finished, it also becomes sīmātikkantikā through the expiration of time, and both impediments are cut off simultaneously. Thus, in other cycles (vāra) as well, as it may occur, the state of Kaṭhina removal and the manner of cutting off the impediments should be understood even in the absence of those specific qualifiers. The statement "In the simultaneous removal (sahubbhāra), both impediments are cut off without priority or posteriority, simultaneously" is said with reference to the possibility of a monk with an unfinished robe undertaking the resolution "I will return"; even if one of those two impediments is absent, it is still a simultaneous removal (sahubbhāra).

## 312-325. The cycle of taking with (samādāya-vāra) is just like the cycle of taking (ādāya-vāra). The only difference here is the prefix (upasagga). Therefore, it is said, "Again, in the cycle of taking with... pe... those very persons."
196:
In the phrase "they are shown," it is said "as it may occur" because the removal of the Kaṭhina ending with departure (pakkamanantika) is not possible when there is an unfinished robe. For that reason, in the section on unfinished robes (vippakatacīvara-vāra), only six removals of the Kaṭhina are mentioned. If the robe is already in hand, the cutting off of expectation (āsāvacchedika) is not possible; therefore, that āsāvacchedika is not mentioned in any of these cycles but is stated separately. In this section on unfinished robes, two sixfold cycles (chakkavāra) are stated by way of the cycle of taking (ādāya-vāra) and the cycle of taking with (samādāya-vāra).

After that, three triads (tika) are shown by way of the triad of completion (niṭṭhāna-tika), the triad of decision (sanniṭṭhāna-tika), and the triad of loss (nāsanantika-tika). Therein, in the third triad, "by one who has not determined" (anadhiṭṭhitena) means by not resolving "I will return" or "I will not return," thus not attending to it in this way. After the third triad, one sixfold cycle (chakka) is shown. Thus, by combining the three triads and one sixfold cycle, it is called the first fifteenfold set (paṭhama-pannarasaka). In this manner, the second fifteenfold set and so forth should be understood.

In the twelvefold set of expectations (āsādvādasaka) of the Pali text, regarding the removals of the Kaṭhina for a monk who has gone outside the boundary, since the robe-impediment remains for them until the completion of the robe by way of the expectation of obtaining a robe and so forth, it is said: "That monk who has gone outside the boundary hears, 'It is said the Kaṭhina has been removed in that monastery'... pe... removal of the Kaṭhina ending with hearing (savanantikā)." Here, it should be understood that at the moment of hearing, the residence-impediment (āvāsa-palibodha) is cut off first, and when the robe is finished, the robe-impediment is cut off.

In the ninefold set of going to a direction (disāṅgamikanavaka), "the monk who goes to a direction departs" means he departs with the thought "I will not return." By this, the absence of the residence-impediment is shown. For that very reason, the removal of the Kaṭhina ending with completion (niṭṭhānantikā) is stated for one who, having gone back to the monastery where he spent the Vassa, has just finished the robe. By the words "desiring the share of the robe," it shows that monk's possession of the robe-impediment; "apavilāyamāno" means desiring (longing for). The remaining words are easy to understand.

## The explanation of the sevenfold section on taking (Ādāyasattaka-kathā-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
## The method of the explanation of the Kaṭhina Chapter (Kaṭhinakkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
197:
## 8. Cīvarakkhandhaka
## Explanation of the Story of Jīvaka, etc.
In the Cīvarakkhandhaka, the term "kammavipāka" (result of kamma) is used with reference to an unavoidable disease arising from weather (utu), mind (citta), and nutriment (āhāra) which has kamma as its cause. This is because there is no [purely] kamma-born disease [in this context].

In the Pāḷi, "saṃyamassa" means gathering or not giving away, just as in the passage "Yo saṃyamo so vināso" (That which is restraint is destruction), etc. The connection of the sentence (yojanā) is: "We know the fruit of this restraint." The merchant's wife, wishing to show that very fruit, said: "Varaṃ etaṃ ... āsittaṃ."
Some teachers, however, say that "saṃyamassa" has the meaning of benefit (āniśaṃsa), and in this instance, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.

"Ussannadoso" means having an excess of humors such as bile (pitta), etc. "Sabbattha" means in the whole body.

"Mahāpiṭṭhiyakojavaṃ" refers to a woolen coverlet/rug that has received the name "mahāpiṭṭhiya" because it is to be spread on the back of an elephant.

338-9. "Upaḍḍhakāsinaṃ khamamānaṃ" means worth five hundred (half of a thousand). In the Pāḷi, "kiṃ nu kho" means "what is it?"

340-342. "Upacāre" means in the vicinity of the cemetery. "Chaḍḍetvā gatā" means they went away having discarded [the item] without saying anything. By this statement, it is shown that if something is discarded with the intention "Let the bhikkhus take it," then a share must be given [to others] even if one is unwilling. However, if it is merely discarded without any prior agreement, and many [monks] enter together, the one who takes it does not have to give a share to the others against his will. The directions such as the East, etc., are the same for those monks; therefore, they are called "sadisa" (similar/same). To show this, it is said: "Ekadisāya vā okkamiṃsu" (Or they entered from the same direction). "Dhuravihāraṭṭhāne" means in the area in front of the monastery.

## The Explanation of the Story of Jīvaka, etc., is finished.
198:
## Explanation of the Story of the Designation of the Storehouse, etc.
"In the middle of the monastery" is said so that everyone may know. "Making various colors (vaṇṇa)" means making equal portions consisting of large and small types/colors using turmeric and so on, in order to know the sufficiency of the portions. Therefore, it is said: "Placing them in equal portions." This refers to giving a half-share to the novices (sāmaṇeras). "Phātikamma" means an act of making sufficient. It means performing manual labor such as binding brooms as mentioned in the Vinaya, to the extent that there is no decline in the monastery. "To all" means to all the bhikkhus and sāmaṇeras who take the rains-residence robes (vassāvāsika) produced in that monastery. "Also in the storekeeper's robe" is said with reference to out-of-season robes (akāla-cīvara). This refers to giving equal shares when an announcement (ukkutthi) has been made. "They act out of turn" means they do not do it at the proper times but at a moment of their own choosing.

"With this much, my robe is sufficient" means "My robe is complete only with cloth worth twelve [kahāpaṇas]; it is not complete with less than that," thus implying a desire to take everything.

## The Explanation of the Story of the Designation of the Storehouse, etc., is finished.

## Explanation of the Story of Dyeing Robes, etc.
"When this is done" means when the dye-water is kept inside the cotton/vessel and the bark is kept outside, thus separating them. "Does not overflow" means it does not overflow because there is no foam arising from the water alone. "Rajanakuṇḍa" is a large pot for holding boiled dye.

"For the long strips such as the border (anuvāta)" refers to the border in terms of length and width. By the word "etc." (ādi), the strip placed in the form of a channel between two sections (khanda) should also be understood as a "long strip" (dīghapatta). "Āgantukapatta" refers to another strip that is added on top of a double-layered robe. It is said that they do not make that additional strip nowadays.

In the Pāḷi, "nandimukhiyā" means having a joyful face, or having a clear/bright direction.

"Acchupeyya" means I would place or establish. "Hatavatthakānaṃ" means of old clothes. "Without removing" means without removing the weak parts, as one would with a patch (aggaḷa).
199:
349-351. In the Visākhāvatthu, 'kallakāyā' means having an untired body. 'Gati' refers to the attainment known through wisdom (ñāṇagati). 'Abhisamparāyo' means the future life reached through wisdom (ñāṇābhisamparāya), as stated in 'Coming to this world only once, he makes an end of suffering' etc., or it means the special destination to be reached by those endowed with path-knowledge. The Blessed One will explain that special destination. The phrase 'dadāti dānaṃ' is spoken in the sense of giving the remaining requisites other than food and drink. 'Sovaggika' means leading to the heavenly realm (saggasaṃvattanika).

'Aṭṭhapadakacchannena' means (sewn) in the pattern of the lines on a dice board called aṭṭhapada.

In the Pāḷi, 'nadīpāraṃ gantuṃ' means the monk's going to the other side of the river. 'Aggalaguttiyeva pamāṇaṃ' means that even a monk who keeps (the robe) for these four reasons for keeping it, should keep it only in a monastery with a secured door-leaf. 'Nissīmāgata' means passing the time limit known as the rainy season (vassāna); it means that robe is no longer a rainy-season robe (vassikasāṭikacīvara).

## The Explanation of Cīvararajanakathā and others is finished.

## Explanation of Saṅghikacīvaruppādakathā

In the phrase 'pañca māse' (for five months), the second accusative case (upayogavacana) is used in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga). 'Vaḍḍhiṃ payojetvā ṭhapitaupanikkhepato' means from the property deposited with interest by donors for the sake of the rainy-season robe. 'Idha vassaṃvutthasaṅghassa' is merely a manner of speaking. Even without the word 'idha', if one says 'We give to the Saṅgha who has spent the Vassa', the same rule applies. 'Anatthatakathinassāpi pañca māse pāpuṇāti' means that because it arises by the power of the rainy-season gain, it reaches even a monk who has spent the Vassa but has not spread the Kathina for five months. Indeed, it will be said later: 'If one says, "I give the rainy-season robe from the robe-month until the last day of winter," whether the Kathina is spread or not, it reaches only those who have spent the past Vassa.' 'Tato paraṃ' means after five months, starting from the first day of summer. The phrase 'Kasmā? Piṭṭhisamaye uppannattā' (Why? Because it arose in the later period) should be seen...
200:
...immediately after the word 'anāgatavasse'. In some books, however, they write the phrase 'kasmā piṭṭhisamaye uppannattā' immediately after 'anatthatakathinassāpi pañca māse pāpuṇāti'; that writing is a scribal error (pamādalikhita). This is because 'anatthatakathinassāpi' should not be said in reference to what arises in the later period (piṭṭhisamaye). Indeed, 'anatthatakathinassāpi' is said in reference to those who have spent the Vassa. A robe arising in the later period does not reach only those who have spent the Vassa, but reaches all who are present. Therefore, it will be said: 'But if one speaks thus from the first day of summer, it reaches all who are present. Why? Because it arose in the later period.'

'Duggahitāni' means not taken (aggahitāni). The meaning is that they are communal (saṅghika). 'Itova' means either only from what is given to the elders, or it means only at this time.

## The Explanation of Saṅghikacīvaruppādakathā is finished.

## Explanation of Upanandasakyaputtavatthukathā

'He causes the dawn to rise every seven days'—this is said to show the state of residing in two lodgings even within a single monastery, according to the method used for monasteries with different boundaries. By causing the dawn to rise, one is said to have resided there, but not for the sake of avoiding the breaking of the Vassa. Even within the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā), a monk who causes the dawn to rise at any unspecified place is considered to have spent the Vassa even if he has not entered his taken lodging. However, he is not said to have 'resided' in the taken lodging; he is said to have resided there only if the dawn rises while he is in it. Therefore, it is said: 'He is said to reside mostly in the first lodging.' By this, it is shown that in the other lodging, he is said to reside only a little if the dawn rises there, and if the dawn does not rise there, he is not said to have resided there.

'Nānālābhehi' means by various regular rainy-season gains. 'Nānūpacārehi' means by various enclosures and various gates. 'Ekassīmāvihārehi' means by two monasteries included in a single precinct boundary because the two monasteries are surrounded by a single wall. 'Senāsanaggāho paṭippassambhati' means the taking of the lodging taken first is relinquished. 'Tattha' means in that monastery where the taking of the lodging is relinquished.

## The Explanation of Upanandasakyaputtavatthukathā is finished.
201:
## Explanation of the Story of the Sick

365-6. "Bhūmiyaṃ paribhaṇḍaṃ akāsī" means that the sick monk washed the soiled area where he lay and had it smeared with cow dung. "Unable to prepare medicine" means being unable to even perform the procedure described by others. In the Pāḷi text, regarding the giving of robes to nursing monks, since novices (sāmaṇeras) do not have the formal determination of the triple robe (ticīvara-adhiṭṭhāna), the phrase "robes and bowl" etc. is used in every instance. Even if it is worth a thousand, it is connected that it should be given only to those who nurse the sick.

## The Explanation of the Story of the Sick is Finished.

## Explanation of the Belongings of the Deceased, etc.

"Aññaṃ" means something other than the robes and bowl. "Appagghaṃ" means something inferior due to being very old, etc. "Tato" means from the remaining requisites. "Sabbaṃ" refers to the bowl and all three robes.

"Belongs only to the Saṅgha in those various places" means it is the property of the Saṅgha in those respective monasteries. In the Pāḷi text, "not to be disposed of, not to be distributed" (avissajjika avebhaṅgika) means it becomes the property of the Saṅgha of the four quarters, present and future, and He allows it so that it cannot be given away or divided by anyone.

371-2. "Akkanāḷamayaṃ" means a robe made from the stalks of the swallow-wort (akka). "Akkadussāni" means robes made from swallow-wort fibers, and "potthakagatikāni" means they are objects of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). "In the middle of a double-layered robe" means it should be given by making a layer in the middle of that robe which will become a triple-layered robe when finished.

Because it is said, "If there is a suitable recipient," it should be understood that if there is no recipient, even if it is distributed without giving, it is well-distributed.

"The libation water is the measure" means they first pour water saying, "I will offer this many robes," and then offer them. Those monks who receive that water are the ones who receive the share...
202:
...are the ones who receive the share. "Parasumudde" means in Jambudīpa. This is said in reference to the island of Tambapaṇṇi (Sri Lanka).

## The Explanation of the Belongings of the Deceased, etc. is Finished.

## Explanation of the Eight Robe-Matrices

"It is stated by way of personal designation" (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) means that although it should be said as "giving in the boundary" (sīmāya dānaṃ), it is stated by way of personal designation as "he gives in the boundary" (sīmāya deti), etc. By the word "api ca" etc., it shows that the second stone's throw outside the area suitable for the first stone's throw is also the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā). The place of regular assembly, etc., should also be taken as being at the limit. In the world, there is no well-known "gain-boundary" (lābha-sīmā) like a village boundary; who allowed this gain-boundary? It is said, "Not by the Fully Enlightened One" (neva sammāsambuddhena), etc. By this, it shows that this gain-boundary is not established by scriptural usage (sāsana-vohāra) but only by worldly usage (loka-vohāra). "Janapadaparicchedo" is said by the power of the meaning of the word 'sīmā' well-known in the world. Everything within the limit is taken as the countryside boundary (janapada-sīmā); the countryside itself is the countryside boundary. The same applies to the kingdom boundary (raṭṭha-sīmā), etc. Therefore, "the place where authority extends" (āṇāpavattitthānaṃ) etc. is said.

"Pathavīvemajjhe gatassa" is said because it is a partial boundary (khaṇḍa-sīmā) up to the water's edge. In unbound boundaries (abaddha-sīmā) like precinct boundaries, it does not reach monks staying everywhere underground; it only reaches monks staying in places suitable for entry like wells, etc., as explained in the Sīmā-kathā below. An object offered in a world-system boundary (cakkavāḷa-sīmā) reaches even monks staying in the water that supports the earth, because the term 'cakkavāḷa' applies everywhere.

"Buddhādhivuttho" means the place where the Buddha resided. "Pākavaṭṭaṃ" means a regular, continuous offering. "Vattati" means it occurs. "Tehi" means with those monks in whose presence this donor gives (it should be distributed). "In the second portion, when reaching the Elder's seat" means after giving a share once to all monks down to the most junior (saṅghanavaka), if the robes are not exhausted, the second portion is given to the Elder to give to all monks again. In the phrase "It is also allowable for rag-robe monks" (paṃsukūlika), they say the reason is that it was not said, "We give to you [specifically]." If it is so, "We give to the Saṅgha"...
203:
Even though it is said, "We give to the monks, we give to the elders, we give to the Saṅgha," no distinction is found because of these words. In this matter, the underlying reason should be investigated.

In the phrase "It is proper to wrap/wear," it is proper for those who wear rag-robes (pāṃsukūlika). In the case where it is said, "I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and to the bhikkhunīs," regarding the point that it should not be divided and given from the middle: because the Saṅgha is not separately touched in the faction of the bhikkhunīs, it is established that the donor's intention is to give a portion according to the number of bhikkhunīs. Such a gift is also appropriate only when the monks are also counted and given. Indeed, otherwise (if only the nuns were counted), it would not be known how much should be given to the monks and how much to the nuns. Therefore, the statement "to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha" is just like the statement "to the monks"; thus it is said, "It should be given by counting both the monks and the nuns."

Therefore, it is said, "The individual... because of not being included by the taking of the Bhikkhu-saṅgha." Because only the monks are taken by the term 'Bhikkhu-saṅgha,' and because the individual is taken separately as "and to you," it should be understood that the individual is not included therein. The meaning is that it is similar to the place where it is said, "to the monks, to the nuns, and to you." In this matter, the term 'Saṅgha' should be understood as emphasizing the individuals. Some teachers write the reading "because of being included by the taking of the Bhikkhu-saṅgha"; that writing is not good, because that statement is a reason for taking a separate gain. For that very reason, "because of being included by the taking of the Saṅgha separately" is stated as the reason for taking the portion of the individual separately. Just as the individual is not included here, so also in the passages above such as "to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and to you," it should be understood that the individual is not included by terms such as 'Saṅgha.' If there were inclusion, one would receive two portions—from the Saṅgha and separately—because of being included in both.

The words beginning with "should be honored" are stated to show that it is not a lay activity. This statement "Carry it to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha" is said with reference to carrying alms-food. Therefore, it is said, "It is proper to eat." By the word "in winter," when the kathina has not been spread, a robe given in the last month of the rainy season reaches only those who have completed the first Vassa. After that, a robe given in winter reaches also those who have completed the second Vassa, because they have completed the Vassa. In the period after winter, a robe given after saying "to the Saṅgha that has completed the Vassa" reaches all monks who have completed the Vassa anywhere, whether in the immediate Vassa or in subsequent Vassas. It shows that it does not reach those who have not completed the Vassa at all. "To all" means it should be understood as to all those who have completed the Vassa in that state of being a monk.
204:
It should be understood as "to all those who have completed the Vassa." This is because it is said, "vassaṃvutthasaṅghassa." In the phrase "sammukhībhūtānaṃ sabbesaṃ," the same method applies. "Atītavassa" means the immediately preceding Vassa.

The phrase "uddesaṃ gahetuṃ āgato" is said because one is an antevāsika (pupil) even before learning the Pali. "Gahetvā gacchanto" means one who goes after completing the learning of the Pali. The phrase "vattaṃ katvā uddesaparipucchādīni gahetvā vicarantānaṃ" is merely an attribute of "uddesantevāsikānaṃ." By that attribute, it excludes those pupils who are not permanent residents, who come at the time of instruction, take the instruction, and then go to live elsewhere.

## The Explanation of the Summary of the Eight Robes is finished.
## The Method of the Explanation of the Robe Chapter is finished.
205:
## 9. Campeyyakkhandhaka
## Explanation of the Story of the Monk Kassapagotta, etc.
In the Campeyyakkhandhaka, regarding the word "tantibaddho," "tanti" is called concern; "baddho" means bound to that concern, or having reached the state of exertion. Therefore, He said "tasmiṃ āvāse," etc.

387-8. "Hāpanaṃ vā aññathā karaṇaṃ vā natthi" means that because the motion (ñatti) of a motion-act (ñatti-kamma) occurs only once, decreasing is not possible. Because that motion is only one, there is no altering by way of placing the motion later or by way of placing it twice. "Parato" means in the surroundings (parivāra). "Tanti" refers to the act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma); "tassa" means for that act.

## The Explanation of the Story of the Monk Kassapagotta, etc., is finished.
## Explanation of the Two Removals, etc.
"Esā" refers to the person indicated by "bālo," etc.; it should be connected as "does not reach." To show the reason for that not reaching, He said "yasmā," etc. There, "āveṇikena lakkhaṇena" means specifically by the state of being a corrupter of families (kuladūsaka), which is uncommon, as stated in the Pali as the cause for the act of banishment. If this monk does not reach that act, why then is he well-expelled? To this objection, He said, "Because it is said that the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform the act of banishment against him, therefore he is well-expelled." There, "vuttaṃ" means it is said in the Kammakkhandhaka.

In this context, regarding a monk who has performed the act of a family-corrupter and has had the act of banishment performed against him, it is stated in the Commentary on the Thirteen (Terasa-kaṇḍa Aṭṭhakathā): "In whichever monastery a monk resides when he performs the act of a family-corrupter in a certain village, he should not reside in that monastery or in that village," and so forth; such proper conduct (sammāvattanā) should also be fulfilled by a monk against whom an act has been performed for a reason other than being a family-corrupter. However, regarding the duty (vatta) stated in that same Commentary for a family-corrupter whose act has been revoked (paṭippassaddhakamma), such as "He should not accept requisites from the families in which the act of family-corrupting was performed," etc.—that duty should not be fulfilled, because the favoring of families (kula-saṅgaha) was not performed. The same applies to the remaining acts. If it is so...
206:
If it is asked whether the words, "He performs the Niyasakamma for one deserving the Tajjanīyakamma... Upāli, thus it is an unrighteous act" (Mahāvagga 402) and so forth are contradictory—they are not contradictory. This is because the state of deserving the Tajjanīyakamma and other acts is established by the decision of the Saṅgha. For if the Saṅgha, having made the decision, "Let us perform the Tajjanīyakamma," recites the Pabbājanīyakamma motion while reciting the formal act (kammavācā), that act of that monk is an unrighteous act (adhamma-kamma). If, however, they make the decision, "Let us perform only the Pabbājanīyakamma for him," and perform that very act, that act of that monk should be known as a righteous act (dhamma-kamma).

Thus, in this context, having shown the meaning by way of the Pabbājanīyakamma intended as "expulsion" (nissāraṇa), now, when expulsion is intended by way of other acts such as Tajjanīyakamma, to show the possibility of the meaning, "He reaches expulsion; the Saṅgha expels him; he is well-expelled," by way of the opposite of the phrase "He has not reached expulsion" (appatto nissāraṇaṃ), it is said again: "If the Saṅgha expels him (tañce saṅgho nissāreti)—if the Saṅgha..." and so forth. In that statement, "there" (tattha) means in the context of Tajjanīyakamma and other acts; it should be construed that expulsion (nissāraṇa) is permitted even by being endowed with just one factor. In the Pali, in the phrase "He has not reached expulsion" (appatto nissāraṇaṃ), the meaning should be taken as: the monk who has committed an offense reaches expulsion, known as Tajjanīyakamma and so forth, by way of a specific procedure.

## The explanation of the two expulsions and so forth is finished.
## The method of the explanation of the Campeyyakkhandhaka is finished.
207:
## 10. Kosambakakkhandhaka
## Explanation of the Kosambaka Dispute
In the Kosambakakkhandhaka, because of the Vinaya expert's words, "If there is an offense, I shall confess it," the Sutta expert elder acquired the view that it was an offense and said so. Therefore, it is said in the Pali: "He has the view of non-offense (anāpatti-diṭṭhi) regarding that offense." Regarding the words "There is no offense," the Vinaya expert, considering that a case of non-offense could occur through lack of intention or mindfulness—such as not knowing water was left, or leaving it and forgetting—acquired the view of non-offense regarding that leaving of water and said so. Therefore, it is said in the Pali: "Other monks have the view of non-offense regarding that offense." The plural "others" (aññe) is used because the view of non-offense also arose among the followers of that Vinaya expert.

"The view of non-offense occurred" means that because the Sutta expert elder was not proficient in the Vinaya, such a thought occurred to him merely by the words of the Vinaya expert. However, that act was indeed an offense for him because he left the water knowing that it remained. For in the case of knowing the physical object (vatthu) alone, the Sekhiya rules are "with intention" (sacittaka), but not in the case of knowing the regulation (paññatti). Therefore, in the Pali, it is stated everywhere as "offense" (āpatti), as in "He has the view of non-offense regarding that offense." The Vinaya expert elder, remembering the words "Yes, friend" spoken by the Sutta expert elder when asked "Did you leave this water?", and being unskilled in the regulation, thought he did it intentionally and thus spoke with the view that it was an offense. Therefore, it is said in the Pali: "Other monks have the view of non-offense regarding that offense."

"Not yet split" means that the Saṅgha is not called "split" merely by the act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) and the following of the one suspended. However, based on that act, the monks of both sides seek their own factions and increase physical and verbal quarrels through mutual anger; it is with this meaning in mind that it was said. Therefore, he said: "And he, by way of quarrel..." "By way of the meaning of sambhama" means by way of the meaning of "haste."

"Without cause" (akāraṇe) and so forth are said with reference to the fact that the act was done for the purpose of harassment through a mind of anger, in a situation where it was proper to free the monk from the offense by making him understand through skillful means without suspending him, out of a desire for his welfare; it is not said with reference to the absence of the factors of the legal act (kammaṅga). Therefore...
208:
For that very reason, it is stated in the Pali: "Monks, this is an offense; this is not a non-offense... p... this monk is one who has been expelled," and so forth. The phrase "one who sits in the faction of those who speak what is not Dhamma" is merely a characteristic to be noted. Even if a monk sits in the faction of those who speak the Dhamma, if he accepts the views of those who speak what is not Dhamma, he is indeed one of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka) from the Dhamma-speakers. The phrase "destroys the legal act" is stated with reference to the part where the group is incomplete without that monk. "In whatever place" means either in the faction of the Dhamma-speakers or in the faction of those who speak what is not Dhamma. "Takes them as Dhamma-speakers" means regarding the monks who have joined those respective factions as "these are Dhamma-speakers," whether it is true or not. This monk makes himself one of the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka) with the monks in those respective factions. "They show" means they bring about. The phrase "this much" in the Pali means: "Having considered that 'if we stay leaving aside this much space, even if an angry mind arises, we will not be able to perform unseemly bodily acts etc. towards each other,' one should stay far away." Therefore, it is said, "leaving the vicinity (upacāra)."

In the Pali, among the terms "quarrelsome" and so forth, the preliminary stage of a dispute is called "bhaṇḍana." Physical contact and such are called "kalaha." Opposing speech is called "vivāda." "With a full treasury and granary": here, "kosa" refers to the inner chamber of a treasury containing gold, gems, and such. The place where grain is kept is called "koṭṭha." A house that is a granary is called "koṭṭhāgāra," which is a place for collecting grain. "Abbhuyyāsī" means he went out facing for battle. "Ekasaṃghātampi" means even a single battle. "Dhovanaṃ" means washing water. "Pariyādinnarūpa" means having the nature of being overwhelmed and seized by an angry mind. "They do not know that matter" means they do not know that quarrel. "Those who harbor a grudge" means binding the aforementioned state of anger in the mind. "Manifest perils" (pākaṭapariဿaya) refers to obvious dangers such as lions and so forth. "Concealed perils" (paṭicchannapariဿaya) refers to hidden dangers such as lust (rāga) and so forth. In the Pali, "There is no companionship with a fool" means that based on a fool, companionship characterized by virtues such as morality (sīla) and so forth does not exist; it cannot be obtained.
209:
"Attakāmarūpa" means those who have the nature of desiring their own welfare. The word "Anuruddhā" is a call to all three clansmen by the method of ekasesa; therefore, it is referred to in the plural. "Is the body tolerable? Is life endurable?"—He asks, "Are you able to maintain the body and endure life?" "Taggha" is an exclamation in the sense of "certainly"; it means "Certainly, Bhante, (we are able)." In the phrase "yathā kathaṃ," "yathā" is merely an exclamation, or "yathākathaṃ" is a single exclamation in the sense of asking for a reason, meaning "in what way?" "I think their mind is one" means because they act according to the will of one person's mind, "the mind of all of us is like one." In the phrase "kacci pana vo anuruddhā," "vo" is merely an exclamation, or it is the nominative case, meaning "Are you...?" The word "amhākaṃ" is in the genitive case in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa), meaning "among the three of us, whoever departs first from the alms-village."

## The Explanation of the Talk on the Kosambī Dispute is finished.

## The Explanation of the Talk on the Journey to Pālileyyaka

In the phrase "yena pālileyyakaṃ," the accusative case is used in the sense of the nominative; it means "where the village of Pālileyyaka is, there he arrived." "Daharapotakehi" means with young elephants. There is also a reading "ogāhiṃ," meaning they descended into the bathing pond.

In the Udāna verse: This mind of the elephant (nāga) whose tusks are like the poles of a chariot, which inclines toward seclusion (vivēka), is equal to the mind of the Buddha-Nāga which inclines toward seclusion. Why? Because he delights alone in the forest; therefore, the connection should be understood thus.

## The Explanation of the Talk on the Journey to Pālileyyaka is finished.

## The Explanation of the Talk on the Eighteen Grounds

"Stand as the Dhamma is" means stand as the Dhamma and Vinaya are established; it means "stand in the faction of the Dhamma-speakers."

"Whoever should obstruct, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)"—this was said with reference to those who do not cause a schism in the Saṅgha. But those who are schism-makers and are opposed...
211:
## Commentary on the Cūḷavagga
## Homage to Him, the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One
## 1. Kamma-kkhandhaka
## Commentary on the Discussion of the Act of Censure (Tajjanīyakamma)
In the first chapter of the Cūḷavagga, the Kamma-kkhandhaka, first, the word "balavābalavaṃ" is a single compound (samāsa) term. Although it should be said as "balavabalavaṃ," it is stated as "balavābalavaṃ" by making an 'ā' sound (lengthening). Since this term is used in the sense of intensity, as in "dukkha-dukkha" and so on, the Commentary states, "Speak back very forcefully." It means to give a response by making it extremely forceful.

In the passage of the Pāli regarding "charging with an offense," although there is no specifically prescribed offense for words that cause quarrels, such as "Venerable sirs, this one has won," because such words do not fall under lying (musāvāda) or divisive speech (pisuṇāvācā), nevertheless, if a monk is told by other monks individually or in the midst of the Saṅgha, "Friend, do not incite monks against each other and cause quarrels; this does not lead to fewness of wishes, etc.," and that monk, due to disrespect, does not desist, or due to reasons such as speaking of things other than what was asked or harassing the Saṅgha by silence, whatever offense arises, that offense should be charged against him, just as an offense is charged against one who has failed in view (diṭṭhivipanna). This is how the meaning should be understood.

Furthermore, if a monk has committed a light offense (lahuka-āpatti) through body or speech, excluding these words like "Venerable sirs, this one has won," an offense should still be charged against him. The inclusion of the word "attanā" (by oneself) in the kammavācā as "those who themselves are makers of quarrels," and the words "approaching other monks who are makers of quarrels..." are taken according to the specific case (vatthu). If a monk is himself a maker of quarrels but does not approach other quarrel-makers to say "do not do this," the Act of Censure (Tajjanīyakamma) must still be performed against him. Those monks performing the act should perform the kammavācā only in this way: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, bhantes. This monk named so-and-so is a maker of quarrels... a maker of disputes in the Saṅgha. If the Saṅgha is ready to perform the act..." and so on.
212: The monk named so-and-so is a maker of quarrels... a maker of legal issues in the midst of the Sangha. The Kammavācā should be performed only with "If it is suitable for the Sangha," and so on. For a monk who also encourages other monks to quarrel, it is proper to perform the Kammavācā in this same way. This is because encouraging others is also included in the state of being a maker of quarrels. A monk who wishes to perform the Kammavācā, having also mentioned the manner of encouraging others, should take only the meaning of the words spoken by them and perform it only after coordinating it to be consistent with that meaning. It should not be performed only according to what is mentioned here in this Kammakkhandhaka, because it is not possible to speak according to what is mentioned here for all monks. It should be understood that only an act performed with true facts is successful and not flawed; any other act is not successful. This method is the same in Niyassakamma and others. ## End of the Explanation of the Tajjanīyakamma. ## Explanation of the Twelve Unlawful Acts, etc. "Appatiññāya kataṃ" means an act performed without making [the monk] admit to the basis or the offense. If a monk, having committed a transgression of the basis while everyone is watching, later speaks a falsehood saying "I did not do it" out of fear of the act being performed, his committing the transgression in the presence of the monks is itself the admission (paṭiññā). The requirement for admission is allowed only for the purpose of knowing the truth. However, where there is doubt, it should be understood that the act should be performed only after making him admit. This phrase "or by a Pārājika offense" is said because a Pārājika offense is a cause for the destruction of the monk's status and is extremely difficult to remedy by a formal act. This phrase "or by a Saṅghādisesa offense" is said because there exists the specific Nissaraṇakamma such as Parivāsa. The statement made later, "He is one who has failed in virtue regarding higher virtue... the Tajjanīyakamma should be performed," is said with reference to a light offense (lahuka-āpatti) caused by factors such as disrespect when being exhorted, "Having stood in future restraint, emerge from the offense." A monk who has fallen into a light offense rooted in failure in virtue is here called "one who has failed in virtue regarding higher virtue" by way of figurative speech (abhedūpacāra), just as in the expression "one who has failed in view through excessive view." Just as an act performed against one who speaks while holding a [wrong] view, without saying "Desist from this view," is an unlawful act performed without an offense because it was performed solely for the failure in view, so too for one who has reached failure in virtue...
213:
The Act of Censure (Tajjaniya-kamma) and others performed for a monk who, having reached a sense of shame (lajjidhamma), desires to rise from an offense in accordance with the Dhamma and remain in restraint, is called an unlawful act (adhamma-kamma) performed by way of a non-confessable offense, because it was performed solely due to a failure in virtue (sīlavipatti). For this very reason, in the Act of Guidance (Niyassa-kamma) as well, it is stated that not remaining in restraint is the cause for performing the formal act, starting with the words: "A monk, being of normal status (pakatatta), gives probation (parivāsa)." Indeed, the Act of Censure and others are authorized only for the purpose of disciplining the untamed.

Some teachers say that this phrase "by way of a non-confessable offense" is stated with reference only to a Pārājika offense and not to a Saṅghādisesa. That statement contradicts the words in the wholesome side (sukkapakkha): "It is performed by way of a confessable offense." If a Saṅghādisesa offense were also to be taken by the term 'confessable' in a figurative sense, there would be no distinction for this section from the section stated as "it is performed by way of an offense." Furthermore, the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) does not show any distinction here. Therefore, the meaning should be taken in this place only according to the method already mentioned.

"Sabbānipi" means all three: the Act of Censure, the Act of Guidance, and the Act of Banishment (Pabbājaniya-kamma). "By the grounds of another formal act" means that there is no fault whatsoever in performing another formal act using the grounds of an act other than the Act of Censure. The reason is stated starting with the words "Why is that?"

"Pannaloma" refers to those whose hair, namely pride, has fallen away.

## The explanation of the Twelve Acts of Unlawful Procedure, etc., is finished.

## Explanation of the Act of Guidance, etc.

In the Pali text of the Act of Guidance, "apissu" is a collection of particles in the sense of "apica" (moreover). Regarding the phrase "you must live in dependence (nissāya)," some teachers say it is stated with reference to living in dependence on a good friend (kalyāṇamitta); others, however, say it means only the taking of dependence (nissaya). It should be understood that by both [interpretations], it is shown that living according to one's own will (serivihāra) is not proper for that monk.

In the Act of Banishment, the words "let the Act of Banishment be settled" are stated with reference to those who conduct themselves properly without departing or doing other such things.
214:
In the Act of Reconciliation (Paṭisāraṇīya-kamma), regarding the phrase "neither the word of a monk nor the word of a layman," even figuratively, monks do not speak words of reviling others. Laypeople, however, although capable of reviling by name, do not speak such words without cause against those who are benefactors. The meaning is: "You have fallen even from the virtues of a layman."

By the phrase "the possession of factors is not the same as the previous acts," it is shown that it is not proper to perform this Act of Reconciliation merely by the reasons stated for the Act of Censure and others. However, by the factors stated here, such as striving for the non-gain of laypeople, it should be understood that it is proper to perform those acts like the Act of Censure as well. And here, because it is stated, "He reviles with low words a layman who is faithful, confident, a donor, a doer of service, and a supporter of the Saṅgha," the act is deserved only by such factors related to laypeople, such as reviling those types of laypeople, and not by reviling monastery attendants, servants, and so on. Even in that case, after the donors and others have been asked for forgiveness (khamāpita), there is no longer a need for the formal act, and the offense should be confessed in any suitable place. If a donor does not forgive even when being asked for forgiveness three times, the monk who has not yet had the formal act performed against him should confess the offense within the sight-range (upacāra) of that donor. If that donor has passed away, or has gone to another place, or the direction he went is unknown, or if there is a danger to life on the way, it is said that whether the monk has had the formal act performed or not, he should inform the Saṅgha of the truth in their midst, ask for forgiveness, and then confess the offense. In the case of not fulfilling a righteous promise (breaking a promise), one should go to those donors and be informed of the sequence of words for asking forgiveness, such as: "I made a promise without careful consideration and could not fulfill it; please forgive me for that."

In the Pali text, "being crestfallen, he was unable to make the householder Citta forgive him" means that although he went again on a journey of thirty yojanas, because of his stiff pride, he did not reveal the fault as it truly was and did not ask for forgiveness. Thus, he was rejected by the householder who said, "I do not forgive," and being crestfallen, he was unable to make him forgive. Although that Venerable Sudhamma returned to Sāvatthī, he was sent again by the Teacher solely for the purpose of subduing his pride. Being unable to make him forgive as in the previous manner, he returned again. Then the Blessed One, having taught the Dhamma starting with "He would desire unreal reputation..." (Dhammapada 73) and having crushed his pride, authorized the giving of a companion monk (anudūta). This is how it should be understood.

Because it is stated, "If he does not forgive... he should be made to confess the offense," it should be understood that if the lay donor forgives from the beginning, there is no need for the task of confessing the offense within the sight-range.
215:
Among the three Acts of Suspension (Ukkhepaniya-kamma), in the case of Ariṭṭha, "having charged with an offense" means charging with a dukkaṭa offense due to the reason of not renouncing an evil view in the midst of the Saṅgha separately, or charging with a pācittiya offense at the conclusion of the formal exhortation (samanubhāsana). In this Act of Suspension as well, the words "Thus I understand from the Blessed One," etc., are stated by the formal act (kammavācā) only by way of the case. In whatever manner those who hold wrong views have spoken, the formal act should be performed by connecting it with those various manners. However, even without specifying the manner of holding the view, it is proper to perform the formal act generally, thus: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. An evil wrong view has arisen in the monk named so-and-so. He does not renounce that view. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha..."

By the phrase "depending on which view he engages in disputes, etc.," it is shown that only disputes and so on that arise depending on a view are intended here, and not mere disputes. However, if a monk holds the view that "there is no fault in engaging in disputes, etc." and then engages in disputes, that view of his is also indeed a wrong view (diṭṭhi). If he does not renounce that view, it is proper to perform the formal act against him.

## The explanation of the Act of Guidance, etc., is finished.

## The method of the explanation of the Chapter on Formal Acts (Kammakkhandhaka) is finished.
216:
## 2. Pārivāsikakkhandhaka
## Pārivāsikavattakathāvaṇṇanā
In the Pārivāsikakkhandhaka, in the phrase "at least those deserving to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanā)," the word "ādi" (etc.) includes monks deserving penance (mānatta), those undergoing penance, and those deserving rehabilitation (abbhāna). This is because those deserving to be sent back to the beginning and so forth remain in the status of a regular monk (pakaṭatta) in the place of those undergoing probation (pārivāsika), and those undergoing probation remain in their place. "Adhovātapadatthanaka" refers to a piece of wooden board or similar where one stands to wash the feet. "Pādaghaṃsana" refers to a potsherd or similar for scrubbing the feet. Since only the words "they perform the duties" are mentioned, it is not appropriate for those such as co-residents (saddhivihārika) to perform acts such as paying homage.

Regarding the phrase "when the pure uposatha is performed," this is said with reference to the pure uposatha performed by those who have not entered the rains-retreat or whose rains-retreat is broken, at the time when the Saṅgha performs the invitation (pavāraṇā) on pavāraṇā days. "With one's own Pāḷi" means reciting in front of the junior monks (navaka).

Regarding the phrase "only for the one undergoing probation," this is said with reference to all heavy offenses (garukāpatti) ending with those deserving rehabilitation. This is because those monks are also permitted the alms-food relinquished on the previous day respectively; only the remaining regular monks (pakaṭatta) do not receive that alms-food.

"Catussālabhatta" refers to alms-food given in order in the refectory. "By one standing within the hatthapāsa" means standing in a place where the reception is valid within the donor's hatthapāsa. "Even in the mahāpeḷabhatta" means even in the alms-food given by placing it in large rice baskets and similar vessels.

"More evil" (pāpiṭṭhatara) is said with reference to the Pārājika offense as the highest. However, compared to the offenses of the formulated prohibitions (paṇṇatti-vajja) such as acting as a go-between (sañcaritta), offenses such as the emission of semen (sukkavissaṭṭhi) are indeed worldly faults (lokavajja); among those worldly faults, acts such as causing a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda) are indeed more evil.

By the phrase "the act (kamma) is the formal act of the probation (pārivāsika-kammavācā)," it should be understood that the meaning of the word "kammavācā" as "the speech which is the act" is established. In the word "savacanīya," it means "with fault." It should be seen here that the meaning is an act initiated by one's own speech; it means that one should not perform an act initiated by one's own authority, such as saying "Do not go" or "Come before the masters of the Vinaya."
217:
Or else, it means one should not perform an act initiated by one's own authority, such as saying "Do not go" or "Come before the masters of the Vinaya." Thus, when a formal admonition (savacanīya) is performed by someone, it is not proper to transgress it with disrespect; if one transgresses, it is called transgressing the authority of the Buddha and the Saṅgha.

"Rajohata-bhūmi" is an attribute of a leaf-roofed hut (paṇṇasālā). "Paccaya" refers to the rains-residence robe (vassāvāsika-cīvara). "Does not receive a lodging" (senāsanaṃ na labhati) means not receiving a place to stay according to seniority (vassagga).

"Apaṇṇakapaṭipadā" is the unerring practice. In the phrase "even if one strives" (sace vāyamantopi), a monk who is unable to strive, knowing his inability, is also included.

"Without distinction" (avisesena) is because it applies generally to both monks on probation and suspended (ukkhittaka) monks. "In places covered by five types of roofing" (pañcavanna-chadanabaddha-ṭṭhānesu) means in places roofed with the five kinds of roofing.

"Obaddha" means oppression (pīḷita) connected with the burden of service and so on. In the phrase "on a bed or a chair" (mañce vā pīṭhe vā), the word "vā" (or) has the sense of inclusion (samuccaya); by this, it is shown that it is not proper to sit even on long seats such as mats (taṭṭikā) or skins (cammakhaṇḍa).

"No offense of breaking duty" (na vattabhedadukkaṭaṃ) shows that there is no dukkaṭa offense even if a senior monk breaks the duty knowingly. The phrase "having laid down the duty" (vattaṃ nikkhipāpetvā) is said with reference only to probation (parivāsa) and so on.

## The Explanation of the Duties of those on Probation is finished.
## The Method of the Explanation of the Chapter on those on Probation is finished.
218:
## 3. Samuccayakkhandhaka

## Sukkavissaṭṭhikathāvaṇṇanā

In the Samuccayakkhandhaka, "vedayamahaṃ" means "I inform, I announce." They also say the meaning of that word is "I experience." However, they praise the former meaning because it is a statement of announcement. The phrase "having announced, it should be laid down" is said for the sake of being freed from the dukkaṭa offense. Some teachers, however, say, "It is also said to prevent the interruption of the nights (ratticcheda) for a monk who wishes to undertake the duty again on that very day and let the dawn rise."

Because it is said "compatible (sabhāga) monks reside," it should be understood that it is proper to perform the duty only outside, without undertaking it in the residence of incompatible (visabhāga) monks. The phrase "having passed beyond two stone-throws" is said for the sake of leaving the vicinity (upacāra) where the sound of monks' recitation and so on in the monastery can be heard. The phrase "having stepped aside from the main road" is said for the sake of passing beyond the vicinity of monks traveling on the road. The phrase "concealed by a thicket" and so forth is said for the sake of leaving the vicinity of sight.

By this Pāḷi, "that monk also goes for some business even before dawn," it is shown that when the announcement has been made, even if all the monks have gone to the monastery, there is no fault of deficiency in the group (gaṇa-ūna) or the fault of living apart (vippavāsa) because the living together (sahavāsa) has been announced. Therefore, it says "ayañca" and so on. "It is not proper to perform the rehabilitation (abbhāna)" means that even if performed, it is as if not performed.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Emission of Semen is finished.

## Paṭicchannaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā

"Suddhassa" refers to one who has not fallen into a compatible Saṅghādisesa offense, or one who has emerged from that offense. "Aññasmiṃ" means in the emergence from another offense other than the emergence from an offense by way of the Suddhanta probation. In the Pāḷi, "the monk Udāyi, having been sent back by the Saṅgha for one intermediate offense... (pe)... sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanā)," this should be construed by changing it through the power of the instrumental case (karaṇa) as "sent back by the sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāya paṭikassito)." Or else, it is also proper to construe it only by the power of the nominative case (paccatta) together with the subsequent phrase "the sending back to the beginning is pleasing to the Saṅgha."
219:
In the phrase "the bhikkhu Udāyī, because of an intervening offense... pulling back to the beginning," it should be construed as: because an intervening offense is the cause, pull the bhikkhu Udāyī back to the beginning, taking the original days, and let the Saṅgha give him a combined probation (samodhāna-parivāsa) for that intervening offense. "Abandoning after making it clear" means making the monk's incurable state clear to the Saṅgha and abandoning him by separating him from the group of conscientious monks (lajjī-gaṇa).

"One hundred offenses" refers to a hundred offenses committed in a single day due to bodily contact (kāyasaṃsagga), etc. "Ten hundreds" means a thousand offenses. "Concealing for a hundred nights" should be construed accordingly. "At the end of all the Kammavācās for probation" means at the conclusion of the Kammavācās for all these probations: the two types of purification probation (suddhanta-parivāsa) and the three types of combined probation (samodhāna-parivāsa) shown below. "In the same manner as before" means in the same manner as stated in the concealed probation (paṭicchanna-parivāsa).

"From the precinct of the monastery" means from the precinct of the monks' monastery outside the village. "Two stone-throws must be exceeded" refers to exceeding the hearing distance (savana-upacāra) of the monks. The absence of the word "village's" does not mean that the village precinct (gāmūpacāra) need not be left. Therefore, it shows that even if monks or nuns stay within the village precinct, if they stay beyond the sight and hearing distance, they do not cause the "breaking of the night" (ratticcheda) for that nun.

"In the same manner as stated for monks who have not laid down their duties" refers to the breaking of the night by monks entering the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā). "In that village" means in the village where the nuns reside. "Showing oneself" means showing oneself in a way that can be made known. "Giving after consulting" shows that even when living with a designated nun, the breaking of the night does not occur.

"For one who has been pulled back to the beginning" means for a monk who has been pulled back to the beginning and has completed the probation again. "Of the three" refers to the original offense and the two intervening offenses.

"If he concealed" refers to an offense committed by a monk who has laid down his duties. In the Pali text regarding the talk on intervening offenses during the five-day concealment period, the phrase "Thus, bhikkhus, six nights of penance (mānatta) should be given" does not mean it should be given immediately after the Kammavācā for pulling back to the beginning. Rather, for a monk pulled back to the beginning, after he has lived on probation for five days...
220:
...it refers to giving penance (mānatta) for a third intervening offense that was not concealed, committed while practicing penance. For a monk who has been given penance in this way, by practicing for one period of six nights (cha-ratta), the penance for all four offenses—including the three offenses for which penance was previously given—is considered practiced. In this way, the procedure should be understood for an intervening offense committed during the time worthy of rehabilitation (abbhāna), and for intervening offenses during the period of concealment for a fortnight (pakkha-paṭicchanna).

"Five by way of days concealed for one day, etc." is said by performing the individual giving of probation, giving of penance, and rehabilitation for each of the four offenses, such as the one concealed for one day. "Four by way of intervening offenses" is said by attributing the giving of penance and rehabilitation to a single instance in each respective pulling back to the beginning.

## The Explanation of the Talk on Concealed Probation is finished.

## The Explanation of the Talk on Combined Probation

"Because the intervening offense was concealed" is the statement of the reason for giving combined probation (samodhāna-parivāsa), but not the reason for the nullification (makkhita) of the days already served on probation. This is because even when pulling back to the beginning is done for an unconcealed intervening offense, the nullification of those days is possible. Therefore, after the phrase "Both the days penance was practiced and the days probation was lived are all nullified," the construction should be: "And combined probation should be given to him. Why is it given? Because there is a concealed intervening offense; therefore it is given." That is why the phrase beginning with "Therefore" (teneva) is stated.

## The Explanation of the Talk on Combined Probation is finished.

## The Explanation of the Talk on Combined Probation According to Value

By the Pali "And based on a single offense," it shows the method such as "one offense concealed for one day, one offense concealed for two days," etc. "To show the state of being unconcealed" means to show the state of being unconcealed by stating the worthiness of penance for an offense that was concealed due to not knowing, etc. "Friends, for one month a bhikkhu...
221:
...is worthy of penance" (Cūḷavagga, 153). In that text, it does not mean he is worthy of probation by virtue of the month concealed through not knowing; rather, the meaning is that he is worthy of penance simply because of having committed the offense. In the Pali, "makkha-dhammo" means the desire to trample or ignore. It should be understood that this chapter is called the Samuccaya-khandhaka (Chapter on Accumulation) because it is a collection of all decisions regarding the giving of probation, etc., for Saṅghādisesa offenses.

## The Explanation of the Talk on Combined Probation According to Value is finished.

## The Method of the Explanation of the Samuccaya-khandhaka is finished.
222:
## 4. Samathakkhandhaka
## Commentary on Sativinaya and Others
In the Samathakkhandhaka, the discipline given relying on the extensive mindfulness of an Arahant, which is the means of removing unsuitable actions such as accusations, is called Sativinaya (Verdict of Mindfulness).

"Cittavipariyāsakata" means having a perversion of the mind that has been committed. In the sentence "They accuse the bhikkhu Gagga...", the habit of an insane monk is called "ummattaka" (insanity). That very habit, because it is done with a perversion of the mind, is called "cittavipariyāsakata." It should be understood that they accuse the bhikkhu Gagga of an offense committed through such an unseemly practice, which belongs to an insane monk and is done with a perversion of the mind. The discipline given to a monk who was first deluded but later reached the state of being non-deluded is called Amūḷhavinaya (Verdict of Past Insanity).

The procedure that brings about the majority status of those who speak according to the Dhamma (dhammavādī) is called "Yebhuyyasikā" (Majority Decision). To show that in this context, this word has the augment "sa" and ends with the suffix "ika," the phrase beginning with "yassā" was spoken. In that word "yassā," "kiriyāyā" refers to the procedure of taking voting tickets (salākaggāha), such as by secret or open methods. The settling procedure that relies on the majority status is called "Yebhuyyasikā"; thus should the meaning of the word Yebhuyyasikā be taken. Only when taken in this way does this Yebhuyyasikā become a settlement of legal issues (adhikaraṇasamatha). This is because when the majority status of the dhammavādī is established by the aforementioned taking of voting tickets, the settlement of the legal issue occurs only by relying on that majority status afterwards. It cannot be achieved merely by the act of establishing the majority status of the dhammavādī.

By the statement "The rest of the meaning here is just as the method mentioned in the Tajjanīyakamma and others," it is shown that like the seven formal acts such as Tajjanīyakamma (Act of Censure), this Tassapāpiyasikākamma (Act for Further Misconduct) is also a separate, single act of suppression (niggahakamma) to be performed against a person who is associated with faults such as impurity and who does not abide by the decision of the Saṅgha. When this act of suppression is performed, that person does not get the opportunity to descend into the midst of the Saṅgha to prove his purity, saying "I am pure," nor does the Saṅgha get the opportunity to give a decision to him. The legal issue is settled merely by the performance of that act.

However, how does that act cease? In this regard, some teachers say, "That person remains suppressed just as he was suppressed; he does not receive reinstatement (osāraṇā). For that reason..."
223:
...it is said that 'Osāraṇā' (reinstatement) is not mentioned in the Pali text (for one subjected to Tassapāpiyasikākamma). Other teachers, however, say that since the Pali text mentions proper conduct with phrases like 'should not be ordained,' etc., for a person who conducts himself well and enters into a state of shame (lajjīdhamma), even though reinstatement is not explicitly mentioned, it should indeed be performed by adapting the formal act (kammavācā) according to the method used in Tajjanīyakamma and others. This statement is appropriate. For that very reason, it will be said in the Commentary: 'If he is virtuous, he will fulfill his duties and obtain relief. If not, he will remain as one who is thus destroyed.' The term 'Tassapāpiyasikākamma' is also an un-elided compound (aluttasamāsa). Therefore, it says 'This (Tassapāpiyasikākamma) is...', and so on.

## The explanation of Sativinaya and others is finished.

## Explanation of Adhikaraṇakatha

Because of the state of perversion, the mind becomes distressed; therefore, it says 'vohāra (expression/usage) for the sake of mental suffering,' and so on. 'Upavadanā' means accusation (codanā). 'Tattheva' occurs in the follow-up accusation (anuvadana).

'Because of the state of knowing each act from the beginning' means that because the section on formal acts (kammavagga) that comes in detail is known through the introductory explanation of the Commentary from the beginning, the decision will be easy to understand; thus it should be connected.

In the Pali text, 'ajjhattaṃ vā' means either in oneself or in one's own group. 'Bahiddhā vā' means either in another or in another's group. 'Anavassavāya' means for the sake of non-arising.

'Is Vivādādhikaraṇa (Legal issues arising from disputes) wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?'—this statement is a question. 'Vivādādhikaraṇa could be wholesome,' etc., is the answer. This method applies to the remaining terms as well.

Even though it is of a conventional nature (paññatti), if an offense is called unwholesome or indeterminate by way of metonymy of cause (kāraṇūpacāra), then since wholesome states can also be a cause for an offense, it should be said by that same metonymy that 'Āpattādhikaraṇa (Legal issues arising from offenses) could be wholesome.'
224:
To show the reason for saying "There is no wholesome legal question concerning offenses" instead of saying it that way, it is said: "In this context, the meaning should be understood by way of what was spoken with a specific intention." The meaning in this statement is as follows: If an offense (āpatti) were of the nature of an ultimate reality (paramattha), then the statement "A legal question concerning offenses (āpattādhikaraṇa) might be unwholesome," etc., would be appropriate. This is because, as shown in the commentaries on the Duṭṭhadosa training rule and others, it is not fitting for it to be an ultimate reality due to being entangled with faults; it is strictly of the nature of a conventional reality (paññatti). Therefore, it should not be said in a direct sense (nippariyāya) that "it might be unwholesome, it might be indeterminate."

If, however, it were said figuratively (pariyāya) as "it might be unwholesome, it might be indeterminate" based solely on its arising from unwholesome or indeterminate states, then it should also be said figuratively that "a legal question concerning offenses might be wholesome" based on its arising from wholesome states. This is because this statement was made with reference to the specific nature of the reasons why an offense is worthy of being figuratively called unwholesome or indeterminate, but not worthy of being called wholesome. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood only by way of that specific reason for which this statement was spoken.

Now, if someone were to take it that the unwholesome nature of an offense was stated only with reference to the mind that completes the factors (aṅgappahonaka-citta), and not with reference to any other specific reason, the teacher said "Yasmiṃ hi," etc., to show the flaw in that view. In that passage, "pathavīkhaṇanādike" refers to legal questions concerning offenses that are faults by convention (paññattivajja) caused by digging the earth, etc. "Kusala-cittaṃ aṅgaṃ" means that when one, without knowing the regulation, performs actions such as cleaning the ground in a stupa courtyard with a wholesome mind, and at that time digs the earth or destroys vegetation (bhūtagāma), the wholesome mind is the cause. "Tasmiṃ sati" means while that legal question concerning offenses exists, there is an offense worthy of being called wholesome because it arose from a wholesome mind. In the Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, however, the phrase "tasmiṃ sati" is interpreted as "when that wholesome mind is taken as the nature of the offense." That is not appropriate. Because the word "tasmiṃ" (that) must refer back to the "āpattādhikaraṇa" (legal question concerning offenses) which was already referred to by the word "yasmiṃ" (which).

"Na sakkā vattuṃ" means that even if it is of a conventional nature, if an offense is called unwholesome because it arises from unwholesome states, then it must also be called wholesome. Therefore, it is not possible to say "There is no wholesome legal question concerning offenses." If it could be said, then the unwholesome nature of that offense would also have to be rejected.
225:
Because, although the three states—wholesome and so on—are equal in being sufficient factors for an offense, only the designation "wholesome" is rejected for an offense, while the designations "unwholesome" and so on are not. Therefore, this statement—"A legal question concerning offenses might be unwholesome, it might be indeterminate; there is no wholesome legal question concerning offenses"—was not made with reference merely to the mind which is the cause and factor in the sense of originating the offense. Otherwise, it would also have to be said that "a legal question concerning offenses might be wholesome." By this, it is shown that the unwholesome nature of an offense is also stated only figuratively for some reason, and not in an ultimate sense. As it is said: "That which one commits with a wholesome mind is wholesome; that which is committed with others is the other (unwholesome or indeterminate)."

In the passages beginning with "Idaṃ pana," the meaning is this: This statement, "A legal question concerning offenses might be unwholesome, it might be indeterminate," was not made with reference to an indefinite cause that occasionally becomes a cause in some training rule. Rather, it was made with reference to that very cause which is capable of being the cause of an offense in all training rules. For unwholesome states are the cause of all offenses for one who knowingly transgresses a regulation. In the case of worldly faults (lokavajja), they are the cause even for one who does not know the regulation. In purely conventional faults (paññattivajja), unwholesome states do not occur at the moment when wholesome or indeterminate minds are active; elsewhere, they occur of their own accord. As for the indeterminate (abyākata) associated with body and speech, it is a factor of all offenses at the moment when wholesome, unwholesome, and other states are occurring, and also in the case of an offense of "sleeping together" (sahaseyya) for one who has entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). Why? Because among the six origins of offenses (āpatti-samuṭṭhāna), there is no absence of the factors of body and speech. Therefore, this unwholesome and indeterminate nature of offenses was stated with reference only to their being the root of all offenses. In cases such as digging the earth (pathavīkhaṇana), where a wholesome state is also a cause of an offense, it is still inappropriate to call the offense "wholesome" by figuratively applying that cause to it. This is because calling blameworthy (sāvajja) and blameless (anavajja) states by the same name is contradictory. To the extent that they are mutually contradictory, to that same extent, it is inappropriate to apply the designation of cause and effect to them. Therefore, even if a wholesome state exists in those acts like digging the earth, it is not reckoned (avvohārika); only the doors of body and speech are the specific causes.

In that context, "it is strictly unwholesome" is said figuratively by way of the cause, because it originates from an unwholesome mind. In that passage, "tatra" refers to worldly faults (lokavajja). By the words "vikkapo natthi," it is shown that the word "siyā" (might be) does not have the sense of an alternative (vikappa). "It is unwholesome" means it is unwholesome by way of figurative application of the cause, because it is originated by the unwholesome. By way of sleeping together (sahaseyya), etc...
226:
The statement that it is indeterminate (abyākata) because of falling into an offense means that since the offense is committed only by the power of the indeterminate form (rūpābyākata), namely the bodily door (kāyadvāra) which occurs through the stretching of the back with a woman and so on, the offense is called indeterminate by way of metonymy of cause (kāraṇūpacāra). In that passage, 'tattha' refers to that legal issue of prescriptive offense (paṇṇattivajjāpattādhikaraṇa). 'Sañcicca-asañcicca-vasena' (by way of intentionality and unintentionality) is said with reference to this nature of variation (vikappa), meaning the state of being unwholesome (akusala) or indeterminate (abyākata), which is intended by the power of falling into an offense either by knowing or not knowing the regulation.

If it is said with reference to such a nature of variation, one might ask: 'In the case of falling into an offense unintentionally, since one can also fall into an offense with a wholesome mind, why is it not said that the legal issue of offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) can also be wholesome (kusala)?' For this reason, the phrase beginning with 'sace pana' is stated. To clarify the meaning already stated as 'acittakānaṃ' (those without intent) by way of the mode of origin (samuṭṭhāna), the phrase 'eḷakaloma-padasodhammādi-samuṭṭhānānampi' is stated. By this statement, 'one might fall into an offense with a wholesome mind' regarding those of unintentional origin, it is shown that it is inappropriate to use the term 'wholesome' (kusala), which is blameless (anavajja), even by metonymy of cause, for an offense that is blameworthy (sāvazza). By the phrase beginning with 'na ca tattha', it is rejected that it is appropriate to call it wholesome even though wholesomeness exists as a cause of the offense, and instead, only the causality of the indeterminate (abyākata), namely body and speech, is shown. In that passage, 'calitappavattānaṃ' means those that are moved and those that are proceeded. For the body is 'moved' (calita) and speech is 'proceeded' (pavatta).
