Here, either the body or speech is the factor (aṅga). And since that factor is ...pe... indeterminate, it is stated only as the cause of the offense. Thus, it is established that the statement 'the legal issue of offense may be unwholesome or may be indeterminate' is spoken figuratively (pariyāyato) by way of metonymy of cause, and not in the literal sense (nippariyāyato).

As for the extensive elaboration in the Sāratthadīpanī to establish the nature of the offense as unwholesome etc. in the literal sense, it should not be accepted as essential, because it is rejected even in the commentary on the Duṭṭhadosa training rule. Therefore, here too, by the phrase beginning with 'the mind which is a factor of the offense...', the unwholesome mind is shown to be distinct from the offense by being its cause. Since what should be said here has already been shown below, I will not elaborate further. In this phrase 'yo vītikkamo' (which is a transgression) occurring by way of transgression, the transgression of the offense arising from the bodily and vocal transgression of a monk who transgresses knowingly with an unwholesome mind is stated. This same method applies in the section on the indeterminate (abyākatavāra).

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Legal Issues is finished.
227:
## Explanation of the Discussion on the Settlement of Legal Issues, etc.

In the Pāḷi, the question beginning with 'vivādādhikaraṇaṃ ekaṃ samathaṃ anāgamma' (a dispute not having come to a single settlement) is the inquiry. The part beginning with 'siyā' (it may be) is the answer. In the word 'siyā', the meaning is that it should be said that settlement would occur only by this means of settlement. 'Sammukhāvinayasmiṃ' should be understood as a description emphasizing the state (bhāva), meaning 'in the state of a verdict in the presence of'. This method is the same in all sections (vāra). The phrase 'the performer reopens [the case]' (kārako ukkoṭeti) is merely an illustration (upalakkhaṇa); any monk who reopens a case incurs a Pācittiya offense. The reason why a Pācittiya offense is not mentioned in the case of criticizing an Ubbāhikā act (referral to a committee) is that there is no giving of consent (chandadāna) in that Ubbāhikā act.

'Vaṇṇāvaṇṇāyo katvā' means having made them endowed with small and large marks. Therefore, it was said: 'having imposed the perception of a sign' (nimittasaññaṃ āropetvā).

In the passage 'kiccādhikaraṇaṃ ... sammati', the meaning should be understood that the act of announcement (apalokanakamma) and so forth are accomplished by the verdict in the presence of (sammukhāvinaya).

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Settlement of Legal Issues, etc., is finished.

## The Method of Explaining the Samathakkhandhaka is finished.
228:
## 5. Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka

## Explanation of the Discussion on Minor Matters

In the Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka, 'aṭṭhapadākārena' means in the form of eight squares on a gambling board (chessboard). 'Mallakamūlasanthānena' means in the shape of the base of a spittoon. This is said with reference to a circular support; it is a designation for a circular bowl made with raised points (spikes).

'Puthupāṇika' refers to massaging the back with open palms without making a fist. With reference to this very thing, it is called 'hatthaparikamma' (hand-treatment).

In the phrase 'muttolambakādīnaṃ', the word 'ādi' includes earrings and so forth. 'Palambakasuttaṃ' refers to a thread in the form of a sacrificial thread worn by Brahmins. 'Valaya' refers to bracelets and anklets.

'Dvaṅgule' is the accusative plural; the meaning is that it is not proper to exceed the measure of two finger-breadths. Here, regarding the Pāḷi 'monks should not wear long hair', they say that even for one who does not know that two months or two finger-breadths have been exceeded, offenses without intent (acittaka) occur based on the count of hairs and beard.

'Kocchena' means with a comb (or brush) made by binding together Usīra grass and so forth and cutting them evenly. 'Cikkalena' means with oil mixed with resin (or gum). 'Uṇhābhitattarajasirānampi' means even for those whose heads are heated by the sun's heat, or those whose heads are covered with dust. 'Addahatthena' means with a wet hand.

248-249. 'Sādhugītaṃ' is a song (chant) connected with the nature of impermanence and so forth. 'Caturassena vattena' means with a complete manner of pronunciation. To show the common characteristic of all manners such as the 'wave-like' manner (taraṅgavatta), the phrase 'sabbesaṃ ... lakkhaṇaṃ' is stated. Reciting with more measures (mattā) than the measures required for a syllable to be complete is called 'distorted recitation' (vikārakathana); reciting without doing so is the meaning of 'characteristic' (lakkhaṇa). 'Bāhiralomi' is a neuter description of state; the meaning is that for one wearing it such that the fur is visible on the outside, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
229:
In the Pali, "taruṇaññeva ambaṃ" refers only to a young mango whose seed has not yet matured. "Pātāpetvā" means only by causing it to fall (by cutting). This statement "mattāvaṇṇitā" was spoken for the sake of the benefit of the Sāsana, meaning "others criticize." "Na pariyāpuṇiṃsu" means they did not learn.

The phrase "cattāri ahirājakulāni" is spoken by including all types of snakes into only four families. "Attaparittaṃ kātuṃ" means to perform protection for oneself.

"Virūpakkhehi me mettaṃ" means "May I have friendship (mettā) with the Nāgas of the Virūpakkha family." It means "May they be happy, free from suffering, and free from enmity." In this way, the radiation of loving-kindness occurs. The same method applies to the remaining terms. The word "apādakehi" and so on shows the radiation of loving-kindness towards all beings, including the snake families, in a limited way (odhiso). The phrase "mā maṃ apādako hiṃsī" shows the arrangement of self-protection through that loving-kindness.

"Sabbe sattā" and so on shows the radiation of universal loving-kindness (anodhiso) towards all beings, using oneself as an example. In that Pali, "mā kañci pāpamāgamā" means "May no cause of evil suffering (unwholesome) and suffering itself reach any being."

After showing the protection of oneself through loving-kindness in this way, "appamāṇo" and so on is spoken to show it by recollection of the Triple Gem. In that Pali, the unwholesome states that act as measures and the results of those unwholesome states are called "measurable" (pamāṇa). The virtues such as morality (sīla) which are the opposite of those measures, and the mundane and supramundane results of those virtues, are called "immeasurable" (appamāṇa). Because the Blessed One possesses those incomparable virtues, He is called "immeasurable." Alternatively, because the Buddha possesses infinite virtues, He is also called "immeasurable." "Pamāṇavantāni" refers to beings associated with the aforementioned measurable states. The term "ahivicchikā" shows the different types of reptiles (creeping things). "Uṇṇanābhī" is a spider that has hair on its navel. "Sarabū" is a house lizard.

"Paṭikkamantu" means "May they depart," meaning "May they not harm me." In the phrase "sohaṃ namo," the remaining word "karomi" (I pay homage) should be added. The grammatical connection (yojanā) should be made as: "Because I have performed protection for you and for myself through loving-kindness and so on, and because I pay homage to the Blessed One and to the seven Buddhas beginning with Vipassī, may these beings depart."

"Aññamhī" means in sensual lust which should be cut off by the reflection on foulness (asubha) and so on. "Aṅgajātaṃ" refers to the male organ without testicles. Indeed, it is said that if the testicles are cut off, one becomes an opakkamikapaṇḍaka who is ineligible for ordination. Some teachers say that even the testicles...
230:
At the moment of cutting the testicles, only a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) offense occurs. When the male faculty and so on gradually disappear, one becomes a paṇḍaka who is ineligible for ordination. At that time, he should be expelled by destroying his appearance as a monk (liṅga-nāsanā). "One who causes such suffering" refers to a monk who causes suffering to himself by striking with a fist and so on.

In the Pali, the phrase "This bowl is yours" refers to the words spoken by the merchant: "To whichever Arahant who is also possessed of psychic power, it is indeed given." "Taking that bowl, he circled Rājagaha three times"—in this phrase, "taking the bowl" is said in reference to the fact that the bowl, which was tied to a succession of bamboos, stayed in the air above the city after circling it three times. It does not mean that Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja himself held the bowl with his hand. However, some teachers say, "By the power of psychic ability, that bowl was released from the succession of bamboos and stood following the Elder; and it was as if it were held by him with his hand." "Taking the bowl from the hand of Bhāradvāja" is said in reference only to its staying in such a manner.

"Those people also... followed" means those people who did not see the psychic miracle at first followed the Elder, saying, "Please show the psychic miracle to us as well." The Elder then manifested vikubbaniddhi (transformative psychic power) by creating forms of lions, tigers, and so on. Those people, being filled with wonder and amazement, made a loud and great noise. Therefore, the Buddha asked, "Ānanda, what is that loud and great noise?"

In the phrase "A psychic miracle should not be shown," vikubbaniddhi is intended, which proceeds by way of transforming one's own body, as mentioned in: "One who gives up his natural appearance and shows the appearance of a youth, or shows the appearance of a Nāga... or shows various military arrays." Therefore, it is said, "But adhiṭṭhāniddhi (psychic power by resolve) is not prohibited." Being one by nature, he reflects on being many. Having reflected on a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand, he resolves with knowledge, "May I be many." The psychic power accomplished by the power of such a resolve is called adhiṭṭhāniddhi. "Gihi-vikaṭa" refers to things belonging to laypeople.

In the Pali, "na acchupiyanti" means they are not touched. "Rūpakākiṇṇa" refers to things crowded with figures of women and so on. "Bhūmi-ādhāraka" refers to a bracelet-shaped bowl-stand made of ivory and so on. Because this bracelet-shaped stand is not high, the bowls placed on it do not fall over. Therefore, it is said, "It is suitable to place three bowls."
231: It is stated that it is allowable to place alms-bowls on a bowl-stand made of ivory and the like, which is in the form of a ring. Because such a ring-shaped bowl-stand is not high, the bowls placed on it do not fall. Indeed, with reference to its low height, this ring-shaped bowl-stand is called a "bhūmiādhāraka" (ground support). Regarding the phrase "on bowl-stands made of a single piece of wood and bowl-stands made of many sticks," these two types of bowl-stands are higher and have the nature of falling along with the bowls. Therefore, it is said, "on well-prepared bowl-stands." A "bowl-stand similar to the edge of a lathe" refers to a bowl-stand that resembles the edge of a lathe where items like a water-strainer (dhammakaraṇa) are inserted and turned. Because such a wooden bowl-stand is not wide, a bowl placed on it is liable to fall; therefore, it is called an "unsuitable bowl-stand." The phrase "in places with high floors such as the front of a house" gives this meaning. It refers to the outer wall of a palace and the like. It refers to a railing. In all places, however, it is allowable to place it only within one cubit (hatthappamāṇa). But on a bowl-stand, it is allowable to place it even outside that measurement. In the Pāḷi, "oṭṭha" refers to the rim of the mouth. "Pattamaḷaka" is a bowl-stand in the shape of a pedestal made higher than the ground to prevent termites from climbing up. "In the shape of a wide-mouthed water-pot" means it resembles a wide-mouthed pot. It is said that for a monk who hangs the bowl itself, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); for a monk who hangs it with a bowl-bag, there is no offense. This point should be investigated. "With another small article" means with a piece of cloth used for tying another load. Since it is said, "tie it and hang it," the shoulder-strap of the bowl-bag should be tied in every way so that it does not slip from the place where it is hung. The statement "even if tied, it should not be placed above" is said because those sitting above might press down on it and break it. The statement "it is allowable to place it there" is said because there is no fear of someone sitting on it. "Or by tying" refers to an umbrella that is kept tied. "Anyone" refers to either a bowl full of alms-food or an empty bowl. "To carry" means to keep it for the purpose of going on the daily alms-round. A monk who cannot obtain an alms-bowl is allowed to discard it after using it for one day's alms-round and eating. Therefore, it is said, "it is allowable to use it temporarily." The same method applies to leaf-cups and the like. "Abhuṃ me" means "my non-increase" or "my destruction." In the Pāḷi, "pisāco vatamam" means "this person is indeed a goblin," or this is simply the reading. "Pisācillikā" means young goblins. "Human skull bowl" is a bowl made from a human skull. The genitive case (saṭṭhī vibhatti) here is used in the sense of the relationship between the original material and its transformation (pakativikārasambandha).
232: "Cabbetvā" means having spat out. Since it is stated "having made it a receptacle for hand-washing," it is allowable to wash the hands by taking water with a hand soiled with food, sprinkling it on the bowl, and then washing and rubbing. Merely washing in this way does not constitute making the bowl a receptacle for hand-washing and washing the hands. "Taking a mouthful of water" means, without touching the bowl, lifting the water into that bowl with a hand soiled with food and rinsing the mouth, or it is also allowable to lift the bowl with the left hand alone and take a mouthful of water with the mouth. "Having rinsed with water outside" means it is also allowable to rinse off the food particles on two fingers and take it outside. In the phrase "one who wishes to eat again," even if one does not wish to eat it oneself, one is allowed to keep meat, fruit, etc., that are fit for others to eat. "Having done it in that very place" means doing it without removing it from the place where it was placed in the bowl. "Having peeled" means completely peeling off only the meat from there. 256. "With yeast powder" means smearing a needle with the yeast powder used in making liquor. "The frame (nisseni) also" refers to a layer made in a rectangular shape according to the size of the robe using four sticks and fastened. On this layer, the edges of the robe are tied evenly and the robe is sewn as desired. "Spread on that frame" means spread above the frame fastened with those four sticks to support the robe. Calling the cord used to tie the robe to the frame known as "kathina" as the "kathina-cord" (kathinarajju) is a compound where the middle term is dropped (majjhimapadalopa samāsa). Therefore, the words beginning with "yā yā" were spoken. In that case, if one of the two layers becomes longer, wrinkles occur; therefore, the cord that ties both layers of a double-layered robe evenly should be known as the "kathina-cord." In the Pāḷi, "the end of the kathina wears out" means the edge of the robe tied to the frame wears out. Here, the robe dependent on the frame is called "kathina" by way of metonymy (nissayavohāra), just as in "the beds cry out" and so on. "Longitudinal border (anuvāta) and transverse border (paribhaṇḍa)" means sewing a longitudinal border and a transverse border with any pieces of cloth to prevent the edges all around the robe from wearing out due to the cords tied to the frame. It means making the kind of border into which small cords can be inserted and wrapped around the sticks so that the robe can be pulled evenly. Some teachers, however, say, "The making of longitudinal and transverse borders is allowed only for mats and the like known as kathina to prevent them from wearing out." "In the middle of that" means inside the old frame itself. "By the measure of a monk" means according to the size of a monk's robe. "Another frame" means tying it by placing other sticks for the length and breadth.
233:
Bidalaṃ is the name for a specific action known as making a double layer. Therefore, it is said to be "making a double layer." Pavesanasalākā refers to bamboo splints and the like that are inserted to prevent folds from being caught. In the Pāḷi text, paṭiggaha refers to a small finger-sleeve (finger-stall) to be worn on the finger.

Pāti is a specific type of vessel for placing utensils. In the Pāḷi text, paṭiggahathavika is a bag for holding vessels such as the pāti. Cinituṃ refers to building with bricks and the like to prevent the edges of a high object from collapsing. Ālambanabāha refers to ropes or sticks and the like for holding onto. Paribhijjati means that mats and the like are torn in the middle of the kaṭhina frame. The word ussāpetvā is spoken with reference to a kaṭhina frame made with sticks.

258-9. Unallowable water refers to water containing living beings. Upanandhi means bearing a grudge. In the context of "a long journey must be undertaken," a journey of half a yojana is called addhānamagga (a long journey). A monk who wishes to go on such a journey and intentionally crosses the precincts of the monastery without a water filter commits an offense. If he goes unintentionally, it should be understood that he commits an offense at every step if he continues without determining the corner of his double-robe (saṅghāṭi) and the like at the place where he remembers. Na sammati means being insufficient.

Abhisannakāya refers to one whose body has an accumulation of impurities such as phlegm. In that context, "in the middle" means in the middle of the door-bolt. "Above" means on the upper part of the door-bolt. A place for keeping water refers to a place specifically designated and prepared for keeping water.

In the Pāḷi text, udapāna refers to a well. Nīcavatthuka means that the embankment around the well stands level with the ground. "Overwhelmed by water" means that rainwater from the surroundings comes and falls into the well.

Vāhenti means pouring out water. Arahaṭaghaṭiyanta is a wheel-shaped machine with many spokes, where small pots are tied to each spoke, and the machine is turned by one or two people.

Āviddhapakkhapāsaka refers to a building with sloping eaves (duck-wing eaves) placed around the central hub. Maṇḍala refers to the central hub. Pakkhapāsake ṭhapetvā means placing planks and the like in a square shape all around.
234:
Some teachers say that namataka is similar to a rug. However, some teachers say it is made of tree bark. Cammakhaṇḍaparihārena means by the arrangement of bedding without formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna). Peḷā refers to a stand for a vessel, made in shapes such as eight-sided or sixteen-sided. In such a stand, hot milk rice and the like are placed, and a food vessel is placed on top so that the heat of the rice does not dissipate. This is the name for such a vessel-shaped support (ādhāra).

Therefore, it is called "āsittakūpadhāna" in the Pāḷi text. The meaning of that term is a support poured with milk rice and the like. They do not know how to make this āsittakūpadhāna support in the border regions; they make it only in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). Some teachers say that all supports made of iron and the like, which are used by laypeople, are consistent with the āsittakūpadhāna. Some teachers say that a support made of allowable bronze is consistent with the maḷorika. This should be accepted after investigation. Formerly, a bowl-stand was allowed for the protection of the bowl. Now, the maḷorikā (eating stand) is allowed for the purpose of eating. Chidda means having holes. Viddha means having holes bored inside. Āviddha means having holes all around.

In the phrase "pattaṃ nikkujjituṃ," the overturning of the bowl occurs only by the power of performing the act of non-association (asambhoga) through a formal act (kammavācā), not by placing the bowls face down. Therefore, it was said, "Let the Saṅgha perform the act of non-association with Vaḍḍha Licchavi," and so on. It means let the Saṅgha perform the act of non-association with that Vaḍḍha Licchavi through a formal act.

"Pattaṃ nikkujjeyya" means one should perform the penalty of overturning the bowl for Vaḍḍha Licchavi. "Asambhogam saṅghena karaṇam" means the Saṅgha making non-association with Vaḍḍha Licchavi. It means performing it in such a way that there is non-association. In the phrase "nikkujjito ...pe... asambhogam saṅghena," the meaning should be understood as there being non-association with the Saṅgha. Because the Buddha commanded the performance of non-association in this way, because it was proclaimed by a formal act, and because it is stated in the Commentary that "no gift should be accepted," it should be understood that a monk who accepts something knowing it belongs to that person while the act of overturning the bowl is in effect, commits only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

"Accayo" means a transgression of proper conduct; it means an offense. "Maṃ accagamā" means it happened by transgressing against me. "Taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma" means we forgive that offense of yours. In the phrases such as "striving for the monks not to receive gains"...
235:
One should take the meaning as: abstaining from striving to prevent gains, and so forth. In the phrase "that which should not be enjoyed together with the Bhikkhu Saṅgha," the remaining word "done" (kato) should be added and understood.

The phrase "up to the last staircase" is said with reference to the first stair-plank. This is said because that first stair-plank was later covered with cloth. The Elder Ānanda said the words "The Tathāgata has compassion for future generations" with reference to the Buddha's compassionate protection, which prevents monks from being blamed in the future for stepping on cloth coverings by prescribing a training rule. "Apagatagabbhā" refers to women who have given birth. Therefore, it is said, "for the sake of an auspicious blessing."

269-270. "Bījanī" refers to a rectangular fan. "Ekapaṇṇacchatta" is an umbrella made from a single leaf, such as a palmyra leaf.

274-275. "Anurakkhaṇattha" means for the purpose of keeping and guarding. "They make it long" means they let the hair remain without cutting it. "Catukoṇa" (four-cornered) means having it shaved so that four corners are clearly visible: two at the upper temples and two at the lower sides of the chin. In the Pāḷi, "they let the dāṭhika remain" means they let the mustache on the upper lip remain without cutting it. "Rudhi" is a small scar.

In the Pāḷi, "lohabhaṇḍakaṃsabhaṇḍasannicaya" means the accumulation of copper (or bronze) goods and brass goods. "Bandhanamatta" refers to binding with metal at the ends of tool handles, such as a billhook, to prevent them from coming off. "Tantaka" is a weaving frame spread out in that shape for weaving the āyogapaṭṭa (meditation strap).

"Wherever one remembers, there it should be tied." By this statement, it is shown that there is no offense for a monk who enters without having tied his waistband unintentionally (without mindfulness). "A waistband made by wrapping in the shape of a muraja drum"—some say this is made by combining many strings into one and using threads of various colors. Even a waistband woven with thread of a single color, showing patterns like bracelets or pots, is also considered a muraja type. However, a waistband that is wrapped continuously and smoothly without showing patterns is allowable. Therefore, in the commentary on the second Pārājika, it is stated: "A waistband made by combining many strings and wrapping them continuously with a single string should not be called 'bahurajjuka' (having many strings); it is allowable." A "muddika" waistband is rectangular...
236:
A muddika waistband is one prepared without being made rectangular. Pāmaṅgadasā (fringes like those on a breast-ornament) are rectangular. Mudiṅgasaṇṭhāna means in the shape of a grain of barley. Pāsanto means the end of the fringe.

In the Pāḷi, regarding the terms "gaṇṭhikaphalaka" and "pāsakaphalaka," it is permitted to attach button-blocks and link-blocks made of wood, ivory, etc., and place them on the robe. "Koṭṭo vivariyati" means the longitudinal border is opened.

280-1. "Pāḷikārako" is a monk who seats other monks according to their seniority. It is not allowable for that monk to wrap his robe in that manner. In the Pāḷi, "muṇḍavaṭṭī" refers to wrestlers and the like.

"Pamāṇaṅgulena" means by a carpenter's inch. Some say "by an ordinary inch." That statement does not agree with the instruction of "at least four inches." This is because it is not possible to eat a tooth-stick four inches long by an ordinary inch without it getting stuck in the throat.

In the Pāḷi, "they corrupt the Buddha's words with their own dialect" means that because the Māgadha language is easy for everyone to recite, even those of low birth learn it and corrupt it.

"Do not let them harass the monks" means let them not harass the monks with the smell of garlic.

"Avalekhanapīṭhara" is a special basket for keeping toilet scrapers (avalekhanakaṭṭha). "Apidhānaṃ" refers to a closing plank and so forth.

237:
## 6. Senāsanakkhandhaka
## Commentary on the Discussion of Allowing Monasteries
In the Senāsanakkhandhaka, *sisire* refers to the winter season (the two months from the full moon of Phussa to the full moon of Phagguna), specifically the harsh cold contact caused by snowfall or by the effects of rain, such as a seven-day downpour. Therefore, it is said, "*samphusitako*." The word "*tato*" (or "*tena*" according to the Nissaya) is in the ablative case used in the sense of the agent; it means that the wind and heat are warded off by that monastery. Thus, it is said, "*vihārena paṭihaññatī*."

*Āviñchanachidda* refers to a hole into which a finger, a rope, or a chain is inserted to pull the door leaf and make it touch the doorpost. To show that nothing is unallowable for use in a monastery, it is said, "*sacepi dīpinaṅguṭṭhena*" (even with a leopard's tail), etc. *Cetiyē vedikāsadisaṃ* refers to a type of window with four holes, where instead of using window timber or mesh, bricks or other materials are used to create horizontal and vertical bars similar to the railings of a stupa. *Thambhakavātapāna* is a window made only with vertical bars, without horizontal ones. *Coḷakapādapuñchanaṃ bandhituṃ* means tying a cloth similar to a foot-wiper according to the size of the window to prevent bats and other creatures from entering (closing it). *Miḍḍhaka* is a turned-post shape made of wood, clay, etc., in the form of a couch.

*Caturassapīṭha* is a perfectly square chair. *Aṭṭhaṅgulapādakaṃ vaṭṭati* means only a chair with legs eight fingers high is allowable. The statement "*pamāṇātikkantopi vaṭṭati*" (it is allowable even if it exceeds the size) refers only to square chairs. Long rectangular couches with high legs, such as those with seven or five parts, are not allowable. A chair made of cane in a square or other shapes is called a *bhaddapīṭha*; hence it is said, "*vettamayaṃ pīṭhaṃ*." *Dārupaṭṭikāya uparī* refers to the time when the legs are inserted upwards from below the wooden plank that stands in the form of a frame (*aṭanī*); thus it is called "*uparī*" (above). Because it has a curved shape like the two hind legs of a ram, it is called *eḷakapādapīṭha*. *Paloṭhenti* means they roll along with the couches. Since all plants except trees and creepers are considered types of grass, it is said, "*yesaṃ kesañci tiṇajātikānaṃ*," etc.

*Upadahanti* means they place or put. *Sīsappamāṇaṃ* refers to a pillow capable of supporting the entire head along with the neck. To show that the width of that pillow is one *muṭṭhiratana* (a cubit measured with a fist), it is said, "*vitthārato*," etc. This statement shows the size of the cloth to be inserted at both ends of the pillow. The width of the pillow is determined by that cloth. Whether the pillow is made round or square, when sewn, the width from one end to the other must be one *muṭṭhiratana*. Exceeding this *muṭṭhiratana* is not allowable. If the cloth placed at the ends is folded twice from one edge to the other, it becomes three-cornered. Among those three corners, the distance between two corners should be one span and four fingers. The middle part, from one edge to the other, is one *muṭṭhiratana*. This is the maximum (*ukkaṭṭha*) size of the pillow. Therefore, it is said, "*tīsu kaṇṇesu*," etc.
238:
*Upadahanti* means they place or put. The head-size (*sīsappamāṇaṃ*) refers to the size of a pillow where the entire head along with the neck can be placed. To show that the width of that pillow is one *muṭṭhiratana* (fist-cubit), the phrase "*vitthārato*" etc., is mentioned. This refers to the measurement of the cloth to be placed at both ends of the bolster (*bimbohana*). The width of the bolster is determined by that cloth. Whether it is made round or square, it should be sewn so that the width from one edge to the other is one *muṭṭhiratana*. Exceeding this is not allowable. When the cloth at the ends is folded twice from one edge to the other, it becomes three-cornered. Among those three corners, the distance between two corners should be one span and four fingers. The middle part, from one edge to the other, is one *muṭṭhiratana*. This is the maximum (*ukkaṭṭha*) size. Therefore, it is said, "*tīsu kaṇṇesu*" etc., as mentioned before.

Because it is generally stated, "*kambalameva... pe... uṇṇabhisisaṅkhyameva gacchati*," it should be understood that even unallowable woolen rugs like *gonaka* are allowable for sleeping if they are stuffed inside a bolster (*bhisi*).

*Masuraka* is a leather-covered bolster. A bolster made of leather is not allowable even if it is filled with cotton. In the Pali, "*senāsanaparikkhāradussaṃ*" refers to cloth kept for making monastery requisites. "*Bhisiṃ onandhituṃ*" means putting it into a bolster bag and tying it. "*Paribhijjati*" refers to the bolster being damaged by friction when being pulled from couches or when people sit on the edges of chairs. "*Onaddhamañcaṃ*" is a couch that is tied together with a bolster. In the Pali, "*chaviṃ uppāṭetvā haranti*" means thieves stripping off and taking away the outer layer of the bolster. "*Phosituṃ*" means making marks or dots on the outer layer of the bolster after it was taken by thieves to serve as identification. "*Bhittikammaṃ*" refers to making decorations on the wall with various colors. "*Hatthakammaṃ*" refers to making any kind of mark with the hand.

In the Pali, "*na nipatati*" means not adhering or sticking. "*Paṭibāhetvā*" means scraping off. "*Na nibandhati*" means it is a non-adhesive substance.

Even directly saying "Do it" is not allowable. Since direct ordering is forbidden, it is allowable to speak to the gatekeeper indirectly, such as "Why is it not done?" By the term "*jātakapakaraṇaṃ*," any figure related to the Jātaka stories, such as figures of women or men, is intended. Because it is said, "Have others do it," one is not allowed to make even a Buddha image oneself. In the Pali, "*pañcapaṭikaṃ*" refers to finishing with five types of colors or surfaces, such as clay.
239: "Upacāro na hoti" means that there is insufficient space to walk around the exterior of the chamber. "Rukkhaṃ vijjhitvā" means piercing the planed heartwood near the tip. "Katvā" means making a hole. A support made by driving in heartwood stakes is called a "portable wall-base" (āharimaṃ bhittipādaṃ). "Upatthambhanatthaṃ bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ" means to support a decaying wall-base by propping up the external weight with the top of a stake and setting its base in the ground. "Parittāṇatthaṃ" means for the purpose of protecting a plastered hut from the danger of getting wet from rain. "Kiṭikaṃ" is a screen made of palm leaves and the like. The phrase "madditamattikaṃ" is said with the intention of closing a leak with kneaded clay. "Ubhatokuṭṭaṃ nīharitvā katapadesassa" refers to a place constructed by joining the wall and the door on either side as a blockage in front of the door, so that those standing outside cannot directly see those sitting inside. "Samantā pariyāgāro" is a porch (veranda) surrounding the room. "Vaṃsaṃ datvā" means planting posts about the height of a man and placing side-beams, similar to ridge-beams, on top of those posts. It refers to spreading rafters by placing one end of the rafter on the very high edge of the monastery wall and the other end on the lower beam. "Cakkalayutto kiṭiko" is a screen tied with a circular binding to facilitate opening and closing like a door leaf. In the Pāḷi, "ugghāṭanakiṭikaṃ" refers to a type of screen that is raised and tied up when not needed, such as in shops, and lowered later; or it also refers to a screen propped up with forked poles and lowered later. "Pānīyaṃ otappati" means the water kept in drinking-water pots becomes hot due to the heat of the sun. "Tayo vāṭe" means three types of enclosures. By the term "veḷuvāṭaṃ," all wooden enclosures should be included. By the term "kaṇṭakavāṭaṃ," all enclosures made of thorn-bushes should be included. "Āloko antaradhāyi" means the great radiance that arose through the power of joy (pīti) directed towards the Buddha—which made the path clear and free of darkness as if a thousand lamps were lit—disappeared when reaching the frightening charnel ground outside the city, which was filled with corpses and foul-smelling, because the momentum of joy diminished due to fear.
240:
In the verse beginning with "Sataṃ hatthī," the meaning should be understood by connecting each with the word "sahassa" (thousand), such as a hundred thousand elephants. "Padavītihārassa" refers to the taking of a single step by one who goes with the intention "I will worship the Buddha," directed towards the Triple Gem; it means the merit which has that single step as its cause. One-sixteenth of that merit is called a "kala." All the aforementioned things like elephants and so on are not worth, nor do they equal, even that sixteenth part (or one part in 256). This statement is merely for the sake of illustration. They are not worth even a millionth part.

"Andhakāro antaradhāyi" means the darkness disappeared when light arose again due to powerful joy. "Āsattiyo" refers to cravings (taṇhā). "Vayakaraṇaṃ" refers to the new construction (navakamma) which is the cost of the gift-objects.

"Dadeyya" means one should give authority over the monastery to manage the new construction. "Dinno" means the monastery is given to perform new construction, or it means the new construction in the monastery is given.

313-4. "Santhāgāre" means in an assembly hall. "Okāse" means in a living space. "Uddissa kataṃ" means something made dedicated to the Saṅgha. "Gihivikaṭaṃ" refers to household items or mats made or spread by laypeople; it means belonging to laypeople.
