## The Explanation of the Chapter on Accepting Dwellings

The repetition of the phrase "chamāsaccayena chamāsaccayena" (after the lapse of six months) is to show the time interval for giving requisites; it is the same further on. To explain the reason for the statement "taṃ na gāhetabbaṃ" (that should not be accepted), he said "paccayeneva hi taṃ" and so on. The meaning is that maintenance and repair will occur by residing there depending solely on the requisites.

"Ubbaṇḍikā" means they will be those who have their belongings packed and carried. "Dīghasālā" is a hall for walking meditation (caṅkamanasālā). "Maṇḍalamāḷo" is an assembly hall (upaṭṭhānasālā). "Anudahati" means it oppresses. By the statement "adātuṃ na labbhati" (it is not allowed not to give), it is shown that an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is committed by entering the place of a senior monk who, with the intention of not giving, blocks the way.
241:
"The village for alms-round should not be affected"—to clarify this meaning, the words "people do not live in that place," etc., are stated. "Cutting off thoughts" means not allowing the occurrence of such thoughts as: "Seeing me going for this reason, they will stop me and offer requisites." "Bhaṇḍapppaṭicchādana" refers to the robe that covers the body, which is the "covering-article." The statement "it is faultless only because of a pure mind" is not intended to refer to explaining the reason when asked. This is because there is no fault in answering a question even for one whose mind is not pure. Rather, it should be understood that it is said with reference to coming with the notion, "If I go like this, they will ask me."

"Should be maintained" means they should be maintained by repairing broken parts, sweeping, and so on. "Muddavedikā" refers to the square railing above the pot-shaped part of the spire (hammiya-vedikā) of a cetiya. The words "Why should one ask?" etc., refer to what is normally obtained from a gatehouse. Even there, it is stated to show the reason for asking.

"Moving away" means departing from the monastery. To show that meaning, it is said, "It is at a distance of one or two yojanas." "Setting aside the deposit" means either setting aside coins, etc., for interest, or designating fields and so on. "Thus, a faith-offering" means it refers to the gains of the rains-residence given out of faith according to the method stated below.

As for "vatthu" (property/object), it is the gold and silver obtained from the produce of those fields, etc. Since that gold and silver arise from fields donated with the words "Please enjoy the four requisites," they are similar to the property donated by donors with the words "Please enjoy the allowable goods" while in the hands of the kappiyakārakas. Therefore, it is said, "For the kappiyakārakas..." and so on.

"Saṅghasuṭṭhutā" means for the benefit of the Saṅgha. "By the power of the individual" means it is stated by way of referring to individuals, such as "Monks are weary for robes," and not by way of referring to the Saṅgha, such as "The Saṅgha is weary."

"By the power of allowable goods"—to clarify the meaning generally stated, it is said, "only by the power of robes, rice, etc." Here, the word "ca" should be understood as having the meaning of "pana" (but/however), not the meaning of conjunction (samuccaya). To show the manner of requesting by the power of the individual and by the power of allowable goods, it is said, "That matter should be done in this way," and so on.

"Noting the robe-requisite" means determining the amount of the requisite called "robes" obtained during that rains-residence by way of the produce of those fields, etc., donated out of faith, as "this much." "Senāsana" has the meaning of accepting a dwelling. "A junior monk for a more senior monk, a senior..."
242:
"...and for a junior monk"—this is stated because it is improper to accept a dwelling for oneself; the intention is that two monks shall accept for each other. It is proper to authorize eight or even sixteen people all at once with a single formal act (kammavācā). Indeed, the Saṅgha does not perform a disciplinary act (niggahakamma) against the Saṅgha itself. For that very reason, it is stated in the Sattasatikakkhandhaka: "In the authorization of the delegation (ubbāhika), even eight persons are authorized all at once."

"Āsanaghara" refers to an image house (paṭimāghara). "Magga" (path) refers to a rest-house (sālā) built on the road facing the village within the monastery precincts (upacāra-sīmā). The same applies to ponds, the foot of trees, and so on.

"They receive" means the monks residing there receive. "Vijatitvā" means separating into portions sufficient for each individual. "Putting into monasteries" means assigning verbally, "Let the gains arising from here reach and be taken by the monks residing in such and such monasteries." "Should enter" means the intention is that one should live in a precinct with great gains and then take the gains.

"This also"—here, the construction is: "the robe-requisite which is given up by a rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika)." "Placing at the feet, they give cloth" means the donors of the requisites give. By this, it is shown that even cloth placed at the feet by laypeople is allowable for rag-robe wearers. However, where they say, "We give rains-residence cloth," it should be construed by supplying the words "it is not allowable for rag-robe wearers." "For monks who have completed the rains" means monks other than the rag-robe wearers.

"Should be caused to be taken by making a bond" means it should be caused to be taken by making a commitment, such as "Stay at these trees, etc., and take the robes."

"Pāṭipada-aruṇato" (From the dawn of the first day), etc., are stated with reference to the day of entering the rains. However, it is proper to accept an "antarāmuttaka" dwelling even after the first day of the waning moon has passed. "Setting aside the constant duty" means having made a commitment (katikavatta) to be performed regarding constant duties such as recitation, reflection, and so on. "Kasāvapari-bhaṇḍa" means preparing the ground with dye-water.

"Threefold" means threefold by way of learning (pariyatti), practice (paṭipatti), and realization (paṭivedha). "Having purified" means having carefully examined conduct and so on. "The duty of wandering alone" refers to the work of meditation (bhāvanā). This is so stated because meditation should be practiced by wandering alone, having abandoned the company of a group.
243:
The ten topics of conversation (dasa-vatthuka-kathā) are: talk on fewness of wishes (appiccha-kathā), talk on contentment (santuṭṭhi-kathā), talk on seclusion (paviveka-kathā), talk on aloofness from society (asamsagga-kathā), talk on the arousal of energy (vīriyārambha-kathā), talk on virtue (sīla-kathā), talk on concentration (samādhi-kathā), talk on wisdom (paññā-kathā), talk on liberation (vimutti-kathā), and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana-kathā).

The duty of using tooth-sticks (dantakaṭṭha-khādana-vatta) refers to the duty mentioned in the discussion on giving tooth-sticks under the training rule on taking what is not given (adinnādāna), such as: "In the place where tooth-sticks are kept, only one tooth-stick should be taken each day." The statement "Even regarding a bowl... should not be spoken" is said for the sake of protecting the bowl. Incompatible talk (vissabhāga-kathā) refers to animal talk (tiracchāna-kathā) which is contrary to the Path and Fruition. The duties of the Khandhaka (khandhaka-vatta) refer to the remaining duties from the Vattakkhandhaka excluding the duty of the alms-collector (piṇḍacārika-vatta). This is because the piṇḍacārika-vatta is taken separately as the "duty of wandering for alms" (bhikkhācāra-vatta).

Now, to show the procedure for handling the rainy-season robes (vassāvāsika) that donors give to monks who have completed the later rainy season (pacchimika-vassa), the text begins with: "On the day of entering the later rainy season..." "If a visiting monk (āgantuka)" refers to a visiting monk who arrives after the robes have been accepted. "In the place reached" means the place reached according to seniority (vassagga). "Those who entered the vassa first" refers to those who entered the vassa on the later entry day (pacchimikā vassūpanāyikā) before the arrival of the visiting monk. "Received, received" refers to the cloths received repeatedly from donors as they arrive.

The phrase "Not the owner of the rainy-season robe" is said because the vassa was broken (vassaccheda). Because an agreement was made from the beginning, it is said "They cannot help but give"; the meaning is that it becomes a debt for the monks who refuse the given robe. "Should be given only to them" means it should be given only to some monks who have not yet received the rainy-season robe during the vassa-entry days.

"Earned through service" (bhati-niviṭṭha) refers to requisites obtained by performing services such as providing water. The passage beginning with "As for what belongs to the Sangha (saṅghika)" shows the view of some teachers. In that context, "accepted after performing an apalokana-kamma" means that because the robe was given by the Sangha after making a formal request (apalokana) in the manner stated previously—"It is pleasing to give the rainy-season robes of those who broke the vassa and the currently arising rainy-season robes to these monks"—even a monk who has disrobed (vibbhamanta) can receive it. Much more so a monk who has broken the vassa. However, some teachers say that regarding a robe accepted by the power of requisites, since it was agreed upon by oneself and the donors to be taken only after residing for the three months, even one who performs service, one who breaks the vassa, or one who disrobes cannot receive it. This latter statement is authoritative because it was said later. For that reason, for a monk who takes the rainy-season robe donated by donors on the very day of entering the vassa, only the residence without breaking the vassa is prescribed below, not the duty of performing service such as providing water.
244:
For a monk who takes the rainy-season robe donated by donors, only the residence without breaking the vassa is prescribed below. The duty of performing service such as providing water is not prescribed. Indeed, if that robe accepted by the power of requisites were only to be obtained by performing service, then only the performance of service would be prescribed. Therefore, it should be understood that those who break the vassa and so on do not receive the robe accepted according to seniority.

By the phrase "It becomes the property of the Sangha" (saṅghikaṃ hoti), it is shown that the portion of the rainy-season robe of monks who have completed the vassa is not released from being Sangha property, and it becomes Sangha property upon their disrobing. It is said "He receives" (labhati) because by having the donors assign it, saying "Give my reached portion to this monk," it is separated from being Sangha property.

The phrase "The excellent portion for the novice" (varabhāgaṃ sāmaṇerassa) is said because it is the first portion for that novice, and because the Elder had already taken the first portion previously, so the portion being taken now is the second portion.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Taking of Lodgings is Finished.

## Explanation of the Story of Upananda

In the Pāḷi, the phrase "Excluded from both" (ubhayattha paribāhiro) is said because he is sequentially free from both periods of taking lodgings; it does not mean he is excluded from both in every respect. Therefore, He said: "In the later... etc... he stands."

320. "That which is sufficient for three" (yaṃ tiṇṇāṃ pahoti) refers to a place, other than a bed or a chair, which is sufficient for three monks to sit comfortably; this is called the last long seat (dīghāsana). In these places that are not beds or chairs, even three monks who do not share the same seating status are allowed to sit. But on beds and chairs, only two may sit. On beds and chairs that are not long seats (adīghāsana), only monks of the same seating status are allowed to sit. Why? Because only a group of two is permitted.

A building is called a "Hatthinakha" (elephant-nail) palace because it has elephant figures at its lower part. The lower part of the palace is called "nakha" because it resembles a toenail. That lower part stands well-decorated with many elephant figures in all directions. Because the palace built above that collection of elephant figures is as if it stands on the frontal globes of elephants (hatthi-kumbha), He said: "Standing on the frontal globes of elephants."

The phrase "ornamented with gold, silver, etc." is said with reference to a monastery belonging to the Sangha (saṅghika). However, a personal (puggallika) monastery ornamented with gold and so on is not allowable for a monk to accept. Why? Because He said: "In no way is gold and silver to be consented to." For that reason, in the commentary, regarding the use of such a palace ornamented with gold, silver, etc., it is not said "whether in a Sangha monastery or a personal monastery."

Only in the case of unallowable items (akappiya-bhaṇḍa) such as woolen rugs (gonaka) is it said "whether in a Sangha monastery or a personal monastery." Why? Because there is no fault for another monk in accepting those floorings like woolen rugs. "By the manner of a layman's decoration" (gihi-vikaṭa-nīhārena) means with the intention that the donors have spread their own property and donated it. "They are obtained" (labbhanti) means they are allowed to sit. The explanation of the story of Upananda is finished.

Explanation of the story of non-disposable items (avissajjiya-vatthu). 321. "Arañjaro" is a large water jar that holds much water. It is called arañjara because it is capable of holding (storing) water.

Among the five groups beginning with "Permanent by permanent" (thāvarena ca thāvaraṃ), it should be understood that the first two are called permanent (thāvara) and the last three are called heavy articles (garubhaṇḍa). In the word "He gives equally" (samakam-eva deti), it should be noted that even if the yield is not equal, it is allowable to take an orchard near the monastery site and give up an orchard that is too far or difficult to guard. Indeed, "If it is of great value to the monks... etc... it is allowable to accept."
245:
It is not specifically stated whether it is communal (Saṅghika) or individual (Puggalika) property; it is only in the context of unallowable items (akappiya-bhaṇḍa) such as wool rugs (gonaka) and the like that this distinction of communal or individual is made. This is because there is no fault even for a single monk in accepting such rugs as gonaka and the like. 'Gihi-vikaṭa-nīhāra' means by the arrangement made by laypeople, in the manner of laypeople spreading out and offering their own rugs. 'Labbhanti' means they are permitted to sit.

## The Explanation of the Story of Upananda is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Story of Non-disposable Items (Avissajjiya)

'Arañjara' refers to a large water jar that holds a lot of water. It is called arañjara because it is sufficient for storing water.

Among the five groups starting with 'thāvarena ca thāvaraṃ', the first two are permanent property (thāvara), and the last three are heavy property (garubhaṇḍa). In the phrase 'samakam-eva deti', even if the values are not equal, it is considered allowable to exchange a distant and difficult-to-guard plot of land for a plot of land near the monastery grounds. This is because it will be said later: 'If it is of much greater value to the monks... [pe]... it is allowable to accept.' 'Jānāpetvā' means informing and requesting the Saṅgha of monks. If owners offer their property without knowing its high value, and one accepts it with a mind of theft while knowing its value, it constitutes theft (avahāra). Therefore, it should be said (truthfully), 'Are your trees not very numerous?'

'A monastery should be exchanged for a monastery' means a monastery with its land, or a monastery without land such as a palace (pāsāda) built on another's land, may be exchanged for a monastery with land. However, a monastery without land should only be exchanged for a monastery without land. This is because a palace alone is not permanent compared to the land. Thus, even among permanent properties, they should be exchanged only after distinguishing the types of permanent property.

By the words 'Allowable couches (mañca) should be accepted', it is shown that even if a gold-decorated unallowable couch is offered with the words 'I offer to the Saṅgha', it is not allowable to accept it. If it is said 'I offer to the monastery', it is allowable for the Saṅgha, but not for an individual. It should be understood as being like fields and lands. 'Etesu' refers to couches and so on. Allowability and unallowability are to be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned. It is the same as the decisions mentioned regarding chairs (āsandī), mattresses (tūlikā), and so on. Unallowable items include chairs (āsandī) and so on.
246:
Oversized pillows (bimbohana) and so on, as well as allowable rugs decorated with gold and so on offered using allowable terminology (kappiya-vohāra), are items that should not be distributed.

Because it is said 'Black iron... [pe]... should be distributed', it is said that a vessel made of brass or bronze (vaṭṭaloha, kaṃsaloha) may be accepted as individual property and may be carried. This is because only items that can be carried by an individual should be distributed. This statement contradicts the words of the Mahāpaccari mentioned above: 'Various vessels made of bronze or brass are allowable either as communal use or as lay-style items.' This is because that Mahāpaccari statement was presented later to refute the statement of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā which said: 'A foot-washing vessel made of any kind of bronze or brass in the island of Sīhaḷa should be distributed.' Therefore, any vessel made of bronze or brass, starting from a small bronze bowl (the size of five betel nuts), is indeed non-distributable. Even if offered by laypeople, it is not allowable for an individual to accept it. 'Not allowable to carry' means it is not allowable to store and use it oneself like requisites such as alms-bowls. If monastery attendants (ārāmika) and others guard and maintain it like lay property, and bring it at the time of use and take it back, it is allowable to use. It is also allowable to say, 'Store it and give it to the monks.'

It is said that 'paṇṇasūci' refers to a stylus (lekhanī). By the words 'even if obtained by oneself', it is shown that there is no fault in receiving it, but only carrying and using it causes an offense. Just as in this case, it should be understood similarly for one's own property such as non-distributable hatchets (vāsī) mentioned above.

'Anāmāsam-pi' means that even if made of gold and so on, it is allowable to touch and use all of it. 'Upakkhara' means accessories or utensils. 'Aḍḍhabāhu-ppamāṇā' means the measure of half an arm. Some say it is half a fathom (byāma). 'Yottāni' are leather straps.

'Aṭṭhaṅgula-sūcidaṇḍa-matto-pi' means even a small thin wooden stick in the shape of a needle, such as a shuttle-pin. 'Rittapotthako-pi' means a blank manuscript book. This is mentioned in connection with leaves (paṇṇa).

'Ghaṭṭanaphalakaṃ ghaṭṭanamuggarao' refers to this: a dyed robe is wrapped around a smooth wooden roller (muggara), placed on a smooth board (phalaka), covered with another smooth board from above, and one person stands on top of it. Two people hold the upper board by its two ends and pull it back and forth. This refers to that device. As for placing it on the hand and striking it with the hand...
247:
A robe that has been dyed should be beaten (with the hand) while it is still wet. Beating it in this way with wooden mallets, however, should be understood as being done when the robe is dry to prevent it from becoming stiff and hard. An *ambaṇa* refers to a water container made of boat-planks the size of a single trough, shaped like a pond. It is also called by that name. *Rajanadoṇī* is a dye-container made from a single piece of wood. *Udakadoṇī* is also a water-container made from a single piece of wood.

The statement "It is allowable to spread it on the ground" is said with reference to unallowable skins. It is indeed allowable to sleep on such unallowable skins when they are spread as a floor covering. By the term "*paccattharaṇagatika*," the large skin spread on couches and so forth is shown to be sheepskin.

The term "*chattamutṭhipaṇṇa*" is said with reference to palm leaves. "*Pattakaṭāha*" refers to the pan used for baking alms-bowls.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Non-disposable Items is finished.

## Explanation of the Discussion on Giving New Construction Work (Navakamma)

In the Pāḷi, among the words beginning with "*piṇḍanikkhepanamattena*," the act of placing a lump of clay on a broken or dilapidated place is called *piṇḍanikkhepana*. *Navakamma* refers to the authorization for new construction (*navakamma-sammuti*). *Aggaḷavaṭṭi* is the post that forms the door-leaf. *Chādana* refers to roofing the monastery with grass and so forth. *Bandhana* refers only to the binding of the roof with sticks, creepers, and so forth. The phrase "*catutthatthavihāre*" (in a four-cubit monastery) is stated in terms of the measurement of width. In terms of height, however, because it may have many stories, it could be twenty cubits by a carpenter's cubit, and it could be ornate with various shapes. Therefore, the new construction (*navakamma*) that must be completed within four years is mentioned for that monastery. The same principle applies to the remaining monasteries.

In the Pāḷi, the term "*sabbe vihāre*" uses the accusative plural in the sense of the locative. It means that one gives the *navakamma* in all monasteries to a single person. "*Sabbakālaṃ paṭibāhanti*" means that those performing the *navakamma* do not arrange the excellent lodgings they have taken for themselves according to seniority for monks who arrive, and they obstruct them even during the proper season.

The passage beginning with "*Sace so āvāsō jīrati*" is a decision not directly found in the Pāḷi (*pāḷimuttaka*). "*Mañcaṭṭhānaṃ datvā*" means giving the place where the couch stands as personal property (*puggalika*). "*Tibhāgaṃ*" means one-third. Such a disposal also falls only under the category of exchanging permanent property for permanent property, and not otherwise.
248:
This is because all monasteries are liable to decay. "If he wishes to give to his co-residents (*saddhivihārikas*)" means that if that monk does not wish to give the storage area to the Saṅgha or the living quarters to other monks, but wishes to give them only to his own co-residents, it means that such a monk should be told, "Take care of it by making it your personal property according to your wish," and everything should not be given to that monk. To show the procedure to be followed in that monastery, the word "*kamma*" and so forth is stated. In the passage beginning with "*evañhi*," it means that if one has taken a third part or a half part according to age, he is allowed to give that portion.

"*Yena*" refers to whichever of those two monks. "*So sāmī*" means that in the construction of a monastery on that ground, only the first monk is the master, and the later monk should not build there by obstructing him. This is because he took it first. "*Akataṭṭhāne*" means in a place where floor-levels and so forth have not been previously made. "*Cayaṃ vā pamukhaṃ vā*" means building a single monastery by constructing a terrace or a porch outside of and depending on a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha (*saṅghika*). "*Bahikuṭṭe*" means outside the wall, in the place he himself has made.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Giving New Construction Work is finished.

## Explanation of the Discussion on Prohibiting Other Uses, etc.

"*Vaḍḍhikammatthāya*" means for the sake of couches, benches, and so forth that are to be made and completed in such a way that they do not decrease from their original value.

"*Cakkalikaṃ*" refers to a cloth made in a circular shape for wiping the feet. "*Paribhaṇḍakatabhūmi vā*" refers to smooth ground made with black color and so forth. "*Senāsanaṃ vā*" refers to couches, benches, and so forth.

By the phrase "It should be used in the same way," it is shown that an offense is prescribed only for a monk who intentionally uses a place where resident monks wash their feet and use it, without washing his own feet.

Because it is stated generally by "*dvārampi*" and so forth, main doors, windows, and so forth should not be leaned against even if they have not been finished with decorative work. Even for one who leans against them without knowing, in this matter of Saṅgha property, an offense is incurred according to the count of hairs.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Prohibiting Other Uses, etc. is finished.
249:
## Explanation of the Discussion on Allowing Saṅgha Meals, etc.
In the phrase "*uddesabhattaṃ nimantananti imaṃ vohāraṃ pattāni*," the word *iti* has the meaning of "and so forth." It means they have come to be called by terms such as allocated meals (*uddesabhatta*), invitation meals (*nimantana*), and so forth. "*Tampi*" refers also to the Saṅgha meal (*saṅghabhatta*).

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Allowing Saṅgha Meals, etc. is finished.

## Explanation of the Discussion on Allocated Meals (Uddesabhatta)
The phrase "in the refectory" (*bhojanasālāya*) is said with reference to the place where meals are allocated. "*Ekavaḷañja*" means that which is to be used through a single entrance. "*Nānānivesanesu*" means in the houses of various families which have various precincts.

In the phrase "*nisinnassapi niddāyantassapi*," the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*). It means that while the senior monk is asleep, having the junior monk take the portion is a valid taking.

"*Vissaṭṭhadūta*" refers to a messenger who is free from hesitation because he is allowed to speak as he wishes. "*Pucchāsabhāgena*" means by way of being similar to a question. To clarify the meaning already stated as "one is called *kūṭaṭṭhitikā*," the words "*rañño vā hi*" and so forth are stated.

"Everything belongs to the owner of the bowl" means that everything, including robes and so forth, belongs only to the owner of the bowl. It means it is not allowable to take them by saying, "I spoke only with reference to the meal, and not the robes and so forth."

"*Akatabhāga*" is called the portion for a newcomer (*āgantuka*); it means a portion that has not been previously given.

"Without saying what is being brought" means without asking the donor, "What kind of meal are you bringing?" "*Pakatiṭṭhitikāya*" means according to the natural order of allocated meals.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Allocated Meals is finished.
250:
## Commentary on the Discussion of Invitation Meals

*Vicchinditvā* means speaking by cutting off, without saying the words "Take the meal." Therefore, it is said, "one who does not say 'meal'."

*Ālopasaṅkhepana* means distributing by the measure of each morsel. This kind of distribution is not suitable for *uddesabhatta* (assigned meals). This is because in *uddesabhatta*, distribution must be made only in an amount sufficient for one monk.

"Eight monks from the Saṅgha who are entered on the schedule (*mātikā*)"—here, it should be understood in connection as: those eight monks who are entered on the schedule. Among the schedules for communal meals (*saṅghikabhatta*) such as *uddesabhatta* and *nimantanabhatta* (invitation meals), for those monks entered in order in the *nimantanabhatta* schedule, they should be taken after being assigned by the meal-assigner or by oneself from the Saṅgha; they should not be taken according to one's own preference. *Mātikāṃ āropetvā* means informing the donor of the different types of schedules, such as "I shall take [monks] from the Saṅgha."

*Paṭibaddhakālato pana paṭṭhāya* means starting from the time when residence in that very monastery is established.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Invitation Meals is finished.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Ticket-Meals

*Upanibandhitvā* means having written down. *Gāmavasenapi* means also by way of a village where gains are generally equal. *Bahūni salākabhattāni* means thirty or forty meals, and should be read by adding "if there be any."

*Sallakkhetvā* means having noted those meals by their measure. *Niggahena datvā* means giving by compulsion, making a monk who does not wish to go far accept it. In the phrase *puna vihāraṃ āgantvā*, it is also allowable to take the meal without returning to the monastery, and then later have it brought to oneself at the monastery to eat.

*Ekagehavasena* means according to the row of houses on one side of the street. *Uddisitvāpi* means assigning by saying, "Ticket-meals at such-and-such a family's house have fallen to you."
251:
*Vāragāma* refers to a village that must be visited by turn because it is very far. The phrase "whether from sixty or from fifty" is said in reference to a water pot for the purpose of a disciplinary act (*daṇḍakamma*). *Vihāravāra* is the turn to guard the monastery when all the monks have gone out for alms.

"Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to those monks whose turn it is to guard the monastery. *Phātikammameva* means merely providing an adequate compensation for the task of guarding the monastery. "They reach only one [monk]" means they are made to reach each monk day by day.

*Rasasalāka* refers to a ticket for sugarcane juice. The statement "it should not be enjoyed because it was taken by way of a ticket" is said because it is improper (*asāruppa*), not because it breaks a dhutanga practice. For it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*: "A ticket from the Saṅgha free from material things (*nirāmisa*)... is indeed allowable." *Aggabhikkhāmatta* means a mere spoonful of alms-food. The phrase "whether you receive it or not, take it tomorrow as well" is said because even if it is received, it is only a small amount. Therefore, He said: "He receives as much as he needs... if he does not receive it, he should be told, 'Take it tomorrow'."

"There" (*tattha*) means in that direction. *Taṃ gahetvā* means having taken that ticket for the village-by-turn for oneself. "By him" (*tena*) refers to another monk [acting] for the monk who has gone to another direction. "Should be made to reach daily" means it should be made to reach any monk staying within the precinct (*upacārasīmā*) according to seniority (*vassagga*). If those [assigned] monks do not come when it is thus sent, it is allowable for monks in the nearby monastery to eat it; otherwise, it would be [wasted] communal property.

The phrase "only in our alms-resort village" is said in reference to the village of the ticket-meal donors. "The ticket-meal that reached the elder in the monastery" refers to the ticket-meal obtained by a single elder remaining in the monastery because all the tickets reached him.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Ticket-Meals is finished.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Fortnightly Meals and Others

By saying "Tomorrow is the fortnight (*pakkha*)," it means that the fortnightly meal (*pakkhikabhatta*) should not be taken today; the meal to be eaten on the eighth day should not be taken for the purpose of eating on the seventh day; it should be taken only on the day designated by the donors. Therefore, He said "But if..." and so on. "Tomorrow will be coarse" means that today, because of a wedding ceremony or such, very choice food is being prepared; tomorrow will not be like that, so [the donor thinks], "I will feed the monks today itself."
252:
Showing the difference between the fortnightly meal (*pakkhikabhatta*) and the *uposatha* meal (*uposathikabhatta*), He said: "Having undertaken the *uposatha* factors," and so on. *Nibandhāpitaṃ* means designated as "Let visiting monks eat at such-and-such a monastery."

The phrase "a departing monk [receives] even a guest-meal" refers to a monk who has arrived from another village and, while staying with the intention of traveling not yet subsided, is going elsewhere again. However, a resident monk (*āvāsika*) who wishes to go receives only the departing-monk meal (*gamikabhatta*). Because it is said "having set a pretext (*lesaṃ oḍဍetvā*)," it should be understood that if there is no pretext, it is allowable to eat as long as the obstacles to the journey have not been removed.

"They send rice and so on... it is allowable" means it is allowable because it is alms-food brought forward. "Because it was received thus" means because it was received under the name of alms-food (*bhikkhā*).

"Undivided communal property" is a demonstration of how remorse (*kukkucca*) arises. The meaning is that there is no need to ask questions out of such remorse; it should be given without asking.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Fortnightly Meals and Others is finished.

## The Method of the Commentary on the Chapter on Dwellings (Senāsanakkhandhaka) is finished.
253:
## 7. Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka
## Commentary on the Going Forth of the Six Sakyans, etc.
In the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka Pāḷi, 'Anupiyaṃ nāma' refers to the town named Anupiya. 'HeṦṭā pāsādā' means outside on the ground floor of the palace. There is also a variant reading 'HeṦṭāpāsāda'. 'Abhinetabbaṃ' means it should be brought into the sown fields. 'Ninnetabbaṃ' means it should be taken out from those fields. 'Niddhāpetabbaṃ' means weeds and such that destroy the crops should be removed. 'Ujuṃ kārāpetabbaṃ' means it should be made into a pile; this reading 'Puñjaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ' is indeed the text.

'Paradatto' means living by means of the four requisites donated by others. 'Migabhūtena cetasā' means with a mind like that of a deer, because of the absence of attachment to any object. 'Manomayaṃ kāyaṃ' refers to the Brahma-body produced by the mind of jhāna. It should be understood that Devadatta did not lose his jhāna at the moment his first thought arose—'Whom should I inspire? If that person is inspired by me, there will be an abundance of gain and honor for me'—because the obsession of defilement was still weak; he lost it only later. Therefore, it is said, 'Saha cittuppādā' (together with the arising of the thought), and so on.

In the phrase 'Dve vā tīṇi vā māgadhakāni gāmakhettāni', a small village field in the Magadha country is one gāvuta in size, a medium one is one and a half gāvutas, and a large one can be many yojanas. Among these, because it is equal to two medium village fields or three small village fields, it means that the Brahma-body of that being is three gāvutas in size.

'Satthāro' means teachers of a group. 'Nāssassa' means it should not happen to this teacher. 'Taṃ' refers to that teacher. 'Tena' means by something unpleasant. 'Sammannati' means he performs honor to us with robes and so on, or it means this teacher is honored by others.

'Nāsāya pittaṃ bhindeyyuṃ' means they would put pig's gall or fish's gall into the nostrils. 'Assatarī' is a mule born from a donkey in the womb of a mare. When she is pregnant and unable to give birth, they cut open her belly to take out the young. Therefore, it is said, 'She takes a pregnancy for her own destruction.' 'Potthanikaṃ' refers to a small sword; it is also called 'khara'.
254:
O elephant, do not approach the Buddha-elephant, who is free from evil, with the intent to kill. 'Dukkha' is so called because it is the cause of suffering. 'Ito' means from this life. 'Yato' means because of which reason, or it means 'of one who goes'. 'Mā ca mado' means you should not indulge in intoxication/pride.

'Tikabhojana' means a meal to be eaten by three people; it refers to food that is the opposite of a group-meal (gaṇabhojana), which is not allowable for more than that number of monks to accept and eat together. Kokālika and other names are the names of the group leaders in Devadatta's assembly. 'Kappa' refers to the lifespan in the great hell (Mahāniraya); some say it is an Antarakappa, while others say it is an Asaṅkhyeyyakappa.

## The Commentary on the Going Forth of the Six Sakyans, etc., is finished.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Schism in the Saṅgha
Teaching by knowing the minds of others is called Ādesanā-pāṭihāriya (the miracle of mind-reading). Purely preaching the Dhamma is called Anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya (the miracle of instruction). Both of these together are called 'Dhammī kathā' (Dhamma talk). With such Dhamma talk, the Elder Sāriputta gave instruction. The various psychic powers are called Iddhi-pāṭihāriya (the miracle of psychic power). Instruction accompanied by that psychic power is also called Dhamma talk. With such Dhamma talk, the Elder Moggallāna gave instruction.

'Make him confess a Thullaccaya offense'—this was said because the Thullaccaya offense for performing Uposatha etc. by one intent on schism was already prescribed in the Uposathakkhandhaka and other sections; otherwise, since they would be the first-doers (ādikammika), there would be no offense.

'Sarasī' means a lake. 'One who transforms the earth' means one who digs up the earth with his tusks. This is a description of the nature of elephants. 'In the rivers' means in the lakes. 'Of one eating lotus stalks' is how the construction (yojanā) should be made. 'Of one who watches' means of one who protects the herd.

'To go on a mission' means to perform the work of a messenger. 'Of what is fit and unfit' means he is skilled in what is fit to be said and what is fit to be done. Alternatively, it means he is skilled in speech that is intended and not intended; he does not stop at the mere literal syllables but conveys the intended meaning.
255:
In the verses, "jātu" means "certainly." "Mā udapajjatha" means "may it not arise," "may it not be." "Pāpicchānaṃ yathāgati" refers to the destination or the state of rebirth of persons with evil desires. In saying "Know also by this reason," it shows the manner to be mentioned later starting with the verse "Paṇḍito" regarding Devadatta.

"Pamādaṃ anuciṇṇo" means having fallen into negligence. "Āsīsāyaṃ" occurs in the sense of the certain accomplishment of a result. Here, "āsīsā" is intended as the certain accomplishment of a result, not as a wish (patthanā). Grammarians desire the use of the past tense in such a future sense.

"Dubbhe" means "should one wrong/betray." "Visakumbhena" means with a single pot full of poison. "So" refers to that person. "Na padūseyya" means he is unable to mix it with poison. "Bhayānako" means terrifying because of being vast and deep. It shows that even such an ocean cannot be corrupted. "Vādena" means by speaking blame. "Upahiṃsati" means harming.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Schism in the Saṅgha is finished.

## Explanation of the Discussion on Upāli’s Questions

In saying "The Saṅgha is not yet split by this much," it is said because the schism of the Saṅgha is not accomplished merely by the taking of voting tickets (salāka). The schism of the Saṅgha occurs only when a formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) such as Uposatha is performed. In performing such acts, it should be understood that the schism is accomplished by the conclusion of the motion (ñatti) in Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, and by the conclusion of the proceedings such as announcement (apalokana) in other acts.

Regarding the statement "He did not speak of being incapable (abhabba)," the Blessed One, while declaring the state of ānantariya by saying "Monks, Devadatta has first accumulated an ānantariya-kamma," had not yet prescribed for Devadatta the state of pārājika known as being incapable (abhabba). By this, it shows that just like an offense (āpatti), the state of being incapable (abhabba) also occurs only after the prescription, not before it. In this case of schism, since it is not stated that the first doer (ādikammika) is free from offense, it should be understood that Devadatta and others are not exempt from the offense.

In the words "Three foundations of mindfulness" etc., saying there are only three foundations of mindfulness and no more, the rejection of one foundation of mindfulness is what is non-Dhamma (adhamma) here; of the three things...
256:
Establishing them as three foundations of mindfulness is because such an establishment is Dhamma. The same applies to the remaining portions that cause decrease. But in the portions that cause increase, establishing one thing that is not a faculty (indriya) as a faculty by saying "six faculties" is indeed non-Dhamma. The same applies to the remaining things. It should be understood that not only regarding these foundations of mindfulness etc., but in any case, such as "four aggregates, thirteen bases," all presentations in a distorted way are non-Dhamma, and all presentations according to the truth are Dhamma. Here, "presentation" (pakāsana) refers only to the mental aggregates (arūpakkhandhā) that originate bodily and vocal actions in various ways. Thus, in this context, it should be understood that presenting any portion of the ten courses of wholesome action etc., which are Dhamma by their blameless nature, or the courses of unwholesome action etc., which are non-Dhamma by their blameworthy nature, or other indeterminate (avyākata) things, according to the order prescribed by the Blessed One is shown as "Dhamma," and presenting them in a distorted way is shown as "non-Dhamma." Indeed, in this matter, the Vinaya and so forth also fall within Dhamma and non-Dhamma by virtue of being presented truly or untruly. However, because they are taken separately by specifying them with names like Vinaya, it should be understood that they fall into the remaining portions of Dhamma and non-Dhamma.

Schism in the Saṅgha occurs only for one who, knowing Dhamma and non-Dhamma as they truly are, presents them in a distorted way based on evil desire, saying "We will make this non-Dhamma into Dhamma," and so on. This was said to show that for one who presents it with the perception that it is so, schism in the Saṅgha does not occur. The same method applies to phrases such as "They show what is non-Vinaya as Vinaya." In that statement, "niyyānika" means "excellent" (ukkaṭṭha). By the word "tathevā," it draws in the meaning stated as "Thus is our lineage of teachers..." and so on.

"Saṃvara, pahāna, paṭisaṅkhā" refers to the Vinaya of restraint, the Vinaya of abandoning, and the Vinaya of reflection. Therefore, it is said, "This is Vinaya." The dyad (duka) "prescribed, not prescribed" is identical in meaning to the dyad "spoken, not spoken." Similarly, the "duṭṭhulla dyad" is the same as the "garuka dyad." For that reason, a similar exposition (niddesa) is made for those dyads, such as "Four foundations of mindfulness... this is called not prescribed." "Sāvasesāpatti" refers to an offense that remains with the rest of the virtue (sīla). When one falls into that offense, there is no remainder of virtue, thus it is called "anavasesāpatti." In the Pali, "favoring those who are in concord" means favoring or giving support in this way so that the concord of those in concord is not broken.
257:
"Siya nu kho" means "Could it be?". In that context, "one with wrong view" (adhammaditthi) refers to having an improper view in declaring "what is not Dhamma as Dhamma". "One with wrong view regarding schism" means declaring "what is not Dhamma as Dhamma", and by performing acts such as reciting the Kammavācā and distributing voting tickets, one separates oneself from the original Saṅgha. While remaining within the same boundary (sīmā), one dissociates from the Saṅgha consisting of a group of four or more, and by completing separate legal acts (kamma) and so forth, one becomes a person with wrong view in causing a schism in the Saṅgha. "Concealing the view" (vinidhaya diṭṭhi) means that when declaring "what is not Dhamma as Dhamma", one hides the wrong view that has arisen in oneself and pervertedly proclaims, "This is indeed the true Dhamma". The meaning should be understood in this way in all sections.

"One with right view regarding schism" refers to one who holds the view that there is no fault in causing a schism in the Saṅgha according to the aforementioned method. This monk, despite having a wrong view when declaring "what is not Dhamma as Dhamma", becomes an incurable (atekiccha) schismatic because he acts while concealing that view. Similarly, for the monk who is "doubtful regarding schism", there is also the concealment of the doubtful view regarding schism. The rest is the same. The monk who is "one with wrong view regarding schism while having a right view regarding that Dhamma" also becomes an incurable schismatic because he acts while concealing the wrong view regarding schism. In the "bright side" (sukkapakkha), however, in all sections, whether in declaring "what is not Dhamma as Dhamma" or in causing a schism, because he acts with a right view (dhammaditthi) and without concealing his view, even though he causes a schism in the Saṅgha, he is one who can be cured (satekiccha). Therefore, it should be understood that the weight of an "immediate karma" (ānantariya-kamma) falls only upon one who, whether in declaring "what is not Dhamma as Dhamma" or in causing a schism in the Saṅgha, or in both, has a wrong view or doubt, yet conceals that view and doubt, proclaims it as "Dhamma", and causes a schism in the Saṅgha by the stated method.

## The Explanation of the Questions of Upāli is finished.

## The Method of the Commentary on the Chapter on Schism in the Saṅgha is finished.

## Explanation of the Duties of an Incoming Monk (Āgantukavatta)
In the Vattakkhandhaka, "pattharita" means to be spread out in the sun. In the Pāḷi, "abhivādāpetabba" means that by asking about the number of rains (vassa) for the sake of paying respect, the junior monk pays respect of his own accord. "Nilloketabba" means it should be looked at.

## Explanation of the Duties of a Resident Monk (Āvāsikavatta)
"Yathābhāgaṃ" means without exceeding the designated place, shaking out and spreading the couch, bench, etc., and then providing a bedspread on top. To show that this is also the "preparation of lodgings" (senāsanapaññapana), it is said: "However, it is indeed proper to spread it after shaking it out."

## The Explanation of the Duties of a Resident Monk is finished.
## Explanation of the Duties regarding Appreciation (Anumodanavatta)
In the fifth section, "nisinne" means when sitting for the sake of expressing appreciation (anumodanā). "Na mahātherassa bhāro hoti" means it is not a burden for the Great Elder to wait for the one who will express appreciation. "Ajjhiṭṭhova āgametabbō" means that one should remain sitting only while the monks invited by oneself are expressing appreciation.

## The Explanation of the Duties regarding Appreciation is finished.
## Explanation of the Duties in the Dining Hall (Bhattaggavatta)
"Manussānaṃ parivisanaṭṭhānaṃ" refers to a place where people, even within the monastery, live with their wives and children and invite monks to offer them food. "Āsanesu sati" means...
259:
...when there are seats. "Venerable Sir, this seat is high" refers to a seat that is equal to the Elder's seat, prepared on level ground nearby. It is not proper to sit on a seat higher than the Elder's seat even after asking permission. If that seat, though nearby, is lower, it is proper to sit without asking permission. "Mahātherasseva āpatti" means an offense is incurred because it amounts to obstructing with the seat. "Avattharitvā" means pressing down on the double robe (saṅghāṭī) that is worn; "anukkhipitvā" means without lifting it.

In the Pāḷi, "The rice should be received with both hands..." is said for the purpose of preventing the bowl from falling when receiving rice, whether the bowl is placed on the palm or on an improperly placed bowl-stand such as the pacchipitthi. However, if the bowl is placed on a well-prepared bowl-stand, it is indeed proper to receive rice while holding the bowl with only one hand. In the phrase "Water should be received with both hands...", the same method applies.

"Hatthadhovana-udaka" refers to the water used at the end of the meal. Therefore, it is said: "After drinking water, the hands should be washed." By that statement, only washing at the very end is prohibited, but it shows that during the meal, it is proper to wash the hands after drinking water and then eat again. In some manuscripts, they write "After drinking water, the hands should not be washed," but that does not agree with the previous statement because only the water used at the end is called "hand-washing water". The phrase "If people say, 'Venerable Sirs, please wash...'" refers to an Elder who has finished his meal and is sitting. "Dhure" means near the door.

## The Explanation of the Duties in the Dining Hall is finished.
## Explanation of the Duties of an Alms-Collector (Piṇḍacārikavatta), etc.
In the Pāḷi, "ṭhāpeti vā" means saying "Venerable Sir, please stand (wait)."

"Atthi bhante nakkhattapadāni" means "Are there known groups of constellations? Do you know the constellations such as Assayuja?" Thus it is intended. Therefore, it is said: "We do not know, friend." In the phrase "Atthi bhante disābhāgaṃ," the same method applies. "Kenajja bhante yuttaṃ" means "With which constellation is the moon associated today?".
260:
"Aṅgaṇe" means in the open air. By the phrase "In this way it should be practiced," it shows that permission should be asked for things like giving instructions (uddesa).

"Nibaddhagamanatthāya" means for the sake of one's own constant travel. In the word "ūhadita," since the root 'had' has the meaning of discharging excrement, it is said: "smeared with excrement on the outside."

## The Explanation of the Duties of an Alms-collecting Monk, etc., is finished.
## The Method of the Commentary on the Chapter on Duties is finished.

## 9. Pātimokkhatthapanakkhandhaka
## Commentary on the Request for the Recitation of the Pātimokkha

In the Pātimokkhatthapanakkhandhaka Pāḷi, the term 'nandimukhiyā' refers to the dawn (aruṇa) which has a pleasant face because the direction of its face is pure and bright. It should be understood that even after saying, "The dawn has risen," the Elder Anuruddha made the request for the recitation of the Pātimokkha, saying, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha," because the training rule (sikkhāpada) prohibiting the performance of Uposatha on a non-Uposatha day had not yet been prescribed. Why did the Blessed One remain silent in this way and let the three watches of the night pass? He did so to make clear to the Saṅgha of monks the fault of performing communal acts (saṃvāsa) such as the Uposatha in an impure assembly, and also to prescribe that training rule for the monks to follow in such a manner in the future.

In this matter, some teachers say: "The Blessed One sat in that manner because, out of great compassion (mahākaruṇā), He could not bear to say 'You are impure' to an impure person in his presence." That reason is not appropriate. Why? Because it should not be said later either, and it would also lead to the consequence that the Elder Mahāmoggallāna should not have taken that person by the arm and led him out. Therefore, only the reason stated previously is the appropriate reason in this matter. For that very reason, the Blessed One said, "Monks, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that a Tathāgata should perform Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha in an impure assembly," and He showed the procedure to be followed in an assembly with offenses by saying, "Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be heard by one who has an offense," and so forth.

'Saṅkassarāsamācāra' (suspicious conduct) means conduct that others remember with suspicion, having seen something inappropriate and thinking, "This act must have been done by this monk," or conduct that the person himself remembers with suspicion, thinking, "These monks know my misconduct." One who makes a living by wearing the monk's robes and taking a share of the Saṅgha's requisites, even if he does not verbally claim, "I am a monk," is effectively making that claim; therefore, it is said, "claiming to be a monk, claiming to be a celibate (brahmacārī)." 'Avassuta' means being wet with the leakage of defilements. He is called 'kasambujāta' (become rubbish) because he has the rubbish of immorality, or because he is like rubbish due to a lack of essence. 'Bahidvārakoṭṭhakā nikkhāmetvā' means having caused him to go out from the gatehouse porch.
262:
"Mahāsamudde abhiramanti" means they find great delight in the great ocean, mostly through seeing it, entering it, and so forth. "Na āyatakeneva papāto" means it is not deep right from the beginning like a great abyss with a broken bank. "Ṭhitadhammo" means having a stable nature. "Pūrattaṃ" means the state of being full. "Nāgā" refers to dragons of the snake species.

## The Commentary on the Request for the Recitation of the Pātimokkha is finished.

## Commentary on those worthy of hearing the Pātimokkha, etc.

"Udāharitabbaṃ" means it should be understood that even if the meaning is expressed in any language without reciting the Pāḷi text, it is still considered expressed.

"Pure vā pacchā vā" means either before the start of the motion (ñatti) or after the conclusion of the motion.

"Katañca akatañca ubhayaṃ gahetvā" means for a monk who has both things done and things not yet done, taking both of those matters of that monk. "Dhammikaṃ sāmaggiṃ" means a harmonious act in accordance with the Dhamma. "Paccādiyati" means he takes it up again with the intention of upsetting or overturning [the decision].

"Ākārādisaññā veditabbā" means it should be understood that appearance (ākāra), gender/mark (liṅga), sign (nimitta), and name (nauma) are mentioned.

## The Commentary on those worthy of hearing the Pātimokkha, etc., is finished.

## Commentary on the factors of taking up a case (attādāna), etc.

Because a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) that one takes up oneself to charge another again is called "attādāna," it is said, "desiring to purify the Dispensation," and so forth. "Vassāratto" means the rainy season. That rainy season is also an unsuitable time (akāla), just like a time of famine, because it is difficult to bring a group of conscientious (lajjī) monks from afar to settle the legal issue, and it is difficult for the arrived monks to practice conduct such as wandering for alms.

"Samanussaraṇakaraṇaṃ" means a cause for recollection because it generates joy and gladness at every moment of recollection. In the passage "vigatūpakkilesa...pe... saṃvattati," the meaning is: just as the moon and sun, when free from the eight impurities such as clouds and mist, possess glory, so too this accuser (codaka) possesses glory by being free from the impurity of being a wicked person.
263:
The meaning is that just as the moon and sun, free from impurities such as clouds and frost, are glorious, so too this accuser is glorious by the departure of the impurity of being a wicked person.

"Adhigataṃ mettācittaṃ" means loving-kindness jhāna that has reached absorption (appanā).

400-1. In the word "dosantaro," since the word 'antara' is a synonym for the mind (citta), it is said, "without a corrupt mind."

Since what is called 'kāruñña' is the state of compassion (karuṇā) itself, it is said, "kāruññatā is the state of compassion." By the word "karuṇံ," it refers to compassion that has reached absorption. The same applies to loving-kindness (mettā).

## The Commentary on the factors of taking up a case, etc., is finished.

## The method of the Commentary on the Pātimokkhatthapanakkhandhaka is finished.

## 10. Bhikkhunikkhandhaka
## Commentary on the Story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī
In the Bhikkhunikkhandhaka, the phrase 'because of the ordination of women' is an explanation for the reason why the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) would not endure beyond five hundred years. The statement starting with 'it will endure for a thousand years' based on the power of dry-insight Arahants (sukkhavipassaka) is stated by taking the view of the Khandhaka-bhāṇaka elders (reciters of the Khandhakas). However, in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, it is stated: 'It will endure for a thousand years through Arahants who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidāpatta), a thousand years through those with the six higher powers (chaḷabhiñña), a thousand years through those with the three knowledges (tevijja), a thousand years through dry-insight Arahants, and a thousand years through those who observe the Pātimokkha.' In the Aṅguttara Commentary and Saṃyutta Commentary, it is stated in yet another way. Although all these statements are contradictory to one another, the Teacher wrote them by taking only the methods found in the Sinhalese Commentaries which were written according to the views of the respective bhāṇakas. Such discrepancies in narrative accounts (vatthu) are not a cause for the decline and ruin of the Dispensation (Sāsana), nor is there a means to rectify them. Only discrepancies concerning the ultimate truth (paramattha) should be rectified using the methods found in the Suttas; discrepancies in narrative paths, however, do not need to be rectified.

## The Commentary on the Story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is finished.

## 11. Pañcasatikakkhandhaka

## Commentary on the Minor and Lesser Training Rules
437. In the Pañcasatikakkhandhaka, regarding the question in the Pāḷi, 'Friends, do you know our Teacher?', Elder Mahākassapa asked this even though he himself knew that the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna. He did so to inform the assembly of monks who accompanied him, and to make the monks aware of the words of the elder-ordained Subhadda which were contrary to the Dispensation. The reason is that Subhadda, upon hearing of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna in the midst of the lay assembly of kings and others who were extremely devoted to the Blessed One in Kusinārā, was very joyful but would not dare to express his joyful state in words due to fear. However, hearing it here in this secluded forest area, he would express his own evil view as he wished. Then, by showing that very reason and encouraging the monks to hold a recitation (Saṅgāyanā) of the Dhamma and Vinaya, the Elder thought, 'I will thwart the desire of this evil monk and others like him, and make the Dispensation endure.' Thus, it should be understood that he questioned Subhadda while already knowing the facts. For this very reason, the Elder, showing the words of Subhadda by saying 'Friends, once I...', had the Dhamma and Vinaya recited.

## 11. Pañcasatikakkhandhaka

## Khuddānukhuddakasikkhāpadakathāvaṇṇanā

In the Pañcasatikakkhandhaka Pali, the Elder Mahākassapa asked the question, "Friends, do you know our Teacher?" even though he himself knew that the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna. He asked this to inform the assembly of monks who accompanied him, and to make the monks aware of the words of Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age, which were contrary to the Dispensation (Sāsana).

The reason is that if Subhadda were to hear of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna in the midst of the lay assembly of kings and others in Kusinārā who were deeply devoted to the Blessed One, although he would be greatly delighted, he would not be able to express his joy verbally due to fear. However, if he heard it here in this secluded forest area, he would express his own evil view as he pleased. Knowing this, the Elder asked that question with the intention: "I will then use that very reason to encourage the monks to hold a recitation (Sangāyanā) of the Dhamma and Vinaya, thereby thwarting the desires of this wicked monk and others like him, and ensuring the stability of the Dispensation."

For this reason, the Elder Mahākassapa, showing the very words of Subhadda starting with "Friends, once I...", had the Dhamma and Vinaya recited. 'Nānābhāvo' means being in different places physically, signifying separation. 'Vinābhāvo' means separation by death. 'Aññathābhāvo' means reaching a different state by passing into another existence.

Regarding the statement, "If [the Saṅgha] so desires... it may abolish [the minor rules]," it should be understood that the Blessed One said this with the following intention: "Because I have said 'if [the Saṅgha] so desires,' the monks who perform the Dhamma recitation, seeing no single training rule that should be abolished and seeing the fault in abolishing them, will declare with an unshakeable formal act (kammavācā) similar to the original enactment, 'We shall not lay down what has not been laid down, nor shall we abolish what has been laid down,' and they will undertake and practice accordingly. Because of such practice, the training rules that should not be prohibited will remain until the disappearance of the Dispensation."

For this reason, the Great Elders also practiced in that very manner. 'Gihigatāni' means those that have reached the laity (meaning, those known by laypeople such as the Khattiya Mahāsālas). 'Dhūmakālikaṃ' refers to the training rule whose duration of existence ends at the time when smoke rises from the funeral pyre.
267:
'Oḷārike nimitte kariyāmānepi' means even while the Blessed One was making a clear sign (obhāsanimitta) which was the cause for requesting, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One remain for an aeon," by saying, "Ānanda, if the Tathāgata so desires, he could remain for an aeon or for the remainder of an aeon."

'Mārena pariyuṭṭhitacitto' means having a mind possessed by Māra.

'Ujjavani-kāyā' refers to [traveling] by a boat going upstream.

'Kulava' refers to that which is contemptible (kucchita) and involves cutting or destruction (lava); it is a useless destruction. 'Taṃ na gacchanti' means they do not reach that contemptible destruction.

## 12. Sattasatika-kkhandhaka (The Chapter on the Seven Hundred)

## Explanation of the Ten Points (Dasa-vatthu-kathā)

In the Sattasatika-kkhandhaka, "bhikkhaggena" means by the number of monks. "Mahī" means frost.

"Avijjānivutā" refers to those who are covered and obstructed by the hindrance of ignorance (avijjā-nīvaraṇa). "Aviddasū" refers to those who are unwise. "Upakkilesā vuttā" means that these things, such as drinking liquor, are taught as defilements for those recluses and brahmins. They are called "sanettikā" because they exist together with craving (taṇhā), which is known as "netti" (the lead).

450-1. "Ahogango" is the name of that mountain. "Paṭikacceva gaccheyyaṃ" means: "I should go first to the place where the monks will assemble to settle that legal issue (adhikaraṇa)." "Sambhāvesuṃ" means they have arrived (reached).

"Aloṇikaṃ" refers to alms-food or a curry without salt. "Āsutā" means prepared with all necessary materials; alternatively, there is a variant reading "asuttā."

"Ujjaviṃsū" means they went upstream by boat. "Pācīnakā" refers to the Vajjiputta monks because they were born in the eastern region. "Pāveyyakā" refers to those living in the Pāveyya region.

"Are you not, venerable sir, an elder?" means: "Are you not an elder who is free from dependence (nissaya-mutta)? Why did the Elder Revata dismiss (rebuke) you?" Thus they speak words of divisiveness. "Garunissayaṃ gaṇှāma" means: "Even though we are free from dependence, we will live only by relying on a teacher who is a worthy and respected person."

"Mūlādāyakā" means the original donors of the ten points (the resident monks). "Pathabyā Saṅghatthero" refers to the monk who was the most senior by ordination among all monks in the world at that time. "Suññatāvihārena" refers to the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) achieved through the gateway of emptiness (suññatā).

"Sutta-vibhaṅge" refers to the word-by-word analysis (Pada-bhājanīya). This statement also refers to the rule in the Sutta (Pātimokkha): "Whatever monk [should eat] food or a meal that has been stored..." regarding only that which is temporary (yāvakālika)...
269:
...because it was considered [in that context], the offense of Pācittiya for consuming salt stored in a horn (siṅgī-loṇa), which is life-long (yāvajīvika), together with food (āmisa), is established by the method of the Vibhaṅga. To establish that this Pācittiya offense appears in the Vibhaṅga, the phrase "Kathaṃ sutta-vibhaṅge" etc., is stated. For in that case, the Vajjiputta monks perceived no fault in food mixed with salt, thinking, "Only salt is stored here, not food or a meal." To show that they are still guilty of an offense despite such a perception, this Sutta Vibhaṅga [passage] "one who perceives what is stored as not stored" is extracted.

"Tena saddhiṃ" means together with the salt previously received. "Dukkaṭenettha bhavitabbaṃ" means: without saying "Monks, a life-long (yāvajīvika) item is received with a temporary (yāvakālika) item," by the power of the words "received on that day," it is established that it is not allowable to consume a life-long item previously received when its taste is mixed with a temporary item, even within the [allowable] time. The meaning is that a Dukkaṭa offense should occur in that case. "Dukkaṭenapi na bhavitabbaṃ" means: if you think it is a Dukkaṭa because of the reason of storage, since there is no fault of storage for salt which is life-long, a Dukkaṭa should not occur. However, do not think it is not a Dukkaṭa because that salt, whose taste is mixed with food, follows the nature of food. The meaning is that at that time, only a Pācittiya should occur because it has reached the state of food. Here, the statement beginning with "yāvajīvikaṃ" does not support the absence of a Dukkaṭa offense.

In the Pali, in all places such as "Rājagahe sutta-vibhaṅge," the meaning should be taken as "in the Sutta (Pātimokkha) and in the Vibhaṅga." Since those various [offenses] such as eating at the wrong time are also prohibited in the Sutta, the transgression of the Vinaya is called "Vinayātisāra." The statement "A sitting cloth (nisīdana) is said to have a border" is mentioned to show what appears in the Vibhaṅga. "Taṃ pamāṇaṃ karontassa" means for one making it the size of three spans by the Sugata-span; however, for the border (dasā), a size of two spans is made. The meaning is that a sitting cloth without a border is also allowable. All other points here are easily understood as mentioned below.

The connection is: I shall now provide the commentary on the obscure meanings of the Parivāra Vinaya, which was recited in the Vinaya Piṭaka after the twenty-two Khandhakas of the Blessed One, who possesses a retinue of pure Arahants and a body of Dhamma aggregates such as virtue (sīla) and so forth.

'Samantacakkhunā' means by means of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). 'Ativisuddhena maṃsacakkhunā' means by means of the extremely pure visual sensitivity (pasādacakkhu), because it can see very subtle forms within a distance of one league (yojana) all around, day and night. In the passages beginning with 'Atthi tattha paññatti', the meaning should be taken as 'Is there a rule (paññatti) in that [first Pārājika]?' and so forth; therefore, it is said: 'The question (pucchā) as to "What rule is there... who brought it?"'

'Pucchā-vissajjane' means in the answering (vissajjanā) of the question. 'Vinītakathā' means the discourse on the cases of those who were disciplined (vinītavatthu), or the text remains as it is.

'Dvaṅgikena ekena samuṭṭhānena' means by a single origin (samuṭṭhāna) which is a combination of two factors. Although there is no origin that is free from these two factors, it is stated as 'by a single origin' to show that this offense (āpatti) cannot occur if one of these two factors is missing. Now, to show the primary factor among those two factors, it is said: 'Here, the mind (citta) is a factor,' and so forth. This is because this designation of an offense, as prescribed by the Blessed One, arises based on those two factors only when there is a mind wishing to indulge in physical intimation (kāyaviññatti), which is defined as the practice of one's own organ in another's organ; it does not arise if such a mind is absent. Therefore, that mind is only the cause (kāraṇa) of the body, which is called physical intimation, and not the cause of the offense. For that offense, only the body produced by that mind is the direct cause (avyavahita-kāraṇa), while the mind is the cause of the cause (kāraṇa-kāraṇa). This same principle should be understood in all subsequent origins associated with the mental factor...
272:
...the meaning should be understood. By the words of the Parivāra such as 'it arises from a single origin,' the ultimate nature (paramattha-sabhāva) of offenses, such as being unwholesome (akusala) and so forth, is stated only figuratively (pariyāya) in the Pāḷi and Commentaries. It should be understood that an offense is merely conventional (sammuti) in nature because the distinction between the origin and what arises from that origin is established. 'With reference to this meaning' means with reference to the fact that a Pārājika offense that has been committed cannot be turned into a non-offense (anāpatti) by any of the means of settlement (samatha).

'The ancient Great Elders' (Porāṇakā Mahātherā) refers to the Great Elders who, after the three councils, conducted the council to record the teachings in books (the Fourth Council), and who were radiant with qualities such as the six higher powers (abhiññā) and the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The council for recording the teachings in books is similar to the Fourth Council.

'In the Mahāvibhaṅga' means in the Bhikkhuvibhaṅga. 'Sixteen sections (vāra) are shown' refers to those sections which, being marked as the beginning, cause this entire Parivāra to be known as the 'Soḷasaparivāra' (Sixteen-part Parivāra).

## The Commentary on the Paññattivāra is finished.

## Commentary on the Origin Headings (Samuṭṭhāna-sīsa)

In the Pāḷi, regarding the phrase 'Nibbāna and designation (paññatti)', designations such as 'person' (puggala), which are conventional truths (sammuti-sacca) established based on conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma), do not ultimately exist. Therefore, it is inappropriate to say they possess the two characteristics of impermanence (anicca) and suffering (dukkha), which are fixed to ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma) involving arising and passing away. However, since they are devoid of a self-nature (atta-sabhāva) conceived as a doer or experiencer, it is appropriate to call them 'non-self' (anatta). Therefore, this designation is also said to be 'determined as non-self' along with Nibbāna, which is an ultimate reality, because of their commonality in being unconditioned (asaṅkhata). Indeed, although convention (sammuti) does not exist ultimately, it is unconditioned (asaṅkhata) because it is not created by any cause.

To show the coolness of the Blessed One's compassion and the radiance of His wisdom, these two terms 'Buddha-Moon' and 'Buddha-Sun' are used. It is called 'hāni' (decrease) because one decreases by it; 'dukkhahāni' means the cause of the decrease of suffering, meaning the cause for the removal of all suffering. 'He taught the three Piṭakas' means that because other Great Heroes, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas, also teach the True Dhamma...
273:
Therefore, the connection is that the Buddha named Angīrasa taught the three Piṭakas. 'Mahāguṇa' means having great benefits. 'In this way, the True Dhamma is upheld' means that if the Vinaya as scripture (Vinaya-pariyatti) remains without decline, because of its existence, the True Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti-saddhamma) and the True Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha-saddhamma) are also upheld, proceed, and do not decline. 

How does the Vinaya-pariyatti remain? He said, 'By both,' and so on. The connection should be made that it remains because it is bound together by the Parivāra. 'In that very Parivāra' means in that specific Parivāra. 'The origin is fixed' means some training rules are made fixed by their origin (samuṭṭhāna). It means that in that Parivāra, it is shown that a certain training rule has a fixed origin that is not shared with others but is unique to itself. 

'Confusion, origin, and other matters' refers to the confusion (sambheda) of training rules through mutual origins, the origin (nidāna) which is the place of enactment, and other things such as persons and objects. These are evident only in the Parivāra Sutta, which was mentioned above and will be mentioned below. Since this is so, one should learn the Parivāra, which is the cause for the stability of the Vinaya that supports the entire Dispensation (Sāsana). This is how the connection here should be understood. 

'Mixed origins' (sambhinna-samuṭṭhāna) refers to training rules whose origins are shared with others. He speaks with reference to the method found in the Pannyatti-vāra, which is the very first of all. In that Pannyatti-vāra, the origin is also clear, such as 'Where was the first Pārājika enacted? It was enacted in Vesālī,' and so on. It should be understood that it is evident in the Sutta that comes later, referring to the fact of its occurrence later. Of the training rule included in that Ubhato-vibhaṅga. 

'The first Aniyata' is expressed in the feminine gender only with regard to the offense; it means the first Aniyata training rule. In the Pali, 'a non-following female preceptor' (nānubandhe pavattiniṃ) refers to the training rule about not following the female preceptor who gave the ordination. 

In the case of the Eḷakaloma training rule, it is stated: 'Bhikkhunīs, while washing, dyeing, and combing sheep's wool, neglect the recitation and questioning (uddesa).' Taking this word 'neglect' (riñcanti), he said, 'The Eḷakaloma washing training rule which appears in the Vibhaṅga as "neglect the recitation"', to show that the training rule is to be noted.
274:
The training rule on the rainy-season robe (vassikasāṭikasikkhāpadaṃ) refers to the training rule concerning the seeking of a rainy-season robe at the wrong time. The training rule on valuables (ratanasikkhāpadaṃ) refers to the training rule concerning the putting away of a treasure or what is considered a treasure.

In the Pali, 'buddhañāṇena' means by the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa) which has been fully penetrated.

By the words, "The Tathāgatas do not preach thus," it shows the prohibition of preaching the Dhamma to one who holds a parasol in their hand.

'Akata' means that which is made without being mixed with other training rules, meaning it has a fixed mode of origin (samuṭṭhāna). Alternatively, 'akata' means that which has not appeared before, meaning it is new.

In the phrase 'samuṭṭhānañhi saṅkhepaṃ', it is called 'saṅkhepa' (summary) because similar modes of origin are collected here; it is the heading of the modes of origin. It is called 'netti' because it guides away from (vinayati) bodily and verbal misconduct; this is the Vinaya Pali itself. Because that Vinaya Pali is itself the Dhamma, it is called 'nettidhamma', as stated by the words 'vinayapāḷidhammassa'.

## Samuṭṭhānasīsavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
275:
## Antara-peyyālaṃ
## Katipucchāvāra-vaṇṇanā
The question 'How many offenses are there?' is asked by presenting the five classes of offenses, such as Pārājika, as a single category according to their nature, without considering the internal divisions such as sexual intercourse, taking what is not given, and so on. In the question 'How many groups of offenses are there?', it is asked by presenting them as a single category in the sense of a group (rāsi) respectively, without considering the internal divisions. This is the distinction in this context.

'Vinīta' refers to 'Vinīta-vatthu' (disciplined cases). Abstaining from offenses are called 'vatthu' (grounds/objects) because they are the cause of states such as non-remorse and joy. Therefore, they are called 'Vinīta-vatthu'. In this context, these disciplined cases are essentially faultless states such as abstinence (virati).

'Veraṃ maṇati' means it destroys the mass of unwholesome states such as lust (rāga), which has acquired the name 'vera' (enmity/danger) because it is the cause of enmity.

'Breaking up the assembly for hearing the Dhamma and leaving' means that while many monks are sitting together listening to the Dhamma, one disrupts that assembly for hearing the Dhamma, stands up, and leaves.

'Anādaro vā' (Or disrespect) means living without making known one's appreciation in a situation where one should be appreciative, or one's sense of urgency (saṃvega) in a situation where one should feel urgency.

'Kāya-pāgabbhiya' (Bodily impudence) is the misconduct of the body proceeding by way of haughtiness.

It is a bodily action (kāyakamma) called 'metta' because it is born of loving-kindness. 'By both' means by both the juniors and the elders. 'Makes one dear' means making that person an object of affection. To whom? As stated by 'sabrahmacārīnaṃ', it means becoming dear to one's fellow practitioners.

The phrase 'consuming by discriminating among persons' is connected to the preceding text. To show that discrimination among persons, phrases such as 'of such and such a person' were mentioned.

'Because of making one not a slave' means because it makes one live at will in tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) by freeing one from the slavery of craving (taṇhā-dāsa). 'Niyyāti' means it proceeds or progresses. The meaning is that it leads well to the complete destruction of suffering.

## Katipucchāvāra-vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## Cha-āpattisamuṭṭhāna-vāra-vaṇṇanā
'By the first origin of offenses' means by the body alone. Since the Pārājika offense definitely has an origin involving the mind (sacittaka), it is stated that 'No' (na hi) should be said.
276:
The five classes of offenses beginning with Saṅghādisesa and ending with Dukkaṭa can also be acittaka (occurring without intention), therefore it is said "Siyā" (it might be). This means that the commission of an offense may occur. Since the Dubbhāsita offense is prescribed only for reviling (omasana) by way of birth and so on, whether low or high, that Dubbhāsita offense is strictly vācācittasamuṭṭhāna (originating from speech and mind). Therefore, it is said "Na hi" (it cannot be).

In the second method of origin, it is said "Na hi" because there is no Pāṭidesanīya offense that must be committed through speech alone.

In the third origin, however, it is said "Siyā" because a Pāṭidesanīya offense can occur due to the reason of not rebuking a bhikkhunī who is in the position of giving instructions, by means of body and speech.

Although the Pācittiya offense caused by reviling (omasa) has the origin of taking what is not given (adinnādāna-samuṭṭhāna), in order to show that the Dubbhāsita offense prescribed for that reason arises only through the fifth origin, it is said in the fourth turn, "It should be said 'Na hi' (a Dubbhāsita offense cannot occur)," and in the fifth turn, it is said "It should be said 'Siyā' (it can occur)." In this context, it should be understood that for one who reviles only by a bodily gesture, although it is a Dubbhāsita, it is only a Dukkaṭa because it is not a case of bodily play.

In the sixth turn, although the body is present, it is not a factor of the Dubbhāsita offense.
