It is rejected by saying "Na hi" to show that the sixth origin is included within the fifth origin, but not to show that there is no Dubbhāsita offense at all in that sixth origin. For it is not that a Dubbhāsita offense does not occur for one who reviles with body and speech out of a desire to play. It should be understood that an offense that is committed through the fifth origin is also committed through the sixth origin, just like the offense regarding the teaching of Dhamma. The remaining words in the section on origins are easy to understand.

## The Description of the Section on the Six Origins of Offenses is finished.

## Description of the Section on Committed Offenses

In the second section, the Kati-vāra, only offenses such as building a hut (kuṭikāra) are extracted and shown for the sake of easily seeing the offenses to be committed through the first origin. It is not because other offenses do not exist, for offenses such as acting as a go-between (sañcaritta) also exist. The same applies to the second origin and so on. By the words "kappiyasaññī" (one who perceives it as allowable), the state of being acittaka (occurring without intention) is shown. By the words "kuṭiṃ karoti" (he builds a hut), the absence of vocal effort (vacīpayoga) is shown. By both of these, it is shown that offenses such as Dukkaṭa can occur through the body alone. The same should be understood accordingly for the following cases.
277:
The statement "Ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhahanti" (They arise from a single origin) is said in this section specifically in terms of offenses that arise from the body alone. Generally, however, those offenses also arise from other origins as appropriate. The same applies to the following cases.

The statement "Tiṇavatthāreka ca" (And by the covering with grass) is said in terms of the four offenses excluding Saṅghādisesa.

"Saṃvidahitvā kuṭiṃ karoti" means that one arranges it by speech and performs it oneself by body.

## The Description of the Section on Committed Offenses is finished.

## Description of the Verses on the Origins of Offenses

The third section, the Gāthā-vāra, is spoken to summarize and show the meaning already stated in the second section. In that third section, although it should be said "The body itself is kāyika," it is said "Kāyikā" by way of grammatical transposition (vacanavipallāsa). Therefore, it is said "arisen from that [body]"; the meaning is that the body is declared to be the origin.

"Vivekadassī" refers to the Buddha who is accustomed to seeing the seclusion from hindrances and Nibbāna, because of being secluded from all conditioned things and being the cause of such seclusion. "Vibhaṅgakovidā" is an address meaning "one who is skilled in both Vibhaṅgas." In this context, although there is no other person asking, the Elder Upāli himself made the questions and answers to make the meaning clear. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all places.

## The Description of the Verses on the Origins of Offenses is finished.

## Description of the Section on the Causes of Failures

In the fourth section, the Vipattipaccaya-vāra, "sīlavipattipaccayā" means because of the cause of concealing a failure in virtue (sīlavipatti).

"Diṭṭhivipattipaccayā" means because of the cause of not relinquishing a failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti).
278:
In the term "ājīvavipattipaccayā," the analysis (viggaha) should be known thus: they live depending on this, therefore it is called "ājīva" (livelihood), which refers to the four requisites. That very livelihood is "vipatti" (failure) because it is ruined by wrong offenses; thus it is "ājīvavipatti." The meaning is: because of the cause of that failure in livelihood, that is, because of the cause of producing and using that failure in livelihood.

## The Description of the Section on the Causes of Failures is finished.

## Description of the Section on the Causes of Legal Issues

In the fifth section, the Adhikaraṇapaccaya-vāra, "kiccādhikaraṇapaccayā" means because of the cause of formal acts (kamma) known as the act of announcement (apalokana), the motion (ñatti), and the proclamation (kammavācā). In the word "pañcā," the meaning is the non-cause (animitta) for those who perform acts by announcing an unrighteous agreement and so on. In the fifth section, the Adhikaraṇapaccaya-vāra, it should be understood that by the cause of a legal issue concerning duties (kiccādhikaraṇa), the Dukkaṭa offense at the end of an announcement (apalokana), and the Thullaccaya and other offenses for those who perform a motion and so on with a certain intention, are included. "Avasesā āpattiyo" (the remaining offenses) refers to the attainment of the fruit of Stream-entry and so on. The statement "Natthaññā āpattiyo" (There are no other offenses) is said with reference to the blameworthy offenses that belong to the side of failures (vipatti) and so on.

## The Description of the Section on the Causes of Legal Issues is finished.
279:
## Classification of Settlement
## Explanation of the Section on Methods of Legal Processes

In the sixth section on methods (Pariyāyavāra), the statement beginning with "Non-greed is the precursor" is spoken with the intention of addressing the dispute of a speaker of Dhamma (dhammavādī) in an unerring manner for the sake of the longevity of the Dispensation (Sāsana). "The eighteen grounds for schism are the bases (ṭhāna)" means that the acts of presenting non-Dhamma as Dhamma and so forth are themselves the "grounds for schism" (bhedakaravatthu) in this context. These same grounds for schism are called "bases" (ṭhāna) because they are the cause of disputes such as physical quarrels; they are called "grounds" (vatthu) because they are the support; and they are called "foundations" (bhūmi) because they are the site.

The phrase "indeterminate roots" (abyākatahetu) is spoken with reference to the disputes of Arahants (asekkha). "Twelve roots" (mūla) refers to: anger (kodha), enmity (upanāha), disparaging (makkha), domineering (palāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), treachery (sāṭheyya), evil desires (pāpicchatā), great desires (mahicchatā), clinging to one's own views (sandiṭṭhiparāmāsa), and clinging firmly and being difficult to persuade (ādhānaggāhīduppaṭinissagga). These six pairs of factors (12 factors) and the six roots such as greed (lobha) and so forth—making twelve factors in total—are the roots of the legal process of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa).

"Fourteen roots" means those same twelve factors together with body and speech are the fourteen roots of the legal process of accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa).

In order to show that an offense can have wholesome or indeterminate thoughts as its root in offenses involving regulations (paṇṇattivajja) such as digging the earth, it is said: "Non-greed is the precursor," and so forth. The statement "The seven classes of offenses are the bases" and so forth is spoken because an offense can arise due to the concealment of the seven classes of offenses. Is it not said: "Due to the legal process of offense (āpattādhikaraṇa), one commits four offenses"? The phrase "six roots" is spoken because the term "cause of offense" is inappropriate for wholesome states, not because wholesome roots do not exist. Is it not said: "Non-greed is the precursor," and so forth? The causes of offense themselves are indeed spoken of by the name "precursor" (pubbaṅgama).

In the passages beginning with "Four formal acts are the bases," the words of announcement (apalokana) and the words of motion (ñatti) and so forth are called formal acts (kamma). These are called "bases, grounds, and foundations" because they are the basis for the legal process of business (kiccādhikaraṇa), which has the nature of the Sangha's or a group's business, defined as the completion of the act of proclamation with the consent of those entitled to the act who have reached harmony within a single boundary (sīmā). The statement "One root is the Sangha" is spoken generally.
280:
In the formal acts of a group's motion (gaṇa-ñatti) and a group's announcement (gaṇa-apalokana), the group is also called the root. "By way of motion" (ñattito vā) is said because in the formal act with a motion (ñattikamma), the formal act with a motion and one proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma), and the formal act with a motion and four proclamations (ñatticatutthakamma), the form of the motion is included, it has the nature of a motion, and it is preceded by a motion. In the two kinds of motions—formal act motion (kamma-ñatti) and motion for the proclamation (kammavācā-ñatti)—the proclamations (anussāvanā/kammavācā) are also included because they are the root of the formal act. This analysis of the motion will be made clear further on.

"These seven settlements... by method" (pariyāyena)—this is the question. "Siyā" (It may be)—this is the answer. "How may it be?"—this is the follow-up question. "Two settlements for the legal process of dispute" and so forth is the follow-up answer. In that context, the phrase "by way of grounds" (vatthu-vasena) is the reason for the statement "Seven settlements become ten settlements." The phrase "by method" (pariyāyena) is the reason for the statement "Ten settlements become seven settlements." It means: by way of the grounds known as the four types of legal processes, and by way of the method known as the order of teaching.

## End of the Explanation of the Section on Methods of Legal Processes.

## Explanation of the Section on Commonality etc.

In the seventh section, the Section on Commonality (Sādhāraṇavāra), "common" (sādhāraṇa) refers to being shared in the task of settling the legal process of dispute. This applies to all legal processes in the same way. In the eighth section, the Section on Partaking (Tabbhāgiyavāra), "partaking" (tabbhāgiya) means they belong to the side of the legal process of dispute because they settle it.

## End of the Explanation of the Section on Commonality etc.

## Explanation of the Section on Commonality of Settlement and Non-settlement

In the ninth section, the Section on Commonality of Settlement and Non-settlement (Samathāsamathasādhāraṇavāra), by asking "Do all settlements settle a legal process together or separately?", it is said: "Settlements are common to settlement, settlements are uncommon to settlement." Wishing to point out the settlements that are the causes for settling those legal processes in the order of dispute and so forth, he said "Yebhuyyasikā" and so forth. Because no settlement is possible without the Settlement in the Presence (sammukhāvinaya), the remaining six settlements are also said to be common with the Settlement in the Presence, ...
281:
These six settlements (samatha) are said to be mutually exclusive (asādhāraṇa) because they do not have mutual regard for one another. In the section on those belonging to that category (tabbhāgiyavāra), the method is the same.

## The explanation of the section on commonality and non-commonality of settlements (Samathāsamathasādhāraṇavāra) is finished.

## Explanation of the section on settlement in the presence (Samathasammukhāvinayavāra) and others

301-3. In the eleventh section as well, "Sammukhāvinayo" and so forth are the questions (pucchā). "Yebhuyyasikā sativinayo" and so forth are the answers (vissajjanā). In this manner, the distinction between questions and answers should be understood in the section on discipline (vinayavāra), the section on the wholesome (kusalavāra), and the subsequent sections.

In that context, in the Pali passages such as "Sammukhāvinayo siyā kusalo" (Settlement in the presence may be wholesome), the wholesome nature of the settlement in the presence and the disputes (vivāda) etc., is stated through various figurative usages (upacāra) based on the power of the wholesome states arising in the persons involved in those respective formal acts of discipline (vinayakamma) and disputes.

The reason is that what is called "settlement in the presence" for that person consists of the presence of the Saṅgha (saṅghasammukhatā) and so forth. Since these factors like the presence of the Saṅgha are blameless by nature, even when unwholesome states exist, it is not appropriate to figuratively label them as unwholesome, just as it is not appropriate to figuratively label the legal issue of offenses (āpattādhikaraṇa) as unwholesome. Therefore, the meaning is: "There is no settlement in the presence that is unwholesome."

In the subsequent sections, the statement "Wherever the decision by majority (yebhuyyasikā) is obtained, there the settlement in the presence (sammukhāvinaya) is obtained" is said to show that the settlement in the presence is invariably mixed with the other settlements, whereas the other six settlements are not mixed with each other.

## The explanation of the section on settlement in the presence (Samathasammukhāvinayavāra) and others is finished.

## Explanation of the section on the mixed (Saṃsaṭṭhavāra) and others

The statement "These things, whether called legal issues (adhikaraṇa) or settlements (samatha), are mixed" is said to show that settlements occur only within legal issues as appropriate, and that those settlements cannot exist separately without legal issues.

"To make known the distinction by separating them" (vinibbhujitvā nānākaraṇaṃ paññāpetuṃ) means: is it possible to make known the non-mixing of those settlements only at the moment of the settling of the legal issue, in order to define the distinction (nānatta) characterized by their state of remaining unmixed with each other, after having separated the settlements from the legal issue so they are not mixed?
282:
The statement beginning with "Adhikaraṇa" (legal issue) is a demonstration of a blameworthy view. "So mā hevaṃ" means that if a person speaks thus, they should be told, "Do not speak thus." By stating that no other characteristic of settlements can be found apart from the characteristic of settling a legal issue, he rejects the distinction known as the state of abandonment (pahānāvattha). However, it should be understood that by way of characteristics, there is indeed a distinction between legal issues and settlements. The statement "Settlements are settled by legal issues" is said with the intention that all settlements reach completion only through the four legal issues of proceedings (kiccādhikaraṇa), such as the act of announcement (apalokana), and not through others. Therefore, it will be said later: "Settlement in the presence is not settled by a legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa). It is not settled by a legal issue of accusation (anuvāda)... or a legal issue of offense (āpattādhikaraṇa); it is settled by a legal issue of proceedings (kiccādhikaraṇa)" (Parivāra 311).

307-313. The section on settling (Sammativāra) beginning with "By how many settlements is a legal issue of dispute settled?" and the section on settling and non-settling (Sammatinasammativāra) immediately following it are stated to show the mixed (saṃsaṭṭha) and unmixed (visaṃsaṭṭha) nature of legal issues and settlements. The section on settlements and legal issues (Samathādhikaraṇavāra) beginning with "Settlements are settled by settlements" is stated to show the settling and non-settling of settlements with each other, with legal issues, of legal issues with each other, and with settlements.

The section on origination (Samuṭṭhāpetivāra) is stated to show the manner in which legal issues arise because of other legal issues. "Not any legal issue" means that a legal issue does not originate any other legal issue merely by its own occurrence. How then does it originate? He said, "Moreover" (api ca) and so forth. In that context, "they are born" means they are not born immediately, but are born through a succession of causes. Due to the cause of dispute between two persons saying "This is Dhamma, this is not Dhamma," their mutual peace is broken. Because of that cause, as they seek factions and increase the quarrel, the dispute might reach a conscientious (lajjī) monk who is a leader of the Saṅgha with a large following, and thus reach settlement. If it is not settled in that way, the dispute gradually increases and originates a dispute within the entire Saṅgha. From there, it leads to legal issues of accusation (anuvāda) and so forth. In this way, when there is no cause for settlement through the successive process, the four legal issues arise. With reference to this, it is said: "The Saṅgha disputes; that is a legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa)." The meaning is that whatever dispute there is of a disputing Saṅgha, that is called a legal issue of dispute. This method should also be understood for the remaining terms.

## The explanation of the section on the mixed (Saṃsaṭṭhavāra) and others is finished.
283:
## Commentary on the Section on Resorting (Bhajati-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

In the section immediately following that (Samuṭṭhāpeti-vāra), it is stated to show the interconnectedness of legal questions, such as 'a legal question arising from a dispute is one of the four legal questions,' even though they are mutually causal in the manner already mentioned. In passages such as 'a legal question arising from a dispute resorts to (bhajati) a legal question arising from a dispute among the four legal questions,' it means that among the four legal questions, a legal question arising from a dispute only enters into the state of being a legal question arising from a dispute, not into the state of any other legal question. It should be understood that among the four legal questions, it relies only on the nature of a legal question arising from a dispute, is included only in a legal question arising from a dispute, and is categorized only as a legal question arising from a dispute.

As for the words such as 'to how many of the seven settlements (samathas) does a legal question arising from a dispute resort?', they are stated to show the fixed settlements in the pacification of the four legal questions. In that context, 'to how many settlements does it resort?' means: to how many settlements does it go for its own pacification, or by depending on how many settlements does it reach pacification? 'In how many settlements is it included?' means: for the purpose of its own pacification, into how many settlements does it enter by way of similarity with those settlements? 'By how many settlements is it categorized?' means: for the purpose of effecting pacification, by how many settlements that are capable of effecting pacification is it taken up?

## The Commentary on the Section on Resorting is finished.
284:
## Section on Inquiries into the Khandhakas (Khandhaka-pucchā-vāra)
## Commentary on Questions and Answers (Pucchā-vissajjanā-vaṇṇanā)

Upasampadākhandhaka is indeed the Pabbajjākhandhaka. 'Saha niddesena' means 'together with the exposition,' thus it is called 'saniddesa.' There is also a reading 'sanniddesaṃ,' which has the same meaning. In this phrase 'together with the nidāna and the niddesa,' the word 'nidāna' refers to the introductory statement that clarifies the place of enactment, the person, and so forth. The training rules (sikkhāpadas) shown based on that nidāna are called 'niddesa.' The meaning is: 'I shall ask about the Khandhaka which is the collection of those parts, the nidāna and the niddesa.' By the words 'excellent words (uttamāni padāni),' the words that enact the offenses are intended. In 'among those words... how many offenses are there?', the meaning is: how many groups of offenses (āpattikkhandha) are enacted by those words? Is it not true that offenses occur only to persons and not to words? Why then is it referred to by way of possession (genitive case) as 'how many offenses of the excellent words'? In response, it is said: 'By whichever word...' In the Pali, by 'Uposatha' and so forth, only the Uposathakhandhaka and so forth should be taken.

## The Commentary on Questions and Answers is finished.
285:
## The Numerical Method (Ekuttarika-naya)
## Commentary on the Section of Ones (Ekaka-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

In the Ekuttarika method, an offense such as digging the earth or sleeping together, committed by one who is ignorant of the regulation or the object, becomes an obstacle for a monk who, even after knowing later that he has committed it, does not perform the remedy.

The phrase 'committed later by those undergoing probation (pārivāsika) and so forth' is stated with reference to dukkaṭa offenses in the breach of duties. Some teachers say it refers to intermediate offenses (antarāpatti) committed during the time of staying in probation and so forth. Since those intermediate offenses will be mentioned by the term 'antarāpatti of previous offenses,' the former explanation is more appropriate. 'Antarāpatti of the original purification (mūlavisuddhiyā)' refers to a saṅghādisesa offense known as an intermediate offense committed during the period of practicing the purification of probation and penance (mānatta) given at the very beginning without having performed the sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanā) and so forth. 'By the purification of value (agghavisuddhiyā)' refers to an intermediate offense committed again during the period of practicing the purification of probation and so forth, which were given again according to the value (duration) of the previous offense, after having sent the monk who committed an intermediate offense back to the beginning and having cleared it by way of inclusive probation (odhānasamodhāna) and combining it with the previous offense.

'With effort (sa-ussāhena)' means with the intention of wanting to commit that offense again; the meaning is that even if such an offense is confessed, it is not cleared (does not rise up). Desiring to show the peak of fault in committing an offense without giving up the burden (relinquishing the effort), he said: 'In the eighth case, for a nun, it is only a pārājika.' Not only for a nun, but also for monks who, without giving up the burden, take small amounts of ghee and so forth with the intention to steal, if the value reaches one-fourth of a māsaka (pāda), it is indeed a pārājika. Some teachers, however, say that because it is stated 'In the eighth case, for a nun, it is only a pārājika,' this statement refers only to the pārājika involving eight grounds (aṭṭhavatthuka).

'Of a righteous promise (dhammikassa paṭissavassa)' means there is an offense in failing to fulfill a righteous promise made in the presence of laypeople, such as 'I will spend the Rains here.' There is no offense for failing to fulfill an unrighteous promise, such as 'I will strike so-and-so.'

'Thus accused (tathā codito)' means accused unrighteously. One who, not standing in truth or in non-anger, conceals [the offense] is also one unrighteously accused. Only the five deeds with immediate result (ānantariya) and fixed wrong views are called 'fixed in wrongness (micchattaniyata).' The four paths are called 'fixed in rightness (sammattaniyata).'

## The Commentary on the Section of Ones is finished.
286:
## Duka-vāra-vaṇṇanā
In the dyads, 'oneself along with the person' is stated in phrases such as 'of one with a soft back' (mudu-piṭṭhikassa). By the word 'ādi' (etc.), offenses such as cutting the genital organ and suicide are included.

'Bhaṇḍāgārika-cittakammāni vā' refers to storing and arranging the goods of laypeople, or artistic paintings of figures such as women and men. 'If one does not give robes, etc., one incurs an offense'—this is stated in accordance with the words (Mahāvagga, 67), 'Monks, the preceptor should support and assist the co-resident... a bowl should be given,' referring to a dukkaṭa offense for a preceptor and a pācittiya for a bhikkhunī who, out of disrespect, does not provide material support. The offense for not giving robes, etc., that have been relinquished (through a Vinaya act) is also included here.

In the Pali, 'desento' (confessing) refers to confessing a shared offense (sabhāgāpatti), or offenses that do not end with confession (adesanāgāminī), and so on. One who does not reveal or confess an offense during the recital of the introduction (nidānuddesa) is said to incur an offense.

'Ovādaṃ aganhanto' (Not accepting advice) refers to one who does not accept the words spoken by monks for the purpose of advising bhikkhunīs (excluding the foolish, the sick, and those on a journey). Offenses incurred by giving away items donated for one's own use to another, or entering a village with only the inner and upper robes without wearing the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi), are also offenses incurred through non-use.

'Pamāṇaṃ' is the characteristic of the completion of the immediate (ānantariya) kamma of schism in the Saṅgha. 'Bālassa' refers to a conscientious but ignorant person (lajji-bāla) who does not know the procedure for taking dependence (nissaya). 'Lajjissa' refers to a wise person who investigates the compatibility (sabhāgatā) of the teacher who will give dependence. Meanings found in the Vinaya are called 'venayika'; therefore, it is said, 'Two meanings are established by the Vinaya.'

In the Pali, 'appatto nissāraṇaṃ'—here, the act of banishment (pabbājanīya-kamma) is intended as 'nissāraṇa' (expulsion) because it is an expulsion from the monastery. Because a person who does not corrupt families (kula-dūsaka), even if they have many offenses, is considered 'not reached' (appatta) by that specific characteristic, it is said 'appatto nissāraṇaṃ' (one who has not reached expulsion). Because it is also taught, 'If the Saṅgha wishes, it may carry out the act of banishment' (Cūḷavagga, 27) for one who has many offenses, etc., he is 'well-expelled' (sunissārito). However, one who is pure and without offense in every way should be understood as 'badly expelled' (dunnissārito).

In the phrases such as 'appatto osāraṇaṃ', the act of ordination (upasampadā-kamma) is intended here as 'osāraṇa' (admission). Regarding that ordination act, some such as those with severed hands, although they should not be reached (admitted) because they are prohibited, if they are admitted (through the act), they are 'well-admitted' (sosārito). For eunuchs (paṇḍaka) and others, they are 'badly admitted' (dosārito).

## Duka-vāra-vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.
287:
## Commentary on the Chapter of Threes (Tikavāra-vaṇṇanā)

Regarding the 'Threes' (tikas), the "offense of shedding blood" (lohituppāda) refers to a pārājika offense. "By the advice of 'āvuso'" means by addressing as "āvuso". "Offense" refers to a dukkaṭa offense. In the phrase "the remaining night and day," all offenses such as the first Kathina that must be incurred at dawn are to be understood as falling into the third group because they must be incurred exactly in the middle of night and day. Alternatively, because they must be incurred after dawn has risen, they are to be understood as falling only among those incurred during the day. Offenses incurred by instructing bhikkhunīs after the sun has set, and the offense of standing with a man in the dark of night, are incurred only during the night.

Approaching families before a meal, eating food that is not leftover (anatiritta-bhojana), and so on, are incurred only during the day. Some teachers, however, say, "The sekhiya rules connected with food, and group meals (gaṇabhojana) and so on, are incurred only during the day." Therefore, it should be known that, excluding such offenses, the remaining ones belong to the third group.

The phrase "one not less than ten years" is stated because it is a training rule (sikkhāpada) prescribed only for a fool (bāla) of ten years. Only a monk of ten years incurs the offense for not behaving properly toward a student (saddhivihārika) and an apprentice (antevāsika), and for giving dependence (nissaya) to the shameless (alajjī). A nun of less than ten years incurs offenses for not following a preceptor for two years and so on. "One with an indeterminate mind" (abyākata-citta) is said in reference to the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta) of a sleeping monk.

"One who does not perform Pavāraṇā" (appavārento) means not performing Pavāraṇā out of disrespect. If a monk, for some reason, does not perform Pavāraṇā when the Sangha performs it on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, and does so out of disrespect, he incurs that offense even during the dark fortnight; thus, a restriction to "only in the bright fortnight" (juṇha) is not seen. However, a monk who has completed the later rainy season retreat is allowed to perform Pavāraṇā only on the full moon of the later Kattika; therefore, it should be understood that such a monk incurring an offense due to not performing Pavāraṇā must be restricted to incurring it in the bright fortnight. The same method applies to the phrase "it is allowable in the bright fortnight."

By the phrase "one incurs an offense in winter without withdrawing (apaccuddharitvā)," it is shown that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred by one who does not withdraw [the determination] because of the restrictive words: "Let one determine the four months of the rainy season." Failing to enter the rainy season retreat and leaving without a valid reason (sattāhakaraṇīya) are also incurred only during the rainy season. Offenses due to performing an enema (vatthikamma) and so on are reached only by the sick. Stepping with unwashed feet and so on are reached only 'inside'. Entering a precinct without informing a bhikkhunī and so on are reached only inside the boundary (upacārasīmā). Going to another place without informing the teacher from whom one has taken dependence and so on are reached only outside the boundary. The offense incurred by not revealing an offense when there is one during the recitation of the Pātimokkha, and all offenses of unlawful formal acts (adhamma-kamma) such as the act of further examination (samannubhāsana) and ordaining one who is not yet twenty years old, are reached only in the midst of the Sangha. Unlawful group Uposatha and so on are reached only in the midst of a group (gaṇa). Taking dependence from a shameless person and so on are reached only in the presence of an individual (puggala).

"The granting of Amūḷhavinaya is of three types that are not in accordance with the Dhamma" means when a monk, though insane, commits a transgression...
288:
An offense is committed. For a bhikkhunī, entering a monastery without permission and so forth results in an offense only within the precinct (upacārasīmā). For a monk living in dependence (nissaya), departing for a region without permission and so forth results in an offense only outside the boundary (bahisīmā). Offenses incurred by not revealing an offense when there is one during the recitation of the Pātimokkha, as well as offenses due to all unlawful acts (adhamma-kamma) such as the formal act of further examination (samanubhāsana-kamma) or ordaining someone under twenty years of age, are committed only in the midst of the Saṅgha. In cases of unlawful group Uposatha and so forth, the offense is committed only in the midst of the group (gaṇa). Taking dependence (nissaya) from an unconscientious person (alajjī) and so forth results in an offense only in the presence of that individual.

"The three ways of granting the verdict of past insanity (amūḷhavinaya) that are unlawful" means: A monk who, though insane [now], was not insane at the time of the transgression and committed the offense intentionally, but when later questioned by the monks, remembers it yet says, "I do not remember." Another monk who lies, saying, "I remember it as if in a dream." Another monk who says, "Everything done during the time of insanity is allowable for all monks." The granting of amūḷhavinaya to these three types of monks is unlawful.

"Apakatatto" means one who is unskilled in the Vinaya (one who does not know the Vinaya rules). Therefore, it is said, "He does not know what is an offense and what is not an offense." Regarding the statement "A formal act should be performed only against those who do not relinquish their view," this means that while being admonished by the monks, a dukkaṭa offense or even a pācittiya offense will certainly arise due to the non-relinquishment of one's view.

"Mukhālambaraka-karaṇādi-bhedo" refers to various types such as playing the mouth-drum. "Upaghāteti" means he destroys. "Bījaniggāhādike" means in such acts as holding a fan and giving thanks (anumodanā).

## The Explanation of the Section of Threes (Tika-vāra) is finished.

## The Explanation of the Section of Fours (Catukka-vāra)

In the groups of four, "so" refers to the requisites (parikkhāra) of a layperson. "Avāpuraṇaṃ dātuṃ" means giving a key to open a room for the purpose of keeping requisites inside. It is also allowable to personally store items brought for the Saṅgha inside. Therefore, it is said, "It is allowable to have them kept inside."

In the case of the first offenders (ādikammika), because the male gender appeared first, it is said, "By way of what appeared first." In the Pāḷi, "anāpatti vassacchedassa" should be understood as the absence of an offense related to the interruption of the Vassa.
289:
The meaning of the absence of an offense related to the interruption of the Vassa should be understood in this way. "Mantabhāsā" means speaking with wisdom (paññā). The phrase "Starting from the ninth bhikkhunī" is stated because, according to the words "I allow, monks, [paying respect] to eight bhikkhunīs according to seniority, and to the rest according to agreement," the first eight bhikkhunīs are to be greeted.

"Even one who says 'these are not allowable in this place' incurs an offense in the outlying regions," etc., shows that for a monk who intentionally says what is allowable is unallowable, or what is unallowable is allowable, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred in all places.

It is said in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) that they are called "pubbakaraṇa" (preliminary duties); the meaning is that these are extracted here in the Parivāra. To show the preliminary duties intended here, he said "chanda-pārisuddhi" and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Section of Fours (Catukka-vāra) is finished.

## The Explanation of the Section of Fives (Pañcaka-vāra)

In the Section of Fives, "the absence of wandering after asking permission" means that for a monk who is a piṇḍapātika (alms-food eater), because the factor "one who has an invited meal" is absent, there is no offense at all for him by that training rule. "Clothes brought back after being taken to a cemetery" refers to the garments worn and then discarded by those who have come out and bathed after performing funeral rites in a cemetery.

In the Pāḷi, "by five modes" means by the five factors of theft (avahāra). According to the gravity or lightness of the object, Pārājika, Thullaccaya, and Dukkaṭa offenses are mentioned. "Paṭibhānacittakamma" (imaginative painting) refers to artwork that is a cause for the arousal of defilements, such as the union of men and women. "He asked a thousand questions" means he asked a young monk who stood having cleared (like sweeping) a thousand questions regarding the meditation subjects of Samatha and Vipassanā. The other, the young monk, answered everything because it was the path he himself had traveled; because of that, the Elder was pleased. "He defined the duty" means he completed the duty of sweeping. It should be understood that the Elder, who was an Arahant, spoke the words "How are you, friend?" and so forth, to make the benefits of sweeping manifest to everyone.
290:
"Resting on the knees near the footprint shrine" is a textual remnant. "I will cause an accusation to be made" means the Blessed One will cause himself to be accused, he will cause himself to be restrained.

"This much speech should be taken" means this much speech is to be taken for the purpose of settling a legal issue (adhikaraṇa); it is intended to be spoken for the sake of helping [the listener] to understand upon hearing. In this context, one factor is "not supporting the end of one's own speech," one is "not supporting the end of another's speech," one is "acting unlawfully," and one is "without confession"; these, together with the two previous factors, make up the five factors that should be understood.

'Subject matter' (vatthu) refers to transgressions such as sexual intercourse and so on. Not knowing the subject matter by way of the sequence of discourse (kathānusandhi) and the sequence in accordance with the decision (vinicchayānulomasandhi) means: not knowing the subject matter through the sequence of discourse by speaking in accordance with the questions and answers of the accuser or the accused as they were spoken. Speaking that same matter by way of the sequence in accordance with the decision, known as the 'decided cases' (vinītavatthu) in the Sutta Vibhaṅga, is called not knowing the subject matter by way of the sequence in accordance with the decision.

"It is a motion (ñatti)" is connected with not knowing that the motion is finished. "Through the motion, it reaches the act (kamma)" means that even when the motion is finished, it simply reaches the act. Only at the point of the proclamation (anussāvana) is the act finished, thus the motion is said to be finished; the meaning is that one does not know the reason for that motion.

In the Pāli, "five purities" refers to the recitations of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkhuddesa), because they are the cause of purity from offenses and because they are to be performed by pure monks.

## The explanation of the Fivefold Section (Pañcakavāra) is finished.

## The explanation of the Sixfold Section (Chakkavāra) and so on

In the Sixfold Section and others, the "six types of disrespect" in the Pāli are the six types of disrespect toward the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training (sikkhā), heedfulness (appamāda), and hospitality (paṭisanthāra). In these same six, the six types of respect should also be understood. "It should be worn for a maximum of six years" is a statement showing the maximum (parama) limit mentioned in the Vibhaṅga.

"By seven factors" mentioned in the Pāli refers to the seven factors mentioned in the training rule on lying (musāvāda-sikkhāpada), beginning with "Even before [speaking], he intends: 'I will speak a lie.'"
291:
Reflecting, "By what means can I find the non-practice of such harm in this person or in the world?", one removes resentment (āghāta).

"The world is eternal," and so on, is said with reference to the ten extreme views (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi) that appear as follows: "The world is eternal; the world is not eternal. The world is finite; the world is infinite. The soul and the body are the same; the soul is one thing and the body is another. The Tathāgata exists after death; the Tathāgata does not exist after death. The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death; the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death."

"Wrong view and so on" refers to the ten wrongnesses (micchatta), which are the eight factors beginning with wrong view and wrong intention, together with wrong knowledge (micchā-ñāṇa) and wrong liberation (micchā-vimutti). Among those ten, wrong knowledge is the delusion (moha) associated with wrong view. The perception of being liberated by one who is not yet liberated from defilements is called wrong liberation.

"The reversed states" refers to the ten states beginning with right view and ending with right knowledge and right liberation. Among those ten, the fruition of arahantship (arahattaphala) is called right liberation. The knowledge associated with that fruition of arahantship, or the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa), should be understood as right knowledge.

## The Numerical Method (Ekuttarikanaya) is finished.

## The explanation of the questions and answers on the Uposatha and so on

In the questions on the Uposatha and so on, "Pavāraṇā verses" (pavāraṇā-gāthā) refers to the very words of invitation (pavāraṇā) made on the three grounds of seeing, hearing, or suspecting. It does not refer to verses (gāthā) of various meters (jāti) defined by the characteristics of prosody (chandoviciti).

## The explanation of the Sixfold Section (Chakkavāra) and so on is finished.

## The method of the explanation of the Great Division (Mahāvagga) is finished.
292:
## Chapter on Designations (Paññattivagga)

## First Collection of Verses (Pathamagāthāsaṅgaṇika)

## Explanation of the training rules laid down in the seven cities

"Three hundred and a half" (aḍḍhuḍḍhasatāni) means three hundred and fifty (350). By the term "viggaha," the training rule on human beings (manussavigga-sikkhāpada) is meant. "Atireka" refers to the first Kathina training rule. "Kāḷaka" refers to the training rule on pure black wool (suddhakāḷaka). "Bhūta" refers to the training rule on telling the truth [about attainments] (bhūtārocana). Abusing bhikkhunīs refers to the training rule stated as, "Whatever bhikkhunī should abuse a bhikkhu."

"Both schisms" refers to the two training rules on causing a schism in the Saṅgha. By the name "antaravāsaka," the rule on receiving a robe from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī is meant. "Sutta" refers to asking for thread and having it woven. "Vikāla" refers to the training rule on eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana). "Cāritta" refers to the training rule on visiting [families] before or after a meal. "Nahāna" refers to bathing within less than half a month.

"Having given a robe" (cīvaraṃ datvā) refers to complaining after the unified Saṅgha has given a robe. "Giragga" refers to dancing and singing. "Cariyā" refers to wandering on tour during the rains retreat. "In that very place" (tattheva) refers to the training rule laid down concerning staying in that very place after completing the rains retreat without departing on tour. "By giving consent" (chandadānena) refers to the rule laid down concerning giving consent to a monk undergoing probation (pārivāsika).

"Four Pārājikas" refers to the Pārājikas unique (asādhāraṇa) to bhikkhunīs. "Sixteen" refers to the first five training rules plus the rule on corrupting families (kuladūsana), making six, and the ten Nissaggiyas unique to bhikkhunīs.

"Thirty-four" refers to the twenty-two rules in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga—excluding the first Kathina, pure black wool, receiving robes, money, having robes woven, mixed silk, washing sheep's wool, and the second bowl—plus the twelve rules unique to bhikkhunīs, totaling thirty-four. "One hundred and fifty-six" refers to the remaining rules after excluding the thirty-two training rules laid down in Vesālī and other cities.
293:
'Dasa gārayhā' refers to the ten Pāṭidesanīya training rules remaining after excluding the Vessāsa training rule and the Appaṭisaṃvidita training rule. 'Dve sattati sekhiyā' refers to the remaining Sekhiya training rules after excluding the three training rules: Surusurukāraka, Sāmiseṇa hatthena pānīyathālaka paṭiggahaṇa, and Sasitthaka pattadhovana. 'Seyyā' refers to the training rule regarding sleeping with one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna). 'Khanana' refers to digging the earth. 'Gaccha devate' refers to the Bhūtagāma training rule. 'Sappāṇakaṃ siñcanti' refers to pouring water containing living beings. 'Mahāvihāro' refers to the Mahallakavihāra training rule.

'Añña' refers to the Aññavādaka training rule. 'Dvāra' refers to the fixing of a door-bolt (aggaḷa) up to the door-frame. 'Sahadhamma' refers to the Sahadhammika training rule. 'Payopāna' refers to the Surusurukāraka training rule. 'Eḷakaloma' refers to the training rule on having sheep's wool washed. 'Patta' refers to the second bowl training rule. 'Ovāda' refers to the training rule on going to the nuns' quarters (bhikkhunupassaya) to give exhortation. 'Bhesajja' refers to the training rule on the four-month invitation for medicinal requisites. 'Āraññika' refers to the fourth Pāṭidesanīya training rule. 'Ovāda' refers to not coming for exhortation or for communal living.

After stating the answer 'Ime kho yāvatatiyakā' to the question 'Ye ca yāvatatiyakā', the answers to the questions beginning with 'Sādhāraṇaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ' should have been stated immediately. However, without stating those, eight questions beginning with 'Kati chedanakāni' were answered in between. Only after those answers were the questions on Sādhāraṇa and others answered out of sequence, starting with 'Vīsaṃ dve satāni bhikkhūnaṃ... chacattārīsā bhikkhūnaṃ, bhikkhunīhi asādhāraṇā'. Therefore, to show the reason for answering out of sequence, the passage beginning with 'Yasmā pana ye ca yāvatatiyakāti ayaṃ pañho' is stated.

The verse beginning with 'Dhovanañca paṭiggaho' is a verse of the Commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariyas). By the term 'Chabbassāni nisīdanaṃ', two training rules are to be taken. 'Dve lomā' refers to the two Eḷakaloma training rules regarding having sheep's wool washed beyond three yojanas. 'Vassikā āraññakena ca' refers to the training rule on seeking rainy-season cloths and the training rule on dwelling in forest lodgings.

'Paṇīta' refers to requesting sumptuous food. 'Ūna' refers to giving full ordination to one who is less than twenty years old. 'Mātugāmena saddhiṃ' refers to traveling by appointment with a woman. 'Yā sikkhā' refers to whichever training rule. The explanation of the training rules promulgated in the seven cities is finished.
294:
"Nisīdane ca yā sikkhā" refers to the training rule regarding having a sitting cloth made that exceeds the measurement. The same applies to the term "Vassikā ca yā sāṭika".

In the Pāḷi, "Sataṃ sattati chaccevaime honti ubhinnaṃ asādhāraṇā" means there are 46 training rules for monks that are not shared with nuns, and 130 training rules for nuns that are not shared with monks; thus, there are 176 training rules that are unshared between both. "Sataṃ sattati cattārī" refers to the count of shared training rules (sādhāraṇa-sikkhāpada) for both monks and nuns, meaning there are 174 training rules.

By the term "Vibhattiyo", the groups of offenses (āpattikkhandha), as well as Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so on, are intended. Indeed, those offenses and so on are classified by way of Pārājika and so on, and by way of the Bhikkhu-Uposatha and so on. Therefore, "Vibhattiyo" etc. is stated. "Tesaṃ" refers to the meaning of the eight groups of offenses such as Pārājika. The words beginning with "Dvīhi" show the settlement of legal questions arising from disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa) and so on by means of the settlements (samatha).

## The explanation of the training rules promulgated in the seven cities is finished.

## Explanation of the Offenses such as Pārājika

The word "Idaṃ" is said in reference to the statement beginning with "Pārājikanti yaṃ vuttaṃ". Indeed, although this statement "Pārājikanti yaṃ vuttaṃ" etc. is not included in the questions extracted below as "Garuka lahuka" etc., it is shown that in the phrase "Sabbāni petāni viyākarohi, handa vākyaṃ suṇoma te", all those other things already mentioned should be taken as "Explain them, now we shall listen to your words." Therefore, the statement beginning with "Iminā pana āyācanavacanena saṅgahitassa" is said.

"Ativassati" means it leaks, meaning the rainwater enters. "Dhammānaṃ" refers to those things that bear the four requisites, and thus are called 'Dhamma'. Therefore, "Saṅkhatadhammānaṃ" is said. "Gāthāsaṅgaṇikaṃ" means a compilation by way of verses. Indeed, in this text, various meanings are compiled and counted or spoken by way of verses; therefore, this text is called Gāthāsaṅgaṇika.

## The explanation of the Offenses such as Pārājika is finished.

## The method of the explanation of the First Compilation of Verses is finished.
295:
## Classification of Legal Issues

## Explanation of the Classification of Reopening Cases, etc.

Regarding the phrase "Alaṃ āvuso" (Enough, friend), it means informing those who are one's opponents. It implies that by merely showing the fault in disputes (vivāda), such as stating that quarreling over requisites like bowls and robes is improper, they inform them, make them apologize to one another, and thus settle the matter. The meaning is that the settlement is not reached by way of demonstrating mutual offense (āpatti) or non-offense (anāpatti). Therefore, it is said, "only by a decision outside the Pāḷi text" (pāḷimuttaka-vinicchaya).

A monk who relies on unwholesome (visama) bodily actions and so forth is called "visamanissita" (one relying on the unwholesome). One who relies on wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is called "gahananissita" (one relying on the thicket). One who relies on powerful men is called "balavanissita" (one relying on the powerful). To demonstrate this, the phrase beginning with "Eko visamāni" is stated.

## The Explanation of the Classification of Reopening Cases, etc., is finished.

## Explanation of the Origins of Legal Issues, etc.

Regarding the phrase "by the power of an offense arising based on an offense," this refers only to the Pārājika and other offenses of Bhikkhunīs who conceal (vajja-paṭicchādī) their own or others' offenses. It does not refer to all offenses. Regarding the phrase "by the power of duties arising based on a duty," this refers to the duties of the third proclamation (yāvatatiya-anussāvanā) of a Bhikkhunī who follows an act (kamma), arising based on acts such as the act of suspension (ukkhepanīya-kamma). It does not refer to the power of all duties.

In the Pāḷi text, to the question "By how many legal issues (adhikaraṇa)?", the answer given is "By one legal issue, namely the legal issue of duties (kiccādhikaraṇa)." To the question "In how many places?", the answer given is "In three places: amidst the Saṅgha, amidst a group (gaṇa), and in the presence of an individual." To the question "By how many settlements (samatha)?", the answer given is "By three settlements." It should be understood that through these three questions and answers, only a single mode of settlement is questioned and answered.

To the question such as "Does a legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) also become a legal issue of accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa)?", the answer given is that a legal issue of dispute is only a legal issue of dispute; it does not become an accusation and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Origins of Legal Issues, etc., is finished.
296:
## Explanation of the Various Meanings of the Seven Settlements, etc.

In the Pāḷi text regarding the questions and answers on legal issues, the phrase "vipaccayatāya vohāရော" refers to verbal and physical disputes intended to cause mutual suffering for the sake of a distorted result. "Medhaga" refers to a quarrel that has reached growth or intensity.

"Anusampavaṅkatā" refers to the state of being inclined by way of repeated association in the accusation of a falling away (vipatti-codanā).

"Abbhussahanatā" refers to the state of having excessive exertion or effort. "Anubalappadāna" refers to providing support even to the accusers. "Kammasangahābhāvena" means because of the lack of inclusion in the duties to be performed by the Saṅgha and so forth, of the settlement in the presence (sammukhāvinaya), which is merely the state of being in the presence of the Saṅgha.

## The Explanation of the Various Meanings of the Seven Settlements, etc., is finished.

## The Method of Explaining the Classification of Legal Issues is finished.
297:
## The Second Collection of Verses

## Explanation of the Questions and Answers on Accusation, etc.

In the Second Collection of Verses (Dutiyagāthāsaṅgaṇika), the Venerable Upāli Thera asked the question beginning with "For what purpose is an accusation (codanā)?" The Blessed One gave the answer beginning with "Accusation is for the purpose of reminding (sāraṇattha)." Some also say that Venerable Upāli Thera himself asked and himself answered.

"Mantaggahaṇa" means taking the reflection or consideration of those Elders; it means taking the intention of the Suttantika Elders and the Vinayadhara Elders. "Pāṭekkaṃ vinicchayasanniṭṭhāpanattha" means knowing the individual intentions of those Elders and taking the methods established by them for the purpose of concluding the decision.

As if instructing an examiner (anuvijjaka) standing before him, saying "Do not speak hurriedly," and so forth, the Elder taught the duties of an examiner (anuvijjaka-vatta).

"Anuyuñjanavatta" (duties of questioning) refers to the sequence of questioning. Since that sequence must be performed in accordance with the respective training rules even in cases of violating all training rules, it is called "sikkhāpadānulomika" (in accordance with the training rules). "Destroys one's own destiny (gati)" means it destroys one's own journey to a happy destination (sugati).

The word "anusandhita" is a state-denoting term (bhāvasādhana); therefore, he said, "Anusandhita means the connection of speech (kathānusandhi)." In the term "vattānusandhitena," the same method applies. "Vattānusandhitena" means by the connection of conduct, by a confession that accords with conduct. Therefore, he stated the phrase beginning with "Yā assa vattena."

In the Pāḷi text, the characteristics of the shameless (alajjī) and the shameful (lajjī) beginning with "intentionally committing an offense" (sañcicca āpatti) are stated by way of Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs, because they alone are the primary subjects of the training rules in every respect. However, for novices (sāmaṇeras) and others, the characteristics of the shameless and shameful, such as intentionally violating their respective training rules, should be understood by way of association.

"Kathānusandhivacana" means not knowing the speech connected to the sequence of the conversation between the accused (cuditaka) and the examiner (anuvijjaka). It means that while they are speaking about a certain matter, one does not pay attention to it and speaks an irrelevant meaning according to one's own preference. "Vinicchayānusandhivacana" refers to speech that is consistent and connected with the decision of offense or non-offense made by the examiner.

## The Explanation of the Questions and Answers on Accusation, etc., is finished.
298:
## Codanākaṇḍa
## Anuvijjakakiccavaṇṇanā
In the Pāḷi, regarding the words beginning with "Yaṃ kho tvaṃ," the meaning is: "Friend, for what offense do you accuse this monk? In what fault do you accuse him? By what failure (vipatti) do you accuse him?" This method should be understood in all instances.

"Asuddhapariśaṅkito" means being suspected with a suspicion that has arisen in an improper circumstance regarding impurity. Therefore, it is said, "Amūlakapariśaṅkito" (suspected without ground).

In the Pāḷi, "Uposatho sāmaggatthāya" means that pure monks, not being indifferent to one another, assemble at the Uposatha place and say, "Venerables, announce your purity; here the venerables are pure; friend, I am pure," and so forth. By means of investigating and announcing each other's purity, they exclude those who are unsuitable and achieve harmony of body and mind only with those who are suitable.

"Visuddhāya pavāraṇā" means for the purpose of achieving purity by having each other speak regarding what was seen, heard, and so on. "Ubho ete" refers to both of these: dependence on material things (āmisaniśśaya) and dependence on persons (puggalaniśśaya).

## The Explanation of the Duties of an Investigator is finished.
299:
## Cūḷasaṅgāmaṃ
## Explanation of the Conduct of an Inquirer
"There" (tatra) means in that assembly. "Personal enemies" (attapaccatthika) refers to enemy persons who desire the harm of a person who is conscientious (lajjī), lovely (pesala), an accuser, and a hater of evil. "Enemies of the Sasana" (sāsanapaccatthika) refers to those driven by craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi) who proclaim the Buddha's words in accordance with their own misconduct. "Having entered" (ajjhogāhetvā) means entering into the midst of the Saṅgha by way of subduing the shameless (alajjī). That accuser is called "one who enters the battlefield" (saṅgāmāvacara). One should connect this with the phrase "even the talk of kings, etc., seen, heard, or sensed," by not speaking of kings, thieves, etc., based on what is seen or heard, nor speaking of food, etc., based on what is sensed (muta). In the phrases such as "depending on what is allowable or not allowable," the term "distinguishing between mind and matter" (rūpārūpa-pariṭṭheda) shows the meaning of the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka. The phrase "associated with the practice of Samatha, etc." shows the meaning of the entire Suttanta Piṭaka. In that context, "practice of Samatha" (samathācāra) is the sequence of developing Samatha meditation. Similarly, "practice of Vipassanā" (vipassanācāra) is the sequence of developing Vipassanā meditation. "Depending on standing, sitting, duties, etc." means establishing respect in the midst of the Saṅgha, etc., depending on the sequence of standing and sitting, depending on the performance of the fourteen great duties (vatta), and by the word "etc." (ādi), depending on fewness of wishes (appicchatā), etc. "When a problem arises" means when someone asks a question. This is just an illustration; the intention is "preach whatever Dhamma has appeared."

"Lineage designation" (kulapadesa) refers to a specific lineage like the royal family of Kāsi among the kshatriyas, etc. Therefore, it is said, "Lineage designation should be understood by way of kshatriya lineage, etc." "In the circle of the assembly" means that to make the Saṅgha aware of one's manner of inquiry, one should not stand up and walk around looking at the faces of others in the midst of the assembly. One should speak while sitting in one's place so that everyone can hear the decision consistent with the Dhamma and Vinaya.

In the Pali text, "in a non-harsh manner" (acaṇḍīkatena) means in a non-rude manner without being harsh. By the phrase "one who compassionately seeks welfare" (hitānukampinā), loving-kindness (mettā) in its preliminary stage is mentioned. By the phrase "one should be compassionate" (kāruṇikena), compassion (karuṇā) that has reached absorption (appanā) is mentioned. By the phrase "one who strives for welfare" (hitaparisakkinā), compassion in its preliminary stage is mentioned. Therefore, it is said, "Compassion and the preliminary stage of compassion should be established is the meaning of both terms." "Lajjiyā" means a conscientious person (lajjinī).
300:
"Having caused the duties of interrogation to be spoken" (Anuyogavattaṃ kathāpetvā) refers to the duty taught in the Parivāra (p. 362) starting with "I will speak at the proper time," and so forth. Interrogating according to the sequence of practice for inquiry is called the duty of interrogation; the meaning is to have that duty spoken and to have the inquiry conducted according to that same sequence. In the phrase "with uprightness and gentleness" (Ujumaddavena), the word "should be approached" (upacaritabbō) should be inserted and understood. The phrase "towards both the Dhamma and persons" (Dhammaesu ca puggalesu ca) should be connected with the distant phrase "one should be neutral" (majjhattena bhavitabbaṃ); thus it is said, "towards the Dhamma and towards persons... one should be known as neutral (majjhatta)." For a person who exceeds what should be done in any given situation is not called neutral; respect should be shown towards the Dhamma. Regarding persons, there should be respect that is free from partisanship through the development of loving-kindness. Therefore, without transgressing this procedure, one should be known as neutral towards those teachings and persons.

"For the purpose of comparison" (Saṃsandanatthaṃ) means that when a doubt arises as to whether there is an offense or no offense, it is spoken for the purpose of making a decision by comparing and cross-referencing. "For the purpose of showing the meaning" (Atthadassanāya) is for the purpose of clarifying the nature of the matter to be established, such as the offense, solely through the confession of the accuser and the accused. "For the purpose of making the meaning known" (Atthō jānāpanatthāya) means that the meaning thus clarified is for the purpose of informing, making them reflect upon, and making the accuser, the accused, and the Saṅgha accept it. "For the purpose of establishing the person" (Puggalassa ṭhapanatthāya) is for the purpose of establishing the accuser and the accused in the state of having an offense or no offense, solely through their own confession. "For the purpose of reminding" (Sāraṇatthāya) is for the purpose of making one remember what has been forgotten. "For the purpose of making him accountable to words" (Savacanīyakaraṇatthāya) is for the purpose of making it a matter of being addressed with words for one who, though reminded of a fault, does not accept it and does not perform the corrective action. The phrase "they should not be rebuked" (Na tē apasādetabbā) shows the intended meaning. In that context, it should be understood that only those who stand in a position of not being deceptive should not be rebuked, not others.

"For the purpose of Parinibbāna without conditions" (Appaccayaparinibbānatthāya) means for the purpose of Parinibbāna which is not a cause for future rebirth. Parinibbāna refers to the aggregates known as the final death-consciousness and kamma-born matter of the Arahants. Because the underlying tendencies (anusaya) have been cut off in every way, those aggregates do not become conditions such as the proximity-condition for renewed existence, as they are also devoid of other causes such as craving. Therefore, it is called "Parinibbāna without conditions." "That" (Taṃ) refers to the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana). That is why it is said, "in that" (tasmiṃ). "Vinaya-consultation" (Vinayamantanā) means the Vinaya decision. "Lending an ear" (Sōtāvadhānaṃ) means inclining the ear, meaning the act of listening. That is why it is said, "whatever knowledge arises." Since liberation (vimutti) itself is the primary goal through the sequence of causes such as Vinaya-restraint as mentioned, that liberation is again extracted and shown as the mind's release; thus it is said, "the liberation (vimokkha) known as the fruit of Arahantship." Or else, whatever Dhamma...
301:
...without clinging to anything, by means of Parinibbāna, there is liberation from the mental continuum and from the continuum of kamma-born matter associated with that mind; there is a departure by means of non-recurrence. It is for the sake of this, for the sake of this departure; thus the meaning should be understood here by way of conclusion.

In the verses on the duty of interrogation, "by the skillful, wise one" (Kusalena buddhimatā) refers to the Fully Enlightened Buddha. "Done" (Kataṃ) has the meaning of produced or manifested. In the phrases beginning with "by that very reason" (Teneva), it means that because of not knowing what has been done and what has not been done, one does not know the beginning and the end; one also does not know what has been done or not done by another bhikkhu. "To one like oneself" (Attano sadisāya) means to one who is like oneself due to being possessed of the aforementioned faults.

## The explanation of the practice of the investigator is finished.
302:
## The Great Conflict

## The explanation of what should be known by one who speaks, etc.

368-374. In the Mahāsaṅgāma Pali, the word "by one who frequents the battle" (Saṅgāmāvacarena) is said with reference to the person who is the investigator (anuvijjaka). "Basis" (Vatthu) refers to transgressions such as sexual intercourse. "Origin" (Nidāna) refers to the place of enactment such as Vesālī. "A person who is not a doer should be known" (Puggalō akārakō jānitabbō)—in this context, it should be understood as a person who is a leader in the Saṅgha or in a group.

"The training rule on emission" (Vissaṭṭhisikkhāpadaṃ) refers to the training rule on the emission of semen (sukka-vissaṭṭhi) spoken of by way of the discharge of the ten types of semen, such as the blue-colored one. That rule is called "colored and non-colored" (Vaṇṇāvaṇṇa) by way of those that have a faint color like oil and those that have a predominant color like blue. Here, in the sense of "many," the "a" in the word "avaṇṇō" is used.

"Up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahmas, they are divided into two groups"—in this context, the Noble Ones (ariyas) who are inhabitants of the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa) such as Aviha, and the Noble Ones in other planes, only associate with the side of those who speak according to the Dhamma (dhammavādī). It should be understood that others (worldlings) may belong to both sides.

## The explanation of what should be known by one who speaks, etc., is finished.
303:
## Analysis of Kathina
## Explanation of Kathina Spreading and Others

In discussing the Kathina, the phrase "by way of the future" (anāgata-vasena) means that when a preliminary effort (payoga) such as fetching water arises, the subsequent preliminary acts (pubbakaraṇa) such as washing occur later. Therefore, that effort of washing and so on is a proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) only by way of the future. The conditions function by depending on the nature of the result to be accomplished by that effort; they do not occur without that accomplishment. For this reason, it is stated in that figurative manner (pariyāya), but not in an absolute sense (sabhāva) in all instances. Thus, it is said: "For the effort (payogassa hi)," and so forth. In that phrase "payogassa," etc., the connection should be understood as: the preliminary act (pubbakaraṇa) is the causal condition that benefits the sevenfold effort. The reason is stated with "Because (yasmā)," and so forth. "For the purpose of the preliminary act (pubbakaraṇassatthāya)" means for the purpose of accomplishing the preliminary act. "In the scope of the pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaye)" refers to the domain of the pre-nascence condition. "This (esā)" refers to the effort. Among the states such as washing, not even one is obtained as a state that is its own pre-nascence condition, because there is no preliminary act that exists prior to its own arising. "Obtains (labhati)" means the preliminary act obtains the status of a post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya); the meaning is that it becomes a post-nascence condition.

In the Pāḷi, where it says "fifteen states benefit by way of conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya)," since other functional states (paccayuppanna) such as the preliminary acts or efforts are not being considered, the meaning should be taken as: the fifteen states benefit each other by way of conascence condition, because there are no other states arising together with those states. This applies to all instances above as well. Therefore, it is said: "But the conascence condition (sahajāta-paccayaṃ pana)," and so forth. In the phrase "the headings and the impediments (mātikā ca palibodhā ca)," it should be understood that the five benefits (ānisamsa) are included by the word "ca" (and). This is also the case in the phrase "of the headings and of the impediments (mātikānañca palibodhānañca)." Those benefits also arise together with the headings and so on, immediately after the spreading of the Kathina. For that very reason, it is said: "fifteen states benefit by way of conascence condition." "Expectation (āsā)" refers to the hope for robes. "Basis (vatthu)" refers to the unobtained robe which is the cause of that expectation. The expectation for robes that arises immediately, depending on a robe promised by donors saying "We will give, we will make," is described in terms of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) and so forth. "Expectations and non-expectations (āsānañca anāsānañca)" refers to the meaning of expectations for robes that arise regarding robes that are obtained, and the non-expectation for robes that arise regarding robes that are not obtained; the meaning is longing and the absence of that longing. The plural form "expectations (āsānaṃ)" is used in reference to the distinct occurrences at every moment.
304:
It is the meaning of the non-expectation of robes arising regarding robes that are not obtained, of longings, and of the absence of those longings. The plural "expectations (āsānaṃ)" is used in reference to the specific occurrences at every moment. Since it is the meaning of expectation and non-expectation, it is said: "both expectation and non-expectation."

## The explanation of Kathina spreading and others is finished.

## Explanation of the Analysis of Preliminary Acts, Origins, and Others

406-7. The phrase "six robes (cha cīvarāni)" is said in reference to any one of the six types of robes such as linen (khoma). However, by way of including all, the plural "robes (cīvarāni)" is used. In this context in the Pāḷi, in the passages such as "basis, expectation, and non-expectation (vatthu, āsā ca anāsā ca)," the expectation for robes that arises by the power of the benefits when the Kathina has been spread is called "basis (vatthu)." It should be understood that the Kathina robe is spoken of using the terms of root-condition (hetu-paccaya).

The passage "relinquishing by three states (paccuddhāro tīhi dhammehi)" and so forth is stated to show that for the purpose of spreading the Kathina, it is not proper to relinquish or to determine and spread any robe other than the triple robe (ticīvara), such as a rains-garment (vassikasāṭika). By the phrase "by breaking of silence (vacībhedena)," it is shown that the spreading of Kathina is not successful by physical action alone.

## The explanation of the Analysis of Preliminary Acts, Origins, and Others is finished.

## Explanation of the Analysis of What Should Be Known Regarding Kathina and Others

"In which states such as form (yesu rūpādidhammesu)" refers to those mental and physical states in such passages as: "monks who have completed the first rains-residence, a Saṅgha of no less than five, the robe-month, a robe that has arisen rightfully and properly." "When there are (sati)" means when they exist. "Combination (missībhāvo)" is merely a collective concept (samūha-paññatti) of association. Therefore, it is said: "In the ultimate sense (paramattha), there is no single state."

"They arise together (ekato uppajjanti)" means they are worthy of arising along with the removal of the Kathina. Indeed, from the spreading of the Kathina onwards, all removals of the Kathina arise depending on various specific causes. Therefore, all are called "simultaneous arising (ekuppāda)." Among those removals of Kathina, only the two—removal in the interval (antaruḍḍhāra) and simultaneous removal (sahuḍḍhāra)—while making that monastery similar to a monastery where Kathina has not been spread, themselves cease along with the entire spreading of the Kathina and reach the state of removal...
305:
...they reach [that state]. However, the remaining removals of Kathina cause the cessation of the spreading of the Kathina, which belongs only to those respective individuals, by way of cutting off the two impediments (palibodha), and they themselves reach the state of removal; they do not, however, cause the cessation of the entire spreading of the Kathina. The so-called cessation of the removals of Kathina is the reaching of the state of removal depending on various causes. Arising in this way is itself the removal of Kathina. Therefore, it was said: "All removals of Kathina arise together with the spreading," and so forth. In that statement, "the first two" refers to the two—removal in the interval (antaruḍḍhāra) and simultaneous removal (sahuḍḍhāra)—which were first mentioned in the Pāḷi as "simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation (ekuppādā ekanirodhā)." "Among them (tesu)" refers to individuals such as those whose removal is upon departure (pakkamanantika). "When they have reached the state of removal" means when they have reached cessation, which is designated as reaching the state of removal. In the phrase "the spreading of Kathina remains (atthāro tiṭṭhati)," it means that excluding the individual who has departed taking the finished robe, the spreading of Kathina remains for the remaining monks because the impediments (palibodha) still exist for them.

## The explanation of the Analysis of What Should Be Known Regarding Kathina and Others is finished.

## The method of the explanation of the Paññatti Chapter is finished.
306:
## Saṅgahavagga
## Upālipañcaka
## Commentary on Nappaṭippassambhanavagga

'Acts to be performed by harmonious monks' refers to acts performed by monks who, having previously been discordant due to disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa), have subsequently attained harmony. Regarding the question of whether modest (lajjī) monks should achieve harmony with a group mixed with undisciplined (asaññata) monks, it was said: 'In the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, etc.' In that context, 'ṭhitāsu' means the cessation or inability to perform Uposatha and Pavāraṇā.

'Support should not be given' means that support should not be given to a quarrel by saying, 'We too will no longer perform the Uposatha,' and so forth, so that it does not continue to occur in the future. The meaning is that after achieving harmony in accordance with the Dhamma and Vinaya, only the harmonious monks should discipline the undisciplined monks. Therefore, it was said: 'If the Saṅgha, having made [them] confess the transgression,' and so forth. 'Disliking a monk' means disliking someone merely upon seeing a slight fault in certain individuals.

'Even having performed diṭṭhāvikamma' means making one's view clearly known to a monk of like mind, saying, 'This matter is not pleasing to me.' 'Upetabbā' means that for the sake of preventing the decline of the Sasana, physical harmony must be given without disrupting the concord. In such circumstances, associating with a shameless (alajjī) monk does not constitute an offense and is indeed allowable. However, one should not associate with those who strive for the destruction of the Sasana. If one does so, it results in an offense and the destruction of the Sasana. Therefore, it was said: 'Where, however, it is contrary to the Dhamma,' and so forth. By the words 'diṭṭhāvikamma is not allowable,' it is shown that an offense is incurred even if one makes one's view known.

'Kaṇhavāco' refers to one whose speech is defiled by lust, hatred, and so forth. Because such a person shows unbeneficial speech, he is called 'anatthakadīpano'. 'Relying on conceit' (mānaṃ nissāya) means relying on conceit by thinking, 'I alone am fit to decide in this matter,' even when the Saṅgha has not assigned the responsibility of making a decision as one's burden. 'Yathādiṭṭhiyā' means in accordance with one's own view. In truth, it means not answering by taking up a belief that is suitable to a particular matter. 'Assa attano' refers to the nature of non-Dhamma (adhamma) and so forth, and does not refer to a person. It means the view that is suitable to one's own nature, which is described as non-Dhamma and so forth.
307:
'Diṭṭhi' means view. 'Laddhiṃ nikkhipitvā' means discarding or not taking up a suitable belief. Therefore, it is said: 'Being one who holds the view of Dhamma in what is non-Dhamma, etc.' Alternatively, one who conceals his own view and answers according to the person is not said to answer 'according to what he has seen' (yathādiṭṭhiyā). In this context, the phrase 'being one who holds the view of Dhamma in what is non-Dhamma, etc.' should be understood as 'being as if one holds the view of Dhamma in what is non-Dhamma, etc.'

## End of the Commentary on Nappaṭippassambhanavagga.

## Commentary on Vohāravagga, etc.

'Kammañatti' means a motion (ñatti) that is an act (specifically, a motion that is an act without depending on the proclamation/anussāvana). 'Kammapādañatti' refers to the motion that is the basis or foundation of the act of proclamation in acts such as the motion-and-one-proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma). 'In nine places' refers to the nine places such as osāraṇā (reinstatement). 'In two places' refers to the motion-and-one-proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma) and motion-and-three-proclamations (ñatticatutthakamma).

'Suttānuloma' refers to the Great Authority (mahāpadesa) that conforms to the Sutta in the two Vibhaṅgas. 'Vinayānuloma' refers to the Great Authority that conforms to the Khandhaka and Parivāra. The 'four Suttantika Great Authorities' refer to the four meanings to be taken according to the method of Suttānuloma, which are allowed or forbidden in the Sutta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas.

'Diṭṭhīnaṃ āvikammāni' means making known the views that are offenses, or the acts of confessing offenses.

'If a view is made known by four or five [monks]' means that when making it known, four or five monks together confess an offense in the presence of a single person; it means they confess in this way. A person who confesses in this way takes three or four monks with him and confesses in the presence of one person. It is not allowable to confess in this way. Even if confessed, one does not emerge from the offense, and a dukkaṭa offense is incurred due to the confession itself. However, it is allowable for two or three to confess together.

'Adassanena' means because of not seeing the practice of the Vinaya-experts who avoid unallowable things, or because of not following the views of those Vinaya-experts. 'Akappiye kappiyasaññāyā' means because of perceiving unallowable things such as gold and silver as allowable. ...
308:
Because of having marks such as tin (tipu) and so forth. In this statement, "whether by asking or by not hearing what others say, one commits an offense," it should be applied respectively as "one who asks but does not hear" or "one who does not hear what is being asked." "By means of passing one night and so forth" means committing a pācittiya offense by being separated from a determined robe (adhiṭṭhita-cīvara) and passing one night. By the word "ādi" (etc.), the passing of six nights and so forth is included.

"Anatthaṃ kalisāsanaṃ" means making an effort to cause harm by presenting angry words that bring no benefit and by pointing out faults.

"Vohāraniruttiyaṃ" means not reaching the knowledge that distinguishes the sounds (words) expressing various meanings.

"Parimaṇḍalavyañjanāropane kusalo na hoti" means being unable to understand the matter through complete words and syllables, or to understand what others have said.

"Anussāvanena" means by repeated speaking. Therefore, he said "nanu tumhe" (is it not you?) and so forth. It should be connected as: "The meaning which we have spoken, that meaning has been manifested." In this context, the word "yaṃ" (which) does not regard the sound but only the meaning of the speech (vacanattha). Therefore, it should be understood as "the meaning which we have spoken," intending to show that there is no difference in that speech. For that very reason, the reference is made again using the masculine gender as "svāyaṃ" (this very one). The meaning of "svāyaṃ" is "this very absence of difference."

"The forehead might strike against the bed-legs and so forth" refers to the forehead or eyes of a monk striking against a bed and so forth, when he bows down to pay homage after spreading a piece of leather in the dark. By this, it is meant that there is no offense for a monk who pays homage, and it shows that paying homage is not entirely forbidden. This should be understood similarly in all cases not forbidden in other Suttas. However, it is not proper to pay homage to naked persons (nagga) and the like. "Turning to one side" means entering or turning towards the side of bias through anger (dosāgati). Therefore, it is said "standing on the side of the enemy."
