"When being paid homage" means when receiving homage by someone bowing down. Among those worthy of homage, even if the teacher of recitation (uddesācariya) and the teacher of dependence (nissayācariya) are junior monks (navaka), they should be understood as worthy of homage just like senior monks (vuḍḍha).

"Only what was said before" refers to offenses prohibited by regulation (paṇṇatti-vajja) such as sleeping together (sahasseyya). "The rest" refers to offenses with consciousness (sacittaka).

## The explanation of the Vohāravagga etc. is finished.
309:
## Aparadutiyagāthāsaṅgaṇikaṃ
## Kāyikādi-āpattivaṇṇanā

With "Kati āpattiyo" (How many offenses?) and so forth, Elder Upāli himself asked and gave answers to gain proficiency in the Vinaya. "For bhikkhunīs only ... etc. ... called aṭṭhavatthuka" means that the single offense prescribed for bhikkhunīs is called aṭṭhavatthuka (having eight grounds).

In this context of "Kammañca kammapādakā ca", because in formal acts consisting of a motion (ñatti-kamma), the motion itself is the act; and in acts with a motion and one proclamation (ñatti-dutiya) or a motion and three proclamations (ñatti-catuttha), the motion stands as the basis for the act known as the proclamation (kammavācā). Therefore, these two are called "tasks of the motion" (ñatti-kicca).

"A wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is committed along with a pācittiya" is said in reference to the wrongdoing mentioned by power of a bhikkhunī ordained on one side (ekato-upasampannā) in the ten training rules. "In the first training rule" refers to the explanation of the first training rule of the Bhikkhunovāda-vagga. "In an unlawful act" refers to the four groups of nine offenses (āpatti-navaka): two groups of nine offenses to be committed if the act of authorizing an exhorter of nuns is an unlawful act (adhamma-kamma), and two groups of nine offenses if it is a lawful act (dhamma-kamma). For a bhikkhunī who asks for and eats raw grain, there is a wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) in the preliminary effort (pubbapayoga) such as asking, and a pācittiya in swallowing. Thus it is said, "A wrongdoing is indeed committed along with a pācittiya."

In the phrases "standing while leaving" and so forth, when a bhikkhunī, having performed some task while standing having left the reach (hatthapāsa) with one foot, then desires to stand having left with the other foot, she then receives the terms "standing while leaving" and "standing having left" in sequence. In fact, if it were understood otherwise, there would be no distinction from a bhikkhunī entering the vicinity of a village (gāmūpacāra), because leaving the reach is also a form of going. In this context of "sits or lies down", according to the aforementioned meaning, it should be applied as: sitting while leaving the reach with half the seat, or sitting having left with the entire seat; lying down while leaving with half the body, or lying down having left with the whole body.

## The description of bodily offenses etc. is finished.
310:
## Commentary on the Pācittiya

"Sabbāni nānāvatthukāni" means that the five Pācittiyas have distinct objects (vatthu) according to the division of the five substances such as ghee, fresh butter, and so on. In the context of fine foods (paṇītabhojana), the "nine Pācittiyas" etc. follow this same method. Thus, although the training rules on medicines (bhesajja-sikkhāpada) and fine foods (paṇītabhojana-sikkhāpada) are laid down as single training rules, they are similar to five and nine separate training rules respectively due to the division of objects, just like the Pāṭidesanīya offenses of bhikkhunīs. That is why it is said "they have distinct objects."

If a monk accepts only ghee, puts it in many vessels, and lets seven days pass, the many offenses arising according to the number of vessels have only a single object (ekavatthuka). Similarly, if a monk asks for food mixed with ghee in many places and eats it either together or separately, it should be understood that the offenses have only a single object.

In the Pali, for the passage "ekavācāya deseyya, vuttā ādiccabandhunā," the word "iti" should be inserted to connect as "deseyyāti vuttā." The same applies to other places.

In the word "bhedānuvattakānaṃ," the word "ādi" is elided. All "yāvatatiyaka" (up to the third time) offenses appearing in both Vibhaṅgas are treated as one due to similarity with Saṅghādisesa and one due to similarity with Pācittiya, thus it should be understood that it is said "three in the yāvatatiyaka." Here, there is a Dukkaṭa for the motion (ñatti) and Thullaccayas for the two proclamations (kammavācā). These are not included in the Matika. It is said "three" here only according to what appears in the Matika.

"Saṅghādīhi" means because of the Saṅgha, the group (gaṇa), or the individual (puggala) who are the cause. "Abbhunhasīlo" refers to one who has newly arisen virtue by attaining a state of purity. Since newly arisen is called "abbhunha," it means one with pure virtue. Therefore, it says "pākatika" (one in the original state).

Regarding the phrase "the benefits mentioned in the Kosambaka Khandhaka," this refers to showing the danger of not seeing an offense in the Kosambaka Khandhaka with "If these monks suspend me for not seeing an offense, they will not perform the Uposatha with me," etc. It is fully declared through the method of the procedure for confessing an offense for the sake of others' faith. It refers to the eight benefits: performing Uposatha together, performing Pavāraṇā, performing Saṅgha-kamma, sitting in a seat, sitting while drinking gruel, sitting in the dining hall, sleeping under one roof, and performing salutation according to seniority.
311:
"Of the four" (catunnaṃ) is said in terms of the individuals appearing in the Vinaya Piṭaka. What is that confession of faults? It means: what is that fourfold confession of faults (accayadesanā)? "Of the assassins" (abhimārānaṃ) means archers sent for the purpose of killing. "To the female attendant" (upaṭṭhāyikāya) refers to the woman mentioned in the origin story of the training rule on sleeping together (sahasayya-sikkhāpada).

"To the eight bhikkhunīs" means starting from the seat of the elder, eight bhikkhunīs should give a seat to a senior bhikkhunī arriving from elsewhere. If a junior (navaka) bhikkhunī arrives, it is allowable for the eight bhikkhunīs not to give a seat. That junior bhikkhunī should sit in the space obtained as the most junior of the Saṅgha. Alternatively, the eight senior bhikkhunīs should give a seat to another who is more junior than them. "Nine actions" (kammāni nava) means exactly nine, such as rehabilitation (osāraṇā), etc.

## End of the Commentary on the Pācittiya.

## Commentary on Persons Not to be Saluted, etc.

"Ten persons" refers to the ten persons mentioned in (Parivāra, 330) as "Monks, these ten are not to be saluted": the five consisting of a junior (newly ordained), an unordained person (anupasampanna), one belonging to a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka), a woman, and a eunuch (paṇḍaka); and the five consisting of those undergoing probation (parivāsa), etc.

"Twelve faults of an action" (dvādasa kammadosā) means twelve actions accompanied by faults. "Accomplishments of an action" (kammasampattiyo) means accomplished actions, meaning pure actions. "This very thing" (etadeva) means the action that is in accordance with the Dhamma and in harmony (dhammasamagga-kamma).

Because he has conquered and attained the infinite Nibbāna, he is called "Anantajina" (Infinite Victor); thus he said "pariyanta" (limit), etc. "That person himself" (sveva) means that Blessed One himself.

With "To one who professes the Vinaya, we listen to your Vinayas," etc., Elder Upāli himself, as if questioning a Vinaya-expert standing before him, made the answer as if that Vinaya-expert were answering. In that passage, "to one who professes the Vinaya" means to one who professes "I know the Vinaya." "Vinayas" means "we shall listen when the Vinayas are being spoken by you."

In the Pali, "Pārājika" etc. are mentioned by way of including what has not yet been included among the training rules appearing in the two Vibhaṅgas.

## End of the Commentary on Persons Not to be Saluted, etc.
312:
## Verses for Releasing Sweat
## Explanation of the Question on Non-separation
In the Verses for Releasing Sweat (Sedamocanagāthā), "akappiyasaṃbhogo" refers only to the communion (saṃvāsa) such as Uposatha, which is prohibited from being performed with unordained persons (laypeople and novices). In the phrase "pañhā mesa", the letter "ma" is a euphonic combination (padasandhi). The word "esā" is also used by way of gender transformation (from masculine to feminine) to mean "this question" (pañho eso). Alternatively, the word "pañha" should be understood as being used in both genders. Therefore, it is said "esā pañhā," etc.

"Garubhaṇḍaṃ sandhāya" means with reference to exchanging heavy property for heavy property. "Dasa" refers to the ten persons not to be saluted (avandiya). "Ekādasa" refers to the eleven excluded persons (abhabba). "Sikkhāya asādhāraṇo" means there is a training rule that is distinct from the monks, by way of the training rule allowing the carrying of razor equipment.

"Ubbhakkhake na vadāmi" means I do not refer to the occurrence of a Pārājika in the mouth-path located in the head above the collarbone. "Adhonābhiṃ" means, excluding the anus and the urethra located below the navel, how could a Pārājika occur in other parts of the body due to the cause of sexual intercourse?

"Chejjavatthu" refers to a Pārājika.

## The Explanation of the Question on Non-separation is finished.

## Explanation of Questions on Pārājika, etc.
In the word "dussakuṭiādīni", the word "ādi" includes huts covered with very thin cloth, etc., as well as those covered with grass, leaves, etc. For a monk standing outside such a hut and inserting [his organ] into the passage of a woman inside, having spread cloth etc. [in the passage], he would also incur a Pārājika. "Liṅgaparivattaṃ sandhāya vuttā" refers to the offense incurred by using [robes or requisites] without re-accepting (paṭiggahaṇa) them, because the previous acceptance was forfeited when the gender changed.

In the Pali, "bhikkhū siyā vīsatiyā samāgatā" means twenty monks have assembled. By this statement, it shows the state of the Saṅgha being capable of performing all formal acts (kamma).
313:
In the verse beginning with "nivattho", one wears the inner robe (antaravāsaka), makes the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) double-layered, and dons the outer robe (saṅghāṭi). Thus, while those three robes are still on the body, if a bhikkhunī washes even a spot of stain as small as a bindu with water, those robes become Nissaggiya (forfeitable).

In the verse beginning with "itthiṃ hane", one should not kill a woman who is one's mother, nor a man who is one's father. "Anariyaṃ" means one should kill only that person who is not an Arahant. By this statement, it shows that one does not become a killer of an Arahant (arahantaghātaka). "Anantaraṃ phuse" means one reaches an immediate (ānantariya) kamma.

"Suppatiṭṭhita-nigrodhasadisaṃ" refers to a tree that is one league (yojana) in extent.

"Sattarasakesu" refers to the seventeen Saṅghādisesa rules prescribed for bhikkhunīs.

## The Explanation of Questions on Pārājika, etc. is finished.
314:
## The Group of Five
## Explanation of the Chapter on Formal Acts
In the Chapter on Formal Acts (Kammavagga), when monks who have postponed Uposatha or Pavāraṇā achieve harmony in the month of Kattika, it is not proper to perform Uposatha while omitting the Harmony-Pavāraṇā (Sāmaggi-pavāraṇā); therefore, it is said, "excluding the month of Kattika." However, if those monks have already performed Pavāraṇā separately in various boundaries (sīmā) on the Great Pavāraṇā day, but harmony occurs within the month of Kattika, they must perform only the Harmony-Uposatha, not Pavāraṇā. This is because it is not prescribed to perform Pavāraṇā again for those who have already performed Pavāraṇā in the same year. The term "Harmony-day" (Sāmaggi-divaso) refers to achieving harmony on a day that is not an Uposatha day. However, if the Saṅgha achieves harmony on the 14th or 15th day, then it is not a Harmony-Uposatha day, but simply a 14th or 15th day Uposatha. The same method applies to the subsequent Pavāraṇā.

"The day kept by postponing" (paccukkaḍḍhitvā ṭhapitadivaso) is only the 14th day of the dark fortnight, which was kept aside by monks who were oppressed by quarreling monks or due to some business, thus withholding the Pavāraṇā. "Two full moon days" refers to the first Kattika full moon and the second Kattika full moon. Thus, including the two full moon days, the Harmony-Pavāraṇā and the 14th-day Pavāraṇā are combined and called "four kinds." This is stated according to regular practice. However, if such a cause exists, the two 14th-day Uposathas preceding the two full moons and the 15th day immediately following the 14th day of the dark fortnight—these three days are also Pavāraṇā days. Excluding these seven kinds of Pavāraṇā days, it is not proper to perform Pavāraṇā on any other day.

"Having performed the proclamation act" (anussāvanakammaṃ katvā) means first announcing the proclamation (kammavācā), then saying "This is the motion (ñatti)" immediately after the proclamation, then reciting the entire motion, and saying "This is the motion" at the end.

"Yွာယံ" refers to the distinction of syllables (byañjana). In the phrase "distinction by the tenfold syllable-intelligence (byañjanabuddhi)," it should be construed as the distinction of syllables in ten ways. If one asks why this distinction exists, it is said, "because of syllable-intelligence." Syllable-intelligence is the wisdom that produces the letters (akkhara) known as syllables which express the intended meaning. By that wisdom...
315:
By 'byañjanabuddhiyā' is meant through the knowledge that produces letters, or simply through the differentiation of the mind that produces letters. It should also be construed that any letter which is made to be followed by a conjunct consonant (saṃyoga) is called 'garuka' (heavy).

In that context, in the passages beginning with 'āyasmanto', those consonants such as the letter 's' and the letter 'm' which immediately follow [a vowel] are called 'saṃyoga' (conjunct). When such a conjunct follows a vowel like 'a', that vowel 'a' is called 'saṃyogapara' (followed by a conjunct). The word 'rassa' (short) refers to a vowel that is devoid of [following] consonants like the letter 'a'. The word 'asaṃyogapara' refers to a vowel accompanied by consonants such as the letter 'y' and the letter 'n' in instances like 'yassa nakkhamati'. A monk who, instead of changing the letter 't' to the letter 'th', produces only a lax sound (sithila) in another group (vagga) and says 'suṇātu me' etc., also commits a wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa), except where it is a suitable substitution (ādesa). For instance, where a word should be said as 'saccikatthaparamatthena', it is sometimes said as 'saccikaṭṭhaparamatṭhena', and where 'atthakathā' should be said, it is said as 'aṭṭhakathā' in various places. It is proper to recite such usages as are evident in the Pali and Commentaries, or what is consistent with them; other [forms of] letters are not proper. Therefore, it was said: 'By one who does not destroy the lineage (paveṇi) that has come down in succession,' and so forth.

In the passages beginning with 'dīghe vattabbe rassaṃ', it is proper to exchange a long vowel for a short one, or a short for a long, etc., only in suitable places, such as saying 'bhikkhunaṃ' when it should be 'bhikkhūnaṃ', 'bahusu' for 'bahūsu', 'na khamati' for 'nakkhamati', or 'upasampadāpekhō' for 'upasampadāpekkho'. However, it is not proper to recite them in unsuitable places, such as saying 'nago' for 'nāgo', 'sagho' for 'saṃgho', 'tiso' for 'tisso', or 'yācantī' for 'yācati'. As for the connection (sambandha) and division (vavatthāna) [of words], it should be understood that these are proper in every way.

'Sesasīmāsupi' means also in the ten types of boundaries (sīmā) such as the 'atimahatī' (very large boundary).

'Catuvaggakaraṇe' means in a legal act to be performed by a Saṅgha consisting of a group of four. 'Anissāritā' refers to those who have not been excluded, either by the suspension of the Uposatha or by being of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka). For it is stated in the Commentary: ''Apakatattassa' refers to a suspended monk, or a monk whose Uposatha or Pavāraṇā has been stayed.' Therefore, it should be understood that a monk whose Uposatha or Pavāraṇā is stayed is indeed 'apakatatta' (not of normal status). By the term 'parisuddhasīlā', those who have not committed a pārājika offense are intended. In acts such as probation (parivāsa), monks who have committed grave offenses (garuka-āpatti) should also be understood as 'apakatatta'. The words 'avasesā... pe... chandarāhāva honti' refer to...
316:
...refer to a monk who stands having left the reach of the hand (hatthapāsa) of the Saṅgha. Those who stand without leaving the hatthapāsa are not eligible to give consent (chanda). Even those who are in excess of the group of four (catuvagga) etc., become eligible to give consent only after leaving the hatthapāsa. Therefore, consent (chanda) or the declaration of purity (pārisuddhi) must be given only by one who stands having left the hatthapāsa of the Saṅgha.

## The Commentary on the Chapter on Legal Acts (Kammavaggavaṇṇanā) is finished.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Act of Information (Apalokanakammakathāvaṇṇanā)

At present, if a novice (sāmaṇera) speaks dispraise of the Buddha and so forth, or represents what is unallowable (akappiya) as allowable (kappiya), this falls under the failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti). For this reason, it will be said: 'He should be made to give up that view.' The same method applies to monks. A 'micchādiṭṭhika' (one with wrong view) is one who takes the meaning of the Buddha's word in a perverted way; such a person is also said to be endowed with the 'antaggāhikā diṭṭhi' (view of extremes). Some teachers, however, say: 'He is endowed with either the view of eternalism (sassata) or annihilationism (uccheda).' That statement is not suitable. This is because holding the views of eternalism or annihilationism is a cause for the expulsion of novices by destruction of their marks (liṅganāsanā), as stated below in the Commentary itself; whereas here, only expulsion by punishment (daṇḍakammanāsanā) is intended.

'To him also [the punishment] should be given' means that based on evident harshness of speech etc., the punishment should indeed be given to one who does not desist from reviling etc. even after the offense has been confessed, without further questioning, without taking an admission, and without formally charging him with the offense. However, it should not be given to one who desists and asks for forgiveness.

The 'giving of the Brahma-penalty' (brahmadaṇḍa) means the giving of a harsh penalty, a supreme penalty. Indeed, when an act of rebuke (tajjanīyakamma) etc. is performed, there is no prohibition against giving advice or instruction. But when that monk is given the Brahma-penalty, it is not proper for those who have undergone acts like rebuke to perform the prohibited action with him. This is because even mere conversation (ālāpasallāpa) is prohibited by the word 'na' (not), as in 'he should not be spoken to'. Upon seeing a monk under the Brahma-penalty, other monks turn their necks away and do not even look at him. Such avoidance is authorized for that penalty solely for the purpose of crushing pride (nimmadanakaraṇattha). Therefore, even the Elder Channa, who was not afraid when the act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) etc. was performed, fainted and fell when the Brahma-penalty was given, saying, 'The Saṅgha has completely avoided me.' It should be understood that any monk who, knowing [the situation], associates with one under the Brahma-penalty and does not avoid him, commits a wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa). Otherwise, the administration of the Brahma-penalty would become useless.
317:
The imposition of the Brahmadanda (the supreme penalty) leads to futility [and thus is to be regarded as a dukkaṭa offense]. 'By him' (tena) means by the monk upon whom the Brahmadanda has been imposed. Just as monks subjected to the tajjaniya-kamma (act of censure) and so forth must conduct themselves, in the same way, and even more so, he must conduct himself properly, pleasing the Saṅgha. This conduct has already been shown in detail with the words 'gentle and humble' (sorato nivātavuttī) and so on. Therefore, it is said: 'The Brahmadanda should be revoked for a monk who conducts himself properly and asks for forgiveness.'

The connection is: 'That avandiya-kamma (act of not saluting) which was authorized by the Blessed One.' After showing the general authorization with 'to perform a disciplinary act (daṇḍakamma) on that monk,' the Pāḷi passage beginning with 'Then indeed' (atha kho) is cited to show the specific authorization. 'This is the occasion for the apolokana-kamma (act of notification)' means it is the occasion for the occurrence of the general apolokana-kamma. Although it does not exist apart from the specific, it is spoken of as if depending on the specific to show its non-occurrence elsewhere. By the phrase 'the act itself is the characteristic' (kammanyeva lakkhaṇaṃ), it shows the definition of 'kamma-lakkhaṇa'; because all other apolokana-kammas—remaining after those taken by way of osāraṇā (reinstatement) and so forth—are taken by way of the general characteristic, the act itself is its characteristic.

This kamma-lakkhaṇa is also the point of decision for the remaining acts not mentioned. It should be understood as being like the saṅkhārakkhandha (aggregate of mental formations) and dhammāyatana (sphere of mental objects), which are the points of decision for the remaining aggregates and spheres. Therefore, it will be said: 'In this matter, there is also a decision on the characteristics of the act (kamma-lakkhaṇa-vinicchaya) not directly found in the Pāḷi' and so forth. Just as it is stated here, it should be understood that the kamma-lakkhaṇa is also stated above regarding the ñatti-kamma (act of motion) and so forth. 'The performance of that' (tassa karaṇaṃ) refers to the procedure for performing the avandiya-kamma.

By the words 'he should not be saluted,' it should be understood as showing that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred by a bhikkhunī who salutes him. Just as one who knowingly tramples upon a pact made by the Saṅgha, an offense indeed occurs for one who disrespectfully transgresses the Saṅgha’s convention.

This avandiya-kamma is also applicable to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. Since it is taken merely as an illustration, the kamma-lakkhaṇa is also applicable to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.

The place for distributing voting tickets (salāka) is called the salākagga (ticket-hall). The places for distributing congee and meals are called the yāgagga and bhattagga (congee-hall and refectory). In these places, the entire Saṅgha assembles as they do for the Uposatha. Such an act is not a vagga-kamma (an act by a fractional group). There are no people who later complain, saying, 'We did not know about this matter.' However, if it is done in a khaṇḍa-sīmā (small boundary), they do complain. Monks who make an announcement (apolokana) to give Saṅghika property to monks whose robes have been stolen and so forth, and who are standing within the upacāra-sīmā (precinct boundary)...
318:
...must perform the act only after obtaining the consent (anumati) of all the monks within the upacāra-sīmā (precinct boundary). If a dissenting person (visabhāga-puggala) should object to a lawful announcement (apolokana), it is proper to perform that act by either using a stratagem to make him go outside the upacāra-sīmā or by entering a khaṇḍa-sīmā (small boundary).

Where it is generally stated, 'he performs an apolokana-kamma,' the passage beginning with 'acchinna-cīvaraṃ' (stolen robe) is said to show that apolokana-kamma by its specific types. If a robe is to be given only after making an announcement, one might ask: 'What is the use of appointing an appamattaka-vissajjaka (distributor of trifles)?' Therefore, the passage beginning with 'appamattaka-vissajjanakena panā' is said. The phrase 'one nāḷi or half a nāḷi' shows the amount of material to be given after making a daily announcement. By this, it is shown that one should announce only enough for sustenance, not an excessive amount. The phrase 'on a single day only' and so forth shows the limit to be given on one day for ten or twenty days. By this, it is shown that it is not proper to announce [a grant] 'for as long as one lives' or 'until one recovers from illness.' 'The encumbrance of debt' (iṇa-palibodhaṃ) should be connected with 'it is proper to give [material] to pay the debt.' That debt should be paid only after making an announcement and designating a proper amount of kappiya (allowable) goods for a conscientious and amiable (lajjī-pesala) monk who is helpful to the Sāsana and is being oppressed by creditors. However, a large debt of a thousand or a hundred thousand should not be given. For such a debt, all the monks should seek [funds] for that monk through the practice of wandering for alms.

'From the deposit' (upanikkhepatော) means from the property placed by the kappiya-kārakas (lay-stewards) after investing it for interest for the purpose of maintaining the Cetiya. 'Even with Saṅghika [property]' (saṅghikenapi) means not only with property arising in that monastery but also with property donated to the Saṅgha by donors for the four requisites.

'It is not proper to prepare a Saṅgha-meal' means it is not proper to have a Saṅgha-meal prepared like those provided by donors of great gifts (mahādāna).

Because it is said, 'he likes to use it as he pleases,' one may take a small or large amount, provided it is sufficient for one's own use. However, one is not allowed to take an excess. 'On the Uposatha day' is merely an illustration. If it is done on any day whatsoever, it is well done. The person performing it should make this pact: 'I like to use the Saṅgha's property within this monastery and within this boundary... as I please.' Likewise, two or three monks should also do so. In this case, the only difference is the wording: 'Do the venerable ones like...?' 'Of them also' (tesampi) means of the trees. 'That same pact' means that a separate pact should not be made.
319:
"Tesaṃ" means "of the trees." The Saṅgha should be connected as the "owner." "Purimavihāre" means in the former monastery where an agreement (katikā) was made for use as desired. The phrase "having made enclosures, they look after them" refers to a place where, if not guarded, the large and small fruits and the trees would perish; it is said with reference to such a place. The meaning is that the Saṅgha's agreement does not apply to those trees. As for those trees that were nurtured from the beginning by planting seeds, they should be enjoyed by the planters themselves after giving a tenth part. "Tehi" means "by the caretakers."

"Tattha" means in that monastery. "Mūle" means in the beginning, in former times. "Dīghā katikā" is an agreement made for the purpose of enjoyment as desired without a time limit. "Nikkukkuccena" means without having worry (kukkucca) such as "this fruit has not been distributed." "This is merely a reproach" means there is no fault for those who eat much because of such a reproach, as they have taken only the amount sufficient for their own consumption. The meaning is that even if there is someone who reproaches, one should take and eat what is sufficient for oneself.

"Take it" should not be said; if said so, they might think as if it were given by that monk himself, and because wrong livelihood (micchājīva) can arise based on that speech, it is said. Therefore, it is said "having wandered around," etc. "Upaḍḍhabhāga" is half a portion of one monk's share. The monk who gives should say, "The Saṅgha has allowed this much to be given," thus freeing himself and speaking in such a way that the donors gain faith in the Saṅgha alone.

"Without longing" means that even when giving his own property to authorized persons such as the sick, travelers, or rulers, the monk should give without longing for any gain. However, it is not proper to give to unauthorized persons even without longing. Only Saṅghika property should be caused to be given according to the agreement. If the donors of requisites and others take the large and small fruits of one's own property familiarly, they should not be forbidden; one should remain silent, thinking "it is an allowable acquisition" (laddhakappiya). "It was already said before" means the reason for remaining silent was already stated before with "An angry person might even cut down a tree," etc. Even if there is no harm done by them, it is proper to remain silent out of compassion. But it is not proper to say "Take it," etc.

"Because it is heavy property (garubhaṇḍa)... it should not be given" means that because living trees are part of the monastery grounds and timber is used as building material for houses, it is not proper to give saying "You take everything." "Having built a monastery not yet built" means when the turn for fruit arrives while looking after a dwelling place that did not exist before.

## The Explanation of the Act of Notice (Apalokanakammakathāvaṇṇanā) is finished.
320:
## Explanation of the Chapter on the Group of Benefits, etc. (Atthavasavaggādivaṇṇanā)

Among the dangers in the future life known as the suffering of result (vipākadukkha), it is called "feeling of the suffering of result" (vipākadukkhavedanā) because it arises due to the enmity of killing, etc., and because it is the cause for the occurrence of enmity. To include unwholesome states that are free from the five enmities such as killing together with the enmities, it is said again "of the distinctions of the ten courses of unwholesome action" (dasa-akusalakammapathappabhedānaṃ).

499-500. "Taṃ kammaṃ" refers to the act itself, such as the Act of Censure (tajjaniyakamma). It should be connected as "the seven groups of offenses (āpattikkhandha) are prescribed." "Antarā kenaci apaññatte sikkhāpade" means in the training rule not prescribed by anyone in the interval from the beginning of this aeon until our Blessed One reached Enlightenment, excluding [the times of] Buddhas such as Kakusandha. "Vinītakathā sikkhāpadaṃ" refers to the decided cases (vinītavatthu) themselves. They are called "Sikkhāpada" because they manifest the various groups of training rules, and "Anupaññatta" because they repeatedly make known the existence or non-existence of an offense.

## The Explanation of the Chapter on the Group of Benefits is finished.

## The Method of the Explanation of the Chapter on the Collection (Saṅgahavagga) is finished.

Thus, it should be understood that the Parivāra is adorned with these three Great Chapters: the Mahāvagga, the Paññattivagga, and the Saṅgahavagga.

## Thus, in the Vimativinodanī Ṭီကာ, which is the sub-commentary on the Vinaya Commentary named Samantapāsādikā,

## The Method of the Explanation of the Parivāra is finished.
321:
## Explanation of the Concluding Remarks (Nigamanakathāvaṇṇanā)

In the concluding verses, in whichever Vinaya Piṭaka there is the teaching with analysis because it is analyzed into Ubhatovibhaṅga, Khandhaka, and Parivāra. The construction is: He said that the Vinaya has the teaching analyzed into Ubhatovibhaṅga, Khandhaka, and Parivāra. "Tassa" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka.

The phrase "The Great Bodhi of the Teacher" is said with reference to the southern branch [of the Bodhi tree]. The construction is: By the one residing in the palace of the Lord of the Great Town (Mahānigamasāmī), which was built as a palace surrounded by a beautiful wall in the enclosure (pariveṇa) named Padhānaghara.

The construction is: The Vinaya Commentary (Vinayasaṃvaṇṇanā), which is successful due to having complete decisions, was undertaken with reference to Elder Buddhasiri, or depending on his request.

"Sirinivāsassa" means of the King named Siripāla, who was the abode of glory (siri). "Jayasaṃvacchare" means in the year endowed with victory. To show the time it was undertaken, it is said again, "This was undertaken in the Year of Victory."

"Kāle vassanti" means having the nature of raining at the proper time. "Devo" refers to the cloud.

## The Explanation of the Concluding Remarks is finished.
322:
## Concluding Remarks

With this sequence of words of such extent, this sub-commentary named Vimativinodanī has been undertaken—a work that is not overly extensive, contains complete legal decisions, and consists of fifty recitation sections (bhāṇavāras) in its textual extent.

This work, produced without obstacles, has now reached its conclusion. Just as this work is completed, may all the heart-felt desires of all living beings be fulfilled.

[This work was] desired by Elders who are experts in the Vinaya, whose conduct is one of pure effacement (sallekha), and who are wary of (or fear) overly voluminous texts.

By the merit I have gained in thus composing this explanation of the meaning of the Vinaya, may I attain Supreme Enlightenment. Having attained it, by explaining the meaning of the Vinaya through excellent means, may I lead beings from the suffering of Saṃsāra to the purity [of Nibbāna]—providing the eye of wisdom that cuts off doubt, and removing erroneous meanings, distorted interpretations, textual knots, and excessive verbosity.

May all beings be endowed with both worldly wealth and spiritual virtues, and may they all delight in the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened Buddha.

## The Vimativinodanī-ṭīkā is finished.
